Unfun and broken experience overall.
I've played this game for a long time, so I feel that this review is most accurate. I've found myself at a brick wall. Over 200 hours in this game, and I'm stil stuck on the gold rank because this game's matchmaking (and fighting in general) is terrible.  Ranked matchmaking is terrible unbalanced. I don't understand how me being a gold rank should pit me against diamonds and platinums, the highest levels in the game. It makes zero sense whatsoever. Worst part is most plats/diamonds have some annoying gimmick to their playstyle because this game reinforces gimmicks, dodge abuse, and spam.
The fighting is fun at first, until you get to the higher level, where no actual fighting is happening. Just pointless spamming and dodge "tactics". All you have to do to win is to just spam dodge with a high speed and/or high dex legend.   There's no actual strategy involved, and the meta itself is broken. There is no reason to play a high strength or high defense legend because
1. The majority of legends are high speed high dex
2. They can spam their sigs and dominate slower characters
Also majority of weapons are broken, especially the lance and the spear. With these weapons (and just about any other weapon) no skill is required since the weapons have high speed and range making them impossible to dodge and making the victim subject to spam more than they already are.
Also every single match is plagued with lag Lag LAG. Up until 2 months ago the servers were at least serviceable. Now not so much. Half of the time what you see isn't what's really going on. It's really annoying when my screen shows me hitting a combo but the server says ♥♥♥♥ you and you find yourself falling off the map.
Another detriment is the game doesn't have any type of followable logic whatsoever, there is zero consistency with the legends, the weapons or the attacks. I don't know how to put it into words, but its one of the things you see after you lay over 200 hours of the game. I've always ending up yelling "THAT'S ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T" at the screen out of sheer frustration.
Also the devs have lost all interest in balancing legends. Back when Kor was introduced, the devs took time to listen to complaints and balance out the legend, now they pump countless new legends out their asses for the sake of selling a few more skins
Last but not least is the cesspool of a community this game has, nothing but♥♥♥♥♥♥talkers and players with no respect for the game or other players. People who go their farthest to either♥♥♥♥♥♥you off or make you feel inadequate. Of all the terrible qualities this game has, this is by far the worst.
I've come to this conclusion after a very long time playing this game, I usually never write reviews this long but I felt the need to get these gripes off my chest. There are other free games you can put more time into without regretting every inch of it. Just forget about this one

Where to start.
The singleplayer is fantastic. However it is let down by Rockstar only adding things to Online.
Driving would also be more fun if you could actualy save cars that aren't the default character ones. Also Rockstar and Take Two are cracking back down on Mods for Singleplayer.
Online is where all the issues are. It's obvious that everything in it is just there to get you to purchase the Shark Cards. Missions get you next to nothing, heists only give lots of money for the final mission and only if you can find people to actually help you get it.
You can't steal others cars, hackers run rampant, if you find a "server" that doesn't have them it's filled with those with tanks or other super expensive overpowered weapons, and finally as it's a p2p network it's full of lag.
In conculsion, stay far away unless heavily on sale. Even then only play for the Singleplayer.

I've always enjoyed fighting games, I've played them since I was little, whether it'd be Soul Calibur, Dead or Alive, or Tekken, or maybe Virtua Fighter. But this is the first Mortal Kombat game I've ever played, and I am very happy with my purchase! Since I just edited this review, I currently have around 10 hours as I'm writing this. I have completed the story mode, tried out the other single player modes available such as the towers and the krypt (towers is basically just your average survival mode, and the Krypt is a place you can spend all your money to destroy tombstones like a complete necrophiliac cyber bully, just so you can get some random skins and fatalities and other juicy unlockables) but I've spent most of my time on this game playing with my friend, who also bought MKX at the same time I did. Both me and my friend have been enjoying the game, it's easy to get into once you crack through the little shell (that being the "HOW THE HECK DO I COMBO YOU FOR MORE THAN 3 HITS" question which will slowly protrude) but not quite as easy to master (or maybe I'm just horrible at the game).
The story itself is something I personally found more enjoyable than the story modes available for other games, simply due to the fact that the plot at least wasn't TOO generic. I did complete the story mode without taking a single break, but I'm unsure exactly how long it took (however I think a fair estimation would be somewhere between 3.5 - 5 hours). Only thing I can say about the story without spoiling it too much, is that you'll be playing as several characters, from different cute little friend circles (no seriously, trust me, you'll have adorable little play dates. You'll even get to see two girls making out, and what 12 year old doesn't want that)  which keeps the story feeling a bit more "fresh" in terms of actual gameplay.
The game has the option to automatically configure the settings for you, to ensure the maximum amount of eye candy, without neglecting the performance. However, unlike most games which just scan your computer specifications and take a wild guess what would be optimal, MKX actually says "f*ck it, let's find out for ourselves" and runs your computer through some quick tests, trying different settings. Hell, even if you've already hit the optimal 60 FPS, the test keeps going with different values for different specific settings going up and down like Sasha Gray being up to no good in those adult films we both know you've seen. This is of course a bit time draining (took me like 3 - 5 minutes I think, but I could be wrong, never been good at estimating time since I smashed a vase with my face as a child) but at least you get the best possible graphics/performance ratio without having to sit there tweaking the settings on your own (because putting effort into stuff is like soooo 2016).
Every single character is quite unique from one another. Some may have a few similarities in certain aspects, but overall, the characters are quite different from each other in terms of the attacks and combo progressions available for them. Every character has 3 different variations to them which you can choose from, which depending on what character and what variation you're grinding your eyeballs up against the monitor like a complete psycho for, will either just change up a few of the attacks available or nearly completely overhaul the character's combos. And of course, the fact that you can tweak each character's arsenal of attacks just a tad, you're kind of able to bend your favorite characters a bit more towards your playstyle.
The combat in the game, which is of course the most important aspect (what's the point in playing a fighting game with bad fighting mechanics?), provides tension as well as eye candy through beautifully animated, fluid attacks and stage interactions. As mentioned earlier, every character comes with 3 different variations to them, whilst still keeping every character unique, which helps the game stay interesting and fun to play, and allows you to explore different combos for different character variations. There's a tremendous amount possibilities in terms of comboing with each character, as you have several attacks (some of which are tricky as heck to use sometimes due to having to flick the analog stick followed up by a button press, with the expertise timing of shaolin monks) and different stage interactions and finishers at your fingertips. Every stage, as mentioned a few times now, has some objects you can interact with, which can be anything ranging from walls, jars, kitty cats, tree branches and poor old women. And when I say "interact" I obviously mean beating your opponents face in with whatever innocent life form you decided to pull out from the arena and use as a weapon (because let's face it, no one wants to crush someone's cranium with the help of an inanimate object, when they can just toss an innocent old lady at them instead). By pressing the start button on your controller (don't use a keyboard for fighting games, that's just silly) at any time you're able to get a quick overview on how to do the more relevant attacks, but don't let the menu fool you, there are in fact plenty more attacks, if you pay attention to exactly how you perform the attacks (I'm obviously not talking about the regular boring old punches and kicks, but the attacks which require the expertise timing of shaolin monks as mentioned earlier) it will become quite evident to you that you can apply the pattern in front of you to other buttons as well, giving you access to even more attacks which you'll never remember how to do and will probably completely fail at using in actual PvP matches (unless you have the expertise timing of a shaolin monk). All obnoxious hyperbole aside, I'm probably the only one who struggled a bit with the timing. The game has a somewhat steep learning curve, so no matter what you do it's probably gonna take a while until you start carving off that rookie flesh from your bones. The steep learning curve becomes even more evident once you proceed with playing online matches, which as several people in the MKX community has stated, is like a raging headache profusely growing like the child you never wanted, due to it mainly just being full of people who has played the game for quite some time, and loves to bully newbies like it's 3rd grade all over again.
So let's talk a little bit about the price tag shall we? Well, to be honest I wouldn't mind dishing out $19,99 for this game at all, as it's in my opinion, one of the best fighting games currently on the market. However, if you intend on getting the XL version of the game, which gives you all of the DLC as well as a 100% larger price tag, I'd suggest either crawling up in a dark corner and waiting for the notorious Steam sales, or grabbing the game from a third party website, which is what I did. But ultimately, whether it's worth the money or not is up to you.
MKX is a fun game with beautiful finishers which will make your skin crawl. Nice little variations to each character which allows you to adapt your favorite characters a bit more to your ideal playstyle is something which is also present. The game also isn't ridiculously overpriced, unlike some other games (I'm looking at you, DOA5). Graphics are looking pretty nice as well, a bit mediocre at times but overall it looks quite nice, but that's something you'll come to regret when you watch Mileena bite someone's entire face off. Game is 5x more fun with a friend.

With that out of the way, let's get some misconceptions out of the way, what VRC-Pro is and is not. First off, it's not a casual racing game. This isn't a knockabout toybox racer like say "Toybox Turbos" or "Blazerush". Whilst VRC-PRO deals with miniature racing cars, it should be treated with the same respect as say Assetto Corsa or DiRT Rally, you will need to either -have- an interest in the subject matter (namely RC car racing) or be willing to learn and take an interest in the hobby to get the most out of this. This is a "simulator" as opposed to a normal racing game, except here we're discussing simulating radio controlled cars, and that's a different mindset. It takes a different approach to get used to, but once you get over the learning curve, it's most definitely an entertaining and satisfying experience.
The core package provides you with a good slew of tracks, both indoor and out, time trial and practice modes, as well as practice against the AI to get you used to the core concepts, it also provides you with an arsenal of components ranging from spec grade controllers, batteries and motors, all the way through to a selection of bodies that come with their own decals and colour schemes. Critically, all of these components can be fine tuned in much the same way that one can tune a full size car in AC, except now you're dealing in the fractions of millimeters and fractions of degrees, but the principles are very much the same.
You'll be adjusting to balance downforce against top speed, working out the best gearing ratio for a given track to optimise for speed versus acceleration, the user interface provides a solid level of information as to what each change will affect, so you're not left in the dark as to what your adjustments will cause. A useful addition is the marker that shows where the original setting -was- before you started tweaking, so you can assess how big a change you're making before you commit. Pitting in track allows you to make some adjustments, but for the full suite you'll need to go outside of the track and take the car apart, that also allows you to change components, and with the deluxe car pack, there's -tons- of options available.
The graphics are solid, the track are well appointed, and the cars are suitably detailed, the game runs at a rock steady 60fps and I doubt it's going to tax anything that's been built in the last five years. The only hiccup is the flat textures that represent the people around the edge of the track, but you won't really be paying attention to them when you're trying to set good times.
An important note is that the physics engine most -definitely- feels convincing. These machines may be light, but they have grip and traction once they're up to speed, and using something with an analog control (such as an xbox pad) is deemed *critical* if you want any chance of setting decent times. The game supports the full gamut of controllers, and in a full nod to authenticity, even supports RC radio controllers if you order a USB dongle from the VRC PRO site. This allows people who are testing their RC setups to port their configurations into the game, and then test them from the PC environment using their RC controllers with full and immediate feedback, this is an important plus.
Sound? It has some. It won't win awards, but it does the job. The music is .. music. I'll be kind and say you can set it to "off" if it doesn't flick your switch. Multiplayer is stable and the netcode is reliable, in the tests I ran it didn't hiccup once, and there's a good and solid community that's been running alongside this game for an extended period of time, which is a nice to have. The skill levels range from hobbyist right the way through to high end (as evidenced by the time trial leaderboards), so there's always likely to be a race that suits your tastes.
The one thing it lacks right now is a true Single Player "Career" mode of sorts (a la Project CARS), which means that beyond Time Trials and Practice VS the AI, you're going to be reliant on the community and your own enthusiasm for the world of RC simulation as for how much you get out of it. In that sense it's going to be a lot like Assetto Corsa, if you have a love for the subject matter, this is an easy sell. It's a very niche product, but what it does, it does exceptionally well.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is one of my favorite games I've ever played. Without actually making a list, I dare say it would easily fall somewhere in the top 20 for me. That said, despite knowing generally how the video game industry works, I somehow never dreamed there would be a direct sequel to the original starring Adam Jensen, so when I saw the first trailer, I looked like a teenage girl screaming wildly at a concert for her favorite boy band. I anxiously awaited the game's release, deliberately avoiding spoilers and information about the game aside from its initial announcement trailer, and pre-ordered it like a sucker.
Before talking about the actual meat of the game, I'm going to throw this out there right now: the pre-order content and season pass are pure garbage. Almost everything in them is a consumable, and the first of the two DLC missions you can buy costs less than half of what the season pass costs. Oh, consumables with the pre-order and season pass. Yeah, so you may or may not have heard, but they're one-time use items. If you make a new save file/start a new game (as opposed to new game +), they're GONE. This is freemium/free-to-play content in a paid game, or as game journalist Jim Sterling calls them, "Fee to Play" games. I urge everyone to avoid purchasing anything for this game that's been announced so far other than the main game and its DLC missions for this reason.
How is the story? Honestly, it's pretty good, but I found Human Revolution's plot to be much more interesting. I'm not sure why at all, really. Perhaps it's because I went so long in between story moments that I forgot a lot of what was going on, aside from the minimal facts the game gives you on its loading screens. You see, if you want to do everything there is to do in this game, most of your time is going to be spent running around the city, hacking computers and digital locks, punching paths through walls, and generally trying to find clever ways to get into almost every building you can see in the most crammed-full hub map I've ever seen in my life. It's my drug, man. I -love- that sort of thing. However, Human Revolution had two hub maps, each far less densely filled, and technically less impressive, but I actually kinda prefer the variety.
Vampire  - The Masquerade: Bloodlines is my favorite game, which is basically Deus Ex in the World of Darkness (vampires), and it had four city hubs, each not incredibly dense with secrets, but the atmosphere was so thick you could cut it with an antediluvian's fang. That glorious atmosphere and colorful (yet dark, somehow) immersion is what puts that game in my #1 spot and few other games can come close. But I digress: Mankind Divded may have just a bit -too- much to do in the one hub; so much so that it stagnates the narrative and the exciting portions of the gameplay, with long stretches of busywork/running and jumping around and no stealth/action.
If you aren't OCD and can keep focused, avoiding every opportunity to score items, money, and the game's limited experience points, the game can probably be completed rather quickly and with a nice, narrative flow, even when taking on the 13 mostly impressive and well-written side quests it has to offer. In some ways I wish I'd done that instead, but I simply couldn't resist getting everything I could. Whenever I play the game again, I may try to avoid this so I can get a better feel for the story.
One last thing about the plot: some people are saying it just kind of ends and it's surprising. You can kinda tell the story is reaching its climax, and if you try to ace the last mission without failing one of two objectives, it's really intense, but the ending stuff afterward is kind of a letdown. Nothing Mass Effect 3 level of bad, and no "choose your ending buttons" from Human Revolution. It's a pretty lame ending, but the true reward of this game is its stealth gameplay.
The gameplay is fantastic. In short, it's Human Revolution with some tweaks to your hud and the gameplay that make it just wonderful. I'm sure when I play Human Revolution again, I'll miss some of the new features this game has, such as a better inventory system (biocells instead fo candy bars, and they stack up to 25, only taking 2 slots per stack), a worthwhile tranq gun, a cooler-looking and better-functioning taser, remote hacking (holy crap, take remote hacking ASAP, it sounds like garbage, but it's one of the top 5 or so best skills in the game with oodles of opportunities for tiny bonus experience boosts, and you -cannot- get this XP with the normal hacking! It has its own special things you hack.), and the list goes on. So it's basically Human Revolution but better when it comes to gameplay.
Sound? Music's nice and atmospheric, very "chill" as the kids these days would say...um...yeah, it's great. Same with voice-acting and sound effects. The controls can be remapped and the default controls were great in my opinion.No complaints here.
I will reiterate, this is a great game. I did not enjoy it as much as Human Revolution, but my own obsessive compulsions of wanting to loot everything and do everything caused this game to take a ridiculously longer time than it should have for me to complete. That's more of a personal problem than anything the game did, and I suspect whenever I start a new game, if I can avoid that pitfall or at least do it faster, I'll have a much more enjoyable time and appreciate the story better.

I think it's totally worth it. I was considering Trine (2) for a while now and I finally got into buying it by buying the Frozenbyte Collection at 80% off for just 5,99€. After 2 days, I spent 10.1 hours playing it together with my sister.
I love the graphics. They run totally fine on my rather low end machine and look amazing in my opinion. I don't think I'll need to go into detail about them since that's what the screenshots are for.
My sister was playing the game on the keyboard while I was playing it with a very old controller. The controller needed a little bit of tweaking since at first the x/y-axis of the right joystick were reversed, however this was an easy fix. Another complaint is, that using the grappling hook with a controler is a little hard, but that's about it. It played wonderfully other than that.
The story was easy to follow, nothing special, though. It does what it's supposed to do, yet the story is not what the game focuses at the most. (It worth noting that I have not beaten the game, yet.)
The music was amazing! Not only did it fit what you were doing perfectly, but it was also very fun to listen to. It was infact, so good that I had to go to YouTube to listen to it after I played the game. I love it.
The controls were easy to pick up (except for the few minor complaints listed above) and getting into the game was very simple. While you are playing it you need to solve puzzles in order to progress, which varied between being very easy to being hard enough to keep us thinking for tens of minutes, which I find really well done. I have to say, though, that playing together with a friend really makes some of a lot easier than playing it on your own, so they would definitely be harder when I did so. However puzzles aren't the only thing the game is made of. Often enough you'll need to fight a horde of goblins or something and combat is actually pretty neat, especially thanks to the awesome music. A gameplay element that is worth noting are the upgrades, which make solving some puzzles easier and make some boni accessible. They are not overpowered (meaning that they won't make the game too easy), yet they also don't feel like there's no difference. The only complaint I got is that I once got a bug that made me unable to buy explosive arrows because they game told me I couldn't afford them, even though I could. This wasn't game breaking in any way though, as we just went for another upgrade instead, which was worth it in the end.
This is where the game shines even more than in the gameplay. Thanks to the atmospheric graphics, the really well done music and well made voice acting, the game scores a high score on this one. Combat feels really nice thanks to good looking effects/animations and really nice combat music and so do the puzzles.
Totally worth it, even at full price. 9.9/10

The Four Horsemen is a beautiful lightweight adventure game with great puzzles and a long play time… although a large portion of that time will be spent by ungodly amounts of constant backtracking.
Although it is not uncommon, it is still interesting to see when a casual series decides to switch genres between games. Lost Lands: The Four Horsemen is a good example for this. Unlike Dark Overlord, which was a hidden object game, this one is closer to a lightweight point ‘n’ click adventure that tried to include as many interesting puzzles as possible as a consolation for HOG fans.
Sadly, it forgot to get rid of the biggest issue of the last game, the constant backtracking that takes up almost half of the 5-8 hour play time. They just masked it with another great story, where we can meet the heroine of Dark Overlord, who this time is summoned back to the Lost Lands in order to help the fight against the titular Horsemen. She may be a little too okay with being dragged into a fantasy conflict against her will, but it is hardly recognisable with this interesting plot and engaging puzzle design.

Sequel to Lost Lands: Dark Overlord and second in the Lost Lands series.  Though Lost Lands: A Hidden Object Adventure is created by the same developers, Five-BN, and quite possibly occurs in the same world, these games are not related by storyline.  Though it would be interesting if somehow the developers managed to tie the storylines together.
Storyline: A few centuries have past in the realm of the Lost Lands and a new threat has appeared in the form of the Four Horsemen: Chill, Flare, Death and Darkness.  These Horsemen are slowly and methodically destroying the Lost Lands world and Maraan, the wizard/druid sets a spell in motion to bring the warrioress and once before savior back to the Lost Lands.  The intrepid Suzanne is teleported to the Lost Lands where she embarks on the quest of defeating the Horsemen and finding the Compass of the Worlds (the key to a magical portal) before one of the Horsemen does.  For help on the quest, Maraan sends a dwarf named Folnur to Suzanne as a guide, to protect, and to provide useful information.
Gameplay:  A quasi-open world with area based bottlenecks, and more of a Point and Click then Hidden Object quest adventure.  The Hidden Object scenes are silhouette finds of the interactive type.  Each Hidden Object scene shows silhouettes which when found are then used to do other things like open boxes, scrap wax from a table, cut roots out of the way, etc.  until the main object of the scene is obtained.  Nothing overly difficult though some intuition (such as looking in baskets or crates) and careful searching is required.
The Point and Clicks aspects are more complex and require not only careful searching of an area to find all the needed inventory items but often travel.  There is a no penalty fast travel map which the further and further along in the story the player proceeds the more and more the fast travel map is needed.  Many items and several puzzles found early in the game or in previous chapters can not be accessed until a later time when the needed inventory is eventually found.  If playing on casual mode these items and locations are highlighted.  If playing on Hard mode, notes or a good memory is needed.  The game will give the player hints about where to find something, such as 'Where have I seen that before?' among other comments.  There is also an in-game strategy guide if one gets stuck or can not find an item needed.
The puzzles are mostly sliders of some variation, straight picture sliders, put the correct piece in the correct place, and rotating sliders.  There is also matching, codes, and picture puzzles.  Nothing overly hard, but there are a few puzzles that do require some thought to solve.  NOTE: One particular puzzle in the beginning of the game has an achievement attached if the player can solve it in less then 70 moves.  The in-game stategy guide does the puzzle in 92 moves, so achievement hunters will have to earn that one on their own.  (This puzzle can also be accessed through the mini-games in the Extra menu after both the main game and bonus chapter are completed.  So no need to play the entire game again just to play the puzzle.  Love, love this feature.)
The bonus chapter concerns the dwarf Folnur who Maraan has asked to help Suzanne after her arrival in the Lost Lands, and Folnur's preparations to do that and to craft a magical dwarven hammer.  In the main game the player sees his arrival which is the conclusion of the bonus chapter.
There are two sets of extra finds: 1) is morphing objects (35 total) and 2) machine parts (35 total) found through out the main game.  If the player finds all 35 pieces of the machine this unlocks a bonus feature which is a set of extra puzzles.
A few words about achievements: All achievements can be earned in a single playthrough since most are gameplay oriented.  For one achievement the player can not use any hints DURING GAMEPLAY in either the main game or the bonus chapter or in any puzzle or Hidden Object scene which is standard.  One achievement is found in the bonus chapter and is a timed picture puzzle.  Also both the main game and the bonus chapter must be completed to earn a couple of achievements.  If the player missed the puzzle achievements during gameplay they can be earned through the mini-game section in the Extra menu.  That is so innovative and eliminates a forced second playthrough.
Extras:  First of all there is the in-game strategy guide which makes playing the game on Hard mode the first time through easier if the player gets stuck or misses some needed item.  This game has many extras which become available after completing the bonus chapter.  Extras include wallpapers, concept art, music and cut scenes.  It also includes a replay of the 21 puzzles found in the game and 3 picture puzzles.  If the player found all of the machine parts there are 20 extra pipe puzzles to solve under that bonus feature.
Overall, an enjoyable game to play, not too hard and not too easy.  Despite a bit of fast traveling near the end of the game, it plays smoothly and relatively logically.  Well worth the price.

I'm right on the borderline of not recommending "Lost Lands:  The Four Horsemen."  It's a shame, because it's very obvious that a lot of work went into the game (good story, graphics, and even puzzles).  But, there are aspects to it that are horribly frustrating:
- The voice acting is horrible.  The first couple of characters you meet are fine.  But, after that, pretty much everyone's voice acting is cringe-inducing.  Worse, once you meet a dwarven guide, he (and others) insist on giving you an ear-bleeding travelogue of stuff you don't need to hear.  It made me want to not click on things because they'd talk at me.
- The Hidden Object Games (HOGs) aren't really HOGs.  My definition of a HOG is a screen full of objects with a text list of objects to find.  Every HOG in this game is what I call a Chain o' Objects Game (COOG).  In these, you've got a "list" of outlines.  You have to find a starting point in the scene and follow the chain of objects until you get to the end point.  Personally, I pretty much hate those COOGs.  It doesn't help that the ones in this game are difficult to do.
- Some of the Achievements are really frustrating.  In my case, I had issues finding some of the collectables.  They're so well camouflaged that after examing each scene minutely 5 times, I finally had to resort to the in-game Strategy Guide to find the last of them.  Similarly, I had another Achievement that I swear I should have gotten, but couldn't without multiple run-throughs.  And, finally, there's one ("Artist") where the timing is so tight I physically can't move the pieces fast enough and I've given up (my OCD is driving me nuts).  EDIT:  I finally managed to get this last Achievement after 50 or so tries.
- A few of the key/lock pairs are so obscure that there's really nothing to indicate you should be doing something except that there's nothing left to try (the spinning top "key", for example).
- And, finally, a lot of the key/lock pairs are so far apart (not just physically, but temporally) that by the time you find the "key" that fits the "lock" you've not only forgotten where the "lock" is, you've also forgotten its very existence.
It's really a shame about all of the above.  I liked the previous game ("Lost Lands:  Dark Overlord") a lot, and it had much the same design philosophy.  I think this game frustrated me so much because these issues got more prevalent in this game (either that or I shouldn't have played them back-to-back).  Still, for the price, and for the amount of gameplay you get (14.9 hours total:  9.6 in the main game, 1.9 in the bonus chapter, and another 3.4 hours back in the main game trying to finish up those Achievements), it might be worth trying even at it's current list price of about $7.  A lot of good work went into this game (with a lot of good ideas) and it'd be a shame to not at least try it.

This is a pack of four games and as such I'm going to review them seperate but I will try to keep it as short as I can.
Blake stone:alien gold
A spirtual successor to wolfenstien 3d. It makes many improvements as well as refines old ones. The shooting is still great and there are more weapons as well. They give you a map which is VERY helpful.  And you also get to go back to earlier levels at any time(you could restock or look for things you missed). You also have to think a bit more with your shots as well since scientists are scattered on every floor and can help you with info and even give you items, but you can shoot them. There are problems though. All the weapons use the same ammo, so some become worthless when you get other ones. The map is better than nothing but while it shows locked doors it doesn't show doors that open on one side only. And this led to me back tracking for nothing at times. It also doesn't show you where your facing in a room, but you can open the map a couple of times to get the idea. While having some npc's are a nice touch you can't tell which are good or bad(as some are enemies) and on higher difficulty levels you can get killed quick so it can make sparing a scientist very risky. Overall while not as remembered as wolfenstein 3d, it's a solid shooter that has aged better.
7/10
Blake Stone: Planet Strike
The sequel to blake stone:alien gold takes what the first one did and improves it in almost everyway. There are more enemy types, more weapons,etc. The graphics while not leaps better, have a few new details and animation. The pacing is also much better. There are less keycards (three instead of five) and more of a focus on level design. The map is on your screen at all times which means you won't have to keep pulling up the map like in the first one. But it's more zoomed in so you may get lost a bit more, however I will take this over the last games setup. There are less levels(1/4th from the first one) but this is a case of quality over quanity as I can see going back to this one more. Not everything is better however, all the weapons still use the same ammo, leading to some weapons just filling up space. I also felt less satisfied with the ending than the first one. But overall, this was great and i'm glad I played it.
9/10
Rise Of The Triad
ROTT was orignally going to be the sequal to wolfenstein 3d and you can tell in many ways the game looks and plays(such as the "triad" being nazis and the levels looking limited since it uses the same engine). The action is quite intense and has plenty of weapons. This game is also very gory to almost mortal kombat-style over the top violence and it's done well. You also get choices in your character which can change your speed,defense,and attack, giving the game some variation. The map is the best in the pack and shows a lot of detail. But the map may not always help, as the levels are very large and that can make you lose track of where you are and it doesn't help that it uses the same level designs throughout making it hard know where you been or not. You are also limited to how many weapons you can take, Only one bullet based (which you can't swap out) and a powerful weapon(rockets or firewalls etc.). The game is made for this design choice but it can lead to fighting enemys that are resisting your bullets. Over all this is my favorite in the pack despite my complaints. It's fun, fast, over the top, and doesn't take itself seriously.
9/10
Extreme Rise Of The Triad
The expansion to ROTT. There are no new weapons or enemies to my knowlege, it's all brand
new levels and I must admit I didn't like this one much. Not to say there is no value here, this is far more difficult than ROTT and some may enjoy it. I found it, straining the gameplay and my patience way too much. I was getting lost very frequently and enemy placement and limited weapons made it difficult to enjoy. However I do think many fans will find something to like here. And it still has the gameplay that I enjoyed in the first one.
6/10
Overall I really enjoyed the game pack with all it's up's and downs. I fully recommend this to anyone who wants some classic shooters, I know I had a blast.

I'm quite mixed about this product. Certainly, the throwback pack sounds like a good deal in theory, but once you play them all you see why it costs so little.
The Blake Stone games are a bland, boring experience that offers little to distinguish itself from the glut of pre-Doom shooters. The controls are inadjustable, the levels show no variety, and the NPCs might as well be cardboard with the way they act. You'd have more fun playing a sci-fi themed Wolfenstein 3D mod.
The Triad games, meanwhile, are exactly worth their price. Even today it still holds up for all the wacky ideas it crammed into the genre: where else can you fire drunken RPGs, earn high scores for destroying every decoration, and fly around the level as a yawning deity? It'd be madness to see such acts in a modern grimdark game.
My advice: grab this collection strictly for Rise of The Triad and its bonus level pack. Even with the other crap attached, it's worth buying even as just a curio.

Here are just a few things that I found of interest in this title:
Multiplayer - Though
can be played solo, the experience is enhanced greatly through cooperative play; the genre typically requires such. This title allows the player to create sessions for friends or strangers to play online or on a local network. A staple for dungeon crawlers can be seen in this game as enemy mobs become increasingly difficult with each additional player added, which also escalates the amount of loot acquired as well as the rarity of said items. As always, cooperation is key since monsters throughout the overworld become more powerful, adding to the play value of
. In summary: garb your friends, or I will gladly play with you if your friends do not own this game.
Gameplay -
combat system is quite simple: click to move and attack, with the Number keys serving as a layout for implementable items and abilities. Other keys can be utilized for certain actions-such as holding down Shift to remain still while attacking-but the core combat retains the simplistic style of the classics. As players gain levels by instilling the ‘f*** up everything in sight’ clause, they gain attribute points which passively improve specific aspects of the character such as Strength and Defense statistics, as well as upgrades to level-specific skills such as the Engineer’s Spider Mines. New items in the form of loot can be obtained from defeated enemies. Said items add to character customization as well as developing a build in which players can utilize their own set of tactics within the game’s limits. The system is actually quite intricate with bonuses influencing the various class skills. Simple fishing holes are also scattered throughout each area, which grant another mini-game and new items to the players.
Map Layout - Each area the player treks to has its own theme and general appearance. For example, you can expect the Blightbogs to assume a marshy look and contain enemies that are apparent to the given scene. These settings have simple background pieces that add to the landscape without distracting the players from combat and exploration, while the map itself is entirely nonsymmetrical-this presents a more realistic stage. Quests typical face the player across the massive span of each set-piece; I have found this to be quite entertaining seeing as though I, myself, tend to explore every inch of the map regardless. Secrets such as golden chests-requiring the defeat of a monster with the designated key to open-as well as mysterious portals to bonus stages are strewn throughout the world.
TL:DR - I had wanted to mention several other functions of
such as its dedicated Steam Workshop contributors and fluid graphics style. I have seen that, as a collective opinion by many of its players, this is one of the few games in which the story is disregarded, yet the game itself is highly enjoyable beyond its writing. I would highly recommend
to anyone who enjoys dungeon crawlers and roleplaying game character building because this game is just more
, and there’s nothing wrong with that. Thanks for reading.

Originally, I was hyped to get this game when it was first launched back in 2015 as it looked like Rockstar had returned to form after their darker outing of GTA IV. However, time and ever more expensive updates has ultimately moved this game from good to awful in my rankings of games to play to unwind.
Whilst the Single Player campaign is pretty solid in terms of game-play, the characters are basically forgettable when you stop to think about them, with two out of the three (Franklin and Trevor) having no real character growth whilst Michael only grows in the sense that he makes friends with Trevor again and is making steps to be closer to his family. Compared to the protagonists of previous GTA games, such as CJ of San Andreas, Niko of GTAIV and Tommy of GTA Vice City, they all go through their own proper character arcs and you learn to appreciate who they are. GTAV just feels like a severe step down from this, with focus needing to be given to either one or maybe two characters at most. Three ultimately just seems to result in things becoming spread thin. Summing up the Single player game-play, it has some good steps in right directions, but still seems to lack greatly when compared to its older, 3D generation counterparts.
With regards to the On-line aspect, this has pretty much turned into a Grindfest ,with ever more expensive DLC resulting in you having to turn your spare time into work so as to get any amount of money to buy the items you might want, or having to shell out real world money for in game currency, which could ultimately be used to buy another game to have fun with instead. Along with this, the complete failure to moderate Hackers/Modder/Griefers means that when you try to earn money via CEO, Biker or Gunrunning activates, you run the constant gambit of losing all the progress you have made. This means the time you have spent stocking up of items to sell becomes wasted due to one selfish person who decides to be a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥for the sake of "playing the game as it should be played". Along with this, having the constant server glitches, lag or drop out risks to contend with also results in you risking losing what little progress you have made in your spare time. This will often result in you trying to confine yourself to a single player public server, so as to mitigate the issues, but at the same time cutting yourself off from the social aspect the game is meant to have. Ultimately, when a game becomes a chore to play rather than fun, it has stopped being a game worth play.
I await to see what GTAVI might hold, but if from what I am seeing from GTAV carries through to the next game (be it due to Rockstars’ decisions or TakeTwos’), this is one game franchise I will not be bothering with again.

VRC Pro is an RC simulation game from developer Virtual Racing Industries that is currently available on Steam as well as on the VRC Pro website. VRC Pro gives you access to the world of modern RC cars and racing and provides a method of training for amateurs and veterans of RC racing alike. While it may be intimidating at first VRC Pro is an excellent way to get in to the world of RC motorsport.
A word of warning, don't expect this to be an RC racing game because that's not what it is, this is a simulation game and a realistic one at that. Also I'd just like to say I've never really raced RC cars in real life, I used to own some RC cars which I used to drive around but that's about as far as my experience with RC cars goes.
+Great graphics
+Realistic physics
+All of the included cars (15) and all of the included tracks (22) are real
+A good variety of different types of car and different types of track
+A huge amount of customization options for the cars included as well as the ability to create your own from scratch
+Has gamepad support as well as support for real RC controllers (adapter required)
+The controls at first seem complex and difficult to use but once you get the hang of them they're great
+Great performance
+A fixed camera view as well as an up close 'following camera'
+There is a practice mode for races, helps to familiarise you with a track before you take part in the main race
+Practice cars (AI) are very good
+Several different game modes both offline and online
+Good amount of people online and I believe it can be played with people who own the non-Steam version also
+Provides a good way to enjoy RC racing without having to spend a lot of money on a real RC car
+The developer is active on the Steam forums
+/-You pretty much have to play this with a controller, personally I'm fine with that but I know a lot of people get annoyed if they can't play with KB&M
-You can't pause the game even when playing offline
-Some of the tracks seen on the Steam store page aren't included in the Steam version of the game
-Not all of the tracks have the option for you to practice or race against AI, kind of annoying if you're like me and only want to play the game offline
-It's not very begginer friendly and it only has a very simple tutorial
Verdict:
8
A great way to learn how to race RC cars with realistic physics, great graphics, a fair few cars to drive and a number of tracks to drive them on. If you have any interest in racing RC cars then this is definitely a game you should pick up.
***This review was written using a key provided by the Developer for review purposes***

Pros:
Good simulator that works quite well as a game.
Cons:

This may not be for someone who wants just to add another racing game to their library and lacks understanding of what is what in R/C. If you are willing to learn this is a great game to help do that since there is so much detail.
I have a history where I was really into electric R/C racing for a few years (10+ years ago). This is my re-introduction to the sport since I do not have easy access to supplies to get back into the hobby. I think to appreciate this game you need to go into it with the mentality that this is a simulator first and foremost, not a game. Thus, I can imagine that tweaking the many parameters for each unique vehicle and component must be a monumental task. Therefore I take my prior R/C training experience an apply it here: I only used to race stock class for the time I spent in the hobby. Why? Because the general skills that are transferrable from class to class do not depend on having the exact setup that you have. If you have a faster motor to begin with you will just spend all day crashing and not having a good time without understanding why. Stock or Spec classes let you get the feel for how you should be driving while making it more approachable. I am again only tinkering around in spec class until I get really comfortable with the Spec classes using lower power motors since you can learn how to handle the car (or SC truck in my case) for the specific track. Once you can race stock class very confidently then moving up to the hotter motors can make sense. This games makes it so that faster does not equal better. A good driver with a stock setup can do quite well against someone who is not such a good driver using the fastest and best setup. As it stands I am mainly playing in the electric short course 1/10 scale class, so I am not too familiar with nitro or road racing. I have tried nitro, and it is an unfamiliar beast for me. I have tried road and I do not have any interest in the class.
Without some sort of controller or game pad the game is not worth getting. I am using an XBox 360 controller which is quite nice, I hope to get the USB adaptor to try using an actual radio transmitter soon. Make sure to calibrate the dead zone since the controls are much less forgiving than in other games.
Edit: I now have had the USB adaptor and use it with a Spektrum SR210 reciever. This requires cutting some of the plastic on the USBs plug to get rid of a corner so that it will plug into the SR210. It works great and I highly reccomend this.

Warband. Oh, where do I begin?
Way back in the summer of 2015, I was a huge fan of the first mount & blade, right? I loved its combat system and it's unforgiving nature paired with its perfect combat mechanics. Block in four directions, attack in four directions. One day I was checking out little things that could help me take over the Swadian part of the map, and a video of a multiplayer siege in Warband was in recommended videos. I loved the game already, but with a multiplayer element? That's a million dollar idea in my eyes.
So on the next steam sale, I bought the game. I was instantly in love with everything it had to offer. Cavalries, archery, and melee. My first server ever was a TDM match, and I was blown away by how much these players were capable of with thousands of hours of practice. Nude Swadians walking around mowing down anyone in their path with a great sword. Simply beautiful what experience could bring you. Likewise, absolutely everything was killing me with ease. I was the newbie in the server.
This brings up my only problem with the game- with all the options for customization of your equipment (gloves, helmets, weapons, etc) a learning curve is caused. It's not all that steep- but its definitely noticeable. Even now, after 100 hours of experience, I don't know at all how much money you get from one kill.
Now we go to what takes up most of the game- the combat. Swords, spears, bows, axes, and shields. Sounds like basic variety, but its hard to describe how interesting the combat is. Blocking is extremely satisfying and will raise your ego every little time you do it, as the swords connecting makes that *clink* sound and your opponent gets visibly more anxious. Blocking also has a weird counterpart that I'm not sure if the game intended to exist-fainting. If you attack, but in the middle of that attack you block and instantly switch directions, you'll give your opponent the illusion that its their turn to attack, and you'll hit them as they go to hit you. Another little thing is kicking, but this one's really risky. If someones shieldhugging and holding W, you can press E to give them a kick. This will make them shuffle backwards and drop their guard, giving you a free hit. So much variety in a simple package.
This game's graphics are definitely subjective. I think it's as pretty as it wants to be- grass is nice, character detail is well done and you'd be surprised how big the maps are. Ever gotten lost in a siege map before? I know I have.
+Good Graphics
+Amazing combat
+Great map size
+Skilled community

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is the sequel to Deus Ex: Human Revolution which was released a few years ago. It is set in a future where humans can be 'augmented' to restore limbs and recieve upgrades that can be weapons or other abilities. Throughout the game these 'augmented' people are referred to as 'augs'. The game is heavily focused on an in depth story which changes depending on the choices the player makes. The game offers a variety of ways to complete missions and objectives which can range from a complete rambo attack play style destroying everything they see to a highly stealthy play style where you are not even seen or heard by one enemy NPC. Your route varies as well as you can crawl through a vent, hack a few door security panels or break through a wall to reach another area.
Your abilities are managed via the augment tree where you can choose abilities for offense, defense, perception, athletic ability and electronic manipulation (hacking). There are many abilities to choose from to suit your preffered play style and have various upgrades to increase their effectiveness or decrease their energy consumption. Initially you have many of these abilities but you will lose them early on, giving you the opportunity to rebuild yourself to your own preffered way.
The game navigates the story well and always provides detailed background behind situations and engaging dialogue. Voice acting is top notch and so are the choices for steering conversations with NPCs. The game tries to steer you on to the main story missions occasionally but you are free to roam the city of Prague and discover all the little secrets and extras that the game has to offer. The game also feels very polished and smooth which shows that a lot of testing was conducted prior to release which sadly does not happen a lot these days as most studios are looking to deliver a product as fast as possible and/or meet a release date. This is also evident as the release date for Mankind Divided was pushed back a few months to fix some problems and smooth some bugs and the finished product was worth the wait. I had no issues with the game and even tried the beta version that supports Direct X 12 too.
I write this review after I have finished the game for a third time on the hardest difficulty where you only have one life for your entire playthrough. Overall the game is of excellent quality, has a great skill tree, has an engaging story and a good combat and stealth system. You do need to enjoy these types of games to get the most out of it and taking a stealth approach is in my opinion, the best way to experience the game.
Highly recommended 10/10.

I've been playing this game for a short while, and I gotta say....It's quite amazing! The way I can describe it, is....Like Super Smash Bros meets Soul Calibur, with the platforming and "The more wounded you are, the harder you'll fly away with a hit" of the former, and the weapon based combat of the later, sort of.
BUT, I gotta say, even if I love the game, it isn't all that well balanced, honestly. And the community is quite toxic. I can mention a few types of players I've had to deal with so far:
The bad winner/loser: This guy will always flame you if you lose, or they will spam♥♥♥♥♥♥like "EZ" and "Noob" and stuff like that if they win. But, if you happen to win against them, they'll get really salty and they will start to call you a spammer, or they will insult the character you picked, calling it a "noob character" or what not. You know, the kind that you often encounter in other games, and in legions in Dota and CSGO, they infested this game, too. This is quite common in ranked play, of course. My advice? Do whatever that's♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥them off, and try to win. And if you lose, just immediatly leave the lobby, don't waste your brain cells with these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Spammers: And I'm not talking about people who use the same attack thrice each 20 seconds or so because let's face it, they are good finishers and there isn't much you can do to attack people in this game anyways. I'm talking about the player that deliberately spams the same attacks over and over and over again. Want some examples? Ada's forward and down special, the pike's forward special with any character, specially if it propels them forward, any of Vraxx's attacks, any of Asuri's attacks (Even if I love her), any of Lucien's specials with the katars, the list goes on. Attacks with a short dely that are quite effective at finishing off your foes. You'll see some players spamming them at least 5 times every 10 seconds or so. Once you learn how to counter the regular spammer, they are quite easy to defeat, unless they are.....
The Advanced Spammer:....Now, these guys ARE a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ They know they are spamming, and they know how to do it well. With some characters like Hattori, which is pretty much 90% of the players that ever reached a high rank in competitive play, you'll encounter lots of these. Unless you're one of these, your chances of reaching high ranks are pretty slim.
My advice for both? try to spam them back. And mercilessly.
The Butt Buddies: These ones are quite annoying, too. I'm pretty sure these guys join the que together. What they do all the time is: They stay at both edges of the map, and they refuse to attack each other, leaving you to your opponent, the other guy who isn't a butt buddy. Extra points if they are taunting, too. As soon as the other player leaves you all battered and with a red status bar, they will go for the kill, and they will attack you, probably with one of the easy to spam attacks, therefore stealing the kill from the other player. Often, the non butt buddy player will be so stupid, that they fail to realize that they are stealing all the kills from them, and will keep giving them free kills. AND if you try to attack the buttbuddy players, they will dodge your attacks or they will hit you back. And if you somehow manage to get more points than them, they will start giving each other free kills 'til they are above you on the scoreboard, too. My advice here? Just do what they do. Stay at one of the edges of the map, and as soon as they try to attack you, slap their ♥♥♥♥ing faces. If the non butt buddy player attacks you, let him or her kill you. If that player is good enough, they'll manage to kill the butt buddies a few times, and with the extra points you gave them, they will surely win, therefore ruining the plan the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s had for free wins. And that, my man, is quite satisfying.
All in all, the game is quite fun, even if it isn't perfectly balanced, but let's face it, unless each character is a carbon copy of each other, that's impossible. You don't want a game like that, do you? Plus, they devs are trying damn hard to update the game and balance the characters with frequent patches, so at least they are trying.
If you wanna play for fun, be my guest. If you wanna do anything serious, or get far in the ranked matches, just forget about it. You'll end up getting an aneurysm.

The prequel, Lost Lands: Dark Overlord, is an excellent game, and this sequel is even better. Though it thematically fits in the "casual point-and-click and hidden-object game" genre, actually it is mature, long, and difficult enough to appeal to fans of "classic" point-and-click adventures. There are actually very few hidden-object scenes, and though there are several mini-game puzzles, most of your time will be spent in thinking about how to use the objects you find.
It's long, with a lot to do. I played it in expert mode, and it was quite challenging indeed. The bonus chapter is a fun prequel that satisfyingly fills in a gap in the story. There are lots of attainable achievements, and they are fully synced with Steam.
The graphics are good, and the cut scenes are exceptional. The story is neither amazing nor original, but serves well to keep the adventure going.
Voice acting here is a significant improvement over Lost Lands: Dark Overlord. The characters feel fleshed-out and flavorful.
Highly recommended for fans of the casual point-and-clicks and HOGs!

The Apogee Throback Pack is a collection of great games from the early 90`s. All the games uses the Wolfenstein 3D engine.
The first game is Blake Staone and the Aliens of Gold, released in 1993. The gameplay is very similar to Wolfenstien 3D. The only real difference is that there are npc's in the game, the setting is in space and the way healing works. There are scientest npc's in the game. Some are informants working for the same agency as the player. The rest are working for the bad guys. The only way to tell them apart is by interacting with them. Healing is done through buying health tokens from vending machines with money found through out the levels. The main way to progress thourgh a level is by finding all the keycards and returning to the starting point. Aliens of Gold has 60 levels that is complete maze hunts.
The second game is Blakestone Planet Strike, released in 1994. Planes Strike`s gameplay is the same as Aliens of Gold. The olny difference is the graphics, levels design and level count. Planet strike has improves graphics wtih better sprites for the weapons, aliens and soldiers. The levels aren't maze hunts and is better designed. Progressing though a level also works differently. The player has to find a bomb and blow up a red security cube to progress to the next level. There are only 20 levels, but that is okay becuase the are waybetter then the levels is Aliens of Gold.
The third is Rise of the Triad: Dark War, released in 1995. This is one of the most unique games from the 1990`s and what they did with the Wolfenstein 3D engine is nothing short of black magic. The player can look up and dow, use jump pads, there are multiple stories in a level (altough no room over room scenarios), outdoor areas, roof and floor textures, realistic looking sprites, all kinds of traps and it was the first game to have rocket jumping. The level design is mostly good, but there are times where the level design quality dips. Gameplay is very unique an entertaining. the player takes on the evil Triad. There are 4 main weapons slots in the game. A pistol, two pistols, what looks like a MP40 and a explosive weapon.
the pistols and MP40 have infinte ammo and no reloads. Only explosive weapons use ammo. There are a ton of different explosive weapons. There is Bazooka`s, heatseeking missilse launchers, flame throwers and more. Then there are the power ups. These include god mode, dog mode and one that puts youre charecter on a high. Included woth the version of RotT is the shareware version, the original version and the extreme version, all of wich have their own original levls.
This bundle of game contains tome classic FPS game from the 90`s that really deserves more love.
I used sourceporst for every game. I downloaded a sourceport called ATP2 which allows me to lauch either the original dos verison or the sourceport version from the launcher and it enables steam to count the time I played the games. This sourceport uses WinRottGL_v1.7 for Rise of the Triad and the bstone sourceport for both Blake Stone Games.
TLDR
Get it now.
It's Rise of the Triad and Blake Stone and all relevant expansions. Two classics and pioneers of the FPS genre that shouldn't go unnoticed. Worth the price.

Originally, I was hyped to get this game when it was first launched back in 2015 as it looked like Rockstar had returned to form after their darker outing of GTA IV. However, time and ever more expensive updates has ultimately moved this game from good to awful in my rankings of games to play to unwind.
Whilst the Single Player campaign is pretty solid in terms of game-play, the characters are basically forgettable when you stop to think about them, with two out of the three (Franklin and Trevor) having no real character growth whilst Michael only grows in the sense that he makes friends with Trevor again and is making steps to be closer to his family. Compared to the protagonists of previous GTA games, such as CJ of San Andreas, Niko of GTAIV and Tommy of GTA Vice City, they all go through their own proper character arcs and you learn to appreciate who they are. GTAV just feels like a severe step down from this, with focus needing to be given to either one or maybe two characters at most. Three ultimately just seems to result in things becoming spread thin. Summing up the Single player game-play, it has some good steps in right directions, but still seems to lack greatly when compared to its older, 3D generation counterparts.
With regards to the On-line aspect, this has pretty much turned into a Grindfest ,with ever more expensive DLC resulting in you having to turn your spare time into work so as to get any amount of money to buy the items you might want, or having to shell out real world money for in game currency, which could ultimately be used to buy another game to have fun with instead. Along with this, the complete failure to moderate Hackers/Modder/Griefers means that when you try to earn money via CEO, Biker or Gunrunning activates, you run the constant gambit of losing all the progress you have made. This means the time you have spent stocking up of items to sell becomes wasted due to one selfish person who decides to be a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥for the sake of "playing the game as it should be played". Along with this, having the constant server glitches, lag or drop out risks to contend with also results in you risking losing what little progress you have made in your spare time. This will often result in you trying to confine yourself to a single player public server, so as to mitigate the issues, but at the same time cutting yourself off from the social aspect the game is meant to have. Ultimately, when a game becomes a chore to play rather than fun, it has stopped being a game worth play.
I await to see what GTAVI might hold, but if from what I am seeing from GTAV carries through to the next game (be it due to Rockstars’ decisions or TakeTwos’), this is one game franchise I will not be bothering with again.

A cathartic, if short, throwback to 80's movies and 90's games. Everything about this game screams nostalgia: a protganist name like Rex Power Colt, dialogue so (intentionally) cheesey that even Snake Pliskin would cringe, and stylistic still-image cutscenes not scene in a decade. All of this utilizing the immensely enjoyable framework of exploring an open world and choosing your playstyle seen in Far Cry 3. The story is straight out of the 80's, with an ending that is nigh perfect for a game such as this.
The guns, when fully upgraded, are immensely satisfying to use; the shotgun and sniper become stupidly overpowered (even on Hard) but it does a lot of work to get there. The real challenge comes from using stealth to get in close to the enemy, marking them all in order to keep track, and then blitzing through them with your takedowns, being able to take out entire groups in the blink of an eye should you possess the skill. The blood dragons you will encounter cannot be so easily slain, and they take patience and methodical approach to kill just one even with a fully upgraded character (on Hard).
Overall, it's a game worth dedicating the day or two it will take to compelte. It's a game that doesn't take itself seriously without being as wacky as games such as Saints Row 4 (though it does come close at times). The only obvious downside is how shallow and short the experience feels, particularly in the postgame, as it does not offer much replay value unless you really enjoy it. However it's cheap so that can be forgiven. Worth the buy if you loved 80s action movies, and worth a look even if you dont.

I am very impressed by a game that had been out/in development for so long and the work put into it shows.
Pros:
-Very realistic
-Real cars and tracks
-Online races/esport type matches as well as series (haven't touched these yet as my skills are lacking so far but look fun)
-Very in-depth custiomization (body, parts, aerodynamics, ride height, shocks, balance, steering, etc...)
-Punishes you for bad habits
-Can use a real rc controller (need to buy an adapter sold separately)
-Has been out/in development for ~14 years, it shows
Cons:
-Slightly misleading info on steam. The videos/pics show some tracks not yet availible in steam version and felt slightly slighted by the fact I thought I would be getting some of the ones in the videos/pics. After reading their forums and the steam forums it seems they are aware of some of these things and are fixing them. The other tracks from what I gathered will be released as a "deluxe" dlc. I am dissapointed that $40 did not get get me the "whole package" or what I was expecting. HOWEVER this is a SIM and a polished one at that and I completely agree with their asking price (for now).
-Will be fixing steam/non steam compatabilty or previous buyer issues. (more forum info)
-Wish more tracks were included
-Is an older game, ~14 years, other than graphics it really dosen't show, and the graphics are not bad by any means.
Conclusion:
-Definitely recommend this game to anyone interested in a sim rc experience or anyone who has had an rc car.
-DO YOUR RESEARCH on what you will get with steam version/non steam license. Steam version contains more than enough to really enjoy this game I just personally wish there were more tracks included. Everything seems like it will make it's way over to steam and the playerbase will only grow from that.
-Asking price is fair.
-Use a gamepad at the very least if not a real rc controller (xbox 360 controller worked fine for me)
if you're into rc this is the game to get, it feels just like Friday night at the track, just a lot less expensive.

Being a total fangirl of DXHR, I was thrilled beyond words when a sequel was announced- I mean, after witnessing the calibre of the first game, who wouldn't? The absolutely stunning designs and visuals, the exciting background and engaging story, badass characters, great gameplay; the talents at Eidos Montreal have set a high bar and garnered even higher expectations from fans from all around the world.
And after half a decade, one of the most anticipated games of 2016, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, was finally released after lengthy delay. Make no mistake, this game lives up to its predecessor's fame as a beautiful work of visual art. And as always it has high levels of detail in game, and good soundtrack too. But these, however unfortunately, are perhaps the game's only saving grace...
Bluntly put, the game felt very underwhelming, in the sense that it has lost the 'scale' of its original story. It has lost its touch of grandeur, the sense of suspense and urgency, It feels like you are no longer chasing after some unknown wrapped in globe-spanning intrigue, you are now some rookie cop solving petty local crimes... The plot barely advances, if at all. The game feels unfinished - AND PERHAPS IT IS. The actual, substantial contents that have been delivered here are comparable to about 1/3 of that in the original.
If this was done as an intentional decision, as part of some ugly attempt to forcibly extend the lifespan of the franchise, I am SERIOUSLY disappointed. And I am not the only one (no doubt other Steam reviews speak volumes already).
Mechanically the game was badly optimised, unpolished and a horroshow of bugfests and glitches upon release. And the actual gameplay has changed little other than some minor quality of life improvements and a new crafting and customisation system.
Do I still love Deus Ex? Absolutely. But would I recommend this game to anyone? No. And not until the powers-that-be can put their acts together and remedy this appalling disappointment.

DLC Quest is a platformer where you collect coins to buy "DLC" that can get you through the game. This game is pretty hilarious, since you need to buy DLC to do even the most basic things, like jumping and moving left.
For the most part, the platforming is pretty easy, and most people should get through the game with little challenge. The game's also fairly short too. I beat both campaigns with 100% completion in 2.5 hours. DLC Quest is pretty much entirely held up by it's humor. If  you're familiar with video game culture in general, it will keep you laughing. You can even buy Horse Armor.
The graphics are basic pixel work, but it looks nice and it's appropriate for this style of platformer. The chiptune music is alright but not really memorable. The game thankfully controls pretty well, except that wall jumping may take some time to get used to.
DLC Quest is easy and very short, but it's funny and it only costs $3. It's definitely worth the minor investment.

Operation Flashpoint: Red River is the final installment in the Operation Flashpoint series.
I go way back with this series. The original Operation Flashpoint was my favorite game in High School. Cold War Crisis (Now called ArmA X: Cold War Assault) was a brilliant milsim. It was a difficult and wonderfully rewarding experience.
Now, this is where things take a turn for the strange. Codemasters and Operation Flashpoint's developer, Bohemia Interactive Studios, had a falling out. Codemasters owns the Operation Flashpoint license, so they name stayed with Codemasters. BIS went on to make Armed Assault: Combat Operations, or ArmA. The original ArmA (as in ArmA 1, not ArmA CWA) was lukewarm in reception. It had loads of issues upon launch. This left people wondering perhaps that Codemasters could make a better game. So, they tried with Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising.
Now, simultaenously, BIS was going to try again with ArmA 2. BIS made a lot of good decisions and even released a demo of ArmA 2. ArmA 2 came out a few months before Dragon Rising. There were still complaints about performance issues, but over all ArmA 2 was a huge hit.
Dragon Rising received no demo before release. Infact, it got a demo a month after. Dragon Rising did feature a better performing engine than ArmA 2, but that was about it. The game even had a mission editor on PC, but it was inferior to ArmA's. In all, I actually enjoyed Dragon Rising a lot, but it's inferior to ArmA 2 in so many ways. The majority of issues that plagued it could be centered around the fact that it was a pretty weak console port to PC.
Now, Red River is more of the same bad, but none of the good. I wish I could go into more detail, but Red River boils down to this:
-Get briefed by a gruff Staff Sergeant
-Scripted shooting gallery section with weak feeling weapons and the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ set of mouse sensitivity in an FPS. You need to have it maxed in order for your view in the iron-sights to have any usable movement. How ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ were you, Codemasters?
-Deal with dumbed down AI. Literally. Prick-in-Command Sion Lenton outright said the AI in Dragon Rising was "too good" at some points. The ♥♥♥♥ planet are you from? Now, enjoy being able to run through a door filled by a Tajik insurgent, get behind him, and shoot him in the back as he menaces you.
-Get back in vehicles for additional banter.
One hallmark of Flashpoint, vehicle control, is gone. In a quote from ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ supreme Sion Lenton, he stated that "Marines don't fly"  despite the USMC operating the 5th largest Air Arm in the world.
Instead, you're treated to a Call of Duty level single player and co-op experience.
Literally, it's pretty much Call of Duty single player.
This game is one you should pass on without a doubt.
If you want tacticool shooting, pick up any of the ArmAs, the original Ghost Recon, and Ravenshield.
If you have those and still want more, Dragon Rising isn't awful

So, What is "The Mean Greens"? Well, It's a third-person multiplayer shooter based on the UNREAL engine, featuring, as might already know, toy soldiers. Gameplay is quite simple, but this simplicity somehow makes this game even more fun. Basically, It's just simple toy-styled game where you can just play and relax in the end of the day. Of course, there are different gamemodes and maps, and, talking about maps, they are very well designed, colorful and full of decorations. Graphics is nice, however, there are some texture pop-ups, but they are not very annoying. Another good point is that game runs nice on my aged hardware (AMD Athlon II X4, 4gb ram, XFX Radeon HD 7750 (1gb vram)). There are some troubles with connecting to servers, but most of them are already fixed.
All in all, The Mean Greens is quite simple but solid game which can bring your childhood back to life. You should definately buy it when it's on sale.

Let me start by saying if you loved playing Army Sarge's heroes on N64 and wanted a spin off multiplayer third person shooter than buy this game!
Pros-
-The graphics are astounding! Seriously the best I have seen from Unreal engine 4 so far.

-Many different unique gamemodes which allow fun filled action to ensue throughout various hours of gameplay.
-No class system, rather all players have access to 5 different guns which represent various ways to play (all need to be used situationally).
Cons-
-16 player max server (understandable fighting within game is already chaotic).
-Animation can at times seem buggy, hopefully this will improve throughout being updated.
-No Autobalance which in effect allows the team with the most amount of players to obtain a very large advantage (especially since maps are at most 8v8)
-Not much other than multiplayer modes.
All in all this game is definetly worth a purchase. A very unique third-person shooter that entails endless hours of fun!
The biggest CON for me is respawn protection (a few seconds would be nice). Because spawnkilling can be an issue...

Being a total fangirl of DXHR, I was thrilled beyond words when a sequel was announced- I mean, after witnessing the calibre of the first game, who wouldn't? The absolutely stunning designs and visuals, the exciting background and engaging story, badass characters, great gameplay; the talents at Eidos Montreal have set a high bar and garnered even higher expectations from fans from all around the world.
And after half a decade, one of the most anticipated games of 2016, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, was finally released after lengthy delay. Make no mistake, this game lives up to its predecessor's fame as a beautiful work of visual art. And as always it has high levels of detail in game, and good soundtrack too. But these, however unfortunately, are perhaps the game's only saving grace...
Bluntly put, the game felt very underwhelming, in the sense that it has lost the 'scale' of its original story. It has lost its touch of grandeur, the sense of suspense and urgency, It feels like you are no longer chasing after some unknown wrapped in globe-spanning intrigue, you are now some rookie cop solving petty local crimes... The plot barely advances, if at all. The game feels unfinished - AND PERHAPS IT IS. The actual, substantial contents that have been delivered here are comparable to about 1/3 of that in the original.
If this was done as an intentional decision, as part of some ugly attempt to forcibly extend the lifespan of the franchise, I am SERIOUSLY disappointed. And I am not the only one (no doubt other Steam reviews speak volumes already).
Mechanically the game was badly optimised, unpolished and a horroshow of bugfests and glitches upon release. And the actual gameplay has changed little other than some minor quality of life improvements and a new crafting and customisation system.
Do I still love Deus Ex? Absolutely. But would I recommend this game to anyone? No. And not until the powers-that-be can put their acts together and remedy this appalling disappointment.
