I like this one more than I liked Human Revolution. There is an abundancy of side missions that can be found and completed during each visit to Prague and some of them depend on whether you completed a previous side mission or not. A nice detail is that if you complete some side missions you gain a "favor" that will make things much easier later in the game, I really liked that when I found out.
Although I have seen the crafting system in Tomb Raider already, I do not mind having it in Deus-Ex as well. In previous games you had to search for cells or candy bars to refil your energy, in DX:MD you can craft biocels, nano blade ammo, tesla ammo, upgrade your weapons and so on. This is great because you do not have search every inch of the map to find a particular item, you can craft it now as an alternative. If you are a heavy aug user you can craft loads of biocells, if you like to shoot your way you can upgrade your weapons to have a higher damage output. This is a great addition because you have more flexibility on how you can play the game.
Jensen Stories, while a nice way for adding DLC stories, they have a small issue. Basically they all happen when you are in Prague. You can go pay Tarvos a visit (Desperate Measures DLC), raid the Palisade Blade (System Rift DLC) and who knows what the future holds... Anyway, the issue with them is that they are stand alone missions (cannot be activated through the main story) and you get exactly nothing (no augmentations, weapons and so on) from what you have in the main story. There is no argument for why you managed to lose everything just when you are about to raid a bank, at least for The Missing Link DLC (Deus-Ex: Human Revolution) you get a solid argument for why you lost all your guns and all your augs, for Jensen Stories there is no explication storyline wise (except desperate measures which happens somewhere in the past).
Last but not least, The Breach. This is a bit different from what I am used to when playing a Deus-Ex game but it can be fun nonetheless. You have your avatar, you can upgrade augments, buy guns, upgrade guns with weapon parts, pretty much evereything you have in the main game, with a few exceptions. Using in-game credits you can only buy standard ammo, you cannot buy Armor Piercing (AP) ammo, EMP ammo, praxis kits, biocells, hypostims, grenades, mine templates and other goodies. What you have to do to get them is either capture reward nodes (they are of limited number) or buy booster packs and hope that once you unpack it you will get the items you were looking for. If you run our of in-game credits you can always get more using real money (yes, REAL money).
I have completed all nodes in Breach without paying extra and I still have 200K (Breach) credits after buying a Rippers pack. But the mechanics of Breach do not seem to belong to a single player game that costs around 50 euros. In my view, Breach would have been a good Free-to-Play version for Deus-Ex. You get some of the standard stuff and can buy more standard ammo and guns using in-game credits. You can play the same level multiple times to get more credits and eventually buy booster packs to further upgrade your guns, get augs and so on. If you really want to, you can pay with real money to speed your upgrades.

Mount& Blade: Warband. A gem from Taleworlds Entertainment, a small group of Turkeys with goals beyond gobbling and stuffing. These brave men and women have forged from the depths a game beyond all depth and meaning, a strategy that is part "Grand" and "Real-Time". Starting with the original Mount & Blade, they expanded from their website and released their game on Steam, as well as "Mount & Blade: Warband", a full remake of Mount & Blade with oodles of new content. Mount & Blade originally started out as an ambiguous product; - The early versions of the game had two factions, Swadia and the Vaegirs, the former being literal undead. (King Harlaus, Long may he Butter, was a skeleton!) After deciding to give a pass on the medieval-fantasy route, they stuck to a more solid plan and focused on creating an artifical world based off of the 1257 timeline, with unique factions, cultures and landscape, in the land "Calradia". Spanning years of development, Mount & Blade, Mount & Blade: Warband and their subsequent additions have been carefully tested, played and play-tested to the point of perfection. An absolute masterpiece of a game that will take hours of your time and leave you wondering where they went.
My personal time on Steam is not even 200 hours, but spanning the original M&B and Warband, which I purchased digitally from Taleworlds, I have accrued around 4,000 hours, if not more, of play-time. This is partially due to the incredibly dense and managed modding scene, where-in hundreds, thousands of people have created their own flavors of Mount & Blade: Warband, leaving you with a buffet of excellency to choose from. There's more than just a bit of choice here, and something will match everybody. The game routinely goes on sales, and the original M&B was created, from my knowledge, by simply two people, who later expanded the team for Warband. They're going on to make Mount & Blade: Bannerlord, a "Sequel" of sorts to Mount & Blade: Warband.
If you're interested in roaming the lands hunting bandits, managing villages and castles, engaging in wars or turning bandit and living off of the land, Warband is for you. Check out the modding scene for hundreds more hours of enjoyment.
Mount & Blade: Warband is in my top 5 "Best-Games-Of-All-Time" list. An absolute 5/5, a 10/10 masterpiece. I cannot think of a single flaw besides the fact I've been waiting for Bannerlord for far too long. Please give this game a try, and you will not be disappointed!

Another Simon Says game, where the entire point of the game is boiled down to twitch reflexes. The twist this time around is that you can either make it harder or easier on you by choosing the input method. So you can either do it via controller or if you, like me, are a proficient typist who averages around 100 words or 500+ keystrokes per minute, you can completely dominate the game by typing out predefined words.
The single-player is limited only to a handful of AI enemies and seem more like a tutorial for the online and multiplayer modes which unfortunately are pretty much dead given the niche nature of the title. This is a typing game and yet it functions like it is everything but.
This is not a traditionally structured review and the reason for that is this game is lacking in 3/4 categories I usually highlight.
To start, the game was fun initially and by that I mean for the first 3 single player rounds. After those rounds I began to notice the cracks in the game which were difficult to ignore. I really thought I was going to be surprised be how good the game was going to be but I couldn't have been more wrong. That feeling came from the game's killer presentation. It really makes a good first impression. You can tell the UI and opening menu is well developed. The narrator is perfect and his comments as you browse the menu had me excited for what was to come. But that was where it ended and where my disdain began.
The game is a breeze and yet it is so frustrating. But before that, this is basically how the game plays out. There are 10 singleplayer bots to face-off against who progressively get faster at typing. You type a single 10 letter word as fast as you can in an attempt to beat the NPC. If you're an avid PC user like most gamers on steam are you're going to polish off the first 7 opponents in under 6 minutes. The last 2 are the only real challenge and where you will probably spend most of your time in the SP mode. I'd like to comment on the multiplayer but there are no servers. And for that it's a damn shame you can finish singleplayer in under 15 minutes. But that's not the worst of it. Oh no. When I said this game is frustrating, I said that because the dev chose to fancy up menus instead of working on gameplay.
Why are the words vertical? I can't quickly distinguish letters from eachother or even quickly read the word half the time this way. Additionally, that makes it a QTE experience because I no longer try to quickly read the word and then quickly type it out. I just react to what's top-most.
Why are the words strictly 10 letters long? You can tell the dev just ran out of 10 letter words to use and started using compound words that aren't official words or using words that were popular in the 1800's. It doesn't make any sense and it just makes it more infuriating when you are trying to read vertically. Because now not only am I reading in an abnormal way but I am also trying to read words nobody in the modern era has seen before. Just asinine.
Why is it 8-bit styled text? I get that that's the art style but it's a massive problem when you're supposed to be acting quickly. For example, W's are too similiar to the H's; H's too similiar to the K's; A's to R's; A's to B's; F's to E's, and the X's to the K's. That's a total of 42% of the alphabet that can be mistaken for another letter. Whoever developed this needs to take a lesson on font. It's actually confusing to me how this was overlooked. It really doesn't help that the words are vertical either and they ♥♥♥♥ing blend with the rest of the game. No, outer glow in a different color or boldness to stand out on the font. So now I'm trying to read vertical words no one has ever heard before in a font that makes it so if you spend more than a quarter of a second trying to recognize you lose. Just so stupid.
Why do we just type one word only? I don't see why every round needed to last just 9 seconds. It's a buzzkill and a half.
The worst part is the game is cool. It has that flair that really nails the western thing but fails completely as the type of game it wants to be. There is nothing else to the game. I didn't note additional modes and couldn't bear to play more. This had potential but there's just nothing that helps me to recommend it. I enjoyed some of my time spent on this game but it was so flawed that I just got angrier typing this up trying to understand why it is the way it is. And for 6$ I think with gameplay tweaks it would have been worth it but right now, even as a cheap game it's not even close. If I had to give this a score...

(THIS IS JUST A REVIEW OF BLAKE STONE IN ALIENS OF GOLD)
Blake Stone in Aliens of Gold was the first game I ever owned on PC and it turned me into a life long PC Gamer!  The amount of hours I spent on this game trying to find every secret door is ridiculous!!
PROS:
- SECRET DOORS!! Oh man... there are tons and tons of secret doors with gold and money and all sorts of goodies.  Secret doors within secret doors within secret doors!! Today's games are seriously lacking secret doors!!!
- Very fun blood and gore 90's retro FPS.
- Kill people for candy bars!!
- If you like the original Doom and Wolfenstein 3D then you'll love this game (unless you don't...)
CONS:
- The controls are backwards 90's FPS... meaning you have to use the arrow keys, shift keys and space bars.  You can use your mouse which makes it better.
- No Steam SHIFT-TAB screen (its a DOSBOX game).
Short Story: It's 1993... I'm 7 years old and my mom got a hand me down PC from her work.  I wanted to  get a game for it but she wouldn't let me get Doom or Wolfenstein 3D because my Aunt let my older cousin get them and she said "OH MY GOD THEY'RE GAMES ABOUT PURE MURDER!!!! BLAH BLAH BLAH... 90'S ANTI VIDEO GAME PROPAGANDA... BLAH BLAH BLAH".  So I hear about this game called Blake Stone from another friend of mine, which at the time was very underated and unknown to parents.  It had all the  blood, the gore, the killing monsters and robots but no parent were raging on it yet because Doom and Wolfenstein took all the heat!  So I was able to convince my mom it wasn't bad and she bought it for me! I can't even imagine how many hours i spent playing this game.  Still holds up pretty well in fun factor considering how old it is.  If you love retro 90's FPSs then try this game out!!

Operation Flashpoint: Red River is something that fills the gap between realistic military sims and the more common mainstream shooters.
I know the series is more known for it's more realistic approach, latest reference is 'Dragon Rising', franchise fans will turn it down because of that. It is somewhat dissapointing to see a series dummed down because the publisher demands to appeal to a broader audience.
But this said, it does try to ease players into a more tactical and realistic approach to their missions. And I do applaud the fact that the developers tried to balance the two playstyles, because by doing so they might just pave the way for all those rushing reflex based players to grow up and become mature tactical players. Because we all have to agree on the fact that military sims have a rather steep learning curve that might scare new players away.
The game is good looking and other than the sometimes superfluous banter the sounds are great aswell. There are even several funny anecdotes from other media. The only thing that is bothersome is the AI, and most importantly those of your squadmates. But if you micro-manage their commands they get the job done though. This being said it is obvious that the game would be tons more fun with coop buddies, and the developers facilitated this through the inclusion of various Fireteam Engagements.
Allround if you're looking for a step-up from your average twitch-based shooter into a more tactical genre of games and you have some friends to play this with you it's totally worth it. You will learn to pace yourself, command your squad and look at situations from a tactical point of view before rushing into a insurgent populated village.
This game was epic.

I've seen a lot of people compare this to Arma or Battlefield, and then say this game is rather dissapointing. The game is more like MoH or CoD, in the sense that it isn't openworld, and the missions are very linear. Where it differs from MoH or CoD however is in the gameplay. Unlike you're generic FPS military game, you are not a walking tank that can run through the battlefield taking little to no damage whilst wreaking havoc on your enemies using an array of weapons. In OF you have 4 distinct classes, with different weapon setups, and by playing as the classes you can unlock different weapons to use and more customization options, none of which however are capable of running and gunning through the battelfield due to how easy it is to be killed. Even on normal you can get killed in as few as 2 bullets. Due to this the gameplay is a lot slower paced than other FPS games you may be used too, but it is still very enjoyable. Personally I found it a nice change from the standard FPS games. The story however is rather dissapointing. It's your standard military story where you are in a foreign country trying to restore peace by killing anything that moves, and overall the story is forgettable.
Now one of the major downsides to this game is the need to install Games for Windows Live. Youll need to install the GFWL client seperatly from the windows/xbox site before being able to launch the game, and you will need to sign into an Xbox live account in order to play co-op/multiplayer and to be able to save your progress. It's important to note however, that the multiplayer and co-op is still functional despite GFWL not being supported anymore, which is a good thing since the game is a lot more fun to play with friends as the AI squadmates generally are not very useful.
The graphics have not aged well and even back in 2011 when the game was launched the graphics weren't that great, and the game isn't optimised that well for PC. With that being said though, the game is still a lot of fun to play, and has a lot of gameplay value, especially for its current low cost. I'd give OF:Red River a solid 7/10
PS: The game plays a little smoother with a xbox controller over keyboard and mouse, but is still playable with them if you don't happen to have a controller. Also GFWL may not be getting updated anymore, but it works fine, so people should stop complaining about the game and giving it bad ratings based on this one thing.

after a half of year of this game, i can finally judge from an unbiased point of view.
Basic overview: The game used to be great.
Ahh, this game was fun. I joined the germans after playing a few days of americans. Spent some cash even, finally got to the point where i unlocked the "generals" part of the game.
The Stragetic game:
(Generals is where you command squads on a strategic map of europe with other generals against 2 other countries: United States, Russia, and Germany. You can join the games to help win territory and capture important cities.)
But it is so broken!!! Germans have no chance of winning... And this is no biased opinions. I only remember winning one war out of the other 50...
People blame the "biased devs" and hackers and what not. But, the truth is, The germany faction is simply overpopulated. because of this, USA and Russia get a 40% XP/Coin bonus... not the best move in my opinion, but i guess its to encourage german players to join the other factions. Also, the huge german generals are slowly giving up, also causing us to lose even more...
It is simply broken and not fun anymore.
Economy System
Overview: Pay to Win or Grind.
Look, I enjoy this game at times because of the fact of having tanks, airplanes, paratroopes, snipers, and infantry in the same battlefield.  But really, thats just kinda the only thing.
Everything is so expensive... dont even get me started on the costs of the classes...
Want to buy a machine gun? 200k or more. med pack? 30k. a decent pistol? 70k.
Yeesh, and keep in mind that each battle u play on average u will get 2-5k coins. But, don't forget the repairs of guns and such. -2k. Grind, grind, grind. get a gun that turns out to be useless.
Don't forget the XP ribbons to unlock those things that u have grind for. ugh.
Gameplay
Overview: Die Die Die, hide in bush, Die.
Ahh, well, gameplay? Could be better. Love the tanks that shoot you from a mile away. Or the hacking sniper that shoots from 2 miles away. or the grenade abusers.
#1 Tank's enemy: Throw 2 anti tanks grenades at a tank and watch as they blow up without warning. Broken.
Also, the machine guns are overpowered. And you cant get one till u pay up. Unless, you want to grind for months, of course.
Graphics/Connection
overview: Bland graphics with decent connection.
The graphics are not good. espicially for pilots: A building looks like a dirt pile in the sky. I mean, they could be decent for their time, but the game is outdated. Connection is pretty A OK. the only ok-ish thing on this game.
Conclusion
Old game that used to be good. Stragetic part of game is broken and gameplay is not that good. The economic side is terrible and Pay 2 Win. Graphics Are old, but the servers are fine.
3.5/10 Would play again if cleaned up.

Team Deathmatch/Deathmatch: get the kill limit and win or have the most kills until the timer runs out. You can respawn
Siege: The defenders must hold the castles flag until the time runs out. The attackers must capture the castles flag. Defenders have limited lives while the attackers do not.
Duel: Duel other players/bots and gain score required to win.
Commander Battle: Maximum players 40. Only available in Napoleonic Wars DLC/ With Fire and Sword Expansion) Players can command bot regiments and fight other players regiments, making huge battles of 200 vs 200. The servers in Napoleonic Wars are often full.

CONS:

Don't be turned away by the "Mixed" stigma and that scary, danger-orange coloring to the same type-written word. This game has real meat to it, real substance that gives the game lasting value.  I've owned this game and played it off and on since its release in 2011: Operation Flashpoint Red River is worth your ten bucks ten times over.
Red River is about as realistic as you choose, and your "Normal" difficulty rating still hammers home that this is a tactical, infantry-based military sim. Some corners are glossed over in a comesmetic way (e.g. Fireteam members completely restored at save checkpoints in the single-player campaign) which some find unappealing and what I'll bet you is the number one focus of complaints.
The multiplayer options of the game are quite awesome if you pause to think about truly seamless the integration of co-op into Fireteam Missions and even the Campaign. Player Progress and Class Setup (rewards for Achievements etc.) are just whipped cream on a trifecta wedding cake.

This game is very fun, but its shortcomings are too much and I cannot recommend this game because of them.
Pros:
+ Game is very fun and side missions are interesting.
+ Ability to tackle a situation anyway you want continues from the other Deus Ex games.
+ Prague is well designed and its ghettos reflects the atmosphere of the story well.
+ The story is interesting and is a modern take on the Civil Rights Movement.
Cons:
- Denuvo. An anti-piracy measure that needs you to be online to play the game, despite it being only a single player game.
- The story missions start off well and continue to do so until the later parts of the game, of which are disappointing and underwhelming.
- Too easy. Even on the hardest difficulty, it is seriously too easy just to shoot everyone up, even more so with armor and health augs.
- Heavily unoptimised. This game runs at 60+ FPS some of the time but frame drops happen too often, this should not happen with a GTX 1080. This is probably due to the fact the Dawn engine is an in-house engine with little development time, it is not even graphically impressive.
I cannot recommend this game at the current price, I haven't even talked about the DLC and Micro-transactions, but I thought I'd just review the game itself. Wait for a sale to play it as it is still a fun and enjoyable experience, but beware of Denuvo and the Micro-transactions.

I'm super into racing games now and rally has become my favorite. After putting a good chunk of hours into Dirt Rally I wanted to try something different so I bought this on sale.
This game gets an undeserved bad rap. In simulation mode the driving is just as hard, and feels very similar to Dirt Rally.
You can also crank the AI difficulty up to extreme and you will probably come in last every single race. Or if you're like me, put it on medium and come in first every time which is kinda nice after not doing so well in Dirt.
Unlike DR this game has different gameplay options from arcade driving to full simulation.
Where this game does lack compared to Dirt Rally is the finishing touches. I use headphones when playing and the sound in the car just doesn't quite sound real. The flying gravel sounds like a recording played on loop that doesn't quite match with what the car is doing. And the co-driver is frankly, awful. His voice clips and he sounds robotic the whole time. Except when you get near the finish and he for some reason yells out "finish!" and it's so jarring compared to the rest of robotic delivery.
At least he doesn't sound mildly disappointed after a big spin out like the co driver in D:Rally.
But this game has an upside compared to DR and that's the career mode. First of all it's real WRC licensing so you get all the cars and drivers and tracks from the 2016 season and there is a real progression not just buying news cars and trying to get into the next racing tier.
We all know Dirt Rally is the current king of the rally games but this game is quite fun and worth playing especially when you can get it for 50% off.

===
Narborion is a mixture between a classic turn-based RPG and an interactive novel. In this title you will impersonate a young page serving a great Lord, in one of the many cities of a rather large and varied dark-fantasy realm. Your training is almost over, so after being victorious in a tournament, the Princess summons you to aid her in an important quest far deep into a forbidden land. This pretty classical incipit is the kickstart of your journey, that will be undoubtedly be riddled with many things to discover, dangers to overcome, but mostly a lot of stuff to read.
===
After creating your character at the beginning, and having selected from a decently sized pool of Feats and/or Spells and having bought your starting Gear as you see fit, our mighty hero will be transported to the city. The main interactions with what happens in the world, and how you react to said events, are done via the text-based interface on the left screen side. There you will spend most of your time reading a very detailed description of many events and places, and then reacto as you see best. This game also has RPG elements, like Inventory Managing, self-explainatory, Character Progression by winning fights, performing actions or training while camping, and most importantly Checks, which are little "tests" of one or more of your attributes, like Strenght or Intelligence, that will be passed or else depending how apt your character is in that feature. The developers tried to implement a very pen-and-paper like style to world interaction, which mostly works. However mind that this game is not one for those who love action or short texts, as there will be a lot of stuff to read, and also Puzzles and Riddles to solve, maybe not mandatorily, but there are. During your travels you will be able (and forced to) set camp, go literally wherever you want, explore exciting new places, meet new people, and then kill them (or not)!
The combat in Narborion is turn-based, very basic and a bit depth-lacking in so. Each turn you will have a number of Movement Points and one Attack or Spell to use, and so do your enemies. Armor wore, attributes, type of weapon used and Feats all are important to the outcome of a fight. A massively armored knight will get a hard time rolling a good dice for hitting an unarmored enemy, while also the opposite applies, well unless you are way more experienced that your foes. On the right side in combat you will be able to see your current statistics, like Attack, Defense, HP etc. the system is done decently enough, does the job even not being the main part of the game, but it also has problems, such fights going on for 50 turns because you can't hit, for example, a light-armored enemy while he can't damage you because too much armor, or your character being unable to attack / move due to simple bugs. The developers apparently know the combat engine is a bit faulty and a Reset button is present to reset the field if something doens't work anymore.
Narborion features a global chat and a multiplayer PvP arena. Sadly we have not been able to test it since nobody was there to play it. It possibly is the same combat system, just PvP.
Content-Wise, Narborion is quite plentiful. There are many locations to visit, items to get, decisions to make, people to meet and riddles to solve. If you look for an adventure with a lot to do, Narborion might be your thing, but be prepared doing a lot of reading. I would say the longevity of this title can go beyond 50 hours, depends how fast you read and how much stuff you do.
Overall, Narborion goes for a realisticly-depicted combat and events. Weapons will do real damage and as many times will happen, one hit is usually sufficent to kill an unarmored, untrained enemy or a medium sized beast, it depends anyway. Balancing-wise, events you interact with during the narration, or Checks, are fair enough if you have the right attributes for them, i have to say though that Luck is overpowered as it can make you avoid any danger for a Luck point price, those anyway are very scarce, hard to regenerate so i guess it is fair, to a point. I noticed prices in markets are quite high and many times even by doing everything, at least early ingame, you won't be able to buy anything decent, so i can say money balance is not very good early on but gets better as you progress.
This can be a quite challenging game, some fights are very tough, riddles are difficult, you will have to remember what you read in places before and then use it later to solve other stuff or determinate interactions. For some obscure reason beyond mortal compresion, this game is described as "Roguelike Dungeoneering", but features a save system called Bookmarks, from which you can reload if you die. How can it be Roguelike if you can save?
===
Graphics, as you would expect from a mostly text based game, are very basic. Character portraits and models in combat are 2-dimensional drawings, done well but a little too small, artist drawings of places though are well done, as are depictions of equipments and items in various shops. UI is sufficently well done graphically, i'd definitely say the graphical style is suitable for this kind of game, just do not expect anything out of basic.
Soundtracks are a few, when you for example enter a tavern and select to hear the Bard's local song, you don't, the soundtrack will be the same. Combat effects are sufficent, there is no spoken dialogue, sounds are overall barely enough to do the job but are not of good quality nor anything special. It works, yes, but just so.
You'd expect this could run on a toaster, well yes it can run on a toaster, but it still has problems in performance. When transitioning from one text screen to the next after, example, some choice, the game can sometimes freeze or take its time to load the text, which makes the exxperience clunky in some fragments. This so far is the only performance issue, not major.
Nothing to report.
AI of enemies and allies is generally good, sometimes tho they take strange paths to reach an objective and perform mysterious actions instead of doing more efficent things they could.
UI, management and panels are accessible and well-thought enough, map could be more zoomed out.
When Steam overlay is used, the game "breaks" its interface, it can be restored by clicking around randomly, but is not very nice. Character can get unable to attack / move randomly in combat, this can be solved by reset button put there by developers. By clicking a sword on top of the name of out character in the interface, we can raise Strenght and Dexterity indefinityl just clicking on it many times, this exploit is a Easter Egg put by Developers but can lead to serious exploiting, since this game has Leaderboards and PvP, i'll let you imagine what happens next.
===
Narborion is a valiant attempt in putting text-based, pen-and-paper like experience on PC gaming, it has good ideas but also problems and inaccuracies. I'd recommend it to fantasy enthusiasts who like lots of reading, things to do, puzzles and some combat. It overall is a rather innovative title but cannot get out of the average in any case.

A fun little game. And maybe also sadly accurate.

Nowadays it's expected that publishers will offer us players some optional, additional content in order to extend our gaming enjoyment beyond the actual end of the game. Most times that extra content is well received and allows us gamers to maximize the bang-for-our-gaming-buck. That said, who among us hasn't (at least once or twice) put up the extra $5, $10, or even $20 for the latest DLC only to come away with the suspicion that we were originally sold what amounts to an incomplete game; the publisher having purposely held back essential content in order to sell that very same content to us later at an additional cost? Afterall, it's no secret that DLC is now a part of the developement cycle from the very beginning.
DLC Quest is an indy developer's jab at the "downloadable content" industry as a whole. It parodies the tendency some less-than-scrupulous publishers have of holding back essential content in order to sleazily fleece their fanbase later. When you start the game, there is no sound or animation. You can hardly move and the game can't be paused. As you progress, you'll find in-game currency which can be used to purchase "DLC" which unlocks these "extra features". Despite the game itself being one big joke, it does actually entertain for the entire duration (though it is very short; you'll most likely beat it from start-to-finish in less than 2 hours). Considering the very low price and the discussion this game's popularity will undoubtedly provoke, everyone should buy it and give it a try.

Here's my philosophy on the games as it relates to this OpenIV debacle: buying a game grants the producer of said game money, and the purchaser limited rights to the game's usage. If a producer (Rockstar) openly supports a new usage of their game (modding the source code of the game that OpenIV enables), then this extends the rights of the end-user to include this new usage.
In this entire event, one must understand the role of Whales (See the Extra Credits video on Whales in F2P games for a better explaination of the term) in freemium multiplayer games, as well as hackers. While a gaming company is fine in supporting whales with a business model, they should never support hackers.
Whales and hackers both ruin the online experience in GTAV. Whales have paid hundreds if not thousands of dollars to get ahead in the multiplayer aspect of the game without needing to grind or extend hard effort for  leveling, while the hackers do so illegitimatly through exploits that the game's developers have ignored in patching. This creates a smalll amount of "top-tier" players who are the most powerful in the game.
This disproportion of high to low level players in the Online aspect of GTAV is what makes for such a frustrating experience for the average gamer. Hackers and whales alike have little or no repercussions for attacking the average Online user. This makes and even more grueling experience as a gamer that does not want to hack or pay-to-win is faced with countless setbacks in trying to make progress in the online aspect of GTAV.
Many users who wished to avoid the litany of wanton unfairness in Online and still wanted to experience Online's content, turned to mods.
Modding  GTAV  requires specific software. One of the more popular softwares for handing, installing and managing mods in GTAIV as well as GTAV is called OpenIV. It was created by a group of Russian developers for the sake of modding. One of the figureheads of this development group, GooD-NTS, has posted a notice on the OpenIV website as well as the GTA forums, detailing their side of the issue. So go look for their statement if you want more clarification, as I will not be detailing GooD's post here.
Essentially, what has ended up happening, days after Take-Two, the parent company Rockstar, has stated they are "undermonetizing users in GTA Online" is that the two companies (Take 2 and Rock*) issued a cease and desist letter to the OpenIV development team. This guts the modding scene for GTAV , as more than half of the mods for the game rely on OpenIV.
Connect the dots, and you can easily deduce that Rock* and Take 2 are trying to push people back to Online to buy needed Shark Cards, the game's microtransactions, to survive in a broken online environment that they refuse to fix.
Both companies ruined their reputation with this bureaucratic idiocy, and I refuse to support them until OpenIV comes back from the grave.

The game has totally under-fulfilled my expectations. Adhering to the same game mechanics, which made the previous game great, everything seems to be in place. Familiar augmentation system powered with new experimental augmentations, dystopian Prague with enough space for exploration, safecracking and vent crawling and intricate story with plenty of interesting characters.
But as you progress further into story you start to realize how slapdash of a game workmanship this game is. Is very short. You can complete the main story line in less than 12 hours, while sidequesnts will consume not more than additional 7. Yes, it took me around 20 to complete the main story line along with the majority of side quests, and around 30% of playtime was reloading last save as I played on highest difficulty setting available for first playthrough. The game ends on a cliffhanger leaving most of the story questions unanswered, as if the game was planned as filler to extend the whole story premise for as many sequels as possible. I did not waste time to search for info regarding DE:MD sales figures , but I sincerely hope this will not turn to be a successful cash-grab as it was obviously planned to be and next installment in the serious will  be more story focused and complete.
As you explore the game world you eventually realize that it is very small. Prague’s districts are open for exploration from the very start and couple of story missions take place in remote locations outside of Prague. And those locations are very small and missions are very short. To be honest, I rarely had a chance to test new augs until the end of the game. This might end up being my favorite Deus Ex game. I loved the first three, but I'm really shocked by how good this one is. I went in with neutral expectations. This game is fantastic, and a vast improvement over Human Revolution, which felt a little dated even when it came out 5 years ago. I still enjoyed it back then, but when going back to it after Mankind Divided it just felt incredibly bland and boring, so I settled with watching the recap video a second time for the story refresher.
Mankind Divided looks absolutely gorgeous and runs really well on my GTX 1060 6GB, at 1080p. Leaving everything on max settings, except for turning contact hardening shadows OFF and volumetric lighting to ON instead of high (which gains you about 15 fps), it rarely dips much below 60 fps. Had a very slight stuttering problem but nothing that bothered me and I think going with double buffering instead of triple buffering might have helped with that.
Aside from looking gorgeous the game is also incredibly detailed, making the apartments you enter actually feel like an apartment people could live in, something the previous game severely lacked. It also plays really well. I love the new smart vision and the way it helps you find the optimal paths, crawling through air vents, punching through walls etc, making the stealth gameplay immensely satisfying. This is another aspect the game does really well, giving you multiple solutions to a problem and ways to infiltrate, not making you feel like you don't have the right augments activated.
One complaint I've seen about this game is the way it handles DLC. Aren't we used to this by now? In the last 5 years almost any game will try to milk the hell out of us with DLC and in game purchases. Yeah, it sucks, but if the core game is still awesome, the game doesn't deserve a negative review.
I love this game and while I've enjoyed previous Deus Ex games, this is the first that really made me a fan of the series, and I look forward to the next major game in the series.

Deus Ex Mankind Divided improves on everything from the last entry. Gunplay, sneaking, hacking and freedom of exploration are all improved. This game really has a strong vibe of the original Deux Ex game, which is something I didn't expect that much, after the Human Revolution being a quite different feeling case, since it lacked many of the wide open areas that Deus Ex had.
Even though the gameplay is great, indeed very enjoyable, there is one major concern: the main storyline of this game is pretty short and you will not discover much of the story without additional (upcoming) DLC. To add, this game is heavy on the PC hardware and it's not totally polished PC experience, but much better than Human Revolution.
So buy only if you can accept these facts and may be prepared to buy the both two rumored story DLCs.

Ready, aim, press.
Western Press is a dueling battle game where players must race through pressing a series of 10 randomized buttons.
Whoever finishes first wins.
The duels last just a few seconds, testing your reaction skills at blazing speeds. The gameplay is simple but can be challenging if you don’t have nimble fingers.
You can duel in a Skill Tester mode against AI opponents, starting with a stack of cans. The difficulty gets more intense each level, and you unlock characters as you beat them.
The Memory Mode offers a bit of a different challenge, forcing players to repeat a continuously growing string of buttons.
There is also an online multiplayer mode, although its as dead as that aforementioned stack of cans. If you want multiplayer, you better have some friends interested in playing.
Developer Bandit-1 included support for both Xbox and PlayStation controllers, as well as dance pads.
The wild west atmosphere of the game is enjoyable and appropriate for the gameplay mechanics. It all fits together well. There’s even a little voice acting tossed into the mix, adding a little more polish to the product.
However, the game lacks any form of a story, other than the winner of the deuls “is right.” Combined with the dead multiplayer, the omission leaves the game feeling a little empty.
Western Press pulls you in with a good setting and challenging gameplay, but has its drawbacks with no story and no real available multiplayer.

As someone who has spent way too much time playing the Smash Bros series ever since its release, I can say without a doubt that even Playstation Allstars Battle Royale did a better job trying to make a Smash clone.  This game is NOT TERRIBLE per se, but I would not recommend it to seasoned Smash Bros fans.
Pros:
-Easy to pick-up and play
-Simple button layout
-Enjoyable enough graphics / sound / overall presentation
-Lots of hats
Cons:
-Gameplay is way too simple
-Awkward UI / HUD
-Floaty gravity with sudden loss of momentum after most actions
-Limited "combos" / abilities
-Very awkward "dodge" ability
-Limited character variety
-Feels like I'm fighting with the controls most of the time (e.g "neutral" and "up" attacks are the same)
-Too much recovery with third and fourth jump
-Too few items / content
Although I would not recommend this game to veteran Smash Bros players, its not actually that bad of a game for newbies to the genre.  Its like the Plants vs Zombies of strategy games.  Its not a bad game, its just not for people that seriously want to play a Smash game (or clone).  Smash isnt that hard to get into for newbies either, so don't bother with Brawlhalla.
tl;dr
Only good for newbies to the genre. But really, just play Smash instead.

Despite there being many perfectly valid criticisms thrown its way, I have to say I still like it. For once - it doesn't have regenerating health - instead, you bleed until you patch yourself up (and then use the the infinite medkit you have, but I guess life isn't perfect). The main problem with it is that it took on the name of a franchise reknowned for its focus on vehicle use and squad (i.e. 8-10 people) tactics taking place in a large open environment. People unfamiliar with the Flashpoint name wouldn't care if Codemasters just called it "Red River" and those who are ended up brewing a turn storm around the game.
Other flaws include glitchy grapchis and overall shoddy optimization, but not to the gamebreaking level. Character models look nice, with lots of detail on the marine characters, missions take place across large patches of terrain, and although you are confined to a certain area battlefield-style, it rarely becomes an issue.
Missions also sport long rides in the back of a humvee, where the only thing you do is listen to the tutorial voice in the form of your platoon's staff sergeant. These rides are tedious, but wrighting is decent and the guy is genuinely hilarious  at times (provided you've ever been in the military or are a fan of Generation Kill), and he reminds me of a sergeant in my old unit.
Speaking of Generation Kill - both this game and the previous one (Dragon Rising) rip entire dialogues straight out of the show - I guess they ran out of creativity half-way through writing the story.
Most annoying of all - the AI. While friendlies can take a little getting used to, but once you get the hang of commanding them they can be made to function, the enemy AI all graduated from the Tajik special ed class and handed an AK - they either stand in the same spot doing nothing or run towards you. Taking cover is also an overly complicated concept for them. Not only that, but they take damage like a china teacup in a bull arena - you'll be lucky to kill one before he♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥himself on a thornbush and bleeds to death.
All in all, the game feels very reminiscent of the Brothers in Arms games, except that actual terrain was used for the levels instead of them looking like a collection of conveniently placed chest-high walls. But I wish they ripped a few more elements off that franchise as well, like the gun accuracy and sway, and maybe the unlobotomized AI while they're at it.

This game takes everything that Dragon Rising was, and improves it immensely.
+Mission flow is highly improved. You fight and feel as part of a platoon in the campaign.
+Campaign is actually very interesting and as a semi-sequel to Dragon Rising, really succeeds at sucking you into the story and the action. It is a MAJOR improvement off of Dragon Rising (Which I can't remember a god damn thing about.)
+Good characters. There is at least one character you will never forget after playing this game, and several other interesting ones with their own distinct personalities that you'll hear plenty of throughout the campaign.
+Combat is fluid and as realistic as this series has ever tried to get. This isn't as realistic as ArmA, and this isn't as Arcadey as battlefield, but that's because this doesn't try to be either. This is a good in-between point of those who can find no joy in either.
+Fireteam Engagements allow for extra gameplay after the campaign
+Player Progression system awards you for doing the best you can on all missions and for completing as many secondary objectives as you possibly can.
+Class Setup module allows you to fully customize the loadout of your entire squad before going into a mission.
+Compared to Dragon Rising, this game features HUGE maps with improved grapihcs that allow for long and intense missions. You really feel like you're fighting in one country rather than several "maps" as you fight along a road from one border to another.
-Windows Live. Sigh.
-Did I mention this uses Windows Live?
-Lastly, the WORST part of this game? It uses Windows Live.
Seriously though, this game is AMAZING and so very worth the full price. On sale? Even better! This is a game that many will pass up, but you definitely won't regret paying for once you get past that first Windows Live login screen. Definitely give it a shot if you enjoy semi-hardcore shooters.

My big complaint is how short the game felt. I finished the campaign in about 25 hours (normal difficulty) while finishing pretty much all of the side quests. There was only one side quest that I didn't finish and that one I chose not to finish because I didn't want to help the guy that gave it to me. The Deus Ex games all have deep levels of intrigue that you uncover as you go through the game. This one feels like it went one level deep before ending the game. There were so many leads that were just never explored. It feels like they meant to do more, but cut off production early.
I enjoyed the game, but I can't help but feel a little disappointed in it. Tentatively recommended, but don't pay full price, wait for at least 25% off.

I hate the gamepad. Mostly because it's not intuitive to control a 3D camera with the thumbstick and you have control with only 4 fingers. Unfortunately most developers design their games for the gamepad when it can be better controlled with a keyboard and mouse. But Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is different. It has a top-down camera perspective and the camera can be rotated in the 2D plane using the bumper buttons. Most of the time the game itself rotates the camera in the desired direction for you so you can forget about the camera completely. And this game has no crazy combos, twitch timing or quick-time events to execute. You must be wondering why I am talking about the controller so much at the start for a game review. It's because in this game the gamepad genuinely has a clear advantage over the keyboard and mouse. If you are not using the gamepad to play this game you will be losing a lot on what this game has to offer.
This game is as the title says a tale of two sons. The brothers are on a journey to find a cure for their father's illness. You take control of the brothers both at the same time and guide them through a beautiful fantasy world in search for the cure. The older brother is a bit serious in character whereas his younger brother is slightly mischievous. You will meet a lot of interesting characters on your journey - some helpful, some in need of help, some being a hindrance, some monsters and even some helpful monsters. The brothers and all the other beings in this game talk in a completely different language. You have to understand what they are saying through gestures and tone of voice. You can interact with certain characters or objects with each brother interacting in a different way. There are some optional interesting side quests in the game which are really easy to miss if you don't scan the environment and most of the Steam achievements are related to the side quests.
You will have to coordinate the movement of both the brothers as well as complete tasks together. For example, the big brother can help a leg up for his younger brother so he can climb up a ledge and pull down a rope for him. The little brother can slip past door grates whereas the big brother can pull heavy levers. The little brother is afraid of drowning so the big brother has to shoulder him while swimming. The platforming sections are real easy and there is really no challenge or difficulty in this game. This game is all about the experience that you get while playing. There are enemies but most of the time it's either about escaping them or trapping them. You will likely die more by falling off a cliff than by an enemy.
The game is made in Unreal Engine 3. So there are some nice visuals. There aren't much polygons to see as this is an indie game but the shadows and ambient particles make up for the visuals giving a great atmosphere to the fantasy world. The music also adds to the atmosphere. The control scheme is really innovative. It uses the symmetry of the gamepad to control the two brothers using the thumbsticks and triggers. You can't find such symmetry on the keyboard. But more important is the feel that it gives you. They is no way to explain this 'feel' but you will certainly understand it by the ending sequence of the game. There are also some cool force feedback effects. The game is short lasting about 4 hours offering very less replayability. But there isn't much to complain about it being short since it was available for as low as 1.49$ on a Steam sale.
The Good :
+ nice little adventure
+ innovative control scheme
+ great atmosphere
+ emotional touch
+ suitable for all ages
The Bad :
- no difficulty or challenge
- short with no replayability
- does not have AAA Hollywood style blockbuster scenes
- not a benchmark tool
Verdict : 86/100

Then there are the power downs, shrooms mode makes you high and it is hard to shoot anything, and elasto mode makes you bounce all over the place. I would definitely recommend it!

*Rise of the Triad -
back in the day was a fun alternative to Doom.  Doom was definitely better but I have fond memories of ROTT.  The multiplayer was fun and I bet it was funner with 11 people.  Doom only allowed 4.  The graphics I'd say might have been better than doom and it just had it's own thing going for it.  Good graphics, good music and sound.  Overall pretty good level design too.  Not too sure about it's replay value though and it's engine limitations are pretty bad, even for it's time.  Basically this is a really advanced WOLF3D engine.  Good arcade shooter and worth a try if money isn't an issue, just remember it's a really old game.  NOW, with that said...
*Blake Stone/Planet Strike -
are a bit different.  They ARE WOLF3D engine games and probably the best ones.  Back in the day I felt Blake Stone was too corny, but now I love that about it.  It's style definitely has charm.  It has a colorful 70's style to it, everyone seems to have sideburns!  Lol.  Great graphics (amusing), awesome sounds and music and gameplay.  I love the variety of enemies.  It's very arcade and old school.  The addition of a good minimap makes all the difference and it's fun to collect the bonuses.  Planet Strike refined all that and added more features.  Hard to critique old games because by now we've seen this all but for what it's worth it is a very well done game(s).

Western Press is a typing game, where you are thrown back into the old west where you fight to come out on top.
In the game you play as a woman who is killing everyone in her path and you this by typing or pressing button combinations.
That's about all I can summarize the game with as it's as simple as it sounds. There's no power ups, nothing, all you do is type and if you're faster than your opponent you win and continue with your journey, you die you go back to the fight and try to win.
The game gets progressively harder as you play through it, but this is rather false, as the game is rather easy, but the last three opponents are incredibly difficult.
Pixel art style for this game, is really really good. The attention to detail in the environments is impressive to say the least, not to mention that you can get community made maps and characters.
The game took me 30 minutes to finish the story mode, but this game has some play value for it's price, like a mode where you have to remember what keys to type and multiplayer which can expand the play value.
The game is rather fun, but it gets bland really fast and I was bored after a few hours of playing it, so I don't imagine grabbing anyone's attention for too long.
In the end, do I recommend Western Press ? Well to be honest it's kind of tough. I enjoyed the game and by no means it's a bad game, but I think it's rather bland to keep it playing after your done with Story and you've tried out multiplayer, so my honest suggestion is to check it out once it's on sale.
Final Rating:
6.5/10
Pros:
+ Great Pixel art style
+Fun.....
Cons:
-....but gets boring fast
-Story Mode too short

Expacting such a high level of FFB - feedback it struck me hard and with a game I loved playing when I only used the Keyboard. All the game can do FFB - wise is rattling in one unchanging manner and make the steering heavy. That's it! Oh dear me, I was so angry because I was so much looking forward to this game and because I'm a real rally fan. I even have an account to follow every event with live tracking and all this stuff.

I was left alone with all my fancy realism games and couldn't play them anymore until I fixed my wheel. (What I didn't because I was so fed up with this stupid sensors hovering and because I already did it three times).

Like: Coming only near a crowd gave you a penalty and respawned you to a full stop.

Something every Rallygame has its problems with, the roadbook:

All in all:
Forget your steeringwheel!!!

This review will focus mostly on the negative sides of the game, it doesn't mean that the game is bad, I just talk about the negative  things more.
I have no idea why do people compare thisto ARMA or Battlefield. This game is totally different than the first Opflash. People should do  some research before purchase instead of blindly buying games then complain about them. This is not an open world or überrealistic  game. It's an arcade shooter just like COD or MOH.The graphics are not the best but they are totally okay. The optimization is not too  good, eats a lot of resources while the visuals are not too satisfying. There is one effect I really loved though - the sun flare. OMG this  game has the most beautiful sun flare I've ever seen! It's a real eye candy, I wish more games would have it. Overall the places are a  bit bland because you are somewhere in Tajikistan. This game was made for consoles anyway so yeah the maps aren't too interesting.  It has some nice lanscapes and nice sky though.
The shooting is really satisfying. It feels good to shoot with the rifles. Yes, only the rifles because there is no use of smg or shotgun.  The reason is simple: there is no close-quarter mission, there are no indoor missions and the enemy is in long range most of the time.  The gadgets are useless too. It takes ages to switch to a grenade, the tripmine has no use at all - the enemy is only approaching from  front most of the time.
You have to choose your class, I played it through with the scout class, you can unlock all kinda cool snipers and scopes. But you  can only attach the nightvision scope to a sniper, so you cant put it to M4 etc.
The story is... well I couldn't care less about it. I did not understand most parts because of all that soldier talk. I had no idea what was  an APC until I googled it. So maybe you would like the story if you are into military talk and all that stuff. The leader of the squad is an  assshole. He talks waaaay too much and the way he talks is very irritating. He is a wannabe-tough guy, really makes you say the n-word. Your sqad is quite weird. They are not too bright so it's recommended to play in coop with at least one human squadmate. They  are cute though. Many times they are rushing to heal you. But they never heal themsleves. So you may find yourself babysitting them.
Giving them orders is useless. The only orders I've used is hold position and follow me. This game is not a tactical one. Doesn't matter  how bad it will look like a tactical game, it's simply not.
The game has some bugs, you will encounter some but for me they were funny most of the time.
Anyway, the game is REALLY fun. After all those negative things I've listed it's a very good game I don't care what people say. I  enjoyed every bit of the game. I've played with a coop partner and it was very awesome. The game lenght was satisfying, the ending  was not.
I really recommend it to all my friends to give it a try. The replayability is high, because you have the chance to max all the classes and  unlock cool weapons and perks. I've played it through as a scout, it was really awesome. If you are looking for a good coop game,  look no further. I enjoyed every minute of it (except mr.assshole's rambling). It's different from most of FPS games because this game is  representing the missions in a more realistic way. I recommend it to everyone who is sick of ww2 nazi killing clichés and want to play a cool FPS in modern setting.
PS: The menu music is incredible.

(Note: I recieved this as an early birthday gift from a friend)
System.Hack is in a very early state, yet the bones of a great game are already present, and the experience of playing it is already very good.
The puzzle and combat mechanics are engaging, and the programming system (which is akin to a spellmaking system in a fantasy game) is very well thought out and has a ton of customizability. A nice touch is that looking down shows a "body" of your character (at least in cyberspace, I haven't bothered looking all the way down in meatspace yet). All in all, this takes the framework of Southwind's earlier Shadowrun Unlimited (a mod for Shadowrun: Dragonfall), focuses it on hacking, and does the job much better.
Despite this, there are a few small gripes. First of all, the lack of music during a run does detract from my engagement during hacking. Some tracker music (and perhaps some industrial music when a trace starts) would be a huge boon to this game's atmosphere in cyberspace. Furthermore, the mouselook is something I wish could be toggled rather than having to hold down the button. The lack of a mouselook toggle key seems like an omission that may be hampering ease of use, since you currently have to hold down the mouse button and drag.
I have heard updates to this game are fairly frequent, and that Southwind is very involved in this project, so these gripes are very minor considering the likelyhood that the underlying issues will be corrected with the next patch.
All in all, this game is a huge reccomendation for anyone who wants to play though gameplay reminiscent of the hacking scene from Johnny Mnemonic, though people who want an action game will be dissapointed by it's ATB combat system, puzzles, and the lack of enemies patrolling each network (Failing to bypass security DOES spawn enemies though).
TL:DR Version: If you want an action RPG with a cyberpunk, netrunning set of trappings, get Black ICE instead... If you want a deep, fullfilling hacking experience that relies on your wits and mental acuity, then get this game. You won't be dissapointed.

Even as an advocate of early access and in-dev titles in the past, I've recently been avoiding them almost entirely. Something about this game just made me curioius and I bought it on a whim after playing a decent amount of other hacking games.
Just keep in mind that early access means the very real possibility of bugs and crashes, unbalanced gameplay, and just the general "unfinished" feel. So you should expect this. That said, the dev on this project is EXTREMELY responsive to feedback and on top of any bugs reported. I have no question that he truly respects the opinions of the fanbase and honestly wants to make his game better. Every time I've posted a bug on the forum, it has been fixed in less than 24 hours!
OK, but what about the actual game?
-There's  a good bit of repitition as you can expect with most hacking games, but in this case you are navigating systems in an FPS style, rather than typing into a console. That may turn off a lot of people right away as "totally not hacking".
-An RPG style upgrade system lets you get better at the things you want to focus on. If you like the combat, fighting more IC's will level you up. If you prefer to break passwords and spoof user accounts, your stealth rating will increase. Not an entirely new concept, but in a hacking game it hasn't been greatly explored so far.
-You have a bit of work to start understanding how the gameplay goes, and it can be frustrating and confusing. My advice is to read all the tutorial screens and absorb the most relevant info at the time. You can refer back anytime for whatever starts to confuse you.
- TL;DR version -
What this boils down to is just so;
-If you want to play a hacking game that isn't like most hacking games then definitely check it out.
-If the screenshots interest you and you aren't afraid of learning how to play a game while playing it, download it.
-If you want to support Indie devs who are here to make the best game they can, and not take your money and run, buy it.
BUT,
-If you don't like the idea of early access and want to play a finished game, don't buy it.
-If you're looking for the next Uplink, Hacknet, [your fav hack game here], dont't buy it.

I bought this game to support the original author of one of my favorite mods for Shadowrun Returns, but I found myself thoroughly enjoying >//:System.Hack on its own merits.  The gameplay just has a great “flow” to it and managed to be great fun even during my learning curve when all I knew was to run around and interact with random nodes, and even after I figured out what I was supposed to be doing it managed to keep that "fun factor".
However, probably one of the best features of >//:System.Hack is “Oracle” which allows you to code your own hacking programs, it’s powerful, extremely flexible, and just “feels” perfect for the setting.
Now, as an Early Release, the game still has a few bugs a couple of minor quibbles here and there, but I’ve yet to run across anything that was Gamebreaking or managed to dent my enjoyment of slicing through systems like a ghost or smashing ICE into oblivion.  The fact that the dev is extremely responsive to both bug reports and feature requests is a REALLY nice change from the usual as well.
Overall this game really is a gem and I’d recommend it whole heartily to anyone that are fans of the cyberpunk genre as well as hacking games in general.

To start off, Im recommending people to LOOK at the game, and not as much as, this is a fantastic game!!
Really, this game is huge, vast, and will let you have hundreds of hours of playing time....trying to figure it out. While it is a very good MMORPG, it has its ups and downs. Let me name the ups and downs of the game and then you'll see the issue's.
Ups: Great graphics, nice world, lots of towns all different and unique in some way. Crafting, class's, Ive seen some players look like knights, on a horseback. really feels like a Medieval England world. Sadly no castle's round Bree. Chatting is nice. Filter blocks bad stuff while it lets good stuff through. The looting system is one-of-a-kind, PvP, PvE, and you can even try out the Monster Play for a change of pace. The PvP is nice, and the PvE is also gonna be a critical role as you progress.
If your the type that enjoys getting online, making online friends, joining groups, battling monsters, players, exploring different landscapes, and socializing, your probably thinking, whats the issue's? This sounds FANTASTIC!! Well let me now show you the downs of the game.
Downs: Too much lag. Especially going into the towns. And towns are where your gonna buy n sell, meet the characters to progress through the story, and mail letters to players. Ive uninstalled two games to see if it would help. It helped, but still a little laggy. Next, the class videos, where it shows what each class is like, is SOO laggy, and usually in some battle/land area where your not gonna be for a long time. Plus it dont show you what weapons you can and cant have. So, you choose a class that sounds good. You complete the tutorial, and are ready to equip that shield you got awhile back. Oh wait, you cant cause its not available for your class. Wouldv'e been nice to know that ahead of time. And weapons aint the only thing lacking instructions. You get some dye to change your armour's colors. You can spend real money for extra amounts. Oh wait, it never said how to use it exactly. But they'll gladly let you spend money on it. How bout a horse? It says visit some guy in Bree-land for a starter horse. But wait! Whats this? No instructions where to find this random guy in a 10+ mile land? And without a horse, it takes ALOT LONGER to get anywhere. Oh and real money is needed to buy a riding trait. Take a LONG time to earn the points to buy the trait. Oh and some lands cost money to unlock.
Ive found an active server on my fourth try. Its called Gladden. An active server will be important. According to some players I met in a kinship, they say level 40-50 is where your gonna have to spend some money to progress. I cant say thats true for certain however. By now, I'd say its safe to say, "free to play" needs a fine print saying "until a certain point" though it still leaves alot to run around and see...until it gets boring. My final overall thought: look at game, find an active server(Gladden) and spend hundreds of hours trying to figure it out. If you figure it out, and got money, you have hundreds of hours to look forward to. If not, hundreds of hours trying to figure it out down the drain. Oh and dont get discouraged when the usual "new player bug" pops up 45 seconds into the game. Just relog. To me, feels like alot of potential going down the drain.
REVIEW UPDATE: It seems LOTRO has a rather dedicated and very loyal following of players, judging by the other reviews. However, when they say it still has an "active community" they either mean seeing no new players, every once and awhile some chat through the world chat box, seeing 2 players on through the week, with one of the 2 being AFK(Away From Keyboard) and then seeing a "crowd" of 4-7 over the weekend, means "active to them. It  dont sound exactly "active" to me. Though on Gladden I have seen lots of new players, and lots of chat through the world chat. Recently, however, even Gladden was rather player-less, but world chat filled. Some places even on Gladden are quiet as a grave. Unless of course they've all gone to another, far-off region where new players needing help wont get to. Or they are all sitting on the LOTRO official website on there forums/community or something like that. I cant say for sure. The game is "ancient" by MMO standards, and even the movies have been out awhile, with one last final movie to look forward to. Reason I even out the "thumbs up" sign was in the hope maybe it'd encourage new players to help clarify the confusion this game creates within itself.

Practically all the negative reviews on this game are about the control scheme using the arrow keys instead of the WASD.
Well sorry, but old games didn't use WASD. The only reason WASD was invented is to make it easier to use the mouse. And back when these games were made, people didn't use mice to play games. These games were not designed to be used with a mouse.
So be warned before you buy.
You can use a mouse on Rise of the Triad. But it's not ideal.
It's never going to be ideal.. no matter how much you wish somebody would spend the time to make it possible for a mouse to be ideal when playing these games....no matter how much you fiddle with the controls....
They were simply just never designed with mice in mind.
So either get used to the old way of the FPS, or suffer.
People like myself who grew up through this evolution shouldn't have much of a problem going back.

Arrow Keys to move, Control key to shoot, alt to strafe, hold shift to run. That's basically all you need to know other than space to open doors.

Western Press is a one-on-one duel where the faster button-presser shoots the slower. There is literally nothing more to it than that. You and one other player are shown ten random keys, and whoever presses them first wins. Rinse and repeat.
One of the blurbs on the store page compares it to Divekick, in that it's a simplified concept taken to the extreme. I guess that's accurate, but what makes divekick interesting is how even in that simplified environment, there's still a great deal of tactics. Baiting, positioning, mindgames; these are all implicit in Divekick, even though there's no buttons for them. WP has no such depth; you are solely tested on your ability to hit the buttons as fast as you can.
Obviously, online multiplayer for this is completely dead, so it's a friends-only affair. And frankly, I'd be a little embarassed to waste my friends' time with this, when there are so many actually good local multiplayer games out there.
All that said, Western Press has great atmosphere. The voice acting, art, and character designs are all well done. If the key-pressing game was just one of, say, six or seven different minigames that were in a rotation, this would be worth the purchase. Unfortunately, all of that is so much wasted effort in a game that takes all of 5 minutes to see everything worth seeing.

I was so, so sceptictal about buying this game after feeling this would be a really poor representation of rallying. I've been a huge fan of the WRC for years and have been going to Wales every year since I was 15. After playing DiRT Rally I was convinced that nothing could surpass the quality and simulation from Codemasters' finest creation. WRC 6 obviously comes nowhere close to DiRT Rally. However, I can't say that Kylotonn Racing Games have made a bad game.
When I bought this I had the mind-set of "this isn't a rally sim. It's an arcade game for everyone from novices to experienced gamers." When I adopted this mind-set my perception of the game totally changed. The handling model isn't bad once you're used to it and the stages are far more satisfying to run than in previous titles.  The sounds aren't like those from WRC 5 nor are the weathering effects to cars. They are actually good (apart from the co-driver who still lacks human emotion-the pace-notes are good though) and shows they have taken the time improve aspects of the game. It even has local co-op which further reinforces it's position as an arcade game.
There aren't tonnes of tracks but there are ones from each of the locations on the WRC calendar, which is nice. The cars aren't all copy and paste replicas of one another either and it actually feels like a step up going from WRC 2 to WRC class.  I'll re-iterate- this ISN'T a rally sim. Approach this game like it is one and you'll ♥♥♥♥ing hate it, but approach it as a game you can pick up and play for a few hours, and you'll see WRC 6 in an entirely different light.
I'll finish up and say no, don't buy this at full price; by no means is this worth £34.99 not when DiRT 3 and other such titles are cheaper. If it's on sale though (steam or otherwise) grab it. If you're an avid rally fan looking for a simple time-killer, go for WRC 6.
FYI: I've had this on PS4 for a while so don't think my opinion is invalid from the Steam game time :)

This is one game that begs for DLC. Only three classes? You've got to be kidding me. That said, onto the good points. This is like Diablo 2, with a few good ideas tacked on, and placed in a fully 3D world. You'll have to forgive the DIablo comparisons, but this game warrants them: it was made by several ex-Diablo Blizzard crew members, and the polish shows. This is about the most comprehensively fun aRPG I have played since the release of D2. Do I like it better than Grim Dawn? Hell yes. Do I like it better than Path of Exile? Well, kinda. Yes, but the price point on Path sells it better; though in my mind, this is a more polished product. Do I like it better than D2? It follows in the same footsteps, so it is a more modern, updated version at its heart.
I must at least add that for the price tag, it is the most fun "Diablo-like" I have played in about 5+ years, and could easily handwrestle the latest Blizzard release, Diablo 3 if it had tacked on more DLC. The endgame content on this, unfortunately, shortened my journey somewhat. The story is miles above the first Torchlight, and feel more coherent. Here, I feel a sense of *fighting* baddies, making my journey more meaningful. In the last game, everything seemed like an excuse to slay everything around me. This game  reverses the flow, putting plot first, and then allows the killing to begin in sequence, as the game world opens up. No more swimming for a portal that leads into an ever-downward dungeon. Here, there are separate areas, and new ideas, including some not present in D3, and certainly a better skill system than the latter. The first game was a nice time-waster. This one ties that problem up with a new plot, and several better ideas.
I still think there should be DLC packs.
This game calls for at least 3 more classes, to add online variety, and inspire players to frequent it more often. The narrative is well-done. The gameplay has a few twists on par with D3's treasure goblins. Visuals and art, check: graphics are top-notch. Audio is sufficient, nothing lacking, plenty of variety, no critical mistakes. Everything has an emphatic and crisp thump to it, and objects and fighting have loud *clangs,* and sound realistic, as well as sufficiently solid. Something Path of Exile lacks, I'm afraid. Collision detection is not finicky, like the latter, either. If anything, the only near miss is that emphatic lack of end-game content, along with replay value; easy levelling up to cap; and the few, uninspiring classes that would have been fixed with a shiny bit of DLC.
At the time of release, this would have been a 9.5/10. At this point, I feel safer giving it an 8/10, as it is fun, polished, and has variety. Time will tell whether Torchlight supports an online community, and is willing to expand open its gameplay to more modes and challenges. Not in this release, I'm afraid. One thing is for certain: I will be first in line waiting for Torchlight 3. Let's hope for future news! Cheers. :D

Since this game is early acccess, the review is about its current state. (However, so far the game got better and better with each new update!!)
When my characterI first logged into the net of >//:System.Hack I was just amazed how well this cyberspace worked for me. The game is also a lot of fun, accessing the systems and performing various tasks like cracking the access codes to a node via a real well-made and fun mini-game and 1:1 battles vs different intrusion countermeasure (IC) codes ranging from simple block programs to pretty difficult battle codes. So far I did only see a fraction of the IC variants, so I am eager to explore more of the net.
The game also has player stats in virtual combat and stealth, cryptology and programming. The latter is fun because it allows the player to create new programs for the character. For this an quite amazing script-like language is already in place.
The player-base is very active and seeing the development of the game first hand is a quite welcome experience. The developers are in close contact with the community and listen to the bug reports and suggestions. When writing this review I own this game less than a week, but there have already been a number of updates.
I fully recommend the game to anyone in love with cyberpunk/sci-fi hacking games and anyone who always wanted to see the matrix in first person.
