I loved it! It took me about 45 hours to get through, though I do tend to do a lot of quick-save/quick-load as I am testing out different strategies (which is part of the fun of this game). I played a non-lethal campaign, I'm glad there were ways of dealing with every situation (including boss encounters) in this way, whether through non-lethal weapons or through being clever in the environment or by manipulating other characters to get the outcome you want.
I miss the globe-trotting of the previous games, but I like revisiting Prague multiple times, seeing how it changes, the people change, and to continue exploring with all the new abilities I've picked up. I wish it felt like the changes were more impactful, as in Dragon Age 2 (which I know was divisive for also having only one main location), which you got to see develop over a decade.
I never felt the need to use any consumable items, so I don't have an opinion on the microtransactions. In no way do I feel that the developer weakened the game in order to force players to use these. They're there for the people who want to get through it faster or play with the abilities and weapons sooner than you would get to during normal gameplay.

This is more like a review for Mankind Divided and Human Revolution comparision.
Starting with the story. A lot more side quests can be found compared to HR, more than double the amount and they're longer and more interesting than those in the previous game, I've probably spent more time in side quests than the main missions. Some are pretty hidden and worth looking out for and mostly they're all great. HR side quests sucked compared to MD.
Main story is good enough. People complain about the game being short compared to HR probably because the travelling parts in HR that helped it feel bigger and fresh and gives you a feel of the international scale of conspiracy.  Compared to being in Prague 80% of the game in MD. You've travelled more as a head of security of biotech company than as a counter terrorism agent with universal jurisdiction. The main story in MD is definitely shorter yes, compared to HR but combined with side quests I've put 50hrs in MD and 3hrs in the first DLC compared to 30hrs in HR. The disappointing part of the story in MD is the ending. The game introduced many characters yet didn't give much time for some of them, probably due to planned sequels.

For the gameplay. Stun gun and tranq got me through the game. There aren't many weapons similarly to HR, difference is varied ammo types helps customizes the weapon. Ammo is abundant compared to HR, I've had a problem in late game HR I couldn't find any 10mm ammo for my maxed modded 10mm pistol while in MD I've finished the game with +600 rounds. Augs are similar, now with more tech trees and an addition of experimental super advanced augs. Remote hacking is a must and doesnt use any energy.
For energy, I like biocells, they take less space and gives decent energy.
While the game is defienetly designed towards stealth it adds more option for going gunblazing now.
Bossfights or rather lack of bossfights isn't that bad compared to most bossfights in HR that sucked. I've only enjoyed 1 bossfight in HR. At least, it has a better end boss than HR.
Both games have great level design. There are many options to go in and out. Paladise Bank being the most level I've had fun with making up routes. Prague is filled with hidden stuff some are hard to get to and exploring is way better in this game.
For the sound; still fantastic and chill. Worth going rogue just for the combat track.
One thing worth noting, I've absolutely despised the UI in HR. Getting around the inventory alone was pain. Glad they fixed that in MD.
I'd give both games 8.5/10. MD made it up for the story with great sidequests and and more polished gameplay.

Now, Eidos has really gone out of their way to give much more freedom in how to appraoch situations, from a better climbing mechanic, to more ventes, more hacking options, and of course an insane amount of Aug toys to play with if you want to just rip through some folk.
Highly recommended, as this feels like an appropriate last step to the Deus Ex 1 reboot we all know is coming.

I liked it. I was too poor back in the day to have anything more than the shareware version of ROTT so this'll give me a chance to delve deeper into that title that I really loved. It's amazing how well it holds up today, once you change the control scheme to something more modern. (which is doable, though I had to substitute middle and right mouse buttons for look up and look down, which thankfully is seldom needed) ROTT has just about everything I like in a classic FPS: The fast movement speed, the exploration, the waves of mooks you get to mow down in droves with your superhuman prowess. But what I also enjoyed is the complete lack of realism, and the platforming which, unlike in the 2013 remake, you could more or less opt out of the more difficult platforming sections which only provided rewards like 3-ups. (I'm a bit unusual in that I like the platforming) I look forward to completing the game and subsequently getting destroyed by Extreme ROTT.
One thing ROTT really has going for it is personality. There are so many little easter eggs to find, like the end-stage music when you finish a level in Dog Mode, the murderous game quit sequences, the ludicrous gibs, and so much more. You can tell the developers weren't making shovelware here, they made something that they can proudly affix their names onto.
Blake Stone is a bit iffy at the moment. It was never on my radar in the 90's. Even though I grew up with the awkward Wolfenstein controls which were designed to be keyboard only, it will take time to reacquaint myself with those. Unlike ROTT, it's not possible to rig a typical modern keyboard and mouse FPS control scheme.
It's not the game's fault at all -- it was the standard for everything, including DOOM, at the time. I do want to give it a shot, as it seems to have more complex objectives than the run-and-gun style of FPS that Wolfenstein was. It'll just take me time to prepare...I haven't used that control scheme since Quake in the late 90's, which I subsequently abandoned after getting annihilated by keyboard-mouse players. FPS controls aren't like a certain plumber whose controls have remained steady, with new moves merely added onto existing controls since the 80's. This difference is mainly due to the lack of mouse driver standardization back in the early 90's -- not to mention many people didn't even have a mouse back then. Trackballs were also strongly competing with the modern mouse in the early 90's, which justified the fact that pushing your mouse up moves your character forward. It wasn't until the late 90's and early 00's that FPS controls settled into what they are today.

I received this game as part of a friend's humble bundle; he didn't want the game, so I took it.
I tried the game with my Xbox360 controller; I couldn't make it past level 2, the easiest opponent. I then tried the game with my keyboard and cleared the whole singleplayer mode in 16 minutes. It was not easy by any means, but I'm far more familiar with a keyboard than I am the button layout of an Xbox 360 controller.
This game provides exactly what you'd expect; you're to input a set of button combinations as quickly as possible, and the person who does it the fastest wins the round. If you input a wrong button, you will be given a time penalty, so you might finish first but lose the round because you made too many mistakes.
There are two game modes; the speed one (which I described in the above paragraph) and memory mode. In memory mode, you're slowly shown a set of buttons to press, one after another, and you're to press them in that order. It starts with 4, but increases each round until someone makes too many mistakes. It's very reminiscent of the Clefairy Memory game from Pokemon Stadium on the Nintendo 64.
Before each round, the characters taunt eachother; this, as well as all cutscenes, can be skipped of your own volition. I personally didn't care for much of their pre-duel blabbering. There are a lot of characters to unlock and choose from, and the Steam workshop allows you to create your own character.
In conclusion, I personally feel very neutral about this game, but I fail to see any poor features or otherwise dislikeable things about this game. As such, if the game's synopsis intrigues you, then you'll like what you get.

This is an excellent puzzle platformer with a bit of light combat thrown in.
The story is told in short failtale verses and the occasional simple cutscenes between levels.
The controls handle nicely and are fairly easy to pick up as the game does a good job of introducing each skill as the player unlocks them through defeating monsters and gathering collectables.
Multiplayer is also handled wonderfully and is supported in both online and local for up to 3 players, with the option of each player either sharing the 3 heros or having their own set of heros to switch between freely.
However, by far the most impressive part of this game is the presentation of the levels. Each level (or chapter) of the game is absolutely beautiful, every part of the environment feels completely organic and looks as if it was pulled right out of a fairytale. Each level is also packed with multiple puzzles, many of which are obstacles needed to be solved in order to advance while others are simply to hide experiance items and unlockables.
The difficulty isn't too hard for the most part, but some of the puzzles can take a bit of luck to work properly, while others can be solved in a multitude of ways. This can be made easier depending on which of the heros is leveled up an which of their skills are unlocked first.
The Wizard mainly for creating boxes and platforms, moving heavy objects and solving puzzles.
The Knight is primarily for combat and protecting the others from either enemies or environmental hazards.
The Theif is easily the most mobile and focused on platforming with her grappling hook, but can also assist in combat with her bow.
If you're even slightly interested in platformers I would highly recommend this game.
My only suggestion is that while the mouse and keyboard controls work well enough, I would recommend using a controller to play as the game felt more natural to be played with one and thus was much more enjoyable once I plugged it in.

Do you enjoy retro 80s dystopian dark/laser/synthpop-filled themes?  Did you enjoy movies like Blade Runner and Running Man?  Do you enjoy first person shooters that don't take themselves too seriously?  Do you want a cheap, short game?
If you answered at least "maybe" to all of these, this intentionally cheesy game is for you!
You must install UbiSoft's Uplay and sign up for an account to play this game.  There are steam cards, but only Uplay achievements.
The best thing about this game is the Far Cry 3 engine (original game not needed to purchase).  Other than that, the production values scream indie flick, so don't expect great cut scenes, an epic plot arc, or sensible voice acting.  As it turns out, I didn't even like Far Cry 2 and skipped 3 (most sandbox games get fairly tedious to me).  But this game is just long enough to require a few sittings and not too long that playing for completionist (yes it has optional collectables) takes more than 14 hours.
The worst thing about this game is there are a couple early on escort missions.  Once you make it to the open-world, they are over with.
The game is not balanced at all.  Your pistol is just about worthless, but showing up with a gun mounted on a jeep will destroy most things.  I switched to "easy" early on because I got frustrated with swarms before I upgraded my arsenal, and I kind of regret that.  There are stealth opportunities and an almost worthless "predator vision".
Falling Damage doesn't exist.
Sprinting, when combined with bastion fast travel, is generally faster than trying to get a vehicle up a cliffside.
You can only hold four weapons at a time, from a larger pool.
Jumping on enemies is more reliable for an insta-mellee kill than waiting for the "F" key popup.
Just use the buy all ammo needed option every time; it's a discount from buying individually.
I found no need for blood dragon hearts in the second half of the game.  They max out at 99 anyway.
You can only hold 3 medkits at a time, but there is still a partial heal when you run out.
Healing and looting were aggravatingly long animations.
For the completionist:
You can earn all achievements on easy.
Capturing every bastion should be done relatively early on just for the levels and money.  If you do that, and stop for a dragon kill every so often, you should have no problem getting to max level and getting the 25 dragon kill achievement.
Collecting animal kills is easy; just know that turtles are a specific side mission.
There is an in-game unlock that acts like a map for each quadrant's collectibles.
Head shots of every enemy is an achievement, but wouldn't unlock for me (no UbiSoft awards for that one so no foul).
Once I started taking down bastions, I always had enough $ for ammo, yet somehow I still finished the game without enough money to get every weapon upgrade.
You can continue to play the game and go after collectibles/upgrades after the final plot scene.
Value $7

What can I say?
I love the Lotr series, and that was the main reason I decided to download this game.
At first I was put off by the turbine point system, but when I realised that points could literally be earned, I decided to make it a personal 'goal' as such to complete as much as I could to expand my way through the game. It may feel daunting and like a grind fest but you get a feeling of accomplishment when you earn your way through a game. I've not come across a real issue with pay 2 win gear since there really isn't pay to win gear (especially since if there was you would simply need to earn the points to gain whatever is needed).
Imagine WoW. It plays very similar to that in terms of questing and PvE (Right click and hotkey).
You have a few classes and 4 races to choose from, which is relatively extensive. Choose your hair, eyes, nose, lips etc, class and race, each race has certain limitations to classes (as expected) but not as limited as one might think. Once you've chosen those, you can choose where you're from, which each come with certain changes to hair colour (unless you want to change is again).
Once you hit level 10 you can do monster play, which as you could imagine, lets you play as one of the monsters from the lotr series, initially you can only choose one to play as, but the turbine system allows you to play as more if you buy them.
Work your way through the universe of lotr and see the world in your own perspective!
Definitely reccomended to anyone who liked the lotr series.
Gameplay: 10/10
Character creation: 8/10 could be a little more in depth but a very sound system.
Quest system: Pretty good, the usual really, talk to... or kill.... or gather...etc.
Lore: Friggin' 11/10. Exceptional since it practically throws you into the mix of the lotr series, witness Gandalf stop Balrog in a dream, and be told that the fate of the free people will rest on your shoulders.
Point system:5/10. Only ranked so low since it can feel like a drag, unless you're one of these grind fanatics that absolutely LOVE grinding in games. Completing deeds will reward you with turbine points, but not a vast amount, usually about 5-15 tp each time. An upside is that most deeds can be completed twice but with an added end value (example: slay 30 orcs > deed completed > 5 tp gained and title bestowed > slay 60 orcs > 10 tp added) and considering you get certain deeds each time you enter a new area, like Bree-land to the Shire, your deeds will change to the area specific deeds allowing you to gain more tp.
I think I've covered everything, and gone on long enough.

Interesting, catching, funny and kind of comfortable game with great graphics and really nice community. If you want to spend some time living your Tolkien dreams, talking to awesome people, questing and deeding and crafting and roleplaying, this is just the game for you.
Main towns and cities are well-arranged (no big chance to get lost, like I did many times trying to play Dungeons and Dragons), there's efficient navigation, quest tracking system and game guide, smooth and sensitive movement control (I don't get why it's so hard to turn in World of Warcraft or Age of Wulin, but perhaps it's my PC's fault), skill queue, automatic movement towards target (e.g. an ore deposit or a vendor) by right-clicking it and it's easy to get around an object in your path without turning (you just kind of slip around, hardly ever get stuck). Game has a honed race and class system, you can chose from basic to advanced difficulty classes and from 3 trait trees focusing on different skills and have real fun figuring out how to fight best. You can buy your own house, have fun with decorating it, store stuff in the chest (purchaseable space), exhibit your trophies. Crafting is easy and various, crafted items are usually far better than any you can buy (except the stock of the Auction House, where you can put something for sale yourself if you have free slots - VIPs get 30, Premium 5). There are many events where you can win great prizes, you can gain reputation with many societies and get privileges and awesome unique items, you can even chose to play the bad guys (Creeps) and create an orc or warg or spider and fight PvP against the Free Peoples (Freeps) at level 85. In the LOTRO Store you can buy whatever you like for real money, there's a great choice of buffs, additional slots (trait slots, inventory bags, chatacter slots,..), steeds, outfits, quests packs and more. It's not even necessary to use real money - you can earn Turbine points used in the Store by finishing deeds (it's slow, but hey - who gives you something for free these days?).
When you're lost, you can always turn to the LOTRO-Wiki, there's usually everything you need to complete any quest or deed, even when you feel it's impossible to figure one out. And if not Wiki, you can get some answers from other players on the Advice chat channel. LOTRO's community is one of the kindest, most generous and most obliging in the gaming world.
It's kind of comfortable to play this game, it's thrilling, sometimes scary, often funny and not always trivial. You don't have to quest and level, you can just relax and roleplay or craft or hunt materials, money and reputation. You can freely use the chat to meet great new people, join kinships and fellowships and have plenty of fun socializing. And beware - it's very addictive ;).

Graphics are dated, there's no getting around that, but that can be a pro and a con as older/weaker systems shouldn't have a lot of problem running this game on low settings, but it can leave a something to be desired with those that are looking for better looking graphics on higher end systems. The game's storyline is first rate however and there is a lot to do within Lotro's many zones. As with most MMO's getting into a quality/active Kin (guild) adds a lot of dimension to the game. Like anything else sometimes it takes doing some extensive homework and time to find both a Kin and a server to your liking, but I believe it's time well spent.
Lotro's quality control standards are lax in areas that developer's don't seem to feel are as important as far as the overall scope of the game, for example player housing and the way furniture fits and can be adjusted as well as surfaces and color variety. It's been a couple of years since some bugs and problems have been widely reporteded in Lotro forums and direct contact with Lotro GM's in those regards with no update fixes in sight. The quality of a game is in the details as much as anything else including fixing minor bugs in a timely manner.
On the plus side the game is very flexible for a variety of player budgets, anywhere from free to play to spending hundreds of dollars on subscription, expansions, perks, and Turbine Points (Lotro's in game currency). In theory you can over a long period of time acquire many of the above mentioned items except for subscription by saving Turbine Points from deeds earned playing the game on different characters in free to play. From a practical standpoint if you don't have either the time or a lot of money to acquire many of above mentioned you can find some compromises by both earning deeds for Turbine Points and being patient and waiting for sales (and there are some good ones) through the Lotro Store and/or Steam, particularly the expansions. A subscription is always gonna cost real money, but the 3, 6, and 12 months subscriptions through the Lotro store amounts to $10 a month which is cheaper then most other MMO game subscriptions for the same amount of time, not to mention there are occasional sales on subscription time on top of that.
If you come from a game like WoW, keep in mind this is more of a niche market and the amount of player support in and outside the game is far less then WoW's. So there aren't many dedicated websites in support of the game that are regularly updated. Be prepared to fly by the seat of your pants in trying to update to the latest/best gear for your class or finding an online spreadsheet to help you number crunch your dps, heals, etc, but then again maybe sometimes it's more fun to leave a little guesswork in the game.
Overall I'd rate Lotro 6 out of 10 points. I'd recommend it for the casual and/or budget player that wants a good game storyline with some immersion, but doesn't have high expectations compared to other MMO's like WoW or SWTOR in regards to graphics, quality control standards and player support.

This game could have been the kind of thing that I fell in love with. I love Sci-Fi, and I also think that one of the important goals of sci-fi is to explore the societal implications of new science, how it affects us and our interactions with others and our surroundings. I also love meaningful (As in, not cookie cutter NPC, procedural generated same-ness, etc etc) exploration, exploring stories of people and their relationships, or histories of a race or of a thing, or exploring a deep mechanic of gameplay, or small secrets that change how I see something, or even beautiful or haunting vistas.
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a game about exploration more than anything else (Unless you sprint from one objective to another I guess). You spend most of the game finding interesting things in random corners, exploring routes around obstacles, and being a vouyeristic cat burglar that steals a couple token credits (but leaves all the expensive valuables of course, we apparently do this for the thrill of it rather than the income) then reads people's emails, diaries, story rough drafts, text messages, etc. With people's personal data sometimes you find connections between people, you might one day break into the apartment of an addict, then later break into his dealer's house, and find two perspectives and two hidden agendas. Or you might see many people talking about a particular police shooting, and learn from many angles and connect dots that no one else in the game could connect. The most rewarding and thrilling thing in the whole game is to step into these people's lives, hacking their apartment AI to recognize you as the owner, impersonating them in a text message exchange with someone else.
It sounds like something I would love. But... meh. Honestly, the world is just not that interesting. Barring some augments, the technology is not any more advanced than the technology that we use today where it matters (People still live their lives the same way, in the same houses, cars, guns, cell phones, computers, societal structures, etc etc).
The writers are decent enough, but they cannot pull off the characters or the stories or the people as good as other video games have done in the past. So they cannot really pull off the voyeur glimpse into people's lives that they try to do in a way that engages you long term. Nor can they pull off the main themes of the game nor the story if I remember to think about that small aspect :)
The rest of the game is all sort of bland. Combat is bland (you can choose to go lethal or non-lethal, but neither matters for plot or character reasons, and both are identical in function and appearance so really there is no choice), and the "unique twist" of augments to combat only makes it worse. The energy function in this game is what kills the combat and makes it mediocre. For 90% of the game it is a small pool that takes a while to regenerate and can only power anything for a couple seconds or a single boost. So rather than make combat interesting, fun, or new, augments and their energy use kills pacing and makes the game take longer as you wait for a recharge.
That said, two of the augments are actually excellent and add a ton to gameplay. Smart Vision often prevents exploration from becoming frustrating (Which is necessary, since the game has the most god-awful map menu and interface that you have ever seen), and Remote Hacking is a great way to organically open up more options for players (Which also becomes necessary, because all TV's play the same story on repeat on a very loud volume, and you cannot reach them all in order to turn them off).
All in all, its a game that is interesting to start playing, but not interesting enough to bother finishing. I give it a meh/10.

DE:MD was a great experience for someone that was blown away by the original DE back in the day. It's not nearly as groundbreaking as the original, but it still offers up some of those freedoms that the original gave us. Dialogue options were not the most varied, but I didn't push too hard for that. Routes to take in areas is what I enjoyed the most. I loved finding flanking routes, knocking enemies out if I could, or taking them out with a suppressed pistol if I needed. I really enjoyed thinning out their forces as much as I could before getting spotted and then going guns blazing. The combat in MD could be a tad more refined, it just felt stiff, just like the movement of running and jumping felt stiff (not nearly as bad as the talking animations but this series has never been known for that). I never bothered with the overclocking abilities. I never used any combat ability that required energy, I was all about stealth and shooting (without ever using the actual cloak). Hacking is the same that was seen in DE:HR and that's fine with me since I loved it. It's fun plotting your way through the nodes and all that, and then the risk versus reward of trying to get those extra goodies before time runs out.
My biggest and only real complaint is with the end. Without spoiling much, one of the boss fights towards the end felt so forced on me. I don't know if my actions led me to it, but it didn't seem like I could have done anything differently that would have let me approach the fight with this boss any differently. Not that I would as, like I said, I loved going in guns blazing. My issue with this one though was that the fighting began directly after a cutscene, so I had no way of stealthing around, hacking the turrets to fight for me, setting traps, or anything like that. To make matters worse, this boss was a crazy powerfull bullet sponge. I cruised through the game up till that point, but this boss killed me four or five times before I just decided to go all out and spam all of my frag grenades, and just fire all of my guns and ignoring any sense of ammo conservation. I finally beat the boss after that, but it just felt so out of place based on all of my engagements up untill that point. Other than that, the game was fun and I got a great deal of playtime out of it.
4/5

From the very beginning (where you start at the apartment), I started out with my augs glitched. By doing so I did a couple of side missions and some that I was not aware of where I picked up vault cards, key story items, places that might have been part of a sided mission for the Dvali, went into a part of town that was Dvali territory and robbed someone named Otar whose vault had some Tai Yong Medical Manufactured Neuroplasticity thing and picked up 8 augments added up to about 18 after I finally finished Koller's. Never met any of the Dvali or got into conversation with them, finished off all the story mission including exploiting the glitch for story missions for Stanek and Versalife vault (look it up on youtube). By doing most of everything (money gaining tips for dummies new to Deus Ex, sell all weapons you find individually, do not collect them all at the same time, they become ammo lol) and going on curiosity runs around everywhere to do everything, I ended up at about roughly 50 praxis points and a little over 100000 + (I also had about 30 neuropozyn vials that I did not sell, each worth 1000 so about 30000 more and could have made a bit more if I actually decided to screw over Gallois for Entity for all the guns he had in the store). Pros
-You like Human Revolution and enjoyed it for exploration, Prague and the Utelek complex will not disappoint
-The simple fact that you do not have to fix yourself up at the beginning to actually finish side missions.
-Conversations that Jenson has with people is always entertaining. Amazing job again Elias Toufexis
-Tars <-----If there was a man that you wanted to get the most annoyed look from as you sell back the inventory they already owned. HE IS ALL YOU NEED. Props to whoever plays Tars, I exploited so much money by selling him guns that I got from all over town.

You can hack cars, ladders, windows, robots, cameras, electrochromic glass switches (<---thank you for adding this), bombs, laser grids and so much more.
-The new augs are awesome, I enjoyed mostly the remote hacking and the Icarus Dash as those two were my main augments that I used most of the game.
Cons
-After I was done, the game felt a bit short and was sad that I could not go back to the Utelek complex (should have stolen all the guns Gallois had)
-Lack of better guns and mods: Now understand, I loved the Devastator Shotgun, helped me kill off Marchenko real fast but I now feel that the previous game did guns a lot better. Target Seeking System for my combat rifle was the best thing ever, The Sabre Direct Energy Rifle (Laser rifle for short) was enjoyable since I can kill people through walls. I feel that there should have been more mods and better guns in this game.
-Decisions Decisions Decisions : The fact that I needed to choose one mission over the other just felt terrible. In terms of the side mission The Golden Ticket I was fine with but I did not like that with the main mission for Stanek and Versalife vault. I tried to find a way to do both without the glitch but from what I found, there was no way.
- Sarif’s voice actor- This is a minor one but I will put it down here regardless. He is not voiced by Stephen Shellen from HR and I really wanted to hear him again. Let’s hope Pritchard kept his in the upcoming DLC. But I will still give some credit here, I am sure the aftermath of losing his company might change the way he would speak so a bit of props to the new voice actor on showing Sarif’s attitude post loss-off-almost-everything.
-DLC stories- They add nothing to the game. There is no point to them. At least the missing link was properly integrated into the previous game. These DLC just do not belong.
-CASIE aug was useless where it was really needed: Nomad Stanek was hiding something and that was a Keycard, I would have instantly given this a positive rating if the devs were smart enough for adding the CASIE aug activation during the first Nomad Stanek conversation so that we can get the church keycard and not do mission 12.
-Story items that were in POIs that never started any mission or I am not even sure they are relevant.
All in all, I invested a total of about 60 hours to beat this game on "Give Me Deus Ex" and another 60 hours on “I Never Asked For this” Difficulty”.

Years ago, people made games that were unapologetically stupid, crass, violent and never, ever serious.  ROTT is everything you could ever want in a video game, and more, though the shooters of today may have you believe otherwise.  Run around, shoot stuff, maybe turn into a dog, sometimes God, and one time a bouncy ball person.  It's still one of the best shooters out there and you owe it to yourself to play it.
Blake Stone is also quite good, think Wolf 3D but with aliens, and scientists you can hold up for money, and lasers.  It's admittedly a bit hard going back to after all these years, but it's (and ROTT too) just as fun as I remember it.  Both games are bundled with their expansions/sequels, so that's great if you never got a chance to play them.  They're also playable right out of the gate, widescreen and all, with none of the tweaking needed for some of the other DOSBox versions you may find.
Complaints?  It's DOSBox so the Steam overlay doesn't work correctly with it, other than that, some annoyances like the lack of an autosave and mouselook retain, but they're so insignificant they barely merit a mention.

These Blake Stone games are cool stuff if you wanna see where first-person shooters were between Wolfenstein and Doom (in particular shortly after Wolfenstein, since this uses the same engine while managing to look a bit more detailed and feel slightly more "alive" with NPC/enemy behavior).  Some of the monsters share a screeching sound effect with aliens in X-Com and so those games are forever linked in my mind.  Rise of the Triad is interesting, too, being a 1994 (or 1995 for the full version) game planned as a sequel to Wolfenstein 3D, even using a heavily modified version of that game's engine well after the release of Doom...!

Do you love 3D Shooters? Do you also love RETRO gaming?
Yes! Then this bunde is definitely for you!
I HIGHLY recommend all the games included in this bundle!!

This game is one of the most fun games I have ever played, with or without mods.
I don't like writing reviews because most of the time I feel that the way a company knows that I like their game is because I'll give it a thumbs up on another review and I haven't tried refunding it. I have, however, found a need to write a review of this game because of the recent conflict I have seen.
Judging this game's vanilla singleplayer content:
Without spoiling too much: this is one of the only single player games that I can honestly say swept me away. The story was a fantastic tale of three unexpected friends, and it constantly keeps the player entertained. I played through it three times before finally hanging up the controller on my ps3/ps4 and switching to PC. If you are looking for a good single player time, this game is definitely the way to go.
Multiplayer:
I can't be too biased with the multiplayer even though that's where I spent most of my time on the PC version of this game.
The multiplayer is grindy. That's it. It's just grindy.
The above statement is very bold, but I admit that I cannot stop playing GTA Online for one reason only. It is the most fun multiplayer game I have to play with friends. I have easily put 200-300 hours combined between the PS4 and PC versions of this game's multiplayer. The heists are so much fun when you're coordinated. The grindy missions become a lot of fun when you can think of creative and imaginative ways to complete them with your friends. All in all, it is a fantastic waste of time to spend with your friends. People complain about hackers and cheaters, but I think that finding ways to thwart them with your friends is a totally new type of minigame for the multiplayer.
Mods:
Here is where my real criticism comes in... I support Take Two for their actions. I know that this will not be  a popular opinion, but it's the truth. The whole time, since before the release of the PC version of this game, they have been adamant and honest about their opinion of modding the game. They released patch after patch trying to stop mods from being a thing. If this wasn't an issue before, why is it an issue now? I don't think trying to take down OpenIV may have been the best decision, but it was a necessary decision that they made to solidify their opinion on the matter. Mods are not an essential part of this game. Any single person does not have to buy shark cards, they don't have to buy this game at all. They have been completely honest and open about the fact that they do not want their game modded. Sorry, but it's the truth.
TL;DR
Great single player. Multiplayer is grindy, but fun with friends. Devs and producers have never wanted mods and tried to ban mods from the game. It wasn't a big issue then, it shouldn't be now.

I already own Dirt Rally and now WRC 6 as well. WRC 6 shouldn't really be seen as a poor man's Dirt Rally. It is simpler to get into and more accessible while still getting a good rally fix.
I was really surprised how much I like this game, especially since WRC 5 wasn't very good. The jittery framerate is gone and the graphics are significantly improved with no ugly pop up. It's my opinion, but having played both the graphics are certainly in the ball park of Dirt Rally and in some stages I think better. I also use reshade 3 with no problems to tweak lighting to my preference.
Positives:
Car handling feels good and appropriately rally like.
Car settings are simplified but not totally dumbed down and affect handling as expected.
Graphics are good  (I get 60fps vsync @1440p on GTX980ti).
Timing of navigator calls can be adjusted.
More forgiving of small off roads than Dirt Rally.
Negatives:
No seat or FOV adjustment for in-car camera.
Default car setups are too loose (good for  handling demo, not so good for times.)
Car interior  graphics are basic.
Controller setup better than WRC 5 but still lacking. (Dead zone still exists when set to zero and excessive input lag with controller, not Sebastien Loeb Rally levels of lag but could be better).

The game is taking place somewhere in the medieval ages called Calradia where many factions exist and are in an endless war. Game begins in one of the cities of player’s choice, then journey starts the way it is desired. Combat mechanics are great with 4 directional swing/thrust option as well as 4 directional weapon blocking correspondingly, shields can be ascended and descended to cover different parts of the body, offering a solid challenge for the archers. Thus it comes as more like a skill-based one rather than trying to catch a lucky moment to attack your opponent.
There’s a huge range of opportunities and functionalities even apart from combat mechanics. You can fight with enemies, loot villages, gather your own men each with varying and upgradable stats across nations, even special companions who can be taken care of exclusively. Build workplaces to gain weekly money income, perform different actions with other NPCs on the map, trade in an actually self-improving environment in a realistic manner, besiege and claim castles, build up different relations with other NPCs and people of villages-cities, join factions, even create your own and many more. Yet the price is fairly light. This game should be in the must see list of every war addict.

It's too hard to describe how addictive it is. Just play it. You won't regret.
P.S. Viking conquest dlc can bring you a pretty good single-player experience, while Napoleonic war dlc is focused on multiplayer. They are not necessary to enjoy the game, but they can add flavor.

~This is going to be a rather long review, please take a couple minutes and read through it if you're considering playing Lord of the Rings Online. :3
Many people have said that this game is 'dying' and that has either scared people away from even starting to play, or pushing away old players who wish to play again. ~I am here to say that this game is NOT dying, NOT on it's last leg, or anything of the sort! The only reason that people from Steam say that is because Steam only shows people who are playing Lotro through Steam, but this amazing game was available, still is available to download through their website. This game has a flourishing community, many helpful people that would happily start playing with you, but only if YOU give this game a chance.
In this next section, I will review what I think are the Pro's and Con's of this game.
Pro's:
~Many friendly people who absolutely love to play together, just waiting for you.
~Flourishing community to answer all your questions and comments.
~Fun and engaging content to keep you hooked for hours.
~Simple crafting to gear your leveling character.
~Many different classes to choose from to fit your playstyle.
~Dungeons just waiting for you and your friends to plunder them.
~The best gear in the game is crafted by players, not bought from a cash shop.
Con's:
~Many servers have a decline in population. (To move to Brandywine.)
~Over-Simplified crafting.
~Lag spikes in highly populated area's (As expected.)
~Longer-than-usual server downtimes for simple repairs and maintenence.
~Many things are still bought from the cash shop. (Personal Con.)
~No real end-game (Yet, but plenty of gearing and skill tweaking to do.)
You may notice that I have crafting in both Pro's and Con's, mainly because in the last massive update they (Turbine) made crafting super easy, but still fun for the leveling character.
If you have read the review and agree, or disagree with what I have said about this magnificent game, go ahead and send a friend request and we can talk it over.

TL;DR version: A solid game, very entertaining for slow and casual playing where you enjoy the leveling and don't even bother to think about "the end-game". Consider this Skyrim, except it's Tolkien, and you might occasionally run into other people.
RP ( on Laurelin ) is good if you find the right people and places.
PVP ( or Monster Play ) can vary on servers but mostly it's rather dead. Don't expect PVP to be at all balanced as it has almost no focus in the game.
End-game: There are raids and bosses but as I said, don't bother thinking about them. Just focus on enjoying the leveling progress - it won't be fast, and the end-game isn't grand enough to be worth rushing your way there.
Rambly version:
First the most important thing: you should really consider this more of a Free to Try game, rather than Free to Play.  It's true that you earn Turbine Points ( = money )  within the game ( quite a lot too, and easily if you don't mind grinding ) but subscribing is still vastly better if you actually want to play the game without significant limitations ( all of which you can remove with Turbine Points though ). Honestly, you shouldn't think of this as a huge drawback - F2P ( P2W ) games are still a rather new thing and the common model for MMOs has for a long time been to require a subscription. LoTRO wasn't initially free either.
That aside, I wouldn't recommend this game to the usual ADHD MMO button smasher kiddie ( for one thing the combat system is queued ). While it has been eased up from what it was, there is still significant grinding involved in the game. Pure, "Kill 300 Wolves for X" grinds, straight up. These are called Deeds and you earn stat boosts ( and Turbine Points, titles and other things ) by completing them, but for the gameplay purposes, the stat boosts ( Traits ) are most important. However, if you are the type of person who just loves to put on some music, audiobook or even just watch TV while sloooowly advancing your character, this game will be awesome for you.
Gameplay is alright, but I admit it's not the greatest out there. Movement is pretty fluid, though some of the animations are a bit stiff. Skills and such don't feel very streamlined ( I feel there's a lot of redundancy - skills are there just so that you have many buttons to press ) and the combat queue is a bit clumsy. It's unique, I give it that but on certain classes I've found it very annoying. Still, it is as planned and the combat is relatively slow as a result. There are also some minor UI annoyances here and there that take getting used to ( stack splitting, cannot vendor items straight from inventory - need to use vendor ui, have to drag and drop a lot ). On the plus side, you can rearrange your UI exactly as you please and also get some nifty 3rd party skins if you're into that ( there are few other plugins as well ).
The graphics are a bit dated but unless you're used to always only playing newest and shiniest games, it shouldn't bother you overly much. However the overall atmosphere with the music and scenery is amazing, especially if you are a Tolkien fan. Even if you aren't in to RP, I expect one would appreciate the first time they see the valley of Rivendell open up to them, or watching the sunrise in the Shire, not to mention many of the other iconic places mentioned in the books, or seen in the movies.
This is a very fun game for those who enjoy Tolkien's world, casual but very grindy PVE, casual to no PVP and any amount of RP. For social people, the community is generally friendly and you shouldn't have trouble finding a Kin ( guild ) that suits your tastes. For lone-wolves, there is plenty of solo content and for the most part you don't really need a group either.

It feels like in recent times that no other developer has been so illuminated and aware of what made PC gaming so great in its formative years.
The new developers for DX really get it. Mankind Divided is an ode to fun. Overflowing with details and distractions it took me some time to make my way through the campaign. The side quests were all fantastic and the main story is multi faceted and layered and I think it will take a while to dig through a bunch of the symbolism involved also.
I could bang on about graphics and style and art direction but there's no point. I don't think there's anyone in the industry putting out anything as good as these guys.
Now its not perfect.

Performance was great on my 1080, but prior to getting that card I was running on two x 980's, and SLI caused a lot of crashing so I had to use a single 980. Performance could be a lot better for a card of that level.
The scope of the gameworld is somehow smaller than the first revisit to the DX universe too. Human Revolution featured all kinds grand architecture and larger scale battles with mechs and the like, and it feels like some of those aspects are missing. It doesn't detract that much plus MD is telling a very different tale.
Overall I'd say Mankind Divided is to Human Revolution what Mass Effect 2 was to Mass Effect 1, though not with as many steps back, just side steps maybe.

Review based on version 1.0.53
If you want a simulation and play with a wheel, than Dirt Rally is game for you and WRC 6 will disappoint you. But if you want a funny and easy-to-learn simcade (mixture between pure arcade like in Need for Speed and simulation like in Dirt Rally or Richard Burns Rally) title, you will have fun with it :) Two different games for different audiences.
It improved a lot compared to WRC 6. The super special stages are new. Random events like tyre punctures, too.
Graphics and sound are only mediocre (much better compared to WRC 5, but still not as good as Dirt 3), but drifting around is a lot of fun, even with a keyboard. Unlike Dirt Rally, this game forgives errors and one small mistake doesn't mean you have to restart the stage. The variety of tracks and cars is great, unfortunately there are no classic rally cars (e.g. group B). The weather effects can create an amazing athmosphere, driving through sweden at night while it snows is something very different compared to the same stage at daylight with sunshine. Set "Digital Vibrance" to 70 % in the Nvidia control panel for much better graphics and more intense light (for Nvidia desktop users only).
I do not have the stuttering some players experience. For the too dark nights or fogs, see the tip with the "Digital Vibrance" above.
Attention: the retail DVD doesn't contain any gamedata! Only the Steam installer and the serial.

Definitely a sim game this time around: functional wipers, manual headlights, time penalties for in-race tyre changes (after getting a puncture), time penalties for getting off-road, authentic engine sounds, more realistic stage designs, narrower roads, and more complex physics. It's more sim than arcade.
Ignore the Dirt Rally Fanboys, like all Fanboys and most Mainstream gamers they are fully content with playing just ONE game from every single genre or niche they come across, and obsess over it like some child.
Dirt Rally is awesome and you should get it, however I don't want to play the same rally game over and over and over. I want variety, I want new and different content. I like racing games, not just 'A' racing game or 'THE' racing game. If you are the same you should have a look at WRC 6, as well as Loeb Rally and all other non-Codemasters racing games.
The standout feature for me so far in WRC 6 is the stage designs. While I enjoyed the aggressiveness of the stages in WRC 5 they felt a bit similar after a while. The stages in WRC 6 are completely new and different from WRC 5. They are much more varied and unique.
I've not had any technical issues so far, 'true' I had to tweak the settings to get the game to run smoothly, but I've been forced to do that with every racing game I've played for the last 20 years, even the mighty Dirt Rally. It's the reality of playing games on PC.

If you are a die hard rally sim fan and are happy with DiRT Rally (and are not tired of the lack of stages), feel free to pass.

Despite how underwhelming the reboot of Rise of the Triad was, the Apogee Throwback Pack is a must have for anyone that remembers the pleasure of PC gaming at the cusp of greatness.
Back when most of these games were unknown to anyone outside of dedicated home PC families, you no longer have to stay the night at the weird kid's house who still wets the bed to play these gems. The Throwback Pack includes the original Rise of the Triad, and it's expansion Extreme Rise of the Triad. Both in their original glory, played through Dos Box.
But what sold me on this was the inclusion of Blake Stone Aliens of Gold and it's lesser known successor, Planet Strike. Back in the days when Wolfenstein 3D ruled the FPS roster, Blake Stone was a refreshing diversion from the dark halls filled with Nazis and trips into hell. Leaning more toward an 80's sci fi horror FPS, Blake gave everything that Doom and Wolfenstien had, plus the introduction of food dispensers, and the ability to return to levels you had already visited to access areas you missed, or to top off your supplies.
All in all, there is no reason that these should not be in your Steam library. My only detraction, is that I wish they had released more of Apogee's titles from this period.

Operation Flashpoint: Red River
+ A nice change of scenery from the previous installment in the series, Operation Flashpoint: Red River takes you to the war-torn areas of Tajikistan and beyond. You'll be fighting against terrorist hostiles in the desert, while also dealing with the People's Liberation Army of China.
+ Story wise I would say the game is decent, but it doesn't feature anything out of the ordinary or ground-breaking. It's a pretty standard tale of U.S forces securing key objectives like dams and defending Fall Out Bases.
+ As with the first title, Operation Flashpoint: Red River closely resembles a military simulator, so it's great for gamers who want to play tactically.
+ Graphics are passable, not top notch in any respect, but reasonable.
- The guns just don't seem as fluid as the original game. I can't quite put my finger on it, but something is odd. The weapons just appear to be less exciting and more generic. The feeling you have when firing isn't the same as in Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising. I'm not complaining about the realism of the weapons, they just have no charm. In Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising, they were both very fun to use and realistic.
- Squad commands are once again a pain to initiate. Really poorly thought-out system that simply doesn't work as intended in the middle of shooting at enemies. Too time consuming and difficult to do. I finished the game purely by solo killing, with my teammates behind me providing default covering fire.
- The game can start out slow, most of the missions aren't too engaging in terms of gameplay. While the new desert atmosphere is nice, it can also be a bit bland at the same time.
- Game is short at 20 hours, although this isn't the worst length for a First Person Shooter I've come across.
- Voice acting is kinda strange to be honest..just a little.
Overall Score: 6/10
Operation Flashpoint: Red River isn't a bad game. It's just not as good as the Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising. It's shorter, the guns aren't as enjoyable, the environment is fresh and new, but it doesn't have the X factor that Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising retained. In the end, it's a game still worth purchasing, but definitely on sale.

Where do I begin? Ah, yes. It all started when I was first introduced to FATE, and all of its sequels (which I have mostly elected to ignore-aside from The Cursed King). So before I decided to pick up one of the other sequels I haven't played, I searched for similar RPG games that were better fleshed out and ultimately more popular, and everything pointed to Torchlight II. I have searched far and wide, and I can now conclude this is my favorite game of all time.
This Torchlight sequel has a unique and entertaining art style and excellent visual aesthetics. The world is large and the terrain offers a diverse range of explorable landscape, from lush forests, to barren deserts, and a whole lot more. While I haven't personally played the prequel, I can't imagine it being more fun than this game so I don't think I should even bother!
Onto the game features I was looking for and found in this fantastic game: Enchanting, socketing, transmuting, and fishing. These four activities have been my primary points of interest in an RPG, and boy was I glad when I tried them out in this game! The transmuting system is the first unique feature I fell in love with. Through this platform you can create random items by combining different types of items together; for example, potions (to create bigger potions!), socketing an unsocketed item, or even unique items! Done right, transmuting could land you some awesome equipment, all the better to prepare you for the treacherous battles that lie ahead! Which brings us to the next point: the combat system!
Combat in this game is a whole lot better than I initially thought it would be. Sick and tired of passive hack-and-slash? Well, look no further! Depending on the difficulty setting, the combat in this game requires fast reactions and alertness, with your fingers constantly mapped to your quick-keys to rapidly deploy your abilities or consumables as you need them. The four character classes are all remarkably different and each of them has the potential to unlock powerful passive abilities with the right choice of weapon. Another great feature in this game is that skills can be activated arbitrarily without requiring previous skills along the tree to be learned. This makes for an altogether more flexible and versatile skill set for any one character, as each skill is independent of other skills.
Another huge plus is the multiplayer mode in this game. Campaigning alone is nowhere near as much fun as playing with a few friends. And loot drops are unanimous, so every player gets loot and no-one can be too greedy. Also, an excellent trading system is in place for when you get loot that might not be suitable for your character. The loot system also allows players to exchange socketables, something I always found useful since I'm always transmuting gems into (hopefully!) better stuff!
While the story was a bit lacklustre and could have used a bit more refinement, I have enjoyed numerous hours of gameplay on the unadulterated version of the game, and have yet to discover the mods currently in place, which are claimed to be excellent additions to the game.
In summation, if you can look past a bland storyline, this game offers countless hours of playability, with New Game + mode and the Mapworks in place if you beat the final boss, and all the various mods. I would definitely recommend this game to any RPG fan looking for an entertaining and immersive game. You would be doing yourself a huge disfavor if you didn't own a copy.

A simple pattern minigame that has no story but a nice setting. There's a sequence of 10 letters/buttons you have to press before your opponent, wrong inputs usually add a time penalty. You can play with either controller or keyboard (and for keyboard, choose words or random letters). Single player campaign (called 'Skill Tester') is a just series of 9 duels with increasingly fast AI. The bulk of your play time should be with online friends or split-screen multiplayer.
The single player difficulty seemed fine for me, but if you're not a relatively fast typist you'll have a tough time unlocking the final characters. For reference, I usually get ~70-80 wpm on Typeracer and about 2.6s per 10-letter word here. The eighth duel (hard AI) was where I lost my first round (although still ended up 2-1 overall). However, the final opponent (very hard AI) consistently beats me. The first time I won he actually made a mistake (though I won by more than 0.3s).
Worth a look if you like pattern/typing games and have people to play with.
Other thoughts:

I like the game's voice acting and the retro look on this game is mostly good, as opposed to just seeming like it was done to be lazy or cheap. However, the blocky graphics do have one major problem: letters sometimes look like other letters. This is a problem because the entire game consists of quickly typing a word displayed vertically along the left edge of the screen. Unless you quickly recognize the word, you might type "K" instead of "H," or even "X," because the letter looked funky. Despite the retro graphics, they should have at least had the letters look nice and clear, because this made the game a bit off-putting for me.
The major downfall of the game, though, is that this is it. I played fifteen minutes, which included watching the intro video/narration, and made it to the final duel, which I lost 3-4 times before not caring enough to try again. There is not enough to do in this game. Afterward, you can apparently play online. I don't know why I would want to try to type a random word faster than someone online. Like I said, that's literally the entire game. =/
The font and word orientation makes this game more of a strugglefest than it needs to be. Maybe I'll hook up a 360 controller and see if that makes it more playable.

After more than 300 hours played of Dirt Rally and SLRE, I just needed an hour to conclude that this game can't be recommended for any rally enthusiast in its actual state. The major technical problem is a horrible frame stutter that, according to the forums, comes from WRC 5 and still wasn't fixed by developers. This stuttering really breaks immersion, and it happens even with a rig capable of delivering a frame rate that more than doubles today's standard refresh rate (60fps). So, definitely it's not a matter of performance in this case. Any proposed workaround haven't fixed this problem for me.
Also, the force feedback feels very off, especially if compared to other racing titles. It's just bad, there's no other way to say this. I tried every racing title on the last couple years. DR, SLRE, Assetto Corsa, RRRE, Project Cars, you name it. WRC's FFB is by far the worst. Adding to the uninspiring visuals, this makes the (many) tracks available look and feel the same. All of them are really flat and boring, with a serious lack of surfacing work. Sound effects are okay.
Unfortunately, this game can't be compared with Dirt Rally at any level, and even Sebastien Loeb's EVO, with all its limitations, offers a much better sim experience. Maybe, like me - and many other people, you just want another rally game to have some "detox" from the so few DR's stages, and were waiting to get WRC 6 with a better price. But even in this scenario, I don't think it's worth it. I know Kylotonn improved a lot if comparing to WRC 5, but they still need to fix a lot of things, with this game-breaking frame stutter as priority. I'm pretty confident that they'll manage to fix some of these problems to make WRC 7 a worthwhile evolution.

When you play a certain type of game a certain type of way long enough, you can’t just go back to the way it used to be easily. Case in point: the old Rise of the Triad and Blake Stone games. This was back when the name Apogee actually meant something.  I say it’s disappointing looking at myself because I’ve forgotten how to not WASD. See, back in the old days, you moved forward and backward and turned with the arrow keys, then had to hold down alt if you wanted to sidestep. It seems rather counter-intuitive if you’re used to the WASD system and it’s really hard to go back.
Worse still, the games don’t make it much easier because the key bindings are hard to manipulate and often don’t want to work with the mouse. That said, IF you can manage to retrain your hands, this is a great set of nostalgia that shouldn’t be passed up. Maybe I can get the joystick to cooperate…hmmmm.  As it stands, though, I can't recommend this one simply because of the control style.  If you're still used to the old control style, go nuts.

Codemasters started a new side studio called "Codemasters Guildford" to handle making these two Operation Flashpoint games, and they sucked so bad that Codemasters shut down the studio and went back to focusing on their racing games.
Got this and a few other games at humblebundle for $1 to try out. This was such a bad experience that I am not even going to bother with the other game, Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising. Out of the hundreds of games I've played since becoming a PC gamer back in 1997, there are only a few games that I have ever quit playing and uninstalled within 30 minutes, and this is one of them.
First, I can without even the slightest hesitation say that this game has some of the worst voice acting of all time. It is cringe-inducingly bad. It is so bad it made me physically ill and I pooped all over.
This games problems start right away. It is immediately obvious how bad this game is when you start by doing nearly five minutes of riding with your squad in a humvee while a guy talks the ENTIRE time, enough to fill five pages of a book. He just very monotonely drones on and not one single word he says is of any importance whatsoever, just incredibly, mind jarringly annoying. After what feels like twenty minutes rather than five, you get out in a little area and get to kill two guys, then five more minutes of driving and him talking nonsense until your ears bleed. You get out in another small area & kill a few more guys, then five more minutes of driving and you get to assault a small town. In the middle of the assault is when I had enough and alt+f4 out and uninstalled. First off, that insane amount of riding in a humvee is unneeded. The guy rambling the entire time talking more than anything I've ever heard, even more than in a Mass Effect game, is uncalled for.
Also, the gameplay is like something out of a paper cut-out book. My rifle barely moved when I fired it, the sound was bad, sounded like a kids toy gun, when your bullets hit an enemy it feels laughably uneventful and generic, the sight aim sensitivity blows, and the squad command menu is without a doubt completely unnecessary and is just a burden. The basic things you can tell your squad to do are things that are automatically done by the ai in any good game because they are basic actions that should be automatically programmed into the game for the AI, but here are left out to make you feel like you are giving them strategic commands, lol. It's like they said "the game's AI isn't finished yet so we gave you commands to do it yourself".
Where Battlefield 3 would be a 8 or 9/10, this game is like a bottom of the barrel, stripped down, generic, awkward copy of BF3 and would at best be a 3/10. BF3 is a guy with a 20,000 dollar suit on and this game is a homeless guy laying in his own p1ss in the gutter begging for booze money. Codemasters' Dirt games, more specifically Dirt 3, is one of the most well made racing games I've ever played. I do not know what they were thinking trying to make this garbage horse crap of a war fps game, but they would have been better off not doing so. Especially since they took a hit on these games financially and shut down the side company they started in order to make them.
To this game's credit, as god awful as it is, its engine is still astoundingly better than ARMA 2's, lol. But then again, Asteroids for Atari has a better game engine than ARMA 2 so that's not saying much.
Anyone who actually likes and spends any time on these two Op Flash games is probably a recluse with no sense of human interaction and a horrible taste in games and should stop wasting time and kill themselves quickly.

This is going to be a very confusing review, and I'm letting you know that now, because of the split between smash players and casuals. The first half of the this review will be for casual people who haven't gotten into smash.
From a casual playpoint:
This game is very good game to play, even if you never want to go into any competativeness. The game is very easy to pick up and learn with a few posts on reddit, you could learn all the combos pretty easily. I learned this never playing many fighting games, and have before Season 1 have become Platnium with just pure dedication. The community is great, and are great for new players as well. There is a whole discord chat for people gold and below learning the game. However this brings up one concern that it feels a bit reliant on the community, and if you don't want to go that extra step to look at the Brawlhalla reddit, you may have a bad time, since there is no real teaching tools in the game other than training mode. Other than that the community is accesable and great, and the game is easy to play, and relativly speaking easy to master as well. One of my real life friends, has for a while, been one of the best in the world, and he isn't some giant e-sport nerd that spent 15 years on the game and streams it for a living, we are still in school! Anyone could be good at this game, without having to dedicate a big chunk of your life. I think the biggest chunk I played this game in was an hour and a half. Not only has it been a great experience to play, it has also been a great entry way to playing games competative. Because of this game I have actually took the time to play smash, and play Rivals of Aether, and it wasn't that hard because of this game being a stepping stone.
Now it's that time of the review, the wave-dashing, multishing, part for smash players.
T H E  S M A S H  R E V I E W  O F  T H I S  G A M E
If you are looking for a a smash experience, you aren't going to find it. The game is much slower, semi rng based, and is a lot easier. There is not 3 frame tech, and there isn't the smash diversity that made each character different. Each character is unique in their own right, but compared to smash, each character feels like a Doctor Mario to Mario, a Roy to Marth. Because of the weapon mechanic, each character can feel stale. and the game itself as well because of the internal longing for diversity. You aren't going to find it. The fact anyone can pick up and play, hurts the small competative scene. There are some pretty advanced things you could do, but it is still nothing compared to smash tech. There is no 20 frame data to tech, there is no 3 tech perfect pivot you can't do it. I'm not saying this as an insult to the game, but it is like the game in the title, Brawl. A more casual game, that can't really scene, and this isn't an insult to either game, but those are my emotions. Most combos are true and there is no DI or tech you want to do. If you play smash competativly, this game isn't for you, and you know what? That isn't a bad thing. You open up Dolphin and play Melee 20XX netplay edition. You sit there for half an hour practicing your multishine approaches. You find the next combo everyone is going to use.
Extra notes
The character system is frustruating. I understand the store and why it's there but having to buy characters, especially at that price, needs a lot of grinding. Just to main a character you need to spend at least a week just to be able to play them, and it is extremely frustrating.
Game updates a lot, and listens to ideas and compaints. Great community and great devs.
If you want to play this game, and want to get good? Go to the subreddit please! This is how I learned, by looking at what people do, and how to combo. The game has no other entry point for learning these.

So here we are with another FPS game to hit Steam. The Mean Greens will throw you for a loop, though, if you think it will just be another grey/brown/green romp through a shiny explosion-fest. The Mean Greens goes at the genre through a different set of windows. It decides to bust through the fun windows. You know the ones that haven’t really been broken recently. Everyone is all up on the hyper-realistic shooters and while a lot of them are pretty stinking cool, they all kind of merge together in my brain at least. In The Mean Greens you play as green or tan army men straight out of your childhood… if you were raised with them instead of an iPad. I know some of you may only be familiar with them thanks to Toy Story… and I’m mostly ok with that.
I’m going to go with what I didn’t like first since that’s a shorter list and everyone always likes to know what they are getting into before they jump into the pool. The shooting is the only thing that troubles me here. For the most part, my friends and I have noticed a bit of a discrepancy between our aim and some of the other players. I’m fairly sure everyone at this point is on the up and up so that leaves me with a few options. Either other people have just acclimated to the spread of the guns better than some or using a controller has some added benefits over the mouse and keyboard option. Some people can just wreck with the regular machine gun while I tend to struggle with it and the shotgun (although most of my kills are with the machine gun). I’m pretty good with the rocket launcher, but that’s like being proud to win with a gun at a knife fight. I may figure it out eventually, but something does feel off about the controls.
On the bright side, with good teamwork, shooting isn’t everything. The Mean Greens is set up as more of an objective based game. I tend to only stick with maps that are not free-for-all based. Luckily that leaves me with… every other map in the pool other than Art Table Shuffle. What that means is you’re left with:
-playing capture the flag in a fish aquarium
-attacking and defending plates of cookies on a toy train driving around a Christmas tree
-playing fußball on a barn themed fußball table
-trying to unfreeze your dinosaur in a freezer before the other team can free theirs
-even more, but I don’t like doing lists like this, go play the game
This game has given so many different takes on similar themes that it just makes my heart happy. Even with dying at times, I’ve found myself having a laugh at the hilarity of the situation my team of toy soldiers have found themselves in. Some of that is in part to learning how the levels are composed and where everything is. Most of it is due to the crazy atmosphere and great music. Ever wanted to assault or defend a birthday cake? Well, The Mean Greens gives you that chance!
I guess I can throw out one last thing. There has been a lot of complaining about servers and being kicked and all that jazz. Yes, I do get kicked automatically from servers at times. Yes, that does suck. Does it happen a lot? No, not really once you find a server. Finding a server would be another complaint if you want to use the “find server” option. They said they’ve patched it, but as of yesterday, it will usually put me into a server all by myself instead of one with room. Yes, that’s unfortunate, but I can just as easily go to the server list and order it by ping and click into a server and Bob’s your uncle. It’s not ideal, but it’s not a deal breaker. Let’s stop being spoiled here. If that’s your only complaint, I’d say be thankful.
Score: Gewd/Tasty
I will reiterate what I said in my tweet in that I believe that The Mean Greens is the “best variation on gameplay in the FPS genre in the long time including Splatoon.” That is not to say that it is without its faults and when they hit you, you notice them. However, it is super nice to see a developer go and create a game in a familiar genre and not simply rehash what is already available in so many different forms already. There are a lot of shooters out there that will run you a bit of money and there are a lot of free ones as well that don’t suck. At the end of the day, a lot of them are simply the same game with a different color of paint. So much is different in The Mean Greens and anyone who even likes to dabble in the FPS genre would be a fool to not try The Mean Greens out. It’s simply way to fun to avoid.

Having played all of the other Dawn of War games, this one certainly seems to be the weakest of the series.  Don't get me wrong, it's still a load of fun, but when compared to the other installments in the series, this one feels a bit phoned in.
If you've ever played Dark Crusade, it's very much like that.  But, in case you haven't, in Soulstorm you choose one of nine factions to lead to victory over the Kaurava system.  The system is divided into territories spanned across 4 planets and 3 moons.  Each faction starts controlling a certain number of territories, whereas the player starts with only a single territory.  Each faction must then battle it out for control of each territory in the system.  You defeat other factions by conquering their primary territory, known as their stronghold.
In Dark Crusade the campaign played out in much the same fashion, but over a single planet rather than a system.  Furthermore, the backstory for the planet and each of the individual territories felt much more fleshed out in Dark Crusade.  The reasoning for the presence of each faction was better explained and the entire game just seemd to have more personality.
Aside from this, Soulstorm is really just more of the same.  And that's great if you're a Dawn of War fan.  It's great to finally see the Adepta Sororitas (Sisters of Battle) added to the game and the gameplay works just as well as it ever has.
Ultimately, I would recommend this game but only if you enjoyed the other Dawn of War installments.  If this is your first introduction to the Dawn of War Series, I would strongly recommend playing the other games first.

This is a great game with an amazing overall story and one of the best f2p models I've ever seen. While it does have it's share of limitations on f2p users they did something I have never seen any other MMO do, they created a way in which you can remove most of these limitations without spending a dime through the use of what are called turbine points which can be earned through completeing certain tasks much like those you do to earn achievements or trophies. Of course the creators are not so stupid as to make these incredibly fast to get and make getting a subscription pointless, it takes some serious time to earn enough points to unlock quest packs and expansions but for not spending money it's well worth the wait. I've been playing it for several years and I still find it massively entertaining and, despite having put in somewhere close to 2000 hours into it, I in no way find it boring and I still love going through the story when I start an alt, it's just that good. If you're a fan of LoTR you'll definitely love this game's story and learning about some of what went on outside of the fellowship when you play this game. It also does an exceptional job at avoiding having to grind for countless hours by having not only multiple quest packs for the same level ranges but also having scaleable instances. That being said the one problem there is right now is that there aren't as many people playing the lower levels anymore so it can be difficult to get groups together for lower leveled instances and, if you wish to do them, it will take either some luck or going back to it at a higher level. In the case of raids and some other group instances it will still be incredibly difficult or even impossible to complete alone so you would still need at least some help. I personally like this fact because it means that having a max level player in a lower levelled raid won't guarantee your victory, you still have to try your best and there is always the possibility of wiping.
Overall I give the game a 9/10, the story is great, the graphics are as good as you would expect for an MMO that's been out for more than 7 years, and the combat is entertaining albeit sometimes a bit clunky.
I feel so sorry for anyone that paid full price for this game. Yes it's alpha but really? Just don't buy it!

The way that I play games with stealth mechanics is likely to have colored my experience with Deus Ex: Mankind Divided. For the first 16 or so hours (on the most difficult setting), I didn't raise one alarm. Nor did I kill anyone. I would methodically work my way through enemy territory using non-lethal takedowns on anyone that got in my way. That's just how I like to approach stealth sequences in games: if I can be the ultimate lawful-good hero, I'm going for it. For a lot of people, that approach might seem tedious and time-consuming. You're not wrong, at times it was. With that said, I had committed to a specific build from the beginning, one that I was determined to stick with because that's the role I had envisioned for Adam Jensen. That's something that is so great about the Deus Ex series: it presents players with the ability to select skills which drastically and meaningfully affect how you interact with the world.
After having spent 27 hours with Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, I can't say that I would recommend it to anyone. It has some good things going for it and I genuinely enjoyed a sizeable portion of my time with it, but by the time I was 2/3 of the way done I had exhausted all that was redeemable in the game: I had completed the vast majority of the side missions, collected everything I could need for 2 or 3 playthroughs, and I could see the direction that the main story was going. I started Mankind Divided with high expecations which gradually disintegrated with each main story mission. I stuck with it with the hope that in the end it would all be worth it. Boy was I wrong.
