A fun little mod for sure, and at just a single hour's length it isn't a big time investment at all to try out, with an atmospheric first half and a bombastic combat-focused second half with a unique modified weapon.  I suffered one crash during my playthrough, but luckily the autosaves are frequent.  The mod includes achievements, so while it is short, there are a few challenges to increase replay value for those who want to play it a second or third time.  I would say just go play it and judge for yourself due to it's short length - as such the remainder of the review contains some gameplay spoilers:
The unique element of the mod is a gravity gun that fires exploding energy balls, and can be used to rocket jump by firing below you as you jump.  It was a fun mechanic, but it felt a bit underused.  There are just a couple of arbitrary moments where you are forced to use it to reach a high ledge, but in combat it is seemingly optional, since the game kits you out with pretty much the entire gallery of weapons from Half-Life 2.  Ammo is a little scarce, but not entirely, making the game feel like it sends mixed messages a little.  On the flipside it does mean you can play with either the new weapon or have a more traditional Half-Life experience, but it does mean neither option is particularly tightly designed.  You also don't get the modified Gravity Gun until about halfway through the game, which was a surprising factor considering it's the mod's selling point.  It feels like the guns are there as a get out of jail free card for when the gravity gun runs out of charge, but I'd rather it retained it's standard close-range jolt to stun enemies, so you can run away and recover - perhaps make it so this mechanic also allows for long jumps for retreats without causing damage to enemies.
The first chapter was nicely designed with the darkness providing some neat gimmicks.  I'd be lying if I said I didn't have to really work up the courage to descend into the pit of zombies, despite being well-familiar with them from multiple Half-Life 2 playthroughs over the years.  The crescendo at the end of the third chapter felt more fun and exciting to use the new Gravity Gun, with tons of toys and traps to manipulate with it to wreck hordes of zombies.  Meanwhile the fourth chapter's finale encounter felt like the epitome of my "mixed messages" criticism, where rather than being used creatively for combat, the gravity gun instead is just a means to get around and collect a finite amount of rockets to take out Striders in a very traditional manner.  While two cranes can be shot to drop shipping containers on the Striders for a very satisfying payoff, once both those chances are used up, that's the end of the only creative idea the finale has.
Overall, I feel if this mod is intended to serve as a proof of concept for this gravity gun idea, it has succeeded very well, the idea has great potential.  I just wish the mod was overall more focused and tightly designed around it, I'm sure some more creative things could be done and the reliance on showering the player with typical Half-Life weapons could be axed.  If however, the mod is just meant to be what it is, it still succeeds at being a pleasurable experience from start to finish.

I've enjoyed playing this game for a very long time, but instead of it feeling like a classic, I'm left with the same disappointment you can expect with pretty much every Mortal Kombat game ever made. The content is wonderful; that isn't the issue... The issue is the complete absence of character balancing and juggling gone completely off the rails. I know every fighter, and can execute almost all of their moves, but this game has serious issues when it comes to juggling. A better name for MKX would be 'Juggling Abuse Simulator,' because that's all every fight boils down to in the end. Some characters don't heavily rely on juggling, but they have absolutely no chance of beating those who do.
For those not familiar with juggling, it is a method of keeping your opponent in the air for as long as possible, and being able to attack them without them being able to do anything to counter it. You only have one way to escape a juggle in MKX, which is your two bar EX breaker, but it won't help. The worst players in the world will spend their entire lives coming up with the lamest combos imaginable, ones that offer you absolutely no way out, and have infinite resets, so that when you DO finally hit the ground, they have a 50/50% chance of starting the combo on you once again. Since some of these ridiculous combos end up doing 50% damage... you can get the picture... That's basically it. I really like the game's content overall, and the fighting system is extremely fun... until you end up facing a juggle ♥♥♥♥♥, and you simply have no chance of winning unless you juggle ♥♥♥♥♥ them back... and I'd rather be doing something better with my time. Personally, when I do one of these combos on another player, I feel like a complete jerk, because I know how messed up it is, but don't expect anyone online to admit it.
So, if you wanna drop a lot of money to have a good time... for a while... then go for it. I have certainly had my share of fun, but if you think you're going to use skill and actual fighting to win fights against juggle ♥♥♥♥♥s... think again. A prime example of this problem is Kotal Kahn compared to Takeda. Kotal has very slow attacks, and a slow projectile, but his combos do massive damage, as he is extremely difficult to use until you learn his moves. He is well designed. Takeda, on the other hand, has a lightning fast teleport, whips that can strike you and open combos on the other side of the stage, very fast, HUGE juggling combos, and a lightning fast low projectile. (can't be blocked unless you're crouch blocking) Can you guess who you'll be fighting online? Takeda. 87% of the time. It gets old after a while, as the game allows you no way to defeat a character that laughably unbalanced unless you do the same thing. Not even the ALIEN or PREDATOR has a chance, and in my book, that's very bad game design, and why I'm not recommending MKX despite enjoying it.
*Update 11/30/2017*
I feel the need to let people know that despite the flaws I've mentioned in great detail, Mortal Kombat X is still 5x better than Injustice 2 because the spamming in that game is beyond atrocious. Deadshot single handedly ruins the game, and is so ridiculous that he makes Takeda look fair. So if you want to try one Netherealm fighter, definitely get MKX between the two. I'm looking forward to MK11 and fully intend to give it a thumbs up if they manage to balance it. It doesn't have to be perfect, but they really need to focus on balancing above everything else to compete with Street Fighter and Teken.

Trine 2 has picturesque and bright visuals, not-quite-elaborate plot and simple but enjoyable gameplay. It's a traditional platformer full of jumping, fighting enemies, grabbing pickups, looking for carefully hidden treasures and evading various traps. Nice fairytale for kids, good time-spending and some eye relaxation for olders and elders.
You have three heroes here, the commonplace set of warrior, mage, and thief; they have their own special skills, and game levels are intentionally designed to make use of all those talents. This puzzle can only be solved with mage's help, and that one is almost impossible to come through without a thief.
Still, the game often allows several ways to handle an obstacle. You might choose one strategy, and it will pay out; you might choose another, and it will work for you either. It is especially evident when you compare singleplayer to multiplayer experience: a puzzle that you and your friend solved in cooperation turns out to be just as easy to crack when you are on your own.
It also has some physics. This means that you can manipulate objects in different ways, making them move, jump, collide, fly, stick, slide, push, support, block, and on and on and on. This adds quite an amount of variability to the ways that you might choose to deal with a certain problem.
Last words to say, Steam has acquired a good habit of providing 90% discounts for this game. Catch a good bargain, and you'll certainly have some money well spent.

DISCLAIMER 1: This review concerns mostly solo (hardcore) Elite gameplay. Please, skip it if you're not interested.
DISCLAIMER 2: This review does not concern achievement hunting. As the previous disclaimer clarifies, it concerns hardcore Elite gameplay, specially my experience with Embermage.
Grind, grind, grind, grind. And once you're done, you're ready to start the real grind.
Look, the achievements say it all. "Sell 50,000 items"? This requires more than 700h of gameplay (or an autoclicker). But then, the grind goes WAY BEYOND ACHIEVEMENTS. That's the core of Elite gameplay: gear grinding.
Regular monsters will one-hit you even if you're overleveled and "decently geared". XP  grinding is barely relevant: it is the "awesome gear" that allows survival. Torchlight II created a new kind of grinding though, different from "kill that boss 2783782934 times" (which would be already VERY BAD). Grinding in Torchlight II is like this:
- Reload the game until the Vendor have the piece of rare gear you want to buy
- Reload the game until the Gambler has the unique you wanna buy
- Reload the game until the Enchanter you're looking for appears in the map
- Reload the game until the Enchanter enchants what you want him to enchant
- Wait 5min for the Boon Vendor to refresh his inventory. Repeat until you find what you're looking for
- Lava "challenge", reload and do it again for Gems and Gold. You literally just open chests.
After staring at the loading screen for MANY HOURS, you'll be ready to play a game in which there is no challenge left even on the highest difficulty with permadeath (I've never tried NG+ on HCE, and I'm not interested after this experience). See my full rant here, post #26:
Many achievements require "pure brainless repetition" which make Cookie Clicker sound like fun. These devs here should beg the guys from Civilization 5, FORCED, Trine and Mount & Blade to give them a lesson on "How to Come up with Challenging & Fun Achievements - An Introduction For The Clueless Developer".
PS: This review does not concern achievements, it concerns HCE gameplay [3]. My review would remain the same without the previous paragraph.

TAKING THE BRIDGE! - Heroes and Generals

I LOVE THIS GAME!
-and devs, if your reading this, Hi to you and thank you so much for making this game. I finally got enough time to write a review and state my opinions on your game.
If you have any disagreements with my review, I respect that. Everyone has a different view and they are free to have thier views.
Alright, let's get down to the nitty gritty.
If you do not play very many first person shooters (FPS), you might find yourself rage quitting as the United States. Since I started playing as the United States, I've probably lost more battles than won on average.
One thing I love about this game is that it tries to be it's own thing, and not like the next Call of Duty or Battlefield. Many games try to mimic these major titles and usually fail. Even though they do a good job, they mimic so much that it almost becomes a bad game.
Heroes and Generals is not one of them.

This game tries to be more of a fun game for the people who play, and not a free spin-off of a major title just to get money. There is an incredible amount of weapons, accessories (including bullets), gear, and vehicles that you can use to fight the other side. The text chat is always active, so communicating is relatively easy, though one thing to improve it is to add a censorship option to block words that the player considers offensive.
My censorship idea is allow the user to type in the words they consider offensive, then it will block those words in the chat, or add a mute button for the people who spew garbage from thier mouths
Most of these items have to be bought with the in game currency "credits". Everything in the game can be earned free through hard work, or through buying credits using real world money (the good ol' green back bills), though I wish the guns and thier accessories were less expensive, so players going the free route don't have to grind so much for little income.
It is understandable though, because the devs need money to make the game a better experience for everyone, so those people who invest more money will help out the devs more than those going the free route
On the subject of income, the game gives you a base salary, and the more kills you get or vehicles you destroy or hijack, the more credits you'll earn. This is where one of my few complaints shines in it's full glory.
If you are a newbie saving up for that awesome scope for your M1 Garand, or maybe that special M1/M2 Carbine... you better learn to play well fast.
I don't want to offend anyone, or trigger the devs (love you guys <3), but if you are going to pour so much effort into just getting the next addition to your scope or new weapon, should you be playing the game so much? I have poured so many hours into just getting an overpriced Grease Gun I named "Greasy McGee" that, to be honest, I could have used somewhere else. Lower prices would definitely help, but I don't want to put all the blame on the devs, so self-control on my part would help as well.
Other than my complaining about prices, I love the game. There are so many players that are better than you that it gives you the incentive that you need to push on and get better in a conservative amount of time (such as a round or two).
Once again, I do not want to offend anyone, or sound angry, and I hope you find this review helpful.
Keep fighting the good fight, and I hope to see you around,
The Minuteman.

My first playthrough took over 90 hours and I loved every minute of it. Exploring Prague, discovering all of its little secrets and stories, studying the level in order to find the most optimal of routes leading to the completion of an objective - all of that was an absolute delight. I enjoyed it just as much as I remember enjoying Human Revolution the first time I played it.
Gameplay, I thought, was much improved over its predecessor. The movement is more fluid and both stealth and guns feel a lot more authentic. On a more negative note, the AI could really use some work. First, the detection problems: Sometimes an unsuspecting NPC won't react to your actions, even if said actions involve hacking into a computer or punching their comrades in the face right next to them. Other times they will be alerted to the tiniest of sounds coming from the room above or below them. Combat AI is even worse. Enemies constantly run into your line of fire and rarely try to flank you, meaning playing through the game aggressively is a breeze even on the highest difficulty and without activating any of the combat oriented augs - you just need a decent gun (such as the Combat Rifle), enough ammo, and a good cover spot. That's why, if you want at least a bit of a challenge, I'd stick to stealth, and refrain from activating certain augs (such as the Cloaking System, Smart Vision and Tesla). Even with the aforementioned detection problems, it's still the way the game was apparently meant to be played. On the subject of stealth, in future DE games, I'd like to see instances of NPC's moving through the level in a more random manner rather than just following dev placed waypoints on the map.
Level design was also taken to the next level. The levels feel less gamey, but no less fun to explore. The game is still filled with vents, but this time they're almost completely optional even for stealth players. Still, I'd like to see less of them in the next game, since you can pretty much (if you want to) avoid every enemy in the game just by using vents (and they're not hard to find or gain access to either). Also, at first I thought having only one hub world was a step back from HR, but after having experienced both games, I can safely say less hubs and more detail is much better than more hubs and less detail.
Plot wise, the main quest was enjoyable enough if a bit uneventful. I enjoyed the conspiracy bits and the way it rewarded exploration in that players who just blindly follow the main objectives don't really get the whole story, since information relevant to the story and the character of Jensen is often hidden in pocket secretaries, computers and sometimes revealed just by listening to NPC chatter. Still, I wished it lasted a bit longer and that more would be revealed. It seems like just as the plot starts to get really interesting, the game ends. I wanted moar. :rage:
The side quest, however, are excellent and reminded me of some of the RPG's of old in terms of quality. There aren't that many of them, but they're all memorable in different ways: either by complementing the main story, fleshing out the main character or telling a story of common individuals just trying their best to survive in this unforgiving, yet strangely appealing world. Quality over quantity is what is all about here.
If not through quests, you can also learn more of the world and its individuals by simply exploring abandoned or not so abandoned places, talking to random NPC's, and so on. There are also these unlogged micro quests (such as making sense of a certain murder, uncovering a smuggling operation, finding answers related to main or side quest before even receiving the said quest, and so on), which will only be apparent to those who explore and pay attention.
The publisher's shady practices notwithstanding, I can safely say that any self-respecting RPG lover is missing out by not playing this game. In the age where almost everything (from food to entertainment) is designed to offer instant gratification, this game feels like a welcome surprise (especially considering it's not an indie game). Games such as these are a true rarity and should be revered instead of shunned if there is to be any hope of similarly engrossing games ever appearing in the future.

Before we get into this review, go ahead and down vote it.  I have an up to date computer, I know exactly which settings it can run on, and I don't care about the micro-transactions.  Done? Feel better? Ok, now move along there little fella, I'm going to continue this review for the rational people.
This game is definitely an improvement to Human Revolution.  The graphics are much better, the soundtrack is still kickass and epic, the environments are richly detailed, and the conversations actually feel better too.  I like the revamped aug system and the cool new experimental augs they introduced.  And they even threw in an NG+.
The story is a typical turn your brain off action sci fi story, nothing amazing there but I am enjoying it so far.  The voices will not match up with the facial expressions, but that doesn't bother me, and I'm typically reading subtitles anyways and finishing the sentence before the voice actor.  That's just the way I play the game.  I only listen to the full dialogue if it's something interesting and I want to hear how to voice actor conveys the tone.
Anyways, the only other disappointment I have is there isn't multiple hubs.  I liked in HR that there were different cities you would visit.  But Prague is richly detailed enough like I mentioned earlier, so there's still tons to explore, and you get to eventually
.
Microtransactions - these are in a completely separate menu, they aren't in your face, and you don't even see them mentioned on loading screens.  They are a non issue and people are blowing it out of proportion like drama queens.
Performance - this is a very detailed game and there are many eye candy options you can enable which will wreck your computer.  Know which ones you should turn off or turn down and stop complaining that your 4 year old graphics card can't handle the game.
Well that's it, I just wanted to give this game a positive review because I am very much enjoying it, it exceeded my expectations despite the lack of cool hubs.  Steam reviews seriously need to be revamped because this game does not deserve a 64% rating because of a bunch of whiny gamers.

Trine 2 has picturesque and bright visuals, not-quite-elaborate plot and simple but enjoyable gameplay. It's a traditional platformer full of jumping, fighting enemies, grabbing pickups, looking for carefully hidden treasures and evading various traps. Nice fairytale for kids, good time-spending and some eye relaxation for olders and elders.
You have three heroes here, the commonplace set of warrior, mage, and thief; they have their own special skills, and game levels are intentionally designed to make use of all those talents. This puzzle can only be solved with mage's help, and that one is almost impossible to come through without a thief.
Still, the game often allows several ways to handle an obstacle. You might choose one strategy, and it will pay out; you might choose another, and it will work for you either. It is especially evident when you compare singleplayer to multiplayer experience: a puzzle that you and your friend solved in cooperation turns out to be just as easy to crack when you are on your own.
It also has some physics. This means that you can manipulate objects in different ways, making them move, jump, collide, fly, stick, slide, push, support, block, and on and on and on. This adds quite an amount of variability to the ways that you might choose to deal with a certain problem.
Last words to say, Steam has acquired a good habit of providing 90% discounts for this game. Catch a good bargain, and you'll certainly have some money well spent.

OpFlash Red River is an odd class of shooter that's both based on a realistic subject, and is quite realistic. It is not superbly realistic like the Arma Series, and it has little RPG elements where you fight to gain XP to level up, and use that to improve your various combat skills like sprint, weapon changing, accuracy, scouting, and so on. However, it is a welcome change from the usual "blistering pace shoot everything" type shooter (such as Call of Duty Modern Warfare series, or the Medal of Honor series). You control Fireteam Bravo, one of the four marines in Tajikistan, where the US had gone in to take out the guerilla forces aiding the Taliban and Al Qaeda. You will have plenty of friendlies in the campaign missions (fireteams Alpha and Charlie) and various support elements (if any). You can play as one of four classes, rifleman, scout/sniper, grenadier, and autogunner/LMG, each with their "skills" and "weapons" and accessories to unlock. There are 10 main campaign missions, and they are quite long, with a lot of sub-objectives and waypoints. When you are done with those, there are "fireteam engagements" (your fireteam against everybody else) you can play. Generally AI handles the other 3 team members, but if you want multiplayer other players can take over those 3 slots. Graphics are quite good, and campaign missions are quite good, if a bit on the difficult side, as even on easy you WILL get killed A LOT and not knowing where you did wrong. All in all, if you crave a "realistic" shooter and can't stand Modern Warfare you may want to give this one a try.

To start off, yes I liked this game. Is it for everyone no. If you are interested in action and highly engaging/action-oriented gameplay then no this game will probably bore you to tears. However, if you like figuring out the game yourself, and piecing a story together through environmental queues then yes this game is definitly worth taking a look at. The game is generally good at giving you a sense of progression. You almost always know what to do next or have an idea of what to look for. Even when you backtrack, you feel like there is something new to discover in these old areas (because sometimes there are ;) ). During this whole thing I felt like I got a sense of what kind of story was happening, yet I found it interesting that the game was abstract enough that anyone could interpret the queues in numerous ways. My only gripe is that there are some areas and items that you may have to look up a guide for. In my game it took a while for me to find the doll, and I would have never found the sea level if I didn't look up a walkthrough. Overall this game is worth getting (especially now cuz its only 60 cents), it's only two hours but I really was entertained in that amount of time. Plus the music is A+ imo.

Well,
came out of nowhere.
I spent a mere 1.5€ on this... and by the time I finished Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons, it proved itself to be one of the most powerful, confident and, yes, one of the best video games I've ever played.
I strongly recommend you go into this game blind, so I'm going to be as vague as I can in this review.
The premise is fairly simple: two boys head out on an adventure to save their dying father. Make no mistake though; this is a mature, sometimes surprisingly dark story that tackles heavy themes.
There's not a single line of proper dialogue: the characters in the game use body language and talk gibberish (imagine The Sims, something like that) to convey emotion and/or move the story forward. The storytelling relies heavily on visuals, and does an immensely good job at transporting you to a fantasy world brimming with personality.
The gameplay consists of controlling the two brothers via the controller's two analog sticks (though you can use a keyboard, I'd say definitely go for the gamepad). These two must overcome obstacles and solve mild puzzles (which, in all fairness, require no thinking whatsoever, but are still fun nonetheless) throughout their journey.
It's funny how a 4 hour game effortlessly packs more creativity, emotion and memorable set pieces than most contemporary AAA titles struggle to achieve in the span of twice (or even thrice) as many hours. Brothers never feels stale or boring, thanks to its constantly throwing new ideas at you (both in terms of gameplay and visuals), toying with each one just enough before moving on to the next.
is also a strong reminder that art direction, when done right, can outweigh technical brilliance. Sure, some textures are bland and low-res, and you'll never come across any spectacular models or visual effects. But the attention to detail here is so staggering, and the world building so impeccable, it will leave you wondering why you care so much about the technicalities in the first place.
All this is elevated by the soundtrack, which is simply
; sometimes overwhelmingly so. There were moments where the visuals blended so perfectly with the soundtrack, it gave me genuine chills.
Really, the only criticism I may have is the somewhat clunky controls. It takes some time to get used to them (if you get used to them at all), as they are not exactly intuitive; there were times when I confused the two brothers and their actions. But that's a very, very small price to pay for such an exquisite and memorable journey.
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is as close to perfect as it gets.

is a short single-player experience, where you play as Gordon Freeman [obviously] from the original Half-Life series. You are not given any objective from the start, you don't know where you are and where to go. All of this creates an unforgettable, dark and immersive atmosphere.
The game looks beautiful, the new, redesigned source engine is just a joy to look at. The gameplay introduces a few new game mechanics, such as zombies can't see in the dark, so you have to keep your flashligh off while avoiding zombies in a pitch black darkness. Also, you are given a new weapon - a reconstructed gravity gun [Element 120], which shoots out energy orbs, killing instantly everything that's in its way.  I don't have to tell you, that it is incredibly fun to play with.
Since the game is not very long, there aren't many action scenes. There are only two big action sequences, both of them at the very end. But when you experience them, you will want more! They are perfectly choreographed, with adrenalin-pumping music and lots of ways to dispatch your enemies. It's evident that a lot of care went into designing these scenes, but it's a shame that the best parts are only at the end.
The only criticism I have is the lack of guidance. There are a few rooms you will get stuck at, trying to figure out what are you supposed to do and where to go. There are moments when you have to use your new gravity gun to blast open barricaded doors or just jump through something, however, they aren't indicated very well, often just blending in with background.
+ fast and enjoyable gameplay
+ immersive atmosphere [play this at night with lights off!]
+ fun action sequences
+ music
+ sound design
+ free to play
- too short [one hour to complete the story + 20 minutes to get achievements]
- lack of guidance/tutorial

Attractive, well-made Half Life 2 mod which will give you 1-2 hours extra HL gameplay - never a bad thing. It seems to be down to the modding community to continue the Half Life experience now, as Valve seem to have given up long ago; this particular episode is compact but fun and action-packed.
A shout out in particular to the design of the environments, which is suitably dark and gritty just as City17 and Ravenholm were at their very best moments (plus some wonderfully moody lighting in places) and the new "gravity cannon" which is especially satisfying to use.
The main detractors would be the short completion time and the lack of any real plot or purpose - a vague backstory is alluded to, but never really built on or made the most of. It's also not going to win many awards for originality (besides the new weapon) as it's the standard trawl through familiar crumbling urban environments battling Combine and zombies. It's a free mod though, so there's little reason not to pick up and play and lose an enjoyable couple of hours to Half Life once again.

Could it be better? Most certainly, but Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is already great as it is, and you would be remiss to leave it hanging in physical (or digital) stores if you care the slightest bit about RPGs with a deep story, lots of choices and a cyberpunk setting.
Full review here:

tl;dr: 7.5/10. Not enough of it. Time for that upgrade.
I finished my second playthrough at "Give Me Deus Ex." difficulty, on New Game+. No matter what your playstyle, there are still questlines which require stealth and quiet takedowns, especially in Chapter 13. There are still side quests I've only seen hints of and haven't activated, but I've unlocked every augmentation, though it's possible to do well with a limited subset of them. This seems like half the game DX:HR was in terms of both locations and number & variety of quests, so let's hope that the coming DLC releases, as well as the additional "Jensen Stories" single mission quests make up for this.
I upgraded my system to 32G ram and a 4G GFX Geforce 970 card for the second playthrough, and the improvement from 10-30fps (with an old GFX Geforce 680 on low settings) to 60fps on high was dramatic (65 max on the Benchmark), especially in the rainy scenes late game. So if you're thinking about an upgrade, this would be the time to go for it.
Most of you know by now that the story is intentionally incomplete. Naturally Eidos Montreal is tight lipped about its plans, but the relative brevity of the game does suggest that there is more -- possibly much more -- to come. If this turns out to be the case, I'll be happy. Otherwise, however attractive the game is visually, and however much fun the gameplay is, there just isn't enough of it.

The gameplay is hands down, "Deus Ex" style. The sneaking is a little too easy with cloak, but the combat is a little too easy with dumb AI. Visually, the game is breathtaking. I love every bit of design direction this team has taken the DX series.
The story on the other hand, be ready to hold your breath because it is the worst part of this installment of the series. The game sets up a TON of strings that are absolutely interesting to me, and I need to figure out, only to drop me in a boss fight.
I would say, yes this game is worth buying at full price but I can't. You pay 60 dolla and you are not getting a full game. Wait for all the DLC and GoTY editions unless you are like me and NEED your Deus Ex series fix.

A welcome improvement on Deus Ex:  Human Revolution. The combat is better than its predecessor and the augmentations are more fun to use. The game rewards you for exploration and encourages multiple solutions to every quest which lends to user creativity. Human Revolution had this as well but felt more limited and penalized certain play styles. This time the game felt more like the original Deus Ex in many ways, especially the variety of approaches you can take to every problem. They removed the problematic boss fights from Revolution and replaced them with fights that allow for every possible play style to succeed. The ending is abrupt and disappointing which is obviously meant to set up another sequel. Despite that, there are so many creative ways to end a story that it just felt rushed/lazy even if you are gearing up for a sequel. If you like this kind of game it is a must play, just don't expect to be satisfied with the story as it is thin and clearly part of a greater whole.

The lord of the Rings online is a pretty rock solid MMORPG.
Players will find themselves dropped right into the action of middle earth regardless of what type of character they decide to play. The events of the Lord of The Rings Online (LOTRO) follow the events of the films as your character follows in the wake of the fellowship to aid the free peoples of middle earth against the forces of sauron.
Players can choose a host of Classes Ranging from DPS to Tanks to Healers or support. The list of all classes is listed below.
Guardian-----Tank
Warden------Tank
Champion----Melee DPS
Hunter-------Ranged DPS
Minstrel------Healer
Rune Keeper-DPS/Healer Hybrid
Lore Master--Dps/Healer/CC support Hybrid
Captain-------DPS/Support Buffer
Players can choose the races listed below.
MAN
DWARF
ELVES
HOBBITS
The game features group play at all levels by means of "Fellowships" that can be made between 2-6 players. Larger fellowships can be converted to Raid groups for 6-24 players. There are tons of instances all over middle earth that will take you anywhere from bree town to Helms  deep at the moment where players get to live their own Middle earth expiriences fighting the evils from mordor and isengard.
A very easy to use crafting system is also in place for players who prefer to craft to benefit themselves or other players. There are many different crafting skills availab;e to tailor to a player's  specific tastes.
This is a great MMO for people  who are newer to MMORPG's, or for the MMORPG veterans who simply want a taste of flavor. Everything in the user interfacce is easy to find and clearly explained throough tooltips if the player so desires them to be in and can be toggled off in the setting menu.

It's time like this where I really wish Steam didn't have just a Yes, or No recommendation button, but rather somewhere in-between. With that said here is a break down of Pros, and Cons:
The Good:
* The maps are nice, and very pleasing to the eye.
* Gun play is ok. You start out with a rifle, sniper rifle, bazooka, flame thrower, and a shotgun. Also a grenade.
* The maps while not perfect feel different from each other, and don't meld into the same gameplay with a different skin on each one. It's hard to explain, but I feel like some online FPS games just feel very bland no matter what the map, but this wasn't the case with the Mean Greens.
* It's just great to see games from the rat perspective (as I like to call it) where you play as something tiny in a seemingly huge environment. I've always loved that for some reason.
The Not So Good:
* Most rounds take as little as 3-5 minutes to complete, and sometimes even shorter. This could be good, or bad depending on what you prefer, but typically I think that 7-10 minutes is golden for your average map. I just felt like with certain maps/modes that as soon as you get into them it's over, and that's all. I think that the pacing needs to be reworked somewhat.
* When falling, or jumping you cannot fire your weapon. I'm not sure if this a bug, or by design, but frankly it's just irritating, and I can't see why it would be done on purpose. There are a lot of times that I've died, because I'm either falling, or jumping, and can't respond to it.
* While the maps are indeed unique, and very nice eye candy I think that some levels just need a rework. Most notably the bathtub one, and the kitchen one. The bathtub one you get on a duck, and float around, try to get a flag, and bring it back to the base all  the while enmities can camp from their base with sniper rifles. Boring. The kitchen level has you run to the other end of the counter top to push a cup over the ledge, and boom you're done. This isn't necessarily bad, but matches last 1-2 minutes which could be nice for some people, but I don't find it very fun personally.
* Player count, and balance - Finally one of my biggest gripes with the game so far is that teams are limited to 5v5. This isn't necessarily a problem, but I don't see why it can't be 6v6, or even 8v8 as some maps just feel sort of boring with so little people. The other issue is teams can easily stack on one team. Last game I played was 5v2 on the fish tank level which was no fun at all, and as far as I can tell there is no auto balance, or penalty for leaving.
Other Stuff:
* You may find that when you load the game, and try to join in sometimes the game will throw an error, and won't connect you. To get around this I went into the server browser, sorted by lowest ping, and highest player count, and got around it that way.
* Also there is an issue where if you alt-tab out the game will freeze up, and you'll have to kill it via Task Manager, or whatever the Linux, or Mac equivalent is.
Frankly I love the game, and I think it has the potential to be great, but a part of me feels like this wasn't quite ready for release, and maybe should have considered early access as an option. I really want to love this game, but there are some really big glaring flaws in its design. With that said I think it will improve with updates, and community feedback.
Overall I'd give it a 3.5/5

Remember the 80's, what a time that was. Personally I wasn't born, so I wouldn't know, yet playing Blood Dragon was like reliving the era that I never knew. While this game is still Far Cry 3 at it's core which isn't a problem as Far Cry 3 was by far one of the best games of 2012, this expansion takes a journey into territory not taken by any DLC or even game before it. In short, it tries to recreate the 1980's nostalgia from dialogue, setting and even its great music composed by Power Glove, which really sets the mood.
The story picks up in 2007 where you play as Rex, a American cybernetic super-soldier. He and another American cyber-soldier named Spider travel to an unnamed island to investigate Colonel Sloan, an elite agent who has gone rogue. Sound cliched? It is. It practically rips off every movie from the 1980's such as the Terminator and even makes clever references to other minor 80's shows such as great easter egg paradying the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (personal favourite), but I won't spoil it here.
While the game does not have a complete new setting from Far Cry 3, a red haze covers the screen to give a retro feel and many new locations, enemies have been added to the mix. The new weapons are also a highlight including a razor disk that demolishes and disentigrates every enemy in your path, it's one of the weirdest yet most fun weapons in years.
The story can be finished in 3-5 hours which may seem short, theres plenty to do afterwards such as saving scientists and collecting classic 80's items such as Television sets and VHS tapes. Those were the days. So with all these things to do Blood Dragon never gets stail, and for DLC you can't get 'better bang for your buck' so to speak.
Best bit is that you don't need the original Far Cry 3 to play it, so anyone can buy this game straight up and play through it's hilarious yet cheesy dialogue and action sequences so bizzarre I can't even begin to describe them here. With Blood Dragon the 1980's are back in fashion, so put on some Michael Jackson full blast and bring back that Flock of Seagulls haircut, sh**s about to go down.

Dreaming Sarah is what I would call an abstract exploration game because of metaphorical representation and unclear goals. The closest thing I can compare it too is Yume Nikki as far as artistic themes go. Even though this game is 2D, it is still reminiscent of ambient RPG maker games where exploration was done for the sake of exploration.Dreaming Sarah provides the player with emotional experience rather than extensive gameplay. The format is very interesting but many other games have already explored this concept.
It is almost like 75% of the game has nothing to do with what happens toward the end. Even though it seems like a random game it leaves you bread crumbs to piece together what happened.  The ending is somewhat open to interpretation but it came together in a way which left me very curious. There were few moments that were shocking and yet most of the game felt very casual.
My only criticism is that game should have been more consistent with tone.
You don't really need the skill to beat this game ( not that kind of a game ) However, I think it may be a little hard to figure out the next step especially when some objectives literally pop up in places that you already explored. I played a lot of games in a similar format so it was almost easy for me but your experience may be different. It is kind of logical but only in a sense if you think like a developer who is hiding things from a player. There is a nice variety of items that interact with puzzles and sometimes add new gameplay mechanics. You can 100% the game in 2-4 hours.
So the meat of the game is about how much you enjoying the ambiance of the world. Pixel art is not remarkable but perhaps it is overly simplistic on purpose. I can't help but feel that backgrounds do not always match the tone of the story. There is not a lot of detail in the background which again makes it feel like a generic platformer when it clearly isn't.There are some events that will play with your mind although I have seen those in other games. To be honest I was not feeling the vibe of the game until maybe the last quarter when story pieces started to connect.

Dreaming Sarah will probably appeal more to people who look for obscure exploration instead of a generic platformer. In my opinion, there are consistency issues with the tone of the game which take away some of the immersion (clashing tones is probably a good way to describe it). Overall this game had few shocking moments but felt mediocre for the most part. If you never played a platformer with more focus on atmosphere maybe you will get a unique experience from it . Personally, I have seen many ideas in this game associated with this "genre" which made it less impactful. I managed to enjoy it but would only recommend on sale.

I believe great artists convey clear ideas or effectively elicit specific emotion(s) through their art without the need of an explanation. If the art fails to translate the above effectively than the artist has failed.
That having been said, I've a question. WTF IS THIS GAME?
This game seems to me like some emo chick sat at a computer after getting high and said, "you know what would be soooooooo cool, making the best saddest game ever!" After which they proceeded to create this mess.
This game is all over the place and as a result you are left bewildered in the end. Was she shot, did she get in a car accident, did she hit children with her car and attempt suicide, what, what, tell me, what is it! But the game never ever does explain itself.
The visuals are mediocre at best. In fact on a lava level my chick thought I was playing Super Mario Bros, lol. I told her what the game was and she replied by saying they ripped of Super Mario Bros. It was then that I realized she was right. This game seems to take levels from other platformers, the forest level, the water level, the dungeon level, the dessert level, the other planet/moon level. All this stuffs been done before and with greater effect.
The controls are fine and you can use a controller which I did like.
But would I recommend this game? Nope, probably not.
The bottom line is this, if you are looking for an exciting adventure or a compelling storyline then you will not, I repeat, ABSOLUTELY WILL NOT FIND IT HERE.
If however you are an achievement hunter and would like to earn 22 achievements in 2 incredibly boring hours, then this may be the game for you.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided continues the momentum Human Revolution gained to produce a satisfying experience that while is freaking amazing, does stumble into some pitfalls.
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided picks right up right where Human Revolution ended, taking place 2 years after the infamous Aug Incident, a ridiculous event in which millions of augmented citizens went psycho and went on a vicious rampage against their will. While the game’s politics, themes, world and characters are all affected by the aftermath of the incident, the whole game focuses a lot more on Jensen’s goal to find out those responsible for a bombing at a train station.

Mankind Divided’s gameplay brings back the player-driven FPSRPG action of Human Revolution, except with a few subtle improvements. The game’s various new augmentations come with a cost, with them overheating your system and requiring you to disable one of your other augmentations permanently to use. This kind of system stresses the player to create a more dynamic build, which really gives the player a lasting effect on how they choose to play the game. Combine this with tightly well-designed levels and surprisingly long side-quests, and there’s a lot of content in the final package that’s fun to play through and provides all sorts of scenarios to solve.

The presentation for this game comes off strong, with its good color palette, atmospheric soundtrack, and huge level of detail. Whereas Human Revolution evoked the tone of another Human Renaissance, Mankind Divided sort of represents a kind of Dark Age following it, and the game succeeds presenting this with such a fantastic setting filled with interesting things to learn about. If there’s one aspect this game gets right, it’s the atmosphere and scale of the series overall.
However, when the game’s polish leaves, the game starts to show a side of it being rushed to completion. Although it has so much vast content, the story feels incomplete and ends just as it gets good. The game has all sorts of strange bugs and at launch, and I wasn’t even able to progress for almost an entire week due to a crash preventing me from getting past the 14th mission. I still found myself really loving the game, but it feels like I’m playing a fight between corporate executives (ironic :/) and passionate developers, which kind of sucks. Microtransactions appear in the game seemingly benign, but the fact it’s here in a single-player game, allowing players to easily breeze through the game is incredibly hard to swallow.

This is further shown in the game’s Breach Game Mode, which is an interesting diversion that allowed me to play with unique playstyles, but was a drag from the start with its endlessly long tutorial and almost free-to-play like design model. It felt like a cheap cash-in rather than a way to complement the game, and I doubt I’ll be playing it often, if at all.

It’s also no short of weird design choices. Upon finishing a unique side-quest path, you can completely remove augmentation overclocking which would sound cool but it also sounds like the game goes back on its attempt for more tight and specific builds. XP Rewards are more balanced but I found myself not needing to resort to any lethal kills with the non-lethal weapons now being very powerful and the lethal takedown once again being something players will most likely not bother with regardless their playstyle. The engine is an absolute joke and seems incapable of running anything above 60fps without issues (although most of these issues on my end seem to have been fixed), and the game skimped on boss battles but only features one major fight that is laughably unchallenging and unremarkable, to say the least.

The PC Port also seems like a strange battle between the laughably bad engine and Nixxes trying to make it smooth on PC. Thankfully, the PC Port turned out to be decent but for some reason is highly demanding when it comes to its specs. It’s a very intensive game, and while Human Revolution can run (although not optimally) on most computers nowadays, Mankind Divided will require some high-level. The game looks fine at its lower settings but it’s preferable to try to get it to run at Medium-Low settings for those who don’t have the latest graphics cards.
Despite the many issues I’ve had with the game, however, I’ve had an absolute blast playing it. I’ve really been itching for a game with this kind of emergent game to be back in my backlog again, and it’s still left me wanting more. I’m not sure if that’s a good or a bad thing. The final product turned out to be quite flawed, but its presentation and gameplay more than enough to make up for it. I just wish a franchise as historic as this didn’t had to fall in the same pitfalls most Triple AAA games nowadays have.
Also, don't get the DLC. It's seriously not worth it.

At its core, DEMD is a good game. However, as you'll see in other reviews, it basically could be called "Deus Ex: Screaming Out For A Second Half Or A Ton Of Content DLC".
I apparently noticed a few things that most players didn't so there's less "threads" poking out for me than you'd think, but there are still a fair few unanswered questions, making this game not finish with a clear resolution. It really does feel like half a game.
Now, pluses - combat is smooth, if you choose to do it, with the gun mods easy to apply, useful and feel realistic. Stealth works well, the HUD addition of running between cover is really, really nice. Some of the new augs are pretty sweet as well, although you can totally get by without unlocking a single one if you so choose.
Game faces and animations are improved from the original - they're still not perfect, but an improvement. Play DEHR and see how many people look like bobbleheads.
Some of the characters in the game are pretty cipheriffic, but again, DEHR wasn't short of similar characters. Alex I think is a good Pritchard equivalent. The Dvali are a poor man's Harvesters, honestly, but you know, not terrible. The dynamics within their organization are interesting compared to the Harvesters, which is barely mentioned in DEHR.
Some quests are really great - what I loved was just randomly running around Prague and finding quest objectives. There are very few plot-gates. If you really want, you can run headlong into the nastiest areas of Prague right away with the jump aug.
There's no real parkour action (a few jumps are possible and can break into random people's houses with some cool fluff inside - and also grab plot coupons randomly before you're required as well) but the sewers are really impressive and wide-spanning, more than DEHR, along with a lot of the ductwork in the city proper.
If you're a bit worried about buying it now, get it via a key site, wait for a sale or wait for the inevitable Game of the Year sort of edition/Legendary Edition where all the DLC will come with it. And there will be DLC or another companion game released soon enough.

Since Steam reviews do not have the middle option between Recommend/Not Recommend, I'll stick with the positive side.
How onto the game itself. It's not a bad game but it surely has where to step up.
- Dialog and face animations. They look like there are 3 animations overall, lipsync is non-existant and that "Jensen looks aside while nodding head" is going to stay in front of my eyes for a long time.
- NPC's are suffering from the extreme sameface. It was funny seeing Tars the merchant and a Palisad security guard as the same. Maybe Tars has a part-time job?
- Overall optimization. The largest issue in community. I have i7-4790k, 970GTX and 16GB RAM, but left my  settings at high. There is no need to set to ultra, because there is no improvement at all. I cannot tell where all resources go as the world does not look THAT amazing.
- Main story is based much less on conspiracy theories, that are the corner stone of DE series and more on today's realities. It does not have such a punch like ones in DE or DEHR had. Faulty writing or publisher's interference made that the game has ended without answering many questions, baiting into the next sequel.
- Some small glitches here and there, like raining inside, mismatched radio calls.
* I did not like revamped stealth. It obstructs your actions by not where you want to go but where the game offers you to go. It makes delays that can end up in blown cover when you could not act fast enough.
* I missed some exotic heavy weapons that have been present in DEHR. No plasma rifles, no laser rifles, no rocket launchers.
* Breach mode. It's ok to break from the game, but I much more preferred a longer main game.
+ Side missions are amazing. Good variety and tells a lot about the world.
+ Detailed map has much more where to go, what to explore and many more route options.
+ Where weapons are lacking, augs are awesome and supports your stealth/full frontal assault lethal/non-lethal gameplay.
+ Gun customization is nice and crafting helps a lot.
+ Music is also nice, Michael McCann is still in his style.
+ Adequate atmosphere and nice architecture. You can see people suffering and trying their best to survive in Prague. Prague looks great, it is exactly how would I imagine looking in 2029.
To summarize, the game itself is fine,
. DLCs/publisher's practices are terrible, stay away. If you have a semi-decent PC and are a fan of Deus Ex, get the base version. If not, wait for a sale or complete edition. Squeenix games get cheap pretty fast.

Grand Theft Auto V evolves nearly every mechanic that was in the previous Grand Theft Auto games. As far as driving goes, the vehicles have been greatly improved, with Rockstar running more complex physics on them. The cars can even hold to the ground slightly better. The driving mechanics feel more like a racing game, particularly the Midnight Club series, compared to Grand Theft Auto IV's rocky, boat-like handling system. The shooting mechanics are better in terms of the feel of the mechanics and larger compared to the melee mechanics in the game, but that doesn't mean that the melee combat won't be fun, as it as been improved over the previous titles as well. Weapon selection has now also been changed. Instead of the old way of selecting through all the weapons, there is now a Weapon Wheel, which is similar to the one featured in Red Dead Redemption, another game made by Rockstar Games. Grand Theft Auto V draws inspirations from many different Rockstar titles in the past, including Max Payne 3, Midnight Club, Manhunt, and Red Dead Redemption.
There are many unique features in the game, one of those features is that when the players are playing as one of three protagonists in the game, the other two are out living their independent daily lives, and you will be surprised by what you find the characters doing when you switch back into them. Another unique feature is that the character swapping feature is executed in a Google Earth-styled manner and was displayed during a Game Informer demo, which was showed to have ran smoothly and without lag. The PC, PS4 and Xbox One versions present an exclusive feature, the first-person mode The whole game can be played through the eyes of the protagonist. This gameplay mode presents a whole new way to play the game. Cars have detailed interiors different from one another, shooting is like that of an FPS game.
New activities have been added, such as yoga, triathlons, jet skiing, parachuting, tennis, golf, and scuba diving. Random events have also been added to the game and can appear any time, while the player is exploring the map. The mobile phone has returned from Grand Theft Auto IV but is now only used for calling the player's contacts, surfing the web, and quick saving. Giving people the middle finger is another new feature the player can use while in a vehicle (which Rockstar recommended you do in various locations around Los Santos to see the outcome of this effect, depending on where the player is at, they will get different reactions from pedestrians).
Rockstar has also made changes to the pedestrian mechanics; some pedestrians can be seen at the bus stops in East Los Santos, and the same people can reappear in Rockford Hills working in the gardens of the opulent mansions. Some minor mechanics that help convey the environment and appearance of Los Santos occur at certain times of day, such as a sprinkler system being turned on in the morning in wealthy areas like Morningwood.
The map is larger than Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, Grand Theft Auto IV, and Red Dead Redemption combined. After some calculations by members of
, that would equal to around 27.5 square miles/71.2 km2 when land and sea are combined.

Okey so this is my first review and I'll try my best to make it helpfull and understandable as well es short. I played it on an alienware gaming lap top and used several mods that add new characters and pet models.
I hope this review will be noticed besides all the positive ones and will help some to rethink if it's worth buying.
Pros:
+ Graphic design (can be a con as well)
+ Pet, is usefull, can be customized in many ways, sell and buy things when you are in dungeons and fight with you
+ Classic hack and slay with easy and good controls
+ Nice requirement system for gear (either skill level or player level)
+ You can play with mods!!! (Awards will be given to you if you play the modded version as well)
+ Characters explode and killing feels good in general
+ Different possibilities to respawn with one option where you lose nothing
+ Also runs well when played on a toaster
Neither nors:
* Unique items can drop multiple times
* Very simple and boring menu, but works
* Sometimes I couldn't pick up loot because it was unreachable. but it mostly was bad items or one or two gold drops, some may get a problem here though
* I always felt like my character looked like a level 2 mmorpg character except for one or two cool weapons
* It has a story. No big plots (needed).
* Manawhisps (monster class) were invisible for me but easy to track because of shot direction
* Bushes and landscape details (like bushes or wood) were flickering every now and then
* No need to buy anything from vendors except for enchantments (maybe!) or identification rolls
Cons:
- Sometimes overpowered loot drops. Some may like it or say that I could use worse loot instead but that's not the point of this game. (examples for op loot: I could use a level 85 weapon with level 35 because I made my armor set so it would boost the stats I needed for the weapon. New damage from 200-400 raised to 1300-2400 and magic damage was similar; other example was a weapon with 500hp lifesteal that gave me 1/4 of my maximum hp every hit)
This is just not the point of the game.
- The inventory of my pet was broken the first 18 hours of the game so my pet could sell the items in its inventory but I could not retrieve them, once they were placed in the pet inventory.
- Only 4 standard classes and 14 boring pets
- Can't change difficulty midgame (I mean wtf?!)
- After playing multiplayer and finding new equipment it wasn't saved which lead to very frustrating moments
- If enemies run away from a melee character it will be hard to kill them because the character has to stand still to attack and won't hit targets if they move away from him. (Yes you could use skills but it shouldn't be necessary)
- Character has a pretty stupid or not working way finding very often
Conclusion:
I think it is a decent game that has a few mayor flaws that may not occur for some players (why else so many positive reviews??). So besides that it does nothing particularly wrong but doesn't stand out either and I think there are better games that are worth investing a bit more money for a lot more or better content. The best thing about this game in my oppinion is that because it doesn't offer a lot itself, it has the workshop so others can add the "missing" content.
I can't really recommend a game that doesn't offer much, has some mayer flaws, doesn't really stand out and where the community has to add most concerning content and possibilities. Still it might be a fun game when it's on sale but not more.

I know the developers and everyone else involved in making the game deserve to get paid for what they worked so hard creating, but the prices aren't realistic. If the prices of the DLC's were the same as what I paid for the game (CAD $4.99 during the 2016 Summer Sale) and they had included the option to have control over your sims like in The Sims 2, then I would give this a 10/10.
Summary? Great good, bad DLC prices, 8/10 rating.

Grand Theft Auto V evolves nearly every mechanic that was in the previous Grand Theft Auto games. As far as driving goes, the vehicles have been greatly improved, with Rockstar running more complex physics on them. The cars can even hold to the ground slightly better. The driving mechanics feel more like a racing game, particularly the Midnight Club series, compared to Grand Theft Auto IV's rocky, boat-like handling system. The shooting mechanics are better in terms of the feel of the mechanics and larger compared to the melee mechanics in the game, but that doesn't mean that the melee combat won't be fun, as it as been improved over the previous titles as well. Weapon selection has now also been changed. Instead of the old way of selecting through all the weapons, there is now a Weapon Wheel, which is similar to the one featured in Red Dead Redemption, another game made by Rockstar Games. Grand Theft Auto V draws inspirations from many different Rockstar titles in the past, including Max Payne 3, Midnight Club, Manhunt, and Red Dead Redemption.
There are many unique features in the game, one of those features is that when the players are playing as one of three protagonists in the game, the other two are out living their independent daily lives, and you will be surprised by what you find the characters doing when you switch back into them. Another unique feature is that the character swapping feature is executed in a Google Earth-styled manner and was displayed during a Game Informer demo, which was showed to have ran smoothly and without lag. The PC, PS4 and Xbox One versions present an exclusive feature, the first-person mode The whole game can be played through the eyes of the protagonist. This gameplay mode presents a whole new way to play the game. Cars have detailed interiors different from one another, shooting is like that of an FPS game.
New activities have been added, such as yoga, triathlons, jet skiing, parachuting, tennis, golf, and scuba diving. Random events have also been added to the game and can appear any time, while the player is exploring the map. The mobile phone has returned from Grand Theft Auto IV but is now only used for calling the player's contacts, surfing the web, and quick saving. Giving people the middle finger is another new feature the player can use while in a vehicle (which Rockstar recommended you do in various locations around Los Santos to see the outcome of this effect, depending on where the player is at, they will get different reactions from pedestrians).
Rockstar has also made changes to the pedestrian mechanics; some pedestrians can be seen at the bus stops in East Los Santos, and the same people can reappear in Rockford Hills working in the gardens of the opulent mansions. Some minor mechanics that help convey the environment and appearance of Los Santos occur at certain times of day, such as a sprinkler system being turned on in the morning in wealthy areas like Morningwood.
The map is larger than Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, Grand Theft Auto IV, and Red Dead Redemption combined. After some calculations by members of
, that would equal to around 27.5 square miles/71.2 km2 when land and sea are combined.

When I saw this game on sale for 59 cents I figure I'd give it a shot. I wasn't dissapointed. It had most of what I look for in a game: ambient soundtrack, surreal and diverse environments, backtracking, meaningful powerups, and plenty of exploration.

The core gameplay mechanic of controlling two characters simultaneously is inherently difficult, but the puzzles in the game don't try to push the limits of the concept much. On the one hand, this means you may feel the game never really gets challenging. On the other hand, it also means it never gets to controller smashing frustration either.
The visual aesthetic of the game provides a great deal of charm, to the point where there are benches along the path to sit and enjoy beautiful views.
The game's biggest strength is probably the emotional penetration of its story. The characters all speak in a fictional language with no subtitles, but the core ideas and major themes are easily interpretted. I cried at least 3 different times during my 2 hour playthrough.

At its core, DEMD is a good game. However, as you'll see in other reviews, it basically could be called "Deus Ex: Screaming Out For A Second Half Or A Ton Of Content DLC".
I apparently noticed a few things that most players didn't so there's less "threads" poking out for me than you'd think, but there are still a fair few unanswered questions, making this game not finish with a clear resolution. It really does feel like half a game.
Now, pluses - combat is smooth, if you choose to do it, with the gun mods easy to apply, useful and feel realistic. Stealth works well, the HUD addition of running between cover is really, really nice. Some of the new augs are pretty sweet as well, although you can totally get by without unlocking a single one if you so choose.
Game faces and animations are improved from the original - they're still not perfect, but an improvement. Play DEHR and see how many people look like bobbleheads.
Some of the characters in the game are pretty cipheriffic, but again, DEHR wasn't short of similar characters. Alex I think is a good Pritchard equivalent. The Dvali are a poor man's Harvesters, honestly, but you know, not terrible. The dynamics within their organization are interesting compared to the Harvesters, which is barely mentioned in DEHR.
Some quests are really great - what I loved was just randomly running around Prague and finding quest objectives. There are very few plot-gates. If you really want, you can run headlong into the nastiest areas of Prague right away with the jump aug.
There's no real parkour action (a few jumps are possible and can break into random people's houses with some cool fluff inside - and also grab plot coupons randomly before you're required as well) but the sewers are really impressive and wide-spanning, more than DEHR, along with a lot of the ductwork in the city proper.
If you're a bit worried about buying it now, get it via a key site, wait for a sale or wait for the inevitable Game of the Year sort of edition/Legendary Edition where all the DLC will come with it. And there will be DLC or another companion game released soon enough.

Since Steam reviews do not have the middle option between Recommend/Not Recommend, I'll stick with the positive side.
How onto the game itself. It's not a bad game but it surely has where to step up.
- Dialog and face animations. They look like there are 3 animations overall, lipsync is non-existant and that "Jensen looks aside while nodding head" is going to stay in front of my eyes for a long time.
- NPC's are suffering from the extreme sameface. It was funny seeing Tars the merchant and a Palisad security guard as the same. Maybe Tars has a part-time job?
- Overall optimization. The largest issue in community. I have i7-4790k, 970GTX and 16GB RAM, but left my  settings at high. There is no need to set to ultra, because there is no improvement at all. I cannot tell where all resources go as the world does not look THAT amazing.
- Main story is based much less on conspiracy theories, that are the corner stone of DE series and more on today's realities. It does not have such a punch like ones in DE or DEHR had. Faulty writing or publisher's interference made that the game has ended without answering many questions, baiting into the next sequel.
- Some small glitches here and there, like raining inside, mismatched radio calls.
* I did not like revamped stealth. It obstructs your actions by not where you want to go but where the game offers you to go. It makes delays that can end up in blown cover when you could not act fast enough.
* I missed some exotic heavy weapons that have been present in DEHR. No plasma rifles, no laser rifles, no rocket launchers.
* Breach mode. It's ok to break from the game, but I much more preferred a longer main game.
+ Side missions are amazing. Good variety and tells a lot about the world.
+ Detailed map has much more where to go, what to explore and many more route options.
+ Where weapons are lacking, augs are awesome and supports your stealth/full frontal assault lethal/non-lethal gameplay.
+ Gun customization is nice and crafting helps a lot.
+ Music is also nice, Michael McCann is still in his style.
+ Adequate atmosphere and nice architecture. You can see people suffering and trying their best to survive in Prague. Prague looks great, it is exactly how would I imagine looking in 2029.
To summarize, the game itself is fine,
. DLCs/publisher's practices are terrible, stay away. If you have a semi-decent PC and are a fan of Deus Ex, get the base version. If not, wait for a sale or complete edition. Squeenix games get cheap pretty fast.

I wish there was a halfway point between recommend and not recommend. Because personally I'd rate this game as somewhere in between, but overall I'm going with "no".
As a game, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is very good. Gameplay is a bit easier and more streamlined than Human Revolution, however it's definitely designed for XBOX controllers or gamepads in mind so consider that when setting yourself up.
Pros
- Good game design, fluid and easy to control and interact with the game world.
- Fun in the way choice makes a difference from how you play the game to dialogue. You can run in guns ablaze or stealth your way through everything. Kill everyone or nobody.
- Good voice acting.
- Excellent story as per the norm for Deus Ex.
- Remote hacking is stupidly fun in realtime and I kinda hope that future installments expand on this mechanic! I like it more than the main hacking minigame with the way it can be done in realtime while in combat or stealth sneaking.
Neutral
- An entire crafting system that seems sorely underutilized to the point where all I ended up crafting, ever, were biocells. It looks like they tried to create a cool user interface to craft useful items, but there's so much loot to get in general, the majority of the options are useless.
- Beat the game on the hardest difficulty setting with minimal effort. Never used a single health kit. Considering I'm hardly a decent FPS player it seems a bit too easy, but Deus Ex is known for its story dynamic, not impossibly hard shoot outs. On my next playthrough I'm just gonna sell all the health items. Storing them took up too much valuable space.
- Really stupid miniquest where you find triangles and download a cell phone app to scan and get "specials" from. I'll save you the trouble. I downloaded the app, signed onto Square Enix, and scanned two triangles, only leading to silly youtube channels, to which I felt like that was a lot of time wasted. There's another minigame for Deus Ex Go that I didn't even try, and really don't feel like I want to. This is neither a pro nor con because it doesn't hurt the game any but I really have no idea what that was supposed to add, if anything.
Cons
- Something's weird about the lip syncing. It's just... Not right. But it's not terrible and easy to ignore. It's just weird since the original Deus Ex is what pioneered lip syncing in gaming and it just comes off so weird here.
- Despite how great the story is, it ends a lot sooner than you'd expect and seems strangely narrow in scope compared to every other Deus Ex game. Even Deus Ex 2. You'll be playing through the game, expecting yourself to be barely 1/4 the way through, and suddenly the game just... Ends.
- That weird in-game store. It exists to tempt you into spending more money on the game than you already have, even though everything there can be attained legitimately through gameplay.
- On release there was a strange bug that caused tutorial text to permanently plaster onto the screen. Literally throughout the rest of the game, it stayed on your HUD. Eventually this was patched, but I still had the issue long after it was supposedly fixed. (It might be good and gone by the time of this review)
After playing through the whole game, I can 100% assure anyone buying this that the in game store doesn't offer anything you can't just get by playing the normal game. It seems to be less of a "pay to win" and more of a "pay to cheat". By the time I was at the finale to the game, I had so many Praxis kits from standard play, that I was just sticking them wherever to try out Augs I wasn't even using.
Here's where I gotta be straight, though. The game was good. But short and narrow. A lot shorter and narrower than I'd like for a triple A title at full game price. Even after doing all the side missions, and completed the main game, I felt like I only played a quarter of a real Deus Ex game and was left unsatisfied. Overall, I feel a lot more like I just played the expansion set to Deus Ex: Human Revolutions, and not a full fledged sequel.
And that's where I'm a little concerned. With the in game cash shop, I feel like that's exactly what they wanted. I can't say for sure, but are they going to gradually release DLC to "finish" the rest of the game, now, and make us pay even more? Or is this the game we got until the next one?
Now here's the thing. The game is still fun. I don't regret paying for it. But after going through it all, I feel like most people will feel very gipped and become disappointed after playing through it, and the in game store makes me extremely worried about what this will mean about the future of Deus Ex. It clearly doesn't 'harm' the game as it is right now, but it's still worrying if it grows from "pay to cheat" to "pay to win" and possibly eventually "pay to actually play the next mission" that we see on cell phones these days. Particularly since a real world cell phone app is required to partake in Triangles and bonus Praxis Kits.
Overall? It's not worth the listed price. But if you're really into Deus Ex, that probably won't matter. Still a good game, but expect it to play like a big expansion set, not a full game in of itself.

I've not completed this yet but I just thought I'd make a point on how good this mod is. The atmosphere is tremendous, environments are detailed and fully immersive. The game is a masterclass of narrative through play. The improvements made to the physics engine are wonderful. Most notably, large objects function in a believable way and certain map points are now largely destructable. The new game mechanics are fantastic, specifically zombie reactions to light and darkness, and the new QR system which delivers plot points in an interesting and unique fashion. The combat scenarios are exceptional and feature much larger encounters than I am normally used to in a Half Life 2 mod. But the most standout feature for me is the Propulsion Cannon. It is a wonderful weapon that functions well in general and even more so for those accustomed to rocket jumping. In conclusion, this is a beyond solid modification to a framework that has already been excacerbated, and has began to show it's age. This is a breath of fresh air. It's free, and concentrated with some potent and solid gameplay. It's rather on the short side, but it is tooth-rottingly sweet. Give it a shot.
