Before starting the game you're given the option to start the vanilla version and the Workshop supported version. You can move your vanilla character to the Workshop version however the character you save your progress with Workshop mods on will no longer be allowed back to the vanilla game.
The game's difficulties range from Casual, Normal, Veteran, & Elite where the differences in these are that the gold drops are lower and enemy damage & health are increased the higher the setting. In Elite mode the game doesn't just feel harder, it feels like more like an endurance because I found myself constantly having to hit, run, heal, hit, run, heal, and repeat wasting more time than I should be wasting if I was on Veteran because everything on Elite can kill you in a flash and it doesn't help that the baddies take a hell of a lot longer to kill because of the artificial difficulty of increased baddie HP.
There's a an option to check whether or not you want to activate "Hardcore" mode for the rest of a character's playthrough where all it means is that one death means you can't play that character anymore so this is really for those who like to be more pressured into being careful to stay alive.
Unlike the first game you now have a choice of 4 classes however the previous classes have been removed though they all use similar & new equipment as the first. Each class has a handful amount of unique skills but I've found that I was really only putting points in an incredibly low amount of them all the way up to the end-game & max level, 100, leaving probably 80% of the skills without even a single point placed. Though effective this leaves the combat to show how simplistic its action is which all-in-all is just hit, run, & maybe heal. No matter how fancy the skills you've put the points on it's still just run, attack, run, and possibly heal up with a potion or a spell so should heavy damage be taken. You can only "respec" the last 3 skills you've placed points on so you can do a small bit of testing to find out what suits your preference.
The controls for the game are typical isometric ARPG style with the all too likely-to-become problematic mouse-to-move and extensively rebindable keys with the exception of the mouse buttons being unrebindable. I found that the mouse controls can often be wonky; when I try to move to the opposite side of a crowd of baddies to get away from them for some reason the character would sometimes move to them and attack instead despite the mouse being nowhere near them. During critical situations it becomes an incredible nuisance.
Though very diverse in skins, models, & sounds almost all enemy attacks are similar to one another so I found that fighting just became repetitive with the exception of having some new skills to toy with but still overall becomes the same hit & run rule in combat. Even the bosses are fought the same and the way they fight you feel hardly any different from mob attacks.
The environment as well are very limited in variety. The general idea of different types of environment aside from the scenery with some different turns and slight elevations are "don't walk on this right now or you'll get hurt", some levers or switches you have to activate to progress the game, and putting items in environmental sockets to again further progress.
Normally when anything dies in a map they stay dead. When setting your game to an "internet" session you can "reset" the entire world so everything can be killed again. Even all the treasure chests will be up for another round of loot.
The multiplayer's functional & pretty basic; go to the lobby, make or join someone's session, and you just play from there either helping one another or doing your own things. Each person in a multiplayer session sees & gets their own loot from drops so there won't really be any stealing of items. If you and some other people have the exact same mods and sometimes load order of mods you can play the modded game with those people.
Despite all its "problems" and for what it is the game works and does pretty well at what it tries to be even if there's not a whole lot new or special when compared to many other ARPGs like this. It can be good fun to just isometrically dungeon crawl seemingly killing endlessly especially with someone you know but because it lacks special things it can start to be incredibly tedious & repetitive incredibly fast where your only possible source of replayability is likely trying out the different classes, workshop mods, and/or the multiplayer.

PROS:
- Great music!
- 10 maps, each with its own game mode.
- 5 players per team (the magic numebr given the size of the maps)
- Immersive and beautiful graphics
- A silly and fun feel reminicent of TF2
- A variety of balanced weapons to choose from
CONS (many of these are likely to change, as the game is very new):
- Hard to connect to a server without being disconnected, and hard to find a server close to me (US west)
- No shooting while in the air
- Scoreboard seems very vague - it's hard for me to tell how much I'm really helping the team
- Not a whole lot of emphasis on teamwork (there should be in an objective based game)
Overall great game, worth the money.

If you're looking for a positive review, then you're in the wrong place, HOWEVER, if you're here for a tremendous chicken Stir Fry recipe, THEN LOOK NO FURTHER!
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) fillet or sirloin steak, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the beef and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the beef to the pan and heat through. Serve with noodles.

Soulstorm was one of the last time that DLC (or expansion as it was called back then) was truly worth it (instead of paying for hidden locked content so common these days). Still, it was not as revolutionary to the franchise as Dark Crusade was or even as good as the first game was.
The Good:
The 2 new factions feel distinct from the rest, especially with their special powers. The AI definitely had improved, especially in campaign (being used to the one in Dark Crusade, the AI did surprise me when I played the campaign - no more steamrolling with 3 Guardsmen squads on easy) and the balance has been somewhat restored (e.g. Space Marine Squad with max. 4 heavy weapons and Imperial Guard can now have 5 heavy weapons per squad).
The Acceptable:
I have conflicting feeling about the campaign. It was pretty much the same campaign like Dark Crusade, except on a planetary system but they introduced some fun innovations like the webway portal provinces, supply lines and stronghold bonuses - all which I strongly approve. But it wasn't long into the campaign before I realized how lazy the storytelling was; the dialogues were minimal (no more taunting in the beginning or after some objectives were completed in the Stronghold missions), awkward and stiff and the characters were forgettable at most. Some cutscenes were so poorly done that you wonder if they use first-year interns to do it.
The Bad:
Terrible voice acting that gave rise to the legend of METHUL BAWKSES, SPHESS MEHREENS and THE EMPRAH (although the new update restored the in-game voices to the good ones from Dark Crusade for some units (SM Force Commander has Thule's, Chaos Lord has Eliphas' [unfortunately they forgot to put Sindri back]), somewhat correcting this problem). Air units, which I was initially excited about, can really destroy the rebalanced gameplay; the Tau Barracuda can wreck an entire base on its own, the Ork Bomma is similarly devastating to infantry and Space Marines will only need the Land Speeder Tempest en masse).

Even if you haven't heard of the Warhammer franchise, but dig even the concept of RTS and dozens of screaming religous space loonatics tearing eachother into bloody pieces, you will love this.
This game is one of the least demanding RTS in terms of player competency so newcomers to the genre will feel immediately welcome.
Also, the resource model is point-capture, meaning that even if you try to build up the ultimate army before deciding it's time to kill the other guy, you still have to issue squads (not single units) out in the open to capture and protect resource points to even start making that army. Like WarCraft 3's hero leveling system, this leaves each match no room for snorefest turtling and it's sweet sweet killing all the time, every time.
But be warned, even though the industry is seriously lacking in game demos, do not try this game's demo. You'll only get to try the wimpiest race in the game in 2 lousy singleplayer levels. For the uninitiated, this would misrepresent the game as it has motherloving 9 RACES to play in Total-War-style singleplayer and 2 for multiplayer (buy the base game and/or the other expansions to play their respective races in multiplayer) - one of which is the goth kid Dark Eldar and the other (my personal favorite), the screaming roid rage space nuns of Humanity itself: The Sisters of Battle.
Note: Game crashes if you alt-tab. Extremely embarrassing bug to leave untouched for however many years that this came out.

Lord of the Rings Online depicts the world of tolkien very effectivly, mixing both the book's and the movie's perspectives on the characters and locations. The Epic Story as named follows much of the original story of Lord of the Rings while adding some background that most might not know, so it adds some interesting stories and their relation to the fellowship of the ring. The game mechanics by themselves are like most other MMORPG's out there -skill trees, quickslots full of skills, quest hubs, etc- causing most to play thorugh the first time not for new style of gameplay but for the story. The Skirmish system at lvl 20 and up provides a very good multiplayer or singleplayer, of which I recommend the former, experiance to the key locations of Middle Earth. However it should be noted that most of the content above lvl 30 needs some form of payment. The Mithril Edition provides a wonderful bargain of USD 20 by digital download or USD 10 at some stores, as it will provide enough content to get a character to lvl 60 without much hassle. From then on however it can be a bit more pricy. The newest Expansion is still at a price of USD 40, but the previous 4 expansions can be purchased for only USD 40 which includes Moria, Mirkwood, Isengard, and Riders of Rohan. This means to get a character to lvl 85 at the moment takes around USD 50-60 and to cap around USD 100. One can earn in game Turbine Points which would allow them to buy the quests for a region, however this takes alot of grinding and I find it better to use those points for the trait slot that a f2p player needs to unlock. For the USD 100 price point and the content it gives the game is wonderful indeed, and if you play it wisely you could spend less than the 100 and still get to cap. All in all I give Lord of the Rings Online a 8.5/10 as it provides a large amount of content for a reasonable price point.
Note: I have had the game before steam and thus my hours on steam do not reflect my game time.

hands down one of the greatest and most addicting games i've played. though it might not be the most graphically impressive but the gameplay is so good that it doesnt need to be. It's infinitely replayable, with a great modding community. It is possible to get burned out on it, but returning after some time it becomes enjoyable as ever.
You lead a warband around the land of Calradia a land torn by civil war, starting the game you create your character, choose your starting stats and backstory, and finally in which faction you want to spawn initially (this has no impact on the game). There is no centeral narrative the story is what the player makes it, You can become a mercenarry employed by a lord, a vassal of a kingdom or a king in your own right, you can marry, take part in tornaments, become a merchant, own buisinesses, or become a bandit and a villain attacking caravans and looting villages.
Arriving in the town of your choice you are immediately attacked and either way, if you beat your attacker or he beats you a town merchant comes to you with a quest, this quest like all quests in bannerlord is optional, but regarding quests if a player decides to take a quest and does not complete it, it can have negative consequences, mainly detoriated relations with the quest giver(which can either be a lord or king, a village, or a town).
To create your warband you recruit men from villages, who over time and through battles you level up through a troop tree to elite warriors, to new players this can be frustrating as initially even looters can destroy your party and take you captive, so you have to carefully navigate the map and only pick to fight when the force is weaker than you but be carefull that no other enemy parties are in the imediate vicinity as those can join the force you choose to attack. other than recruiting villagers you can visit taverns to find mercenaries and companions. companions are very usefull in the game as you can form a special skill set for all of them (healer, tracker, trainer, trader, engineer etc.) so the player himself can focus on his fighting and leading skills.
The battles, which are the main draw of the game, are grat fun.Most players prefer horse archery which is a very rewarding expierience especially against mounted targets, as your enemies ragdolls are dragged behind horses after you kill them. You can charge at the enemy like an idiot or you can be a more strategic and issue commands to your troops, and manipulate them the way you want. If you charge you should know that if you fall your troops loose morale and if you are unable to fight the auto-resolve battle option isn't really trust worthy you can even loose elite troops to a band of looters with it.
Sieges are a big part of the game because thats how you gain territory, but they are also the weakest part, as there is usually only one ladder on the walls and results in a slaughter for the attacking side, and if you climb up the ladder youll usually be promptly cut down, its advisable for the player to just shoot arrows at the defenders, from down bellow.
Another part of the game that can be a bit frustrating and immersion breaking is that later in the game most lords become turncloaks or are charged with treason and every few game days the each kingdom has different lords.
the game also has a multiplayer component which is usuallly utter chaos, but fun none the less. It doesnt have auto blocking so you'll have to learn directional blocking. initially the skill gap can be very high.
Over all this game is a one of a kind expierience, and evidently by the footage that has been released so far, the sequal will iron out the few weaknesses it has, but we dont know when that will be so i do recommend getting this game for the time being, especially if it's on sale.

As a story experience, Mankind Divided is lacking. The overall story doesn't feel as deep as they would like you to believe, certainly not as much as Human Revolution. It was clear that the devs were made to stretch the conspiracy across 2 games. There is plenty of world building for you to find if you take the extra time to search Prague, and that remains strong, just where it all leads is a bit disappointing.
As a gameplay experience, Mankind Divided is immensely satisfying. The level design is improved greatly upon Human Revolution's already stellar foundation (yes I know that was game 3, but it's a new team compared to the original). The gameplay is also greatly improved. Getting into cover can be a bit wonky at times (say if the object is movable), but movement within cover is easier than ever. Augmentation use is a little weird using the F1-4 keys, so I recommend switching them with the regular 1-4 keys, particularly if you are a stealth/non-lethal focused player.
On a technical level, it looks great and maintained a really solid framerate on my GTX960, loading new areas can cause some stuttering though(after subway rides). Just sit there a second and let it pass, and then back to buttery smooth.
Overall, I recommend the game. The improved gameplay does make up for the lackluster story in my opinion, and I'm currently playing a second run with new game+ and noticing new scenarios based on differences in how I screwed up the first time to how I aced it the second.

For example, your city advisor may give you a quest to clear out a nearby mine so that miners can be sent in to extract resources for your growing city.  So, not only do you tackle this "dungeon" from an action RPG perspective (fighting its denizens, finding loot, etc.), but once it is cleared, your city will benefit from its resources.  Also, some of the loot you find will directly add to your city's resources.  Another exciting example is that the soldiers you recruit from the RTS aspect (the barracks) can be tasked to follow you so that you can take on, for example, an outlaw base from the action RPG perspective.
The game is still early in development and many RTS features have not yet been implemented, but from the interface, you can see where the developers are going.  I was excited just reading the developers' posts in the forums to get an inkling of the features that are in development.  Also, while there are bugs, the developers are extremely responsive and helpful.
This is a unique game, and enjoyable in its present state.  With the responsiveness of the developers, you can genuinely feel that you are part of its development.  So, if a blending of action RPG and RTS appeals to you, then I highly recommend this game.

I don’t recommend to buy this early access product.
On the other hand the game is also as cheap as a pizza. Nevertheless I recommend to buy the pizza.
If you are searching for excuses, then let’s just say the game is in a way too early stage of development.
I expect the game to be of good quality in around 10 or even 20 years (I’m serious), if I extrapolate the development of the last half year. This is somehow the best case. Actually I think the game will never be good, because the stuff that is already implemented is implemented badly. Of course you can say that basically EVERYTHING in the game is a placeholder and will get better – but what’s then left to review?
What you can do in the game is walking around, building 5 types of uninteresting houses, which do uninteresting things and hitting clone bandits and goblin with your metalstick of choice. That’s basically everything. With an emphasize on walking around.
You can talk about potential and what will be implemented in the future but the stuff that is already there is of very low quality so that I’m not really hyped but afraid by future plans.
To make a mediocre game out of this, the first step would be to remove all content that is currently in the game and rework it from scratch.
Review on the current state:
The “rpg”:
There are quests. You get all the quests from one person. When you are done with that, your quests will come from a different person. The quests are written by someone who definitely doesn’t like the job. They are extremely boring and full of logical inconsequence, that you might think a 5 year old came up with them. The execution of the quest is, again, unappealing. You will walk from A to B, kill stuff and come back. Most of the time you have to walk, walk, walk. This becomes quite boring fast because everything looks the very same.
The world:
Boring, empty and on top of that also a bit cheap: looks like a the-elder-scrolls mod from a beginner, tiles in dungeons are not fitting together, floating houses etc.
“AI”:
feels very very cheap. You will wipe out dozens of enemies with placing a ring of fire on the ground and wait for them to walk through it (open area) and die.
Controls:
clunky to say the least. I like that your character has mass and accelerates. However, the execution of related animations is completely buggy.
Sound:
ok but completely bugged when there a more enemies around (trying to) making noise.
Graphics/engine:
good. Something tells me that they just bought the engine.
”RTS”:
completely non existing. In the end you kill all the stuff yourself, because your bot-companions (5-10) will not follow you into a “dungeon”. When there’s finally an outdoor “quest” (‘walk there, kill everything, walk back’), your “army” will be killed by the first 3 goblins on the way, while you will kill the remaining 50 on your own (easily, because the AI is so ♥♥♥♥ing stupid). They could just remove this militia pseudo rts stuff for now, the game would be the very same.
Dungeons:
everything looks the ♥♥♥♥ing same. You will even have complete areas that will look exactly the same but its not (takes a while to find out…) ! Don’t try to draw a map on your own, you will get even more confused because of the geometrical failure of how areas are connected.
Town building:
completely without any strategic component. Place the stuff on the ground and you are done. No decision matters. After 5 hours of playing of which you spent 3,5 hours of walking through emptiness or making a coffee in the kitchen (while your resources increase over time like in a mobile game) you have built everything that is allowed to be build (like 10 houses or so. Built means you have placed them on the ground and now they produce resource over time that you need for nothing but placing houses or suicide paper bots called army if you wish)
In the end you may ask yourself why the ♥♥♥♥ did you place the first house on the ground? Wasn’t it the very same? Now there are houses, and I have 3000 of some resource I don’t need – but who cares?
I guess the sandbox is that you can rotate the house before placing.

The game is good! It has alot of potential. It also has alot of work to go. That said, unlike most early Access games that charge up front 29.99, no need to feel skeptical about this one. Not to mention, it isn't 29.99, but way less.
To put it simply. If you like TES series, if you like Fable, or if you just like RPG games in general, this game is for you. The developers continue to perform updates every month, requests feedback from the fanbase, and executes that feedback or taken in consideration. Mostly executed though!
What I really like about the game is the combat is old school hack and slash. Have to be tactical or you'll get hit or ganked. The building system is pretty cool. Can give me a nice crisp highly graphic game and it can still suck, whereas you have something like Undertale and it's a god send.
The only down side is jaggy combat and some issues with AMD cpu's. Both are being worked on.
Other than that, I'd give this game a try. Whether it be now or wait for a sale. I give it at least 6 months down the road, and LOTS of awesome content will be in this game to where it'll be in the Overwhelmingly Positive status.

If not the best, then it's definitely the second best in the entire Dawn of War series, and possibly the best out of all WH40k games. It remains more accurate in squad size than any other RTS based in the WH40k world, and keeps everything pretty well balanced.

NOTE: This is the final version of Dawn of War, and really the only one you need. Dawn of War had four races. Each expansion pack added at least one additional race. Soul Storm was the final expansion, and includes all of the races for the game (except Tyrannids, but there's a great mod that adds them!) The only things it lacks are the individual campaigns from the expansions, but frankly, they're not interesting enough to bother with. JUST BUY SOULSTORM, and you've got everything you need.
Alright, the review. Dawn of War is a real-time strategy game the relies very heavily on position. Unlike most RTS games, where you can simply hunker down and build up an army, here you have to go looking for the scarce resources you need. That means taking risks. Once you have what you need, you get to see a Warhammer 40,000 army in action in a way never before seen. You move your troops in squads, and those squads act on their own. You can only do so much; march them into certain death and they'll break, panic, and end up getting destroyed. You are very much the commander here, not a fighting participant, and your orders mean less than the situation in front of them. The won't retreat, but poorly thought out orders mean a quick death.
In terms of appearance, the game is authentic to the table-top models. The Space Marines look clunky, the Necrons like an ancient Egyptian nightmare, and so forth. The models are well detailed and reasonably individual. When standing idle, they look around, check their weapons, and do what idle solders do. When in battle, they really look like they're fighting it out, making contact with their enemies, and experiencing the impact of their enemy's weapons.
The sound is about what you'd expect. Unit acknowledgments are race specific, so the Space Marines end up sounding like the fanatical, long-lived Army of the Damned they are. The Eldar come off as arrogant. The Chaos forces sound a lot like that guy in your office who has been stuck at the same job for twenty years, hates life, and has sworn allegiance to the terrible, dark gods. (Sorry, is that only this one guy I know?) In the end, the audio cues do what they're supposed to; remind you that there are no good guys in Warhammer 40K. The music is, in a word, generic.
The campaign in Soulstorm is much as it was in the previous expansion; a territory-hopping game stretched over several planets. Each race takes turns moving, reinforcing, and attacking. It's nothing special, but an enjoyable way to learn all the races.
In the end, I highly recommend this game.

A very fun game. The level designs are very creative and lovingly crafted, with each having its own game-mode attached to it. This ensures that you're able to play something different every round, whether that's free for all, capture the flag, or the many bespoke game types such as table-football.
Weapon balance is cleverly done, in that everyone has an assault rifle, a sniper rifle, a shotgun, a bazooka and a flamethrower. These weapons have limited ammo and are renewed after a long period of time - this makes the game harder the longer you survive as you gradually run out of tools at your disposal, which helps level the playing field.
Character movement is very fluid, and the closest comparison would be Pandemic's Battlefront games. The use of Unreal Engine 4 makes the game very scalable for different systems - I'm playing on a 7 year old PC on low settings and it runs fine, however you'll be able to attain impressive visuals and gorgeous art design on higher end systems.
An excellent low-cost title, which provides a lot of scope for future content.

This is a beautiful game with a unique control scheme.  You control two brothers (hence the name of the game) at the same time, guiding them over obstacles, through puzzles, and through a fantasy world.
The world itself is quite unique and imaginative once you get past the first few areas.  The controls are a bit wonky, especially at first, but honestly that is a draw.  The unique two character controlling dynamic is the game's draw and the most unique thing it does.
Unfortunatly I found the gameplay to be lacking at times.  The game makes use of being able to contol two characters, and while there was the occasional clever use of this mechanic, the puzzles were never difficult and I was never forced to really think.  As such, I never felt a sense of accomplishment.
In fact, the only real difficulty is controlling both characters.  If this was any other game, that would be a major critique, but in Brothers, it somehow manages to be a plus rather than a minus.
Overall, I never actually had fun.  But I'm recommending it beause I appreciate this game from a critical standpoint.  The environments were well put together, the core idea is unique, and it is short enough that the tepid gameplay doesn't become too much of a drag.
It's not an enthusiastic recommendation, but if this looks like something you would enjoy, go ahead and pick it up on sale.

Get ready for a feel trip that nobody's signed the permission slip for. This starts and ends with the brother's compelling reason to traverse the wonderful world they live in - as their widowed father lies on his deathbed, his two young sons set out to find the cure. From there, you embark on a tour around their worlds, and in it you're able to catch glimpses about each brother's personalities. Even though the biggest story barrier for me was their inability to use intelligible language, the game's themes of brotherhood and overcoming loss were crystal clear and packed a wollop when they came along. This isn't as evident towards the middle of the game (where the intricate level design more than makes up for it), but instead bookends the story quite nicely.
Along the winding path of a 3.5-4 hour playthrough, you’re exposed to a host of innovative level design. Perhaps it was the length of the game, but the gameplay itself wasn’t all that repetitive. It could have been. But half of the time you’re not so focused on the actions you’re performing. You’re marvelling over the ingenuity of the level design from an art standpoint.
Yes, the game is truly as beautiful as the art style makes it out to be. If you’re not convinced, sit on every damn bench you can find and soak in the scenery - they go out of their way to make it the most breathtaking damned sitting simulator.
Aside from the language, my smallest gripe comes with the control scheme. While it actually serves as a meaningful plot device towards the end of the story, you can't skirt around the fact that each analogue stick controls a brother. I mean, it's simple, but there aren't many mainstream games where you're controlling two people with the two sticks. But for such a short story, it's manageable.
Brothers is a poignant story that leaves you wanting more despite such a satisfying ending. You'll fumble with the controls more than once, but it definitely won't detract you from the game's natural beauty from both a level design and aesthetic standpoint.
If anything, it’ll make you hug your brother a little bit tighter. Or wish you had one.

Quiet honestly with all the overwhelming praise I've heard from this game. I expected more.
Gameplay: The controls are interesting and unique at first, but it grows tiring really quick. The puzzles are easy and never really changed. I wish they had a couple of actions toggable so that my fingers could rest. I also never felt like I was in danger.  Even later in the game in parts where you were supposed to be terrified in, I didn't feel scared because there was no difficulty in the puzzle. If you like this coop/single player puzzle style, I would recommend you more to Cookie and Cream on the PS2.
Story (Spoilers Warning): So yeah. Everyone praises the story for how good it is. I saw someone play the first chapter and got interested. The set up was good and the somewhat somber atmosphere was a nice touch. When I heard all the praise for the game, I honestly hoped that it gave me a good story, but it's a bit lack luster. I guessed that either something absolutely mind boggling happened in the story, or one of the brothers died. Unfortunately it was the latter. It felt so cliche and forced when it happened. Cutscenes came and went at random slamming us in the head with "OH LOOK IT'S MOM." It would have been better if they showed us a cut scene with the mother that was a happy memory so I could at least relate to it more.
Overall: It's a good first attempt at a game. The atmosphere is the best thing about this game and frankly that's about it. People argue that the characters bloom when you interact with other objects like the flowers or people, but it's only on the brothers and in the beginning. A good story makes you care more as you play, but this was front loaded. Why should I care about the parents? They only show up now and then just to remind you of the "story." The death had little inpact on me because so many other stories have done so much better.  There is no replay value to the story or gameplay for me.

I got this game from a friend who got it from the Humble Bundle pack. At first, I got it as a game just to play another game, since I was fed up with Dark Souls and currently can't really afford Civ 6 at the moment. I checked some ratings, saw it was a good game, and after letting it sit on my screen for a few days, I finally decided to give it a whirl. And boy, am I glad that my friend gave me this game.
Beautiful story, let's start with that. Was the game short? Yes it was. But it was short enough to do what it had to do, and that was create a story set in a fantasy, almost Nordic style region. The last 15 minutes or so of this game hits you right in the feels the entire time, and I really didn't know whether to scream or cry. So even though it takes most people anywhere from 3-4 hours to beat it their first time around, it's a game driven by a great plot.
Artwork was phenominal. Everything in the game was detailed and put together masterfully. Controls are weird to get past, but what can you do when you control 2 people at the same time. The only real cons that I had were the voices and soundtrack. Everytime something bad happens, you get Ms Opera Lady singing the entire time. I thought it took away a little from the emotional side of it, because the first two times it happened, I burst out laughing. And the voices are in a fictional language, so nothing much can be said about it. The only way you can tell what's going on is when a name is said and gestures are made in the game. I think it could have been better if it was set in the player's desired language, be it English or some other language.
All that being said, this was an extremely well thought out game. And even though it's short, it tells the story in its short time and wrenches your heart out (twice). 9.5/10

First off, I totally adored Deus Ex: Human Revolution to little bits, even though I have not played any of the other Deus Ex games. That said, I cannot compare the new game to the old games and I certainly don't think it would be just to do so anyways.
I bought the Collector's Edition earlier this year and went mad with anticipation about this game. And it did not let me down once. The story is really intense and leaves a lot open, which I don't think is necessarily a bad thing. There's a lot of room for further games, more stories and for your own imagination. Some people don't like this. That's personal preference, imo.
I felt it was kinda short because the ending came somewhat abrupt, but I guess that was because I hate it when games end and I want them to continue endlessly so I have more time to explore the world.
As you might have guessed, I like this game. I like the main quest, the music (big plus, SUCH A BIG PLUS), the NPCs, the sidequests (so intense holy), the graphic, the animations, it's like... damn this is a really good game. People might argue it's too little content for too much money, but I haven't had that impression. It was the right amount of money, for the right amount of story. For me at least.
I also did not find it offensive, that you can (!!!) pay for more XP and Praxis, because you do not have to. You can and that's the point. If you want to pay for your single player to have an advantage over the computer, well do it. As I did not need it and do not find this a good idea, I didn't do it ;) Easy as that. No need to be offended.
I will need to play Deus Ex: Mankind Divided several more times, since I missed some sidequests and I want to explore the alternative endings. :) Overall, I can only recommend this game to anybody who's a fan of the Deus Ex games and who likes a good shooter with a lot of story and the possibility to sneak around as much as you like.

Torchlight II is the new game in the Diablo series. The plot is that you're always one step behind Diablo and then you fight him at the end. There are many acts with very unique environments, like the wilderness in act I, a desert in act II, a jungle in act III, and hell in act IV. Matt Uelmen composed the music as always in the diablo series so expect that. There are some great improvements made since the last diablo game, like introducing running and multiplayer! Lastly you can play as all new classes, like the assassin, sorceress, amazon/necromancer, and barbarian/necromancer.
Seriously though, Torchlight I and II are basically the same game as Diablo I and II with names being replaced to avoid any lawsuits from Blizzard. Torchlight I took place in one town with a big dungeon that reached "hell" and Torchlight II made you chase the big baddy across four acts. It doesn't really bring much of anything new to the genre but if you still like Diablo II then you can't really go wrong with this game.
The game is good, especially with friends, but I have a few gripes about it which could just be me. I disliked Torchlight I as it felt like a grind however Torchlight II only felt like a grind in the last dungeon as it was 8 floors long. By the end of it I had zero motivation to play a bunch of randomly generated maps or replay the game in new game+.
Also a lot of the skills that buff and debuff need to be refreshed way too often. Even the summon skills only last for around 30 seconds to a minute. You'll find yourself rebuffing and resummining constantly every 10 seconds to a minute. I could only get myself to play through the whole game using a simplistic embermage prismatic build where I only used 5 skills: prismatic bolts, teleport, fire aura, ice cage, and the 15 second elemental buff.
This could be just me, but you should be able to respec a character's stats and skills. The game lets you respec your last 3 skills but using a console command to respec all your skills will label you as a cheater. What this creates are players that don't want to be labelled as cheater and will have to start a game from scratch just to refine their build.
The last gripe I had was the messed up damage you can take on elite mode. Sometimes you take very little damage then one move takes off almost your entire health bar. Stacking armour and puttings points in vitality will not help. I found that stacking +% reduced damage taken stats in gear was the only way to not get too frustrated. I guess the devs figured there had to be some challenge if healing pots rapidly refilled your health bar but I think it could have been balanced in a much better way. Maybe make healing pots refill health slowly, making there less of a need for rediculously huge damage spikes.
I still recommend this game as I do have fun playing with friends. However I don't see myself making any max level characters in this game like I did back in Diablo I and II days.

I usually don't get EA games, especially above a certain price range, but this looked too interesting.
This is a prime example of a what we, as gamers, should expect when buying an Early Access game. It has a tone of areas that needs work, but you can see that there is substance here and the promise of a good game if development continues.
Think of this as an early-beta, third-person version of Skyrim or something. That might turn off some first person players, but I usually play in third person. In fact, it would be really good if the developers just followed the schemes that Skyrim has already established (controls, avatar response, etc). It's almost half and half at the moment, so you get some wonkiness going on, but doesn't really hinder gameplay too much.
Although there is a game here (which is more than we can say for a lot of EA games), everything looks like a placeholder. Keep that in mind when playing.
So far, these are the other parts that need work:
- Model quality (characters and environment)
- UI/UX (user interface and user experience for the uninitiated)
- Dialogue system (major -- really, really looks like temporary placement)
- Environment Lighting (lighting elements are placed weirdly -- lots of times, important elements aren't lit very well)
- Environmental Look (a good ENB for those familiar with modding)
- On-screen text quality (at standard 1920x1080, the text looks low quality, even when set at higher settings. UI scaling is probably not implemented well for the text)
- Lack of interaction with NPCs & environmental items (À la Skyrim, again -- maybe not NEEDED, but would be nice)
- RTS texturing/coloring (looks too ...um... hard to describe, but it doesn't look like one would expect it to look. Green grass almost looks florescent, for example)
This is what I've seen so far, and is of course in addition to what the developers say they need to add.
Their notes say the game is "in late development stages", this is not really the case. There has been a lot of work put in, but there is still lots more to go (and that doesn't even include polishing. I don't know their patching schedule/development cycle, but the initial 1 year in EA deadline will be hard to meet. As long as they continue to move forward and incorporate feedback though, it should be a interesting ride to be on.

This game honestly, in my opinion, has a lot of potential to become something great. I mean, the game itself is JUST not ready for RTS elements yet but I can see where they would really come into play in this game. Plus, plus the fact that you can just switch back character view once your done placing everything and managing your town? This game is the answer to many RTS/RPG players' dream. I recommend it to anyone looking for something new or a different perspective on those genres.
There are some cons to this game, though. Of course, it's still in early access but I'm hoping this will help improve it's quality too. However, I'm not a picky critic, so I'm just going over more general details I've noticed.
1. The game is good and it plays well! However, I am playing on a very high end computer and yet, I am still lagging at staggering 10 - 25fps. However, I still have yet to install some new hardware and the fps will increase, it still says a statement. The game itself really needs some better optimization, or some lower end computer may, and I said MAY, not run the game very well.
(10-17fps outdoors, 15-25 indoors)
2. I love the transition between character and town management, but it would help a lot if there were indicators stating the building costs when picking a spot for them. I tend to be forgetful sometimes and that little detail would honestly help a great deal.
That's honestly all the cons I feel for this game, other than that it really just needs more work before people play it more and more, but of course, that's stating the obvious that most gamers would know. Other than that, I hope this helps, not just for you to decide if this game is worth it, but the developers improve their game to something better. I have high hopes for this game, but even if that doesn't come true, I still feel it'll become something really great!

Legends of Ellaria is a Third Person RTS RPG with a lot of great features and ideas.
Though the game is far from complete it is still Quite enjoyable in its current stage.
The Pros:
The Game has a good Set for lore and deepening it later right now there isnt a huge amount but gives RPG fans something to look forward to!
The art style is reminescant of Fable 2/3 it is a great looking game, even goes into higher than 1080p resolutions without major performance hits on my 760 although be prepared for glitches to occur if you are using a weak GPU
the Combat reminds me a bit of pirates legend of black kat mixed with a few others, its rather simplistic but its still challenging to lets say hit an enemy thats running with a fireball
the quests, they arent all there yet but there are quite a bit of quests and while they tend to lead to caves or decrepid ruins theres actually a lot to explore a quest might bring you halfway through a cave or castle and then you can either face the treacherous halls of enemies with whatever supplies you had brought or retreat and finish the quest as is. and the dungeons themselves provide enough rewards to make it feel like a  positive action to go dungeon crawling.
Cons
Resources, it wasnt well explained that the resources are scattered throughout dungeons and the map and that they lead to permanent additions so if you go to save up for a building make sure its not going to take too many resources it could make it harder to build more in the future
BUGS i will not accept the fact that people complain about this for odd reasons but i will warn you as of 12/21/2017, the game had a lot of bugs and while not all are really even bad at all, just report them theyll be fixed rather quickly :P i had 1 game breaking bug so far that a restart fixed so not horribly unstable or anything.
the companions, while i understand the game is an EA title, the companions do need a lot of work they are great protection while walking around but they dont go into dungeons and the like with you they wait by the entrance most of the time.
advisor, right now the advisor basically hands out most of the quests if not all. but his dialogue is rather monotonous and can be a bit, boring to read. this is a very early build and im sure since hes currently one of the biggest characters you notice in the game (since you cant talk to most villagers and all) i feel he will be well flushed out by next year because they are adding more and more content and he'll only get more dialogue
spelling, this isnt a huge issue but there are typos just mention it in the discussions and it should be fixed these arent major but when you see a sentnce that is like this. its usually more of a typo everything is rather coherent.
the city building, there isnt a lot of help with the city building although my tutorial glitched out (although i seem to be one in a million with that glitch) it would just be nice if they could make an in game guide or help menu to just explain some of the basic features.
OVERALL
I would give this game in its current stage a 74/100 because it still has a lot of work to go as of 12/22/17 but it is still a great game, a great concept, and a great dev team.
im sure my score will raise by the time they get the systems more flushed out. the game is playable albeit it can be a bit shorter for some (if you catch on quicker) but seems about 12 hours or so of gameplay already there if you wanted to do it all.
if you like the idea, so do many of us and the game is actually living up to is expectations update wise, we are getting a lot of great content sooner rather than later so it can be refined earlier as well.
if you enjoy Mount and Blade, Fable, oblivion, or similar RPG's you may want to support this game early because this could lead to quite the game. i would say right now you dont get 100% of your moneys worth however if they keep doing large updates like this every 4 months or so, you could easily get  your moneys worth by the end of next year.

In all honesty I only bought this game because I got a coupon or something for it that made it ridiculously cheap and didn't even cost me a dollar, but rather a few measly cents. It sat in my library ever since and I hadn't touched it. Until today that is, and I can in all honesty say I was very surprised by it. Very indie with nice pixel graphics and great music to boot. I got goosebumps at certain points in dimension changes when the music switched, and by the end I'd actually grown attatched to Sarah. The game is great at making you question what's going on and little quirks - like chaning your characters colour - make the game fun to play.
However, I would only recommend buying the game if it is on sale. In a little over 3 hours - with pausing and getting coffee - I was able to 100% complete the game with all the achievements. If the game was a little longer I'd be yelling at you to go and buy it, right now, but in fairness, if you'd like a nice little indie game that is quick to play with good pixel graphics, this is the game - just be sure to buy it on sale to make it worth while.

Despite all the bugs and technical problems, Dreaming Sarah is a nice and cheap indie game. Inspired by Yume Nikki, you'll mostly be running around trying to figure where to go all by yourself(since the dialogues are fairly vague) through a surrealistic and dreamy world. The puzzles are not too hard and there's nothing special about the platforming. Considering the low price, the mistakes made by the devs can all be forgiven. It's a very amateur game, but you can clearly see as you play that it was made with lots of love.

Fun little game.
Can get confusing and frustrating due to the lack of information given what to do next.
It mostly depends on your own intuition. I found myself stuck in verious situation and therefore I read in an walktrough from time to time.
But despite that I had good fun with this short game.

It's a puzzle-pixel-platformer, yea. But there is more to say: Dreaming Sarah's atmosphere is overwhelming.
The ambient-like and minimalistic soundtrack creates a lost, strayed and cold vibe, often rapt. In addition to that, the visual aspects are very interesting, for the show the whole story. The story itself is not concrete (only the outer plot). Various actions, dialogues and phenomenons seem senseless, sometimes. But they create feelings. It all is totally abstract and surrealistic, which is good! Why? It grants the freedom to express emotions and to create particular visualized atmosphere. The whole feeling of a dreamy adventure is stunning and forces the player to, at some points, find an interpretation. All these very different locations and vibes... they feel like a whole life.
The developer's thoughts on this game could be expressing and/or assimilating this profound theme of coma and life itself. We can, I guess, enjoy this product without his knowledge. This art is alive in it's effect!

I was pleasantly surprised by this rather fun Smash Brothers clone. Being that it's early access, I'm willing to forgive the rotating roster, the limited number of pick ups, and the two weapon limit. Deus Ex Mankind Divided (MD) is, in my opinion, a really good sequel to the game. But why is it? Well to start off let's talk about the story. It has a good story but not great. It was able to catch the ball Deus Ex Human Revolution (HR) threw to it, but it didn't run too far with it. That's all I can really say about the story, good but not great. Now let's talk about gameplay. Deus Ex MD really improves on the gameplay compared to HR. First is that the stealth has been improved a lot, with my favorite being able to perform takedown moves from cover. Another is giving you an indicator when and where you are being seen. They also toned down on how fast enemies spot you, however I feel like they turned it down too far. In HR enemies acted like they were on cocaine and would immediately start shooting as soon as the saw your foot. But in MD they act more like they're trying to walk off a hangover so it takes awhile before they react. But that's a few things about stealth, now what about combat. Now when I played I tried to go all stealth so I rarely entered combat(so take this with a grain of salt), but the moments that I did it was really fun. With the ability to custom weapon attachments, change ammo types on the fly, and good amount of upgrades. But it seems the main reason that this is getting down votes is because of the microtransactions. Now I want to shoot this down before it bombs a game that doesn't deserve to be bombed. Yes they're micros but they are so far away tucked into the corner that you won't even notice it unless you think about it. Infact the micros are a game balance breaker so don't use them unless you want the game to be unbalanced. Now yes it was a bad thing to put them in the game and it shouldn't be ignored, however we shouldn't burn it at the stake because it hasn't done anything too bad, just give it a light stoning to teach it a lesson so it doesn’t do it again. Overall it's a solid game and don't let the micros sway you away.

This is one of the best games I got and played in 2013. In a time where people are big on nostalgia and referencing the 1980s, Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is one of the few games that perfectly encapsulates the 80s and delivers it to you in game form without going too far. From the enemies that literally look like someone shone a blacklight on a random schlub in a motorcycle helmet to the collecting of VHS tapes, everything about this game screams 80s and all of it works.
Your weapons are peak-80s as well. The Pistol is Robocop's Auto-9, the SMG is a heavily modded Calico (the go-to SMG for sci-fi schlock), The sniper rifle is the Cobra Assault Cannon from Robocop, plus you get to eventually walk around with a Ol' Painless (chaingun) as part of your normal arsenal.
In addition to all of this, you have Michael Biehn (Terminator, Aliens) voicing the main character on your trip through this neon-tinted wasteland which is just so perfect. It plays well, looks great, has a great soundtrack, and it doesn't wear out its welcome. I hope more AAA devs take risks like this using their big engines for little crazy one-off ideas like this more often.
Buy this game, it's worth the $15. If you don't think it is then buy it on sale, but BUY IT.

The Sims 3 is a very interesting game that can be incredibly tricky to get into.
First off, don't buy all the expansions. If you play the game whilst running every single expansion at once, your performance will tank and there will be so much♥♥♥♥♥♥in the game that it will be impossible to play with any kind of focus.
The best way to experience THe Sims 3, in my experience, is to install the Seasons, Ambitions and Generations along with any of the stuff packs that interest you, if any (though most of them aren't worth it.) Your game will still run silky smooth, you'll have loads to do and your sims' lives will be flushed out to the best degree possible without the sheer amount of content becoming overbearing.
I know many people think that EA is cheating them by splitting the game up into 20 some expansions, but it's not meant to be played all at once. It's designed for you to pick the expansions that interest you most, playing with all of them simply isn't possible unless you really enjoy consistent lag spikes.
The game has a lovely sandbox feel to it. You can make a sim that looks like you and see how your children could end up looking 20 generations down the line, or you could make a fat black man with a voice that could break glass named Nethaniel Ticklehack that really enjoys setting other people on fire and sleeping with balding men in his spare time.
While the vanilla game alone can be rather barebones, it's still incredibly fun and worth the buy at the price.

I got this game from a friend who got it from the Humble Bundle pack. At first, I got it as a game just to play another game, since I was fed up with Dark Souls and currently can't really afford Civ 6 at the moment. I checked some ratings, saw it was a good game, and after letting it sit on my screen for a few days, I finally decided to give it a whirl. And boy, am I glad that my friend gave me this game.
Beautiful story, let's start with that. Was the game short? Yes it was. But it was short enough to do what it had to do, and that was create a story set in a fantasy, almost Nordic style region. The last 15 minutes or so of this game hits you right in the feels the entire time, and I really didn't know whether to scream or cry. So even though it takes most people anywhere from 3-4 hours to beat it their first time around, it's a game driven by a great plot.
Artwork was phenominal. Everything in the game was detailed and put together masterfully. Controls are weird to get past, but what can you do when you control 2 people at the same time. The only real cons that I had were the voices and soundtrack. Everytime something bad happens, you get Ms Opera Lady singing the entire time. I thought it took away a little from the emotional side of it, because the first two times it happened, I burst out laughing. And the voices are in a fictional language, so nothing much can be said about it. The only way you can tell what's going on is when a name is said and gestures are made in the game. I think it could have been better if it was set in the player's desired language, be it English or some other language.
All that being said, this was an extremely well thought out game. And even though it's short, it tells the story in its short time and wrenches your heart out (twice). 9.5/10

5.4 hours into the game and I've decided to leave a review. My first 2 and a half hours was a bit clunky, but then a patch came out that seemed to smooth the game out a bit. Still waiting for some of the features they have listed, but so far I really enjoy the game. I've done some quests, and some of them finish a bit weird, with no apparent reward for doing them. Although some quests the reward is a bit obvious (clear a mine and miners get those resources faster and such) it'd be nice to see other quests offer up rewards. I only explored a small portion of the map because I was reading that some of the quests glitch if you go to the areas early. This hasn't happened to me yet, but we'll see. I think my favorite thing about this game so far is the immersion. You really start to feel like a lord of a village after awhile. Ordering people around and such. I can't wait to see where this game goes from here. It has so much potential that I can't imagine the pressure on the developers. I look forward to another day in Ellaria, and perhaps in the future, maybe even more of a story to it. That, and perhaps going head to head with a friend in a neighboring village/city. Sharing resources and such I think it'd be really cool. Good work and good luck @Larkon Studios. Can't wait to see what you have in store for me.
Pro's
Great dynamic with a very interesting twist to how we play games. I love the ability to switch between rts and fps (though right now it's tps)
The game has some wonderful visual effects (at least in my opinion)
Basic fighting structure
Cons
Basic fighting structure
some of the game is a bit buggy still (to be expected in early access)
Needs some basic features like the ability to rotate the screen in RTS as well as a mobile map to tell where you are in the world. Should offer different quest markers or different colour markers for different quests.
As of yet, I have not seen any sort of leveling feature, and the story is a bit vague. We've come to a new world for a fresh start and to get away from our old enemies only to find that they too have come to this world for a fresh start and are now bandits that want to attack us? To top it off, the only real goal right now is to ..? I'm unclear at the moment. We build buildings, and collect resources? Maybe eventually we'll conquer other villages/cities/empires and establish our rule, but then we're just going back into the mess we just left where we use up all the resources and have to start all over on a new plane of existence. Don't get me wrong, the concept seems idealistic. I've enjoyed this game so far, and believe that I can play for at least another 20 hours or so. So, not a bad game for 25 hours of game play. However, with the promised updates that time could quadruple, easily.
Another con is some of the visuals (Wood carriers walking in place and such. Invisible people that you can click on in rts but not do anything with and are invisible. They don't even move around.)
Inventory management: You fill up your inventory quite quickly, and while there are various boxes around town to shove crap in, you quickly find that you're unable to buy/sell anything until you've created a market. Something I have just managed to do in the game so we'll see if all my hoarding has paid off :D
Death: At this time it seems the only thing you lose on death is resources, and an unknown amount at that. It'd be nice to have a list of what was lost on death, and or the loss of the players inventory?
Aaaand the last con I can think of right now: Not enough dialogue. The dialogue seems a bit bland, and can get boring quickly. There doesn't seem to be any way to gather information from different quests yet, nor to really interact with much of anyone around. The main advisor offers up quests and going back to him to complete the quests can be an excercise in futility sometimes. You click E on him to start the dialogue, and then you get a list of things you can say to him (why a him anyways? Maybe a feature to hire new advisors male and female would be nice? Maybe even an advisor for the different races if any can become friendly with your village?) you click on one and he offers up some more options but they're very limited. You'll see when you start to play :)
Now, after all that there is plenty I enjoy about the game so far that will keep me playing and waiting for the updates. Good luck my fellow Ellarians, and happy goblin hunting.

I was finally compelled to play this after recently completing
, for reasons I cannot divulge if you have yet to do the latter. Dreaming Sarah is one of those spooky-artsy platformer-things, but if you've watched the trailer then you already know this. It's like a pixelated
with subtle hints of
in it's colour-coded, mood-coded environments. Speaking of which, the level design is pretty good - the pastel colour palette gives the backgrounds an appropriately surreal quality and the scenes and characters encountered are just the right amount of crazy to represent a fever dream without actually jumping the shark. The controls are smooth (when they work), jumping is satisfying and precise, and some of Sarah's sprites are quite adorable (ex. umbrella descent).
I was gonna say I'm pleasantly surprised by Dreaming Sarah, but I actually had above-average expectations of this game and it still met them. The one major downside that comes to mind, is that the technical aspect is lacking. The game is apparently built on an engine related to browsers and as a result, when I press F12 to take a screenshot, the Chrome Inspect Element popup appears. Yes, "Chrome" as in - the browser. Yes, it comes from the game.
. Other than that, I've had several instances of graphical bugs and major control malfunctions, and trying to jump over the giant tonsil as a fish leads to a surprisingly scary freeze. The game is rather buggy, but admittedly, only once you set out to break it. Luckily, in this genre and particular niche, that is of little significance. It's also quite short, but on par with its aforementioned spiritual peers.

Summary: Dreaming Sarah's a good game with much lore, and a potential sequel. I rate it 9/10
*Spoilers Ahead*
Dreaming Sarah is a game where a girl goes through a coma and you must try to get her out of the coma. the controls are very responsive and tight. The areas you visit are very detailed but some can be forgotten, like the Desert, you go there once to obtain an item or two and never have to go back again. The game has many comic relief characters and many characters that make you feel sad and creeped out. Half the time I thought it was a horror game because I see small things that i fear can pop out and jumpscare. This game is very atmospheric, and can suck you in until upon completion of the game. Sadly the game's not mod compatable which would make it a very strong selling point. It has high potential for custom quests, new items, skins, etc. The game leaves a wierd taste in my mouth when you complete it. Depending how you complete it that is. One of the endings without obtaining all the items is a blank room with you waking up in a hospital without a clear indication of whether you got or you can get a different ending. Which is a downside but is not a major issue, a simple google search or a walkthrough fixes this,
Overall this game is amazing, great characters, good plot, an amazing atmosphere that just leaves you at awe with some of the places like the alien home planet. This game is a must buy for people who want a deep emotional expirience and wish to complete satisfying puzzles that make you feel like you want the ending.

For people who liked Human Revolution, this is really a continuation of that.
For people who disliked Human Revolution (unless it was due to the boss fights), this won't change your mind.
For those who have not played Human Revolution, this isn't the best place to enter the series, but it's not a terrible one.
The real take aways for me are that this is a masterwork of level design and world building. Most other aspects are competant to good to make a decent driving plot a good enough reason to keep playing.
This wouldn't be an honest review without talking about how it runs. I recently built a new top of the line machine with a 4ghz skylake processor, 32 GB ram, 2x 1080 GTXs, and both my OS and game running off of NVMe drives (rated at 2600 MB reads). Of course I wanted to play this at 4k (with the money I just spent on the machine, I had to justify it). And the menu totally hits 60 FPS. And that's about it. Even the credits at the end ran at 45 FPS. The game itself actually stayed around 40-45 most of the time though there were a couple dips all the way down below 30. So overall it was definitely playable though tragic that it still ran poorly. I can say that with my fast hard drives, load times really weren't a problem.
Diving deeper into the game, the story stars Adam Jenson again, though he isn't much of a part of it. There is a sidequest that is relevant specifically to him and a couple references, but overall you play as a dry-witted augmented interpol agent. Personal stakes are functionally non-existant.
That isn't to say the story is bad. It's not amazing, but it's competant even if any of the "twists" seem to have billboards announcing them minutes to hours ahead of time. The side quests and the stories you can discover on PDAs and people's email are really where the game shines though. This is probably the first FPS (and let's be honest, this is mainly an FPS and less so an RPG) where it felt like people actually could populate. There were places to live that looked livable. There were restaurants and shops. There was a sense of being in the city where you spend so much time. And that's awesome. I spend probably the first 20 hours of the game mainly wanting to explore and enjoy the city. And I did some missions because why not.
For gameplay, that's where this really feels like Human Revolution. There are some new augs. I used remote hacking which adds a little, but didn't even touch any of the other "new" augs. I admit, playing a non-lethal, stealth, hacking approach didn't really look to add a lot of the new augs (much more combat oriented), but there was something there. I didn't find myself feeling like I was missing something for not having new augs to use.
The sneak-steal-escape pattern I found myself in for actual missions as well as just exploring works super well. Having such an open city to explore gave me lots to do and shops to stop by and sell all the stuff I just stole but didn't want (which I found to be almost everything). Throughout the game, I think I used... 2 gas grenades, 2 emp grenades, ~20 bio cells, and probably about 6 tranq darts.
Because of my approach, I actually had 10 spare praxis by the end of the game. Those microtransaction you've heard about? This is a game where they really really don't push them. I _never_ clicked the store button and never felt the game wanted me to. I find it a shame to know they are there, but the game does not suffer from them.
Breach mode? I guess it's extra content but I see no reason to play it. It's not what you're buying the game for (probably).
Oh, there's crafting now. I can't really comment because I generally didn't use weapons and had plenty of items from stealing.
This might sound like a weird positive, but I feel like the additions in this game really are just additions that you can play with if you want, but the game doesn't feel you should have to. It's a Deus Ex approach to expanding a game that was already fun.
And this game really is fun in the end if it's the type of game for you. Well done overall a great use of time. My first playthrough + 1 Jenson Story (which is a nice free mission I guess but not essential at all) took 28 hours which is respectable in my book. I know I will come back to this game in time and play through again which is even better.

One of the best FPS games i've played in a long time. A true 80s throw back. Its like a bad sci-fi film, filled with lots of cheesy one liners and clever moments. 16-bit cutscenes and a great synth soundtrack. And the original Kyle Reese (Michael Biehn) is the voice of Rex Power Colt. What more could you want! The island is not as big as FarCry 3's Rook Islands but its still quite large. There are side-quests to complete which can be unlocked by taking over enemy bases. There are also VHS tapes, T.Vs and Papers to find that are scattered through out the map. Outposts are now replaced with Garrisons which are like mini cyborg fortresses. Sadly the game is not perfect, and every game has its flaws. Some of the cutscenes drag on a bit to long. Also the side-quests more or less the same. Save this scientist. Hunt this animal. Kill this dude with this weapon. The missions are less varied as FarCry 3 which will put some off. Also there are not as many weapons to collect. But hey, its a smaller game. The map is about the same size as the second island in FarCry 3 and for $17.95 (last time I checked) its a very good deal. Stop reading and buy the game. 9/10

My negative rating is based entirely on the lack of accomodation of a server that provides decent latency for South African gamers and the frustration that follows.

I have stopped playing now, when there is a South African server or at least one with around 100ms latency I will continue; however I don't see that ever happening unless players can start their own private servers or until the world starts caring about South Africa again for the first time since 1994-1995.

Lord of the Rings Online hasn't captivated players as World of Warcraft has, and there are reasons for that. After playing the game again after the remake of the classes, there some personal reasons I have as to why LOTRO isn't so great.
1.  Early Levels - This is a big problem for Lord of the Rings in my opinion, because the early stages of the game are incredibly boring. When you play as a Human, you are hunting down spiders and bandits from level 1-20-ish. Afterwards, the game picks up slightly by introducing the Barrow-Wights but the bandits will still appear from time to time. The Elf and Dwarf starting areas are a little interesting because it involves goblin invasions and shaky alliances between the two races, though it also involves killing wolves and birds from time to time. The Hobbit starting zone is by far the most utterly dull place in the game. I spend most of my times carrying pies from town to town, delivering mail and helping people with their chores.
2. Enemy Design - This might not turn people off as much as it did to me, but the enemy designs are recycled. If they aren't, then someone put a lot of work in for nothing. The fact that the only difference between a bandit in the tutorial and a demon bandit overlord in the shadowy pits of Mordor is only their number, gives the impressions that no-one seemed to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥in the design of the game.
3. F2P is a Lie - Okay, this might be an exaggeration since developers need money and they can't just make the game completely free. Turbine doesn't seem particular successful with their MMOs. I believe their sister MMO, Dungeons and Dragons Online at launch was about to fail miserably (don't quote me on this. They decided to convert LOTRO and DDO into a F2P model worked, at least for a short while. The game promises that you can unlock game content by grinding for Turbine Points but the rate in which you gain Points is painfully slow. The F2P model added some juice to LOTRO but you basically have to grind the early levels over and over to play the next area in each play through. Referring to the first point, the early levels are boring as hell, so your patience will get tested.
If you have never touched an MMO before and/or also a fan of Tolkien's work, go ahead and try the early levels. If you want to access the higher-level content, I hope you are willing to pay because grinding and grinding will take away any interest you have for this game.

I didn't really like the control sticks and RT/LT buttons being used to control one brother each. Your progress is being saved in the background, if you can stand the sluggishness [mostly caused by the forced on V-Sync I think] do buy it! it offers good things and promising future updates, worthy of the money
if u want the full and better experience, come back in another 1-3 months! the game should be much better imho [depending on how fast the major patches is released], do put them on your wishlist and follow section though, good games with dedicated devs like this requires some show of support!
Detailed Review:
devs already mentioned that the starts is recorded innately through the game, so progress will be saved along the way
devs mentioned should the character customization got improved, extra customization can be done down the road
number 1 & 2 clarified, only the performance optimization [mainly lack of option, but it's still playable]

the concept itself is interesting [a good mix of mount and blade, skyrim, and warcraft/age of empire imo :D]
the plans the devs had is grandeur and promising
should the execution is just as good, this game will offer us a great deal of fun and enjoyment for a long time, just like good ol' skyrim

OK. This *free* game is additcting. It can't combat my addiction to Team Fortress 2, but it can keep you playing for a while. When you play this game, play with friends. I haven't tried the online gameplay myself, but my friend plays online and he's said that playing online is annoying and the player's tactics are bull. The devs are continually updating the game and they've been adding characters recently. I may not have many hours, but when I do play with my friends I have an absolute blast.
There are items such as spike balls, mines, explosives, magic horn things, and ofcourse the weapon drops. Its style of gameplay is like Super Smash Bros. There are many characters to play as and level up. Leveling up characters will unlock things like different color schemes for them, different stances (which can switch up the gameplay style of that character), or just coins.
Now, because of its style of play you need a controller to play better. While I haven't used a controller with it myself, my friends seemed to play a little better with controllers after they started using them. Basically, controllers are a must have.
Now as much of the game as I've seen I've has a blast with. You can get the occasional spike ball kill, which aren't very strong unless you double the damage, and will definately give you a chuckle. You have to come up with your own combinations with each character, which I thought was a good element instead of pressing a bunch of keys to perform one almighty move that will destroy everyone infront of you. There is a character in this game for many playstyles. Characters for a harassing playstyle (the one I like the most), tanking playstyle, the bull playstyles... Moving on.
*Begins rant about how his friend uses all the characters that 'don't' take skill*
I recommend this game with what I've seen. Play it with friends and you'll have an absolute blast.

I played for about an hour. Or rather I tried to play. Because the experience is anything but pleasant. The concept of the game is appealing, merging RTS and RPG elements. However the execution is dreadful and make this game a chore.
Let's start with the RTS part. You can construct buildings alright. But you have no idea what you get for building them. How much does the tavern increase income by? Is it worth investing all my gold in it? Or should I build a house first? You have no clue what each building is producing, there is no large map overhead to help you plan a settlement. It's basically the worst RTS interface I've seen.
Next, the RPG elements. The movements and attacks are so clunky that the game can seriously compete against games from 20 years ago. Furthermore the lack of a map makes it almost impossible to figure out where to go to get your quests done. I don't see any leveling or skills, only equipment. The dungeons are full of repetitive design elements so that every chamber looks exactly the same. And with only the small map it is easy to get lost.
They may have a decent game when it's done but right now it's only a half-baked project not worth your money.

I bought this game on a hunch, to round up a purchase of other things… I guess I just liked the presentation, and I don't have enough female-protag games so this felt like an investment.
I absolutely don't regret it.
I don't know anything of the more popular game everyone was naming as its model or inspiration, so I had no idea what to expect. I found a fun, colorful, peaceful game I wanted to explore and wander about until I uncovered all its secrets.
I particularly liked the way previous areas liven up with new characters and events as you re-explore them after some more progress, and how all the areas get linked to each other so you don't have to constantly tread through everything linearly to get back to some place. It prevents the game from feeling boring or redundant, especially if you get stuck at some point and need to re-explore everything to find what item you've missed or where you're supposed to go next.
I got "85% completion" on the stats screen at the end though, despite having all the items, secrets and achievements, or so I thought. Maybe there are a few more places I still missed… I guess I'll have to play again to check!
In conclusion: quiet, simple, agreeable game to pass time when you're not feeling like engaging with a heavy or stressful environment. Great before sleeping, or on the contrary when not quite awake yet!
