One of the greatest turn based roguelikes out there. A game with hidden depth, surprisingly hard difficulty, and the good ol' "one more run" feel.
You control a hacker that navigates their way through a system full of viruses and daemons, and most of the time end up dying trying. The enemies all have unique movements, such as the virus moves two spaces instead of one, or the cryptog isn't visible until it's in your sights. Getting trapped by a bunch of enemies at once is common, especially if you don't play smart!
Luckily, to counter the horde, there are a lot of powerups. These powerups each counter a specific enemy type, and make tough situations possible, that is if you have resources. To use powerups, you need either Energy or Credits. You collect these with siphons. But you only get two per floor, adding a descision making element to the game. "Do I want this powerup? Should I just grab these resources instead? Or how about take some score?" And to add on to this, each time you take a powerup, it spawns a specific amount of enemies, making each situation risk/reward.
The controls are great, just a simple WASD and number keys, or you can even just use your mouse.
A lot of your deaths will be because of RNG, and that is one of my only complaints. RNG is such a gamble, and a lot of the time ends with the game over screen.
This is the perfect coffee break game, each run is about 10 minutes long, and it saves your progress if you exit the game.
Easily 9.8/10! Grab the DLC too!

For people who liked Human Revolution, this is really a continuation of that.
For people who disliked Human Revolution (unless it was due to the boss fights), this won't change your mind.
For those who have not played Human Revolution, this isn't the best place to enter the series, but it's not a terrible one.
The real take aways for me are that this is a masterwork of level design and world building. Most other aspects are competant to good to make a decent driving plot a good enough reason to keep playing.
This wouldn't be an honest review without talking about how it runs. I recently built a new top of the line machine with a 4ghz skylake processor, 32 GB ram, 2x 1080 GTXs, and both my OS and game running off of NVMe drives (rated at 2600 MB reads). Of course I wanted to play this at 4k (with the money I just spent on the machine, I had to justify it). And the menu totally hits 60 FPS. And that's about it. Even the credits at the end ran at 45 FPS. The game itself actually stayed around 40-45 most of the time though there were a couple dips all the way down below 30. So overall it was definitely playable though tragic that it still ran poorly. I can say that with my fast hard drives, load times really weren't a problem.
Diving deeper into the game, the story stars Adam Jenson again, though he isn't much of a part of it. There is a sidequest that is relevant specifically to him and a couple references, but overall you play as a dry-witted augmented interpol agent. Personal stakes are functionally non-existant.
That isn't to say the story is bad. It's not amazing, but it's competant even if any of the "twists" seem to have billboards announcing them minutes to hours ahead of time. The side quests and the stories you can discover on PDAs and people's email are really where the game shines though. This is probably the first FPS (and let's be honest, this is mainly an FPS and less so an RPG) where it felt like people actually could populate. There were places to live that looked livable. There were restaurants and shops. There was a sense of being in the city where you spend so much time. And that's awesome. I spend probably the first 20 hours of the game mainly wanting to explore and enjoy the city. And I did some missions because why not.
For gameplay, that's where this really feels like Human Revolution. There are some new augs. I used remote hacking which adds a little, but didn't even touch any of the other "new" augs. I admit, playing a non-lethal, stealth, hacking approach didn't really look to add a lot of the new augs (much more combat oriented), but there was something there. I didn't find myself feeling like I was missing something for not having new augs to use.
The sneak-steal-escape pattern I found myself in for actual missions as well as just exploring works super well. Having such an open city to explore gave me lots to do and shops to stop by and sell all the stuff I just stole but didn't want (which I found to be almost everything). Throughout the game, I think I used... 2 gas grenades, 2 emp grenades, ~20 bio cells, and probably about 6 tranq darts.
Because of my approach, I actually had 10 spare praxis by the end of the game. Those microtransaction you've heard about? This is a game where they really really don't push them. I _never_ clicked the store button and never felt the game wanted me to. I find it a shame to know they are there, but the game does not suffer from them.
Breach mode? I guess it's extra content but I see no reason to play it. It's not what you're buying the game for (probably).
Oh, there's crafting now. I can't really comment because I generally didn't use weapons and had plenty of items from stealing.
This might sound like a weird positive, but I feel like the additions in this game really are just additions that you can play with if you want, but the game doesn't feel you should have to. It's a Deus Ex approach to expanding a game that was already fun.
And this game really is fun in the end if it's the type of game for you. Well done overall a great use of time. My first playthrough + 1 Jenson Story (which is a nice free mission I guess but not essential at all) took 28 hours which is respectable in my book. I know I will come back to this game in time and play through again which is even better.

As someone who likes story driven games and had followed the Deus Ex universe in some way, I found myself looking forward to the newest installment. After I finished the campaign here are my thoughts on it.

The compelling story that I found in Human Revolution is nowhere to be found here, sadly. The story in Mankind Divided is on a smaller scale and is mostly tied around a terrorist group. On other side, the main hub that is the city Prague is as detailed and a joy to discover. Plenty of detail and gamers who enjoy exploration will have plenty of things to discover here.
Now, the gameplay is where MD has improved from HR in some way. The traversal is more fluid and dynamic, the verticality in MD is easily one of my favorite things. The simple way to use your augments to traverse the pathways you wouldn’t think of at first, becomes natural. It is great in the regard of stealth play. I can’t say much about the gunplay as I played non-lethal way.
Still, the things I did use form augments, to items and stun weapons felt natural and responsive. After finishing the campaign I had to agree with most of reviews I read, that the end and the story in general just feels like something that is setting up the bigger things which I found rather disappointing.
In the end, if you are first and foremost thinking of buying because of the gameplay you saw MD won’t disappoint, with engaging side quests that at the times I found more interesting than the main mission, you don’t need to look further than Mankind Divided. If you were hoping for a compelling story with choices that impacted a much bigger scale, you will be disappointed and for you I recommended to pick this game up on a sale in the future. Anyways, it is enjoyable and worth your time. It is a step in the right direction and hopefully a sure set up for even bigger things in the next installment.

Have you played Human Revolution? Did you like it? Do you want more?
If your answers are "yes" for all of these, then that game is a match for you. It is essentially (much) more of the same.
I am one of these players. I found HR (Human Revolution) to be a very good game. I can say the same about this game as well.
What I find strangely dissapointing is clumsiness of menus. Much the same in this alley as HR.
Dragging items, context menu fade-ins and popup initial delay, strange sliders as checkboxes. What is disappointing about it? Devs had plenty of time to fix these I would say "minor" issues.
Some default Keyboard shortcuts are still bad(SE trademark). What annoyed me the most was weapon holstering assigned to 'h' key. So in like 1 out of 10 cases I would throw grenade('g' key) instead.
Another disappointment I had is that game seems easier than HR. Enemy routes are easier to read or simply neglect. You could easily sneak in front of enemies without they caring about you, slowly filling yellowbar just tells you how much over the board you went. Is it bad that game is easier? Judge it by yourself, but got warned.
Hubs are even better than before. Prague is big enough, same with Golem City. Level design in these two locations is wonderful.
Quests are great as well. There are no "fetch" quests. MD is a reference material for other RPGs out there. The number of quests might seem low (around 30?) but man, they are long and fulfiling.
Story - altough quite fragmented (GoT style) - is very rich and well written with many interesting characters(not all perfect, mind you). Some might feel "offended"? for game moodines (BLM and stuff) But I found it fitting and probable.
Game looks fantastic. Engine seems very effective but some locations are obviously not optimized. There are terrible framerate drops in places which could easily be spotted during development. They just seem neglected.
Microtransactions...
Yeah. There are some elements but they are quite optional for main game. But microtransactions are aggresively being pushed in "breach" mode.
This way of serving microtransactions I find scary. Play, Play, Play, Play, Pay, Pay, Pay.
In the end I find that game worth it's price.

Trine 2 is a very fun game to play. It is a platformer with puzzle elements (and also a very little bit of rpg).

Trine 2 also consist of the Goblin Menace DLC. This DLC consists of extra levels which begin after you completed the game. (turns out that the goblins weren't defeated)
I really liked this game. It is an easy game to just pick up and play. The graphics are beautiful. I was really surprised by how much i liked this game. This is a must-buy if you are looking for a platformer.

Trine 2 has a very quaint, cute, quintessential fantasy story, though it is really more of a backdrop than anything. The soundtrack is nice and adds to atmosphere. However, it does get repetititve after prolonged sessions of play. The aesthetic of the game is quite nice, and also adds to atmosphere. The graphics options allow one to supersample the game, which can make the game look exceptionally pretty. For a smaller game, Trine 2 is comparable to even AAA games in the visuals department. However, all these elements really take a backseat to the gameplay, which is the focus of Trine 2 by a mile.
Single player and online multiplayer would do in a pinch, but this game is at its best with local multiplayer. Plug in a few controllers and disable player levitation (why play a puzzle game with a feature that allows you to bypass puzzles?) and you'll be sure to have a great time with your friends. While there is virtually no replay value since the level designs and puzzles are static and fixed, the game feels long enough and involved enough to warrant a discounted purchase. 20 dollars seems too steep for the simplicity and one-time-through play value of it all, but if you can get it on sale or part of a humble bundle, you will definitely get 5-10 dollars worth out of it.

I cannot recommend this game more. Certainly for anyone who remembers it's source material, but for any early '90's kid' who grew up on their older brother's 80's cartoons, their parents 80's action VHS tapes, and was entranced by the cartoons of their own era that still had that offbeat style that haunts them to this day. For those of you who see modern cartoons that lack the macho hero, the two-dimensional love interest, and the evil cyborg who wants to control the world. The shows that take themselves too seriously and are slathered with so many unsubtle moral messages they make no sense. For those of you who have had their experience ruined by modern storytelling and adult cynicism.
This game is your outlet.
Everything you miss about those old cartoons and action heroes.
Crammed with references to series I never thought I'd hear about again (And some I never have, I'm sure), characters ripped straight out of more of the same, and a soundtrack so full of 80's synth you'll have flashbacks.
And of course, more one-liners than I've heard from Arnie, Stalone, and Van Damme.
Combined.
Blood Dragon's action and story moments are what you're here for. A barebones kill-the-bad-guy plot that's not about who you're after, but how you take him down, and how everything explodes nonsensically along the way.
The gameplay is simple enough to understand, effectively identical to Far Cry. For those not familiar with it, don't panic. It's a brilliant system reknowned for attention to realistic detail that plays well into the action-movie aesthetic Blood Dragon draws from. Even some of the weapons here are movie references.
Perhaps the strangest part of Blood Dragon is the moments between its story and combat that provide moments for reflection, particularly with the travel methods taken from the Far Cry series.
It is in these moments that you are likely to notice Blood Dragon's flaws, of which there are very, very few.
Perhaps the most voiced flaw of Blood Dragon is the requirement of a UPlay acount to play Blood Dragon, as it is a Ubisoft game. This can be a valid concern, as loss of any account details can mean a lack of access to the game and requirement of technical support. Every buyer should take care in setting up their UPlay account if they do not have one already. The experience of Blood Dragon is too good to ruin with haphazard account setup, and is most definitely worth it.
The first of the game's ACTUAL arguable flaws is its length. Blood Dragon is definitely not a very long game, and after your first full playthrough, you're likely to notice that there is nothing else out there except a week long 80's movie marathon that can come close to the feeling of your first Blood Dragon playthrough. Which is it's second flaw, the difficulty in defining why Blood Dragon captures its nostalgic essence so well can make it difficult to find anything like Blood Dragon except... More Blood Dragon. Or trying to watch Jonny Quest and Terminator at the same time while posing Dino Riders figures.
Besides the possibility of account issues, Blood Dragon's only downfall as a standalone game may be that there isn't more of it. Or that it's not a war simulator that's been rehashed twelve times for its multiplayer.
Blood Dragon delivers where a lot of games fail, making your protagonist a certified hero you WANT to play as. Rex 'Powers' Colt has no flaws, except maybe that he's TOO badass.
And he's voiced by Michael Bien, who might not be the BEST known action star, but he's the hero from Terminator. And he's in Aliens, so Rex Colt really IS an 80's action hero.
Anyone who feels a pang of nostalgia the moment someone mentions aliens of any kind, has a fear of man-eating sharks with uninspired names, or says 'I'll be back.' without even the slightest hint of an Austrian accent will find a moment of solace in Blood Dragon.
Part Duke Nukem and part Far Cry, surreal colors and enemies, and a lot of 8bit era flashbacks. The best fun in quite a while!

pros:
=Game is just awesome (as free peoples of course) you could role play as anything you want from a brave captain to a humble farmer, merchant, or bard, with loads of options to choose from.

=hundreds of armours and weapons to choose from with a paintable customization, and a crafting system which means no overpriced armours from merchants (some), which means you have to earn what you want.
=choose sides from evil or good
="Encounters" Basically a bunch of singleplayer and multiplayer missions involving the war of the ring.
="music porting" as a bard you can play the music you downloaded and play it with a sort of tune depending on wich instrument you have used
=In server housing, yup the houses you buy show up in the actuall world.
=Earn premium stuff from just regular quests (would take some time though)
=See scenes from the events of "LOTR".
=Explore middle earth and even see the places you have read in the book (Like the sun touched trolls in "the Hobbit")
cons:
=PvMP (Player vs multiplayer)
monsters have no RP (role playing) which means you cant be a miner nor a woodchopper, you strickly have to stick with killing the "Freeps" (Free peoples) to get any traits.
=Low server activity as a beginner
="Freeps" are unbelievably OP if you are just a regular "free to play orc or goblin" which means you need to pay up for VIP to get a couple of decent kills.
="Terrible combat system" its not the basic RPG style of hit and miss chance stuff, basically all you need to do is jump around in circles while spamming attacks to kill ,cause you cant hit what is not infront of you and your characteer wont auto face the enemy. which is a terrible factor in PVMP considering all you have to do is be an archer, lore master(mage) or a really fast character to even hit anything. oh that's another thing, the melee combat is pretty slow for an mmo.

="no hit boxes", stay behind a tree where an archer cant completely see you, and he will still hit you as long as you are targeted.
Final Verdict,

I have to say I was pretty impressed with Brothers, but I wouldn't call it a game as much as an interactive story. That being said, it is a beautifully atmospheric story delivered in an impressive way. The whole story is told without words, which is quite a feat and a bold undertaking by the designers. I was also surprised by the level of morbidity in this game. It references death quite a lot. The game isn't too graphic by today's standards but it is a refreshingly dark tale very much in the spirit of Grimm's fairy tales and the like. Parents might want to know that in advance.
The game took me about 4 hours and it was a pretty painless process. No grinding, getting lost, or spending enormous amounts of time on frustrating puzzles. The whole story is entirely linear which I found a bit disappointing. I was totally expecting a casual game but this one was far too easy. Given the adult themes in the game I was hoping for something that might challenge adults more. I'm also very thankful the developers didn't smother this game with tedious "achievements" that often cheapen titles like this.
Overall, the game is really a masterpiece. Some of the plot elements at the end are a bit off and the camera might occasionaly give you difficulties, but everything else in the game more than makes up for these minor flaws.
Buy this game, especially if it's on sale. It's a real piece of art.

868-HACK is an interesting beast... one of those rare games that really gets it right when it comes to both creativity and depth.  But what's also interesting is that it's easy to grasp the basic principles.... despite that the game's difficulty is then quite high.  However, some of that difficulty will be entirely your own fault...
At it's core, this is a turn-based Roguelike where your goal is simple:  make it through 8 sectors (each a single screen in  size) by reaching the glowing green box at the end.  And more importantly, do so while getting your score as high as possible.  There's no point in hacking anything if there's no gain after all, right?
In your way are exactly four types of enemies, and knowing exactly how each one works, and how to deal with each, is of utmost importance.  Demons, the red ones, are very basic in how they move, just coming straight at you, however, they take 3 hits to kill instead of 2. Viruses, the purple ones, move 2 times for every 1 time that you move. The blue orb things are invisible unless you are in a direct horizontal/vertical line with them; however, the spot they initially spawn on will have a blue box thing around it until they've been destroyed, so you're never surprised by them, the game ALWAYS lets you know they are there somewhere, and the spot where they started.  And finally, the pink angular whatsits can go right through walls; fortunately, you can strike them while they are in a wall so long as there is not another wall between you and them.
Your attack is a bit different than in many turn-based roguelikes.  Instead of adjacent attacks, you strike in a horizontal or vertical line with infinite range.  You do this by simply attempting to move towards any enemy you are in a direct line with (this, however, also means you CANNOT just walk towards them; you will always fire instead).  Every enemy that isnt a Demon takes 2 hits to destroy, and the first hit stuns them for a moment.  This mechanic is very basic on paper, but in practice, you really need to time your movements and your attacks carefully.
But the real thing that makes the game interesting is the hacking, and the programs. In each sector you can acquire 2 "Data Siphons".  Using these basically sucks stuff out of the tile you're on, and the 4 adjacent to you, be they floors or walls.  For floor tiles, you recieve the resources displayed on the tile (credits or energy, or both).  For walls, if the wall has a large number on it, you gain that many points for draining it.  If the wall has a program listed on it, you permanently gain that program.  However, EVERY wall also summons more enemies when you hack it; this is displayed as a number also.  On score walls it's always equal to the score value.  You need to be very, very careful, and weigh your options; is that anti-virus program worth the danger of the 4 enemies it's going to send at you?  Should you grab that Step program, despite that it's position means you cannot get it without hacking a second wall at the same time?  Is that big tempting 7 point wall worth a go, do you have the programs to deal with it?
Using your programs well (and making decisions on which to go for) is the key to victory.  The game ends up being like a big (and cruel) puzzle.  Figuring out which programs to use, and in what order, is never easy, and ALL programs are useful in some way... but they all cost credits, resources, or both.  Make a mistake, and you can go down fast; 3 hits and your run is over, though you heal 1 point of HP every time you enter a new sector.  The depth here is huge, and it's what makes the game so good and addictive.  There are numerous programs to unlock, as well.  Each new one brings all sorts of strategic possibilities to the game when you encounter it.
And the way the spawning works means that to some degree, you create your own difficulty.  Yes, enemies constantly appear, but aside from the loading of a new sector, they do this slowly.  Other than that... your actions will determine when, and how many, enemies will spawn, based on which walls you hack.  Once you've taken an action, you need to use your programs, basic attacks, the level structure, and even the enemy's own behaviors against them in order to escape certain doom.
All in all, this is an absolutely fantastic game.   Very, very addicting, very very fun, and the nature of it means that as you get better, you can up the challenge by simply going after bigger and bigger scores each time.  And above all else, it has alot of depth.
I've played this absolutely to death on the iPad, and I'm very glad to see the port of it appear on here (and it's a good port, too).  I definitely can recommend this one.

Trine 2 has a very quaint, cute, quintessential fantasy story, though it is really more of a backdrop than anything. The soundtrack is nice and adds to atmosphere. However, it does get repetititve after prolonged sessions of play. The aesthetic of the game is quite nice, and also adds to atmosphere. The graphics options allow one to supersample the game, which can make the game look exceptionally pretty. For a smaller game, Trine 2 is comparable to even AAA games in the visuals department. However, all these elements really take a backseat to the gameplay, which is the focus of Trine 2 by a mile.
Single player and online multiplayer would do in a pinch, but this game is at its best with local multiplayer. Plug in a few controllers and disable player levitation (why play a puzzle game with a feature that allows you to bypass puzzles?) and you'll be sure to have a great time with your friends. While there is virtually no replay value since the level designs and puzzles are static and fixed, the game feels long enough and involved enough to warrant a discounted purchase. 20 dollars seems too steep for the simplicity and one-time-through play value of it all, but if you can get it on sale or part of a humble bundle, you will definitely get 5-10 dollars worth out of it.

Trine 2 is a gorgeous physics-based 3D platformer, and it’s meant to be experienced with friends.
The most important difference from the original Trine is that this game supports three-player co-op over the internet. It may seem like a "well, duh" feature, but it makes a world of difference over the previous local-only game.
By building on its successes rather than messing with its entertaining gameplay, Trine 2's simple concept of trekking toward the right side of the screen feels more like an otherworldly adventure than just another platformer. The abilities of your three playable characters - Wizard, Rogue, and Warrior - synergize superbly. Though at times you may feel overly dependent on another character's unique skills, the often misplaced trust you put in your friends’ talent will generally lead to hilarious and unintended successes.

Frequently, the way to figure out a puzzle is to throw yourself at it until you discover a solution. A side-effect of this is death, but thankfully, it’s hardly a penalty. As long as one character remains alive and makes it to one of the many checkpoints in a level, the others are instantly revived. If everybody dies, all progress is saved and everybody is reincarnated at the latest checkpoint. This serves the flow of the game well, because your sense of adventure is never punished; indeed, being practically immortal in a platformer is surprisingly fun!
Don’t expect much from the story; other than giving a reason to run to the right, it exists only to provide context to Trine 2’s challenges and puzzles. The reward for figuring out each scenario is mainly a sense of progression – but it works. Progression could mean accumulating experience potions that grant each character improved skills or new abilities, or it could mean discovering hard-to-reach chests that contain pieces of concept art or a narrated stanza from the main antagonist’s journal. Simply getting to the next level is often reward enough, because this game’s vibrant visuals are stunning.
Trine 2's artistic merit is absolutely jaw-dropping. The title screen alone sets the bar for the rest of the game. (Try starting the game at different times during the day!) Half of my play-time was spent taking in the stunningly beautiful backdrops and set pieces. I felt guilty when I solved a puzzle without fully admiring the obscene amount of effort put into the graphical presentation of this game. The quality is consistently superb - worthy of your attention all the way through to the last chapter - and every shade of the rainbow gets a feature performance.
The fun to be had in applying home-brewed solutions to solving puzzles with your friends is what sustains Trine 2 until its end. Along with constantly being rewarded with beautiful vistas and remarkably decorated interiors, finding all the hidden goodies will definitely tempt your inner completionist. Although you may need to set personal goals to warrant a second play-through, Trine 2 is a very entertaining game to play over a week with one or two of your friends.

Welcome to one liners: the game, wait no, eighties: the game, wait no, EXPLOSIONS: the game.  Yeah, that last one is about right.  Blood Dragon is not Far Cry 3, it takes place on an island has guns and even features Far Cry 3 in the title, but this is a lie.  Blood Dragon is an amazing, weird little thing that just happened to happen, and thank goddness it did.  The gameplay is great, running around as a cyber comander (or whatever the right phrase was) and blowing up everyone and everything with ease was great fun.  Now Far Cry 3 had a stealth and fear element, a small group of pirates could kill you pretty easy early on.  In Blood Dragon this is not the case: nothing can kill you unless you let it.  And this isnt a difficulty problem (though the game is a tad bit on the easy side) this is the Rambo factor, you can run and gun through the entire game because you are a cyber god.  The music and sounds in the game are so eighties it actually started to hurt at one point, but in a good way, like pulling off a hangnail, it just felt right.  The story of the game was stupid, it was so astoundingly stupid (but not as stupid as Far Cry 3's story, just sayin').  BUT I LOVED IT.  The game was made to be dumb and it hits this mark on every level.  The npc dialouge, the cheesy one liners and the premise of the game itself were so awful that I couldnt help but be charmed.  Also, I think my favorite feature may have been the ability to flip people the bird: pressing f while not close enough to anything to knife causes the character to stick up his middle finger, mashing f makes him fire them off from both hands.
All in all 7/10.  The game was charming and funny but to easy and much much to short.  If you love cheesy eighties sci-fi or just running around with robocops pistol and capping everything in the head then you'll love this game.  If you want a serious, story driven game with some real challenge you probably won't enjoy this (as much as the rest of us).
Also, get Far Cry 3, it's bloody fantastic

***EARLY ACCESS REVIEW***
11/11/17
I logged about an hour or so before writing this, and what I have seen so far is good, overall. The concept is fairly unique, combing RTS, 3rd Person RPG elements, resource management, city building and exploration elements quite nicely. This game definitely has potential, as long as some of the more glaring issues are fixed, as I trust they will be.
I have seen a few reviews complaining of a lack of polish in terms of graphics. While I tend to agree, I must state the obvious fact that this game is in Early Access, so there are going to be problems in terms of appearance and variety of content. I am not a huge stickler for grpahical quality; it is my honest opinion that too many games sacrifice content and mechanics for graphics. It looks fine for the most part. That being said, give the developers some time, and I am sure they will straighten this out.
The sound design is average, as of this writing, with some effects that are a bit muddy and others simply not there at all. For example, there are no footfall sounds when the player, monsters, and NPCs move around. This is especially problematic when exploring caves and dungeons, as the enemies are all ninja assassins, moving about with nary a sound to be heard until they take a chunk out of your backside with a sword.
There are some things that people may see as lazy or just plain odd design choices, but in reality are just placeholders. For instance, every enemy, and I mean EVERY enemy I have seen (with the exception of the rock golems) shoots arrows at me as soon as they see me, even the little Lovecraftian tentacle guys that don't carry bows. I assume this is because the devs simply haven't coded the attacks properly yet, so it doesn't bear weight in this review. I just wanted to mention it becasue I have seen other folks complaining about it. Most of the weirdness you will see stems from the fact that this game is still very early in its development.
I'm not going to list pros and cons, as it would be pointless to do so at this stage. I will simply say that this game shows real promise, and the developers could use your support. It's worth the asking price, if it helps get the game closer to completion.

If you were waiting for a game where Skyrim meets Sim City, where you finally are a leader who doesn't have to complete all tasks all by himself, this game does exactly that. From what I've seen during my short gameplay I can say they have interesting mechanics, and I won't complain about graphics — yes, it looks outdated, but for games of this complexity the solution is perfect.
If authors will accomplish all their goals, especially if there will be mod support, this will be a legendary game.
Devs, please continue this great work, it looks very promising.
For people who are still doubting about buying this title — honestly, it's risky to invest in such complex games, be aware of the fact that due to this complexity the game may take way too long to finish. But if you believe that this kind of deep genre-mixing is what really lacks in modern gaming world, please show your support for authors — it will signal the market that there's a demand for such games as this one.

*Controller Required*
This is a great little gem with a really nice environment and fairly unique gameplay.
You control 2 brothers at the same time using the analogue sticks and have to help each other get through different obstacles.
Incredible cinematic experience. Enjoyed the controls. Beautiful visuals.

With overwhelmingly positive reviews my expectations were high, but I tried to not let that affect my judgement too much.
I liked the graphics style for the most part, although I admit to being slightly distracted by the younger brothers hair looking like he'd had a bowl of custard poured over his head. Seriously though, the game looks nice.
I got on fine with the controls (you really do need a controller), nice to see some original ideas and a new way to solve puzzles.
The story is a simple one, two brothers go off to find some special healing stuff to save thier dying father.
The ending... Well, I was little disappointed. But only because I didn't feel any connection to the characters. Maybe because the game is only a couple of hours long, and not very challenging. If there had been more time and longer puzzles to solve to create the bond between the brothers it would have had much more effect. If you look at Shadow Of The Colossus, despite the underlying simplicity of the game I still nearly broke down in tears the first time Agro falls down the ravine. You spend so much time with Agro as a truely reliable and faithful companion it's impossible to feel nothing. This game does nothing like that. You just jog your way between puzzles, completing each one with ease then on to the next. Despite this I will admit that the use of the control scheme to evoke an emotional response is genuinely remakable and remains the best bit of the game.
So to summarise, if you're a casual gamer you'll probably like it more. If you play a lot of games and have mastered games like Portal then you'll find this a doddle, and will be less likely to feel the emotional ending. It would have been better if it were 10 hours or more with more intricate puzzles.
It is a good game, and definitely worth playing, but for me it was too short and a too easy to buy into the story fully.

Best MMO I have ever played. World is fantastic, even just the F2P. Story is interesting and well told and everything is very close to Tolkein's works. The game is never impossible but also has a good level of challenge and will keep you occupied for hours. However, the shining part of this game is the business model. Downloading it gets you the whole world (until Western Rohan) to explore and the main quest (again until Western Rohan), though you are unable to access any misc quests after the first four areas (Ered Luin, The Shire, Bree-land and the Lone-Lands). Further questing requires quest packs, however these can be bought using money OR Turbine Points, which can be earned in game and, in fact, many quest packs have the potential to return the investment with just 2/3 characters going through it, which, with many, will be irresistable. Personally I loved Evendim, which is worth roughly £6, or 595 Turbine Points. It kept me hooked for many hours, was fantastic for levelling and returned about 100TP of my investment in just one day. I got it with the Eriador bundle which includes Evendim, North Downs, Forochel, Trollshaws, Angmar, Eregion, Enedwaith and Misty Mountains and costs 3995 TPs (about £30 worth) and gives a huge game world which feels to be at least three times bigger than Skyrim. The combat is standard MMO fare, quickslots and auto-attack, but is fairly well-balanced with improvements planned in the next couple of updates.
I only have two major flaws with the game. Firstly, the download time the SECOND time you load it up is ridiculously long for some and only takes a couple of minutes for some. My other flaw is some store items (like the Riding Skill) will slow progress if you want all QPs and Expansion packs using earned in-game points. To get about some of the later, and larger, areas, you will NEED a mount. However, it costs 95TPs to get the riding skill for each character. There are also a few dubious paywalls, or at least they seem that at first, but these are minor. For example, the quild access packs take a while to show much benefit, though later on do give some very good bonuses: making and improving your own legendary item which allows you to not rely on randomised drops and relics. However, every MMO needs consistent income, especially when more expansions and QPs are set to come (Gondor and Mordor all planned for the coming couple of years). The community is also the most helpful I have ever encountered. Overall I would give this a 9/10, the game being a little out of date graphics wise, but in terms of story, gameplay and the world itself, this is perhaps the best MMO I've ever had the pleasure of stumbling across.

A game that, in theory, sounds fun. Politics an intrigue? City building? Technological progression, dynastic elements? All sounds great, but it falls very flat in implementation.
Politics boil down to managing your influence and choosing which votes you want to win and which ones you don't mind losing. It sounds like it will be fun, but it devolves into tedium extremely fast, to the point that every time you open up the vote screen (which isn't skippable...) you want to groan a bit and get it over with because the outcome of the vote - pass or fail - is known well in advance the majority of the time.
The city building is obtuse, with a UI that does a very poor job making clear what would be of most benefit to your city at any given time. Further, you have very, very little control over the city, as almost every single thing you do goes to a vote, and many times you just can't win. Reminiscent of reality? Sure. Fun gameplay? Hardly.
Really, one of the problems the game has is the fact that is has many different systems - politics, dynasty, city building (kinda), technology - and it does a very, very poor job of making them comprehensible to the player and 'connecting the dots' between the systems so it's transparent in how that interact. Transparency in systems is an essential part to any strategy game; without transparency, strategy becomes random (frustrating) chance, which is too often what you get in Urban Empire.
Icing on the bad cake - optimization is poor. The best thing the game does is lag on higher speed settings, even if you have a beefy machine.
The game sounds great on paper. I love strategy games. I love city builders. I love RPGS. Match made in heaven? But I've tried playing this game on several occassions and every time the game has lacked one essential thing - fun. Go ahead and skip this one, you aren't missing anything.

I ignored the negative reviews and bought it on sale.  Had I known this was as good as it is, I would have paid full price.  It is exactly as the description says, so do not think you are getting a city builder.  This is more or less a political city simulator.  This is a MAYOR SIMULATOR.  You cannot build without permission, the city council has to approve projects, just like in real life.  You want to add electricity to a district? Then you better make sure you have the budget, and the support behind the many political parties behind you.
It is not as complex as many on here make it seem.  Yes, it is hard, but this type of game is for those who like a strategic challenge.  You played for 3 hours and think you wasted your money? Then you have no patience, or concept of mastery.  This game literally requires practice, patience, and strategy.  You won't learn everything the first time, but as you play, you figure it out (its within its design).
Buy if:
You want strategic, different, challenging.  You want to have a management challenge, and dare to dap in simulated politics, economics, and wish to feel like what it is like to deal with city councils.
Do not buy if:
You wish to buy a Sim City or Cities: Skylines type game. If you want a Dictator like city builder (Buy Tropico for that).  If you want the game's playbility handed to you.

Heroes and Generals is a generally fun, realistic "F2P" FPS. It's just what you'd think: A WW2-based shooter with classic nuances like semi-automatic rifles, machine guns, rocket launchers, trucks, jeeps, tanks, airplanes, etc.
The gameplay itself is actually pretty fun in the beginning. For the first few matches of the game, you're eased in alongside other new players and bots against a team of enemy bots on a relatively simple map with a relatively simple objective. It's easy enough, and anyone with brains can pass this part and get into actual gameplay. In the actual game, the first few matches/ranks are very, very fun. It feels like an infantry fight you might see in WWII. Semi-automatic rifle fire, slow-rate machine guns and the occasional mounted gun.
Then, you begin to realize that it's not always gonna be this simple.
As you rank up, gain currency and all that jazz, you get into new games against new types of enemies. Airplanes, tanks, people with sniper rifles and LMGs. And, unless you pay for the friggin' veteran perks, buy gold for guns, etc- you'll have a real hard time getting anywhere.
Be amazed as you get absolutely OWNED by some dude with a limitless trust fund and an airplane, CONSTANTLY dropping bombs on you! Also, tanks aren't suseptable to grenades.. yeah. You heard me.
Wanna take out a tank? Get that land mine, get a Panzerfaust. Oh, don't have enough slots for a mine? BUY THE VETERAN UPGRADE FOR A MONTHLY PAYMENT! You get 1 extra slot. Also, an insignificant XP boost. Also, some more vehicle slots. Really, you just need to buy gold and you're *golden*.
Point is, it's a fun game until you realize people just pour money into anything just to seem good, and the companies entertain this notion by providing the outlet. Man, if you're gonna do that, make the game something you have to buy first. Turn the poor, unmoney commoners away.

(Ubisoft's own flavour of DRM) which adds another level of frustration. So I got bored of waiting around and traipsing about dungeons and decided to take a walk near Riverside after guaranteeing them my protection on a quest. I walk past and discover this neat looking outpost and castle wall, realizing that it certainly wasn't me who built them.
Fast forward a minute later and I'm being assaulted by a horde of trained outpost soldiers and guards who don't take kindly to my presence, after all, I'm wearing really fancy clothes, and nobility could always be ransomed for good prices back in the day.
I of course, being a Mage, massacre the group using the OP Ring of Fire spell... until a fresh horde of double the size spawns after me. Outposts typically had an off-duty reserve force of reinforcements after all.
I'm low on mana, low on health, and♥♥♥♥♥♥outta luck, so I decide to run away, and as I pass Riverside, I realize that I was followed the entire way.
One thing leads to another and Riverside ends up being raided and its villagers butchered. Clearly my excellent guarantee of protection at work.
I barely make it back and swear revenge. I recruit my own massive army which is five times their size and decide to return the favour. Soon as I arrive at their camp, me and my elite band of soldiers, archers, and eight ragtag local serfs carry out a genocide of such utter magnitude... that the enemies stopped respawning altogether.
I'm still mad, and realize that there's a wall manned by enemy archers standing in my way, so, being the excellent commander that I am, I order my loyal soldiers to assault the wall and bring me some heads.
Of course... I forgot to bring siege equipment, and so spent half an hour sitting amidst the corpses of the slaughtered outpost guards as my archers traded fire with theirs and my soldiers clumsily attempted to parkour over the walls.
Suffice to say, the siege did not result in my victory, but instead in a stalemate. Both sides agreed to call it quits, and my force retreated since I ran out of
supplies and had no way of breaking the gate.
10/10 would slaughter and fail siege again.
Devs, you better be assembling my siege equipment for the next assault.

Some games doesn't need awesome graphics, expensive cutscenes and cinematics or entertaining combat's finishers with slow-mo effect. Legends of Ellaria is all about gameplay. And that's a good thing for me.
This game was in my wish list since the very first day of its release. I've decided to give it a go yesterday, just to play something for half an hour before I'll go to bed. Somehow I ended up in the middle of the night building a house. And that's a good sign!
The game is pretty raw at the moment, but its potential is huge. For those who expecting an almost finished product I suggest to wait. But if you do care about the game I believe it is the right choice to support developers and buy it.
There is a lot of work to be done, of course. The biggest problem for me so far is interaction with objects: you ought to be very precise to do anything, I hope developers will fix it as soon as possible. Movement feels unusual and it takes time to get used to it. Tutorial is confusing at some points. Hint's font is hard to read. A lot of placeholders yet but this is just a niggle. Some people also complain about bad optimization but I had experienced just a one tiny lag during tutorial, in the rest of the time the game's performance was okay, except maybe pretty slow launch in the very first time. And I don't have a high-end PC, my specs are pretty average (GTX760).
Anyways, the game is fun overall but you should keep in mind that it is in the very beginning of its path and there are a lot of flaws yet. It is a fresh Early Access title, after all. Moreover, some flaws can deliver a lot of fun. For example, a worker finished building another house for me but still hammering the wall... with an axe! Stop breaking my house, you prat!
I am looking forward to future improvements and wish the best to the developers. And, of course, I expect to see a decent title in a year or two. Don't let me down!

A fantastic fighting game: simple enough to pick up quickly, but incredibly deep and loads of fun.  It's a lot like smash bros in terms of the mechanics, which some people might be bothered by, but I really like smash bros, so I'm always down for more games in that style.  The training mode may be my favorite part of the game so far: it actually lets you pause, play frame-by-frame, and gives you data on each move: startup and ending lag, hitbox duaration, the precise location, size, shape, damage, and knockback of every single hitbox - it's incredibly detailed and technical.  It's mostly online, so endless gameplay, and the difficulty curve is somewhat steep, but not unreasonable or overly frustrating.  You can pay to unlock all the characters straight away or unlock them with coins from playing online matches, and pay for additional character and weapons skins, but neither really give you an edge; it's not pay to win.  You can set the controls any way you like, and play with up to four other people on the same computer, which is just awesome.  I'd recommend this game to anyone if it were $20 and fully complete, so considering it's still just a beta and it's free to play, I don't really know what you're waiting for.

I adore this game.
The art style is visually pleasing throughout. A lot of love and care went into the tiny details, and it shows in the background scenery. The developers have every right to be proud of the beautiful world they created. Please take the time to really look at it when you play! There are lots of things to look at and interact with, and there are benches placed along your path for the two brothers to sit and enjoy what there is to see. Make sure you use them all.
At its heart, Brothers is an exercise in showing, not telling. The plot is revealed in flashback scenes, but there is no real dialogue between characters. Even written instruction to the player is minimal, which is refreshing in the age of gamer handholding. The environments contain all the context you need to solve puzzles. If you can't figure out what to do, it's usually your fault: slow down a little and pay attention to the world around you.
Brothers controls beautifully, and the controls are integral to the way the game is played and how the plot unfolds. If I had anything negative to say, it would be that my controller was acting strangely so I was obliged to finish playing with a keyboard, but that is my only gripe and it's entirely my fault, not the game's.
The guy in the beginning who won't let you pass is one of the most real things in Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons. Even though the game has a very fairy tale vibe to it, it actually gets more real the further you play. Brothers will make you feel things. Unhappy things. I legitimately cried. Multiple times.
If you have a brother, or are a brother, Brothers will speak to you. It's an amazing experience packaged and sold for only fifteen dollars. If even that pricetag is too high, you can also find it on sale from time to time. Please, buy yourself a copy. I cannot recommend the game enough.

This game is so good, and it also has so much potential for the future.
Nothing about it as it stands is really bad, and compared to other selections in the genre it's fully competitive in it's own right as currently presented. That isn't to say it could just stand a few more features, like a better server browser and search, better party formation outside of just creating your own server, and some neccesary bugfixes. However, these small criticisms aside, the game's really very fun. The gameplay is solid, the community is already rolling pretty well, and gameplay balance is pretty much established. From a graphical and technical perspective UE4 is gorgeous (still the best AO of any engine, imo) performant, and remains my favorite modern engine, crytek and it's perpetual z-fighting be damned.
I do wish you could fire while in the air, for balance perhaps with diminished accuracy (or maybe you can and it just freqently won't let me), and the game stealing the mic and forcing a team-only p2t is a bit annoying. It would be nice to have an option to not lock the mic so I can keep a call going with friends in Steam. Server browsing as a group is pretty frustrating as well since partying up only really allows you to form your own server.
Even with the above notes, this game is certainly worth purchasing and playing, just from a cost to entertainment value perspective. It's as good to better than all the other modern 3rd person multiplayer AAA shooters that keep getting pumped out like Scream sequels, and it costs 1/5th as much. Plus you get the gratification of not contributing to EA or Ubisoft's slow strangling death of multiplayer gaming. With these facts in mind, how can that purchase decision even be a question?
So long as they keep out microtransactions and unlockable crap, I can see myself playing this for a while. Shame on those who, in other reviews, have suggested that sort of thing. Keep the cancer of modern gaming out of this, it's too good to die that way.

So far, so good, i received this game as a gift, a beautiful gift that make me chuckle quite a bit upon seeing it. Also, brings me alot of childhood memories.

Soulstorm is the last expansion for the original Dawn of War. However, instead of a last hurrah in honour of the glorious emperor of mindkind, it just a convoluted mess of gimmicks and glitches.
Before we discuss the technicalities, lets look at the content. Soulstorm adds two new races to Dawn of War: The Sisters of Battle, and the Dark Eldar. Neither are genuinely unique races, but they are different from the race their branched out of. The Sisters are a cult of fanatics who wield a wide assortment of flamethrowers and use divine powers to make themselves invincible. The Dark Eldar on the other hand are all about speed and hit and run tactics. Each race also gets a new airplane unit which reflects the race's general playstyle. Both of the new races also come with their own unique resource that can be spent to unleash special abilities on the field.
Both races feel rather uninteresting. The Sisters feel space marines without the brawn, while the Dark Eldar feel like a swarm of gnats that cannot really put out any damage.
Unfortunately, the problems have only just begun. The expansion is unfinished; many abilities and weapons just don't do anything. The guns on some aircraft really do no damage, while other abilities just stack ad infinitum to create an indestructible unit. It is a shame, because the campaign tries to go above and beyond what Dark Crusade had set up. More planets, more abilities, more options. However, just like I mentioned before, a lot of it just doesn't work properly.
To be fair, Soulstorm's development was a mess and as a result the final product is a mess. It functions, but only barely. Playing Soulstorm is like driving a Ferrari with its tyres deflated; You may have the best car in the world, but you just can't enjoy it to the fullest because there is a glaring fault wherever, and whatever you do.

Best MMO I have ever played. World is fantastic, even just the F2P. Story is interesting and well told and everything is very close to Tolkein's works. The game is never impossible but also has a good level of challenge and will keep you occupied for hours. However, the shining part of this game is the business model. Downloading it gets you the whole world (until Western Rohan) to explore and the main quest (again until Western Rohan), though you are unable to access any misc quests after the first four areas (Ered Luin, The Shire, Bree-land and the Lone-Lands). Further questing requires quest packs, however these can be bought using money OR Turbine Points, which can be earned in game and, in fact, many quest packs have the potential to return the investment with just 2/3 characters going through it, which, with many, will be irresistable. Personally I loved Evendim, which is worth roughly £6, or 595 Turbine Points. It kept me hooked for many hours, was fantastic for levelling and returned about 100TP of my investment in just one day. I got it with the Eriador bundle which includes Evendim, North Downs, Forochel, Trollshaws, Angmar, Eregion, Enedwaith and Misty Mountains and costs 3995 TPs (about £30 worth) and gives a huge game world which feels to be at least three times bigger than Skyrim. The combat is standard MMO fare, quickslots and auto-attack, but is fairly well-balanced with improvements planned in the next couple of updates.
I only have two major flaws with the game. Firstly, the download time the SECOND time you load it up is ridiculously long for some and only takes a couple of minutes for some. My other flaw is some store items (like the Riding Skill) will slow progress if you want all QPs and Expansion packs using earned in-game points. To get about some of the later, and larger, areas, you will NEED a mount. However, it costs 95TPs to get the riding skill for each character. There are also a few dubious paywalls, or at least they seem that at first, but these are minor. For example, the quild access packs take a while to show much benefit, though later on do give some very good bonuses: making and improving your own legendary item which allows you to not rely on randomised drops and relics. However, every MMO needs consistent income, especially when more expansions and QPs are set to come (Gondor and Mordor all planned for the coming couple of years). The community is also the most helpful I have ever encountered. Overall I would give this a 9/10, the game being a little out of date graphics wise, but in terms of story, gameplay and the world itself, this is perhaps the best MMO I've ever had the pleasure of stumbling across.

Torchlight II isn't just an average diablo-like game, it's an experience that every gamer must try at least one in a lifetime.
The story takes place right after the ending of the previous chapter, where the Alchemist has gone rogue because of the Ember, a magical substance that is the fuel of the steampunk tecnology within this world.
The new classes are the Berserker (something like a barbarian, or an inn brawler), the Embermage (a sorcerer that may use the great three elemental magics, fire, frost and lightning), the Engeneer (a steampunked fighter and creator of various steambots) and the Outlander (the ranged character, agile and deadly).
The pets are a nice extra in this Diablo-clone (you will have as pet a wolf, a cat, a ferret, an hawk, an owl, a panda, or many others).
Even if it's a really good game in a singleplayer game, Torchlight II shows its best in multiplayer mode.

868-HACK is incredibly simple, and this is its main selling point - it's very feasible that you'll memorize all the content in the game and its interactions within the first two or three hours. why is this a selling point? because despite this, you're given the full breadth of the roguelike experience - you're taught to be cowardly, cut your losses, squeeze the most out of your dwindling resources and feel unbelievably smart and agile doing it. every piece interlocks, so there's no need for any others. it feels a little like playing chess should. buy this game.

It's hard to describe 868-HACK any other way than, "Simple and Elegant."  While screenshots may make the game appear to be complex, this lightweight little roguelike/turn-based arcade game operates on a very simple and easy to understand set of rules that make playing it and replaying it a breeze. Seriously, a game of 868-HACK will likely only take you anywhere from 5-10 minutes, but it's a game that really thrives on replaying for better scores or just booting it up for a quick run to the end of its 8 sectors.
Taking place on a 6x6 grid, your main objective in 868-HACK is to simply get to the exit without being damaged three times. Clearing a sector will heal one point of damage you've taken. There are only four enemy types and each operates on a defined set of movement rules. One enemy type gets two moves to your one, another type is only visible when you share the same column or row, one can move through obstacles uninhibited, and the final enemy type takes three attacks to destroy rather than two. These patterns are easy to understand and pick up on, but puzzling your way through each sector without getting pincered by your randomly spawning foes is what makes each playthrough exciting.
"Data Siphoning" (or collecting) helpful programs and the resources to use them is the key to overcoming the overwhelming odds. Some programs can instantly destroy foes, others can push them away, and there's always the helpful Reset program, which is a full heal. As you complete the game, you'll continue unlocking new and fun programs which can randomly spawn on every sector, which again, greatly increases the game's replay value.
You really can't go wrong with this one. It's simple and fiendishly addicting, capturing the same spirit of "Just one more try" that longer and more involved games like The Binding of Isaac have, but with a much smaller time investment. This one's not leaving my installed folder for quite some time.

To start I would like to say that the game is very fun but probably not worth the current price tag. I actually got it for a lower price for an activation key and I reccomand to wait for the game to go on sale or find a better deal for an activation key.
Since my overall review is positive I will begin with what I didn't like about the game.
Negatives:
While the city hub is very big and there are many side missions, the campaign missions are quite short and are less interesting than the previous game.
The campaign itself is very short and can be finished in about 10 hours if you don't care for anything else.
The story is less engaging than the previous game and seems to lack some of the pathos in some of the trailers. Specificly the guy in the yellow trench coat that appeared in many of the trailers where he was first harassed by police officers, begged Jensen for help as Jensen was forced to not intervene and later would join the terrorist organization was absent from the game itself and could only his computer can be found. In addition the Viktor Marchenko who I thought would be an interesting morally ambiguous antagonist turned out to be a quite generic villain.
Tne ending in particular felt weird, as if the game shouldn't have been over at that moment, like there were still things going on and many questions are left unanswered.
There seems to be a problem with the lip syncing, the characters were saying something and the lips move in a way that doesn't match what is being said.
Breach mode, while an interesting idea doesn't add much to the game and by my opinion isn't very fun. Using one time modifiers that make a stage harder to increase your score or finishing a map in less than 30 seconds just doesn't match the planning and choosing between multiple paths in the main game.
And lastly microtransactions. While microtransactions are bad anyway for a game that costs 60$ the good thing is that they are completely unnecessary and the game was balanced to work perfectly fine without them. I just hope that future games won't expect to purchase one time upgrades in order to finish a difficult mission.
Positives:
The city of Prague is very detailed and has many little things beyond just the main and side missions. Every apartment is distinguishable from the others and eachy computer feels like it belongs to a different person (the exception being corporate computers but even most of them feel like they are used by different people in the company), unlike the previous game where many apartments feel like they were made en masse, each one with the same furniture, an NPC standing as you hack into his or her computer and read the same e-mails you read hunderds of times before.
The city of Prague also holds many secrets, from hidden passageways to buttons that reveal a secret room and safes hidden behind paintings, there are a lot more secrets to find by simply moving through Prague than Human Revolution had.
The voice acting is very good and despite the lip syncing problem really make the characters come to life.
The side missions are very fun and interesting and there are plenty of them. Not only that, but these side missions sometimes affect the main story as well. The side missions are much larger than in Human Revolution and usually involve multiple sateges compared to the usually single objective side missions of the previous game. It feels to me though that they should have made less side missions and focused more on the main story like in the previous game. To illustrate, the game took me 50 hours with the side missions and exploring the city, and 10 hours without the side missions.
By my opinion tha fact that the game has only one city hub allowed that city hub to be much more focused and the changes in the city are felt better than in the prevoius game where the difference between the first visit to a city to the second is that you have one more area to explore.
The graphics are beautiful and Prague looks really great, every part of the enviornment and the objects in it is very detailed.
As always the desicions you make will affect the story later, don't save a witness in time and the witness dies, fail to retrive evidence and you won't have access to that information later.
The most important part of the game, the gameplay, is very good. The levels are designed with many paths available to you, most of them hidden. The levels involve a lot more verticality than the previous game which I enjoy immensely. Biocells and Multitools return from the first game, giving you even more options to solving your problems. The new energy management system encourages you to use your augmentations gor a long time but few times overall, instead of the previous game in which there really was no difference than 3 batteries to 2 batteies and Cyberboost Proenergy Bar.
Overall while I think the game shouldn't be bought over Human Revolution or the original Deus Es it's a fine addition to the series. The game does disappoint in some areas but the most imprortant part of a Deus Ex game, the multiple ways to achieve an objective is certainly there. One of the things I enjoyed the most is when I entered a level from one place and had to advance slowly and stealthly to reach an objective and afterward I left via another path and on my second playthrough I enterd the level from the other path and basicaly skipped the entire level. That is what a good Deus Ex is for me.

Pros
+ The maps all look nice and are asthetically pleasing
+ The scale of the maps are impressive; you really feel like a toy soldier in a huge room
+ The weapons are balanced pretty well (apart from the rocket launcher being pretty OP)
+ The gamemodes are very creative and fun (although some are not obvious what the objective is at first)
Cons
- A few connectivity issues; sometimes hard to join a server (have to keep trying before it lets you in)
- The rocket launcher is a bit OP and, despite only having 1 shot, is usually the most-used weapon
- A few maps make the matches feel either too rushed or too drawn out
- Can't shoot while jumping, which is forgettable sometimes but annoying other times (like on maps with jump pads)
Overall the gameplay is very simple but fun, with easy to understand mechanics. This game has a lot of potential and I hope that it succeeds so that we can see more updates in the future, such as more maps, gamemodes, and vehicles.

This game has a huge amount of potential, and as many have said in the review section, the ground work is there. Unfortunately, this game has one glaring issue. You see those 0.5 hours of playtime there? Yeah. 0.4 was spent TRYING TO FIND A F***ING GAME. I understand the game isn't being published by those big AAA companies but it is inexcusable to have your game launch and have it take 30 minutes to find one game. Oh, but it doesn't stop there. Once I got into a game, crash. I tried again, crash again. 3rd time is a charm, as I finally got into a game. I think I should start with the pros of this game.
*Pros*
-Amazing atmosphere and level design. The levels all feel unique and are perfectly catered to their respected game mode. The levels give off, to me at least, a V20 Blockland vibe.
-OST is perfect. The 30 minutes I waited to get into a game was both frustrating and uplifting. Why? The OST is so damn catchy. The OST fits every level and moment perfectly and keeps you pumped up while you're playing the game as opposed to how other FPS games have no background music (I'm looking at you Battlefront).
-Combat Rolling is wonderful. Combat rolling in games like Battlefront 2 was very fun and unique because not many games at the time had mechanics like it. It forced people to make new strategies and adapt to a new gameplay style. This carries over perfectly with Plastic Warfare.
*Cons*
-Weapon Balance needs reworking. Everyone has the same equipment at all times. While this means the game is more fair in a sense, from what I've played, everyone just ends up using the Rocket Launcher and Sniper. I think this could be improved by adding in a class system or having some weapons be map pick ups, sort of like Halo.
-No Single Player mode. I can't believe I'm saying this, but even EA's Battlefront has a better single player. Why? Because there is no single player in this game. Having an offline mode with bots would greatly benefit the game, as it would not only help new people become adapted to the gameplay, but it would also make the game more playable, especially with the...
-God Awful Connection. I was able to get into 1 game, 1 f***ing game. I would either..
A. Lose connection to the host (even when I was the host)
B. Server would be full (even if it was 7/10 on the browser menu)
c. Join a game, but crash.
-Movement =/= Control set up. The sprint is extremely fast, so it would make sense that sprint jumping would be effective. Unfortunately, there is a 1-2 second delay in jumping and sprinting, which means you end up stopping and jumping or not jumping at all. Also, double tapping forward should set the player into a sprint.
As it sits now, I don't recommend it. However, I'm sure the game will change for the most part and most of these cons will be irrelevant in 6 months.

If you love MMO's and you love Lord of the Rings then look no further.  This game brings together all the features you enjoy in an MMO and all the characters you love (and hate) in the realm of Middle Earth make this game a top of the charts game with top f the line gameplay. I hope you all enjoy this game as much as I do.

As MMOs go, The Lord of the Rings Online: Shadows of Angmar isn't half bad. Although it's gone through several permutations over the course of its lifespan, it is currently a free-to-play title with a very hefty amount of actually-free material. As a man, hobbit, elf, or dwarf, you must rise up and begin fighting back against the various forces of Sauron, indirectly aiding the Fellowship of the Ring as they make their march to Mount Doom. Fans of the LotR universe and devout Silmarillion enthusiasts will have a lot to enjoy here; the world is packed to the gills with obscure names and lore trivia, and seeing every square inch of Tolkien's world fleshed out is actually rather thrilling (according to the massive Tolkien nerd I live with anyway). As a moderate fan of the books, I personally found the world better designed and more atmospheric than most MMO worlds, but nothing to freak out about.
As for the gameplay, it's solid and incorporates many of the best features of modern MMOs. Forming groups for skirmishes and dungeons is easy, quest tracking is convenient, and inventory management is a breeze... assuming you're willing to pay a couple bucks here and there for content. Playing the purely free version of the game is a little more aggravating, but still playable and enjoyable. You miss out on some inventory space, some class options, and eventually a lot of quest access, but by then you'll know if you like the game, and as game costs go everything is pretty reasonable.
Along with the usual assortment of MMO quest grinding (so many boar heads and bear butts for strangely insistent random strangers...), there's also a surprisingly substantial Epic quest chain for each race, making up the actual storyline for the game as your character works with Strider, Gandalf, and many others to save the world from the generic eeeeeevil of Mordor. While I hesitate to call it "gripping", it's a hell of a lot better than it could have been. The only aspect of the game I found lacking was the near-absence of PvP. While players who pay the monthly fee for VIP status get access to a MONSTER PLAY mode, it seems a bit essential to include that in base play.
I could go on, but there's not much to say here beyond it being a solid, high-budget, free-to-play MMO that provides decent returns for your investment in the expansion packs, and which fans of a particular legendary fantasy writer may go nuts over. I had a good two weeks tromping from Shire to Moria, and I'm throwing in the towel without a bad taste in my mouth. For an MMO, that's a hell of a lot better than average.

I missed the boat when this came out for mobile. It plays great on PC, but now it's a must have for my bus trips. Very simple and quick, and has that compelling "one more time" feel.
Your goal is to score the most points across 8 short levels. Capturing score blocks or special abilities causes enemies to appear. You also need to capture resources to feed your special abilities. Everything else is about carefully positioning yourself to manage the enemies. It reminds me a lot of Ending, but with an added risk/reward balance so that you can decide when to play safe or increase your score.

You've gathered cash and resources. You've raided secure nodes for the best programs. You are now ready for the big scores, the hard data. That's how you get the rep. Are you a slick enough cyber-dude to get the goods and slip out?
868-HACK is a roguelike with tactics and strategy so tightly integrated it feels almost like a puzzle game. Hordes of enemies can be overcome with careful application of movement, abilities, exploitation of enemy behavior and the environment. Enemies and abilities operate in clear and logical fashion making it a lot of fun to analyze seemingly impossible situations for the perfect solution. It's so well done when you come up with the answeres you can almost hear the click as everything snaps into place. So even though the game lends itself to short sessions making it perfect for casual play the play itself is not at all trivial. Every move and choice you make will have consequences, immediate and long term. The game is so cleanly designed and clearly presented that the decision making process is highly intuitive making play fast paced and fun. If you play well you'll complete all eight levels, or sectors in the game's terminology, of a run. A run is what the game calls a dungeon. Surviving a run allows you to keep your previous score as you go into your next run. Continued success on runs means you can string these scores together. Can you string together enough conservative runs before the worst happens to climb up the leaderboards? Or are you going to smash and grab your way to the top? Careful, the bigger the score, the higher the risk. This roguelike isn't of the impenetrably punishing variety. Once you learn the rules the only thing that will punish you is your own greed and arrogance. Or who knows, maybe you are really that good.
This game is a must for fans of short form puzzle roguelikes like Desktop Dungeons or Road Not Taken. Easily worth the full price and then some for fans of this style of roguelike, and I believe it could even make some converts.

I read all the reviews, half negative half positive.  I almost skipped out for now due to all the negative reviews.  I am truly glad that I didnt and picked up this game, it is very well worth the money and a worthy successor to human revolution.
I spent 37 hours in the game on "give me deus ex" mode before I completed it.  I was pretty thorough with my exploration but a few times I did get ancy and just cut to the chase because I wanted to know the next step in the story, which was pretty good I must say.  The story is not quite as good as human revolution,  But that is hard to trump considering how good HR is.
The good dialogue is still here, plenty of options to delve deep in each conversation with meaningful dialogue choices.
Combat is extremely satisfying. Tight controlls, powerful abilities, good AI, great feeling weaponry and tons of optiopns on how to approach each encounter.
I was completely absorbed in the game until the very end, which I felt concluded perfectly for the game considering this will be a trilogy and the "real culrpits" Im sure will be the target of the next title, which is perfectly acceptable to me. What turns out to be the main antagonist of this title was someone I wanted to deal with ever since the first encounter with them and it seemed fitting that they were the final boss.
TLDR:  You wont be disapointed if you liked human revolution.  Its basically a continuation with much better graphics, better combat and more abilities to have fun with.  Enjoy!

Warband: ITS ALMOST HARVESTING SEASON
Warband is an example of "gameplay triumphing over everything else". The graphics are ok, the story is pretty ok, but the pure entertainment that you can get from this game makes it worth the money. You start off as some lowly twit with a rusted sword and a shield and can be whatever you want to be. You can lead a horde of bandits across Calradia stealing from every faction in the game, you can start a massive army funded by businesses that dot every city in the realm, or just organize a band of farmers and beat up local deserters for trying to steal your wheat.
The combat system is simple enough to get into, and the game's menus help you cover almost any detail you'd need to know to prevent yourself from walking headfirst into enemy territory. You can juggle inventory items ranging from bags of salt and spices to incredibly heavyweight armor that might make you invincible in battle until some mercenary hits you with a mace. You can hire all flavors of companions who will begin to make some drama at you like it's some 1990's sitcom. And there's many factions you can ally with/go to war with/steal from, ranging from angry Nords, Mongals and the Sarranids who can be of great use as you slam 80 Mamluke cavalry into a Swadian army composed of normal troops.
So yeah, get this game, do some stupid things and watch the chaos unfold as you burn down half of the villages in Calradia because free stuff.

This game has a lot of cool, unique things about it. It's got 4x, RPG, and 1st/3rd person shooter/brawler elements, not to mention horseback combat.
The coolest unique thing about it, for me, though, is how you actually aim and control the swing of your sword with the mouse. Landing some long distance archery shots is cool too, but there's just nothing like coming cruising up on your horse and just landing the perfect neck-slice as you ride by one or more opponents.
So yeah, you'd call it a swordfighting game, too, I guess. And, it's been a while since I played either one, but .. a bit more nuanced than Chivalry, IIRC.
Game does have its issues. Some achievements are glitched, last I checked. And to be honest it's probably showing it's age a bit at this point. But it was always a little underwhelming graphically, which is part of the secret to being able to being able to have actual hundred-person battles onscreen.
Still, a truly unique game. There's nothing quite like it except for maybe other M&B games.
If you think you'd be into it, you can't go wrong on sale.
