OK, story time! I have an eight year old cousin, and since he likes to play Mario and other of Nintendo's more puzzle-ish games I thought he and I could play this one together. Those of you who have tried this game know how the controls work, and it's actually easier to play this game with two hands from two different bodies than two hands from the same body(all puzzle games should have a ♥♥♥♥ed control system that takes 5 years to get used to, it was fun as hell ¯\_(ツ)_/¯) so we had a go at the game.
And then we came close to the ending, and that's when you suddenly realise that the game has PEGI 16 for a reason, first one in a while eh, and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥was it ♥♥♥♥ed. Long story short, after this game he and I discussed life, death and depression.
Replayability is high on this one, the stages are really fun, and to try to replay the toughest stages and get all the achievements are just two reasons to replay. When you've finished the game you can choose with chapter to play, if you want to do just that!

The award-winning action RPG is back, bigger and better than ever! Torchlight II takes you back into the quirky, fast-paced world of bloodthirsty monsters, bountiful treasures, and sinister secrets - and, once again, the fate of the world is in your hands!
Torchlight II captures all the flavor and excitement of the original game - while expanding the world and adding the features players wanted most, including online and LAN co-op multiplayer. Torchlight II is fast, fun, and filled to the brim with action and loot. Adventure solo or online with your friends!
Key Features:
Multiplayer - Play co-op with your friends via LAN or over the Internet for free. No subscriptions, no item sales. Our new matchmaking service lets you find friends, start new games, and join existing games. And, as always, you can play single-player offline as well.
Customizable Characters - Players will create and customize a character from one of four brand new classes. Each class can be played as either male or female, with customized cosmetic features and looks to make each individual character stand out. Moddability - TorchED, the Torchlight II editor, will give players the ability to create their own mods, adding even more content to the world. Have your friends download the same mod and play together. TorchED will be available as a separate download very shortly after launch.
New User Interface - Torchlight II boasts a new and improved user interface, designed to be easier than ever for new players to pick up and play. This intuitive interface ensures you can focus on playing the game the way you want to.
Open World - We're not only in the town of Torchlight anymore! Explore vast overland areas and multiple hub towns, fight through rain, snow, day and night. Our level randomization ensures new layouts, paths, loot, and monsters every time you play.
New Game Plus - In New Game Plus, the game's not over until you say it is. Once you've beaten Torchlight II's primary campaign, you can start again with the same character for a significantly greater challenge. You'll keep all of the skills, gold, and gear you worked so hard for!

If you love MMO's and you love Lord of the Rings then look no further.  This game brings together all the features you enjoy in an MMO and all the characters you love (and hate) in the realm of Middle Earth make this game a top of the charts game with top f the line gameplay. I hope you all enjoy this game as much as I do.

As MMOs go, The Lord of the Rings Online: Shadows of Angmar isn't half bad. Although it's gone through several permutations over the course of its lifespan, it is currently a free-to-play title with a very hefty amount of actually-free material. As a man, hobbit, elf, or dwarf, you must rise up and begin fighting back against the various forces of Sauron, indirectly aiding the Fellowship of the Ring as they make their march to Mount Doom. Fans of the LotR universe and devout Silmarillion enthusiasts will have a lot to enjoy here; the world is packed to the gills with obscure names and lore trivia, and seeing every square inch of Tolkien's world fleshed out is actually rather thrilling (according to the massive Tolkien nerd I live with anyway). As a moderate fan of the books, I personally found the world better designed and more atmospheric than most MMO worlds, but nothing to freak out about.
As for the gameplay, it's solid and incorporates many of the best features of modern MMOs. Forming groups for skirmishes and dungeons is easy, quest tracking is convenient, and inventory management is a breeze... assuming you're willing to pay a couple bucks here and there for content. Playing the purely free version of the game is a little more aggravating, but still playable and enjoyable. You miss out on some inventory space, some class options, and eventually a lot of quest access, but by then you'll know if you like the game, and as game costs go everything is pretty reasonable.
Along with the usual assortment of MMO quest grinding (so many boar heads and bear butts for strangely insistent random strangers...), there's also a surprisingly substantial Epic quest chain for each race, making up the actual storyline for the game as your character works with Strider, Gandalf, and many others to save the world from the generic eeeeeevil of Mordor. While I hesitate to call it "gripping", it's a hell of a lot better than it could have been. The only aspect of the game I found lacking was the near-absence of PvP. While players who pay the monthly fee for VIP status get access to a MONSTER PLAY mode, it seems a bit essential to include that in base play.
I could go on, but there's not much to say here beyond it being a solid, high-budget, free-to-play MMO that provides decent returns for your investment in the expansion packs, and which fans of a particular legendary fantasy writer may go nuts over. I had a good two weeks tromping from Shire to Moria, and I'm throwing in the towel without a bad taste in my mouth. For an MMO, that's a hell of a lot better than average.
Perhaps it is not the best MMO in the world but it's a good game. You can walk through middle-earth and enjoy the beautiful scenery. All LOTR fans should give it a try.

(Single player review) Every species and faction from the previous Dawn of War main game + Expansions, with two new factions and a campaign that is almost a copy of Dark Crusade. Which is a good thing, considering how much fun Dark Crusade was with the added burden of choices and a persistent battlefield.
The two new factions possess enough uniqueness to make them viable alternatives to the series mainstays. I've personally come to prefer the Sisters of Battle over Chaos due to the Sister's faith mechanic, where faith serves as a resource for various units to use for healing and attack bonuses in addition to whatever normal abilities the units possess. The Sisters also have a much greater reliance on melee and flame-based weapons compared to many of the other factions. I personally have no interest in the Dark Eldar, but the new faction's soul-harvesting mechanic dosen't sound like anything the other factions have.
My only real complaint agianst Soulstorm is that the additions to the single player campain seem poorly planed. Firstly, there's very little in the way of additions from Dark Crusade, but this isn't automatically a bad thing. What is troublesome, however, is that the main change, a move from a single planet battlefield to multiple, dosen't allow for zoom or any perspective changes. This means you may encounter difficulty seeing areas of the main battle map, where you view your territories and the territories of your enemies, at higher resolutions. Some tactical planning may be hampered by this, but this is not a large complaint.
If you have any interest in 40k, or if you are tired of Dark Crusade, or even if you just want to see a mostly-female (not all female, for some reason) human faction (I can't tell when it comes to the Eldar, but I guess they're female, too), pick up this game.  You don't need the other Dawn of War 1 games unless you really like space marine (Dawn of War base game) or Imperial Guard (Winter Assualt) plotlines. You will need the other games to unlock the other factions in multiplayer (already have all factions unlocked for any and all single player aspects).

One of the few series left that cares about plot and gives you a good cinematic experience blended with gameplay. It's also an improvement over MK 9 in almost every way. Online is dead, though, due to the horrible launch, so only buy if you're in it for the story.
Pros:
-Environmental maneuvers added.
-Better voice acting.
-A lot more action in the cutscenes, as well as solid plot. The cringey moments from MK9 are gone. Even Johnny Cage stops goofing off. Cutscenes can go longer than MK9 and have much more drama and/or action.
-FMV sequences are actually rendered at a high resolution, so you can't tell where the in-engine cutscenes begin or end.
-New and original characters, it's not like other fighting games where the devs feel pressured to return the same exact roster every installment. They're not afraid of killing off characters for plot.
-Three fight styles per character.
-Button mashing is much less rewarded.
-Alien, Predator, Leatherface, Jason (DLC)
-Bo Rai Cho
-They actually fixed the issues the game had at launch, unlike WB did wit Bamham: Hambam City
Cons:
-The music absolutely sucks compared to MK9. It's just a bunch of nothing. Not a single memorable track.
-Everyone's voice actors improved, except for Sub Zero, who just has a generic throaty Hollywood voice now.
-The input read has been changed a bit to prevent button mashing. Consequently, you no longer have characters like Jade or Kitana, who can just chain a lot of melee moves together, rapidly. Every character shares the stiffness now from characters in MK 9, such as Jax or Scorpion. The roster can feel a little less varied because of this.
-Online is dead after a horrible PC launch tanked reviews and made people leave.
-Most people hate Quick Time Events, which the campaign has during cutscenes, so I'll list it here. I like them, personally. Plus, it's actually kind of funny if you go through the game and fail every one of them.
-I do kind of miss the campyness of MK9's plot, sometimes, but it's no big deal.

I give this game a thumbs up with reservations.  The gameplay is exactly what you'd expect and the options available to you are varied and interesting.  My issue is that the game is short for a $60 AAA title.  I'm someone who invests a lot of time and option choices finding all the odd corners and side quests.  I'm also someone who finished a "pacifist" runthough.  Those things being said, I was still done in 46 hours.
I also have complaints about the story line.  There are plenty of cool references to the past games: characters and organizations from both the most recent game and the original Deus Ex.  There are amusing easter eggs, too (there's a companion cube in a random basement, for instance).  The main plot, though, is devoid of big, sweeping global conspiracies.  I'm not going to spoiler it, but the story, compared to the rest of the series, was small and insignificant.
It's a step forward on gameplay, but definitely backward on plot.  If you love "immersive sims," you'll have a good time.
Technically, it's a system hog and load times in the main city are egregiously slow.
I'd be remiss in not mentioning "Breach Mode."  Breach mode is a separate game that allows you to earn money for the main game and offers snippets of story.  They are basically stylized, low-res levels that you can play to complete or play to particular benchmarks.  There are even global leaderboards and whatnot.  It's interesting, but not exactly compelling.  I played the tutorial and a chunk of the first set of levels.  What's nice about it is that you can build a totally different character to play through Breach as well as preview augs you might not be sure about for the main game.  The micro-transactions that allow you to upgrade the experience definitely show that they plan to support future Breach content.  That could be a plus or a minus depending on your point of view.

I'm going to be the odd man out on this one. Blood Dragon has cool visuals, a very campy 80's feel, some decent bits of humor, and a kick-awesome soundtrack.
Yet where Blood Dragon suffers is when it tries to be over-the-top ridiculous and use the Far Cry 3 game mechanics at the same time. You're given a rifle that can shoot lasers, turrets, a minigun, a laser you mount on your wrist, and you're supposed to feel like the ultimate badass that can kill everything.
Yet the Far Cry mechanics call for stealth, not run-and-gun. So for example if you do a hostage mission, you have all these cool guns that you just want to go pew pew and boom boom with, but if you get spotted by the guards then you have seconds until the hostage is killed. What? These mechanics that fail to properly invent exciting combat are fully realized with the Blood Dragons. There is no real strategy to kill them, other to mercilessly run and shoot. Left 4 Dead makes this fun because the gunplay makes sense. Here it simply does not.
Oh, and by the way, you use the same button to heal yourself and to extinguish fire on you. Due to the first person perspective, it's difficult to tell when you are on fire and when there's just fire around you. So you press Q before you are given the prompt to do so thinking you can put out the fire early. Instead, you just waste a syringe/time healing yourself and then you're still on fire.
Overall, if you enjoyed Far Cry 3 and just want to have a more absurd version of that, this will suit you well. If you want to be the ultimate badass, play Serious Sam or Saints Row or anything else that is actually BUILT for that.

Zoya: she offers ranged attacking with her arrows(which you can enchance once you gain some levels) and great amount of utility with her hook

Amadeus: he offers a great deal of utility. His main ability is to create magical boxes you can jump on to, naturally you will learn to create differnt kind of things when you gain more levels. Amadeus is the only one who can not harm enemies with his abilities alone.

The kind of game that you'd like if you like to play chess. Planning every move against your enemy and using the board to your advantage is critically important. It's the type of game that you can easy pick up and play rather quickly, but can frustrate you as you try to get the most amount of points. While it's visual style may put people off, it's a game that's simple in concept but complex in its hidden mechanics, and honestly is worth the price of admission.
For some gameplay and other first impressions:

Pretty Sweet, I can't think of anything else I've played that it's like.
At first there is a lot of trial and error as you figure out how each enemy moves and attacks. Some move once, some move once but have stealth and take less hits, one can move through the blocks, one moves twice.  Then getting use to all the different abilities you can use.  There are 8 levels and each level gives you two "hacks". When you use a hack you get any of the energy or credits that are watermarked in the squares up, down, left, right, and the one you are on.  If any of those squares of a box with a number on it you get whatever skill is listed on it. Also whatever the number says is how many enemies spawn in when you "hack" the box.  Hacking the boxes with just numbers and no power ups is how you earn points.
Each Level starts with a handful of enemies. Then once they are dead one will spawn autamatically every so 2-3 moves.  To move from each level there is a green square that takes you to the next level.  If you go to the next level with enemies still alive they will go to the next level with you.
Once you get all this figured out (which takes only 20 mins of eating your♥♥♥♥♥ then the real puzzel part comes into focus.  You have to think about which moves to make to be able to kill everything and not get hit 3 times.  Even when there is no enemies figuring out the best thing to use your hacks on is tough.  " Should I farm resources?" "should I go for points?" "Can I handle 7 enemies right now?"

I'm a Greedy Little Hacker and I've played the freeware prototype for well over a year. I'm very pleased with the PC port and the updated progs and whatnot compared to the freeware version is well worth the price of entry.
It's a very tight package, and deceptively simple. It's like a mix of Cave Noire and Desktop Dungeons with Decker aesthetics, and it just tickles that puzzle roguelike feel like no other game does. It has simple and clean graphics, and the ambient noises of the various enemies that come to smash you under their digital heel are a fantastic touch.
Every enemy has a distinct pattern and way they move, the game opens up when you learn to start exploiting that fact in positioning and managing your resources for the various progs. Also the risk reward mechanic of trying to go for a high point run, but doing so in a way where you aren't swarmed into a situation that you can't handle is fantastic.
The best part is it can be played in a short amount of time, but if you are like me you'll start wanting another run... And another. The streak mechanic really ties into that addictive itch to see if you can better your best streak of wins, or others for that matter.
In short, if you are looking for an easy to access puzzling game, with roguelike mechanics, tough as nails decisions, far deeper strategy than you though possible, and a slick hackery sci-fi drizzle of aesthetic on top , than pick it up, and I'm sure you won't be disappointed.

Who I am: I backed this game way back a few years ago now. I saw it on Kickstarter and it was like a dream come true. The type of styled game I've always wanted to play. A mix of The Elder Scrolls and Total War. Making a city, an army and then still having a fully customized and developed character. I've been one of the major forum posters on their website, and have by no means pulled my punches on pulling Larkon up for things that seem to be not working or a bad idea in general.
Larkon Studios: Frankly put, they're the best. The developers themselves have been in constant contact with every back since the campaign personally. You can email them, talk to them on discord or the forum, they answer questions in regular intervals including community Q&A's. They tell you when there is delays and don't bat around the bush as to why. They'll tell you straight up if they made a mistake or if they were just being over-amibitious for example. The company has also kept it's promise to keep us involved in development, with loads of community votes for features and allowing us a say as to what gets put in first.
Pro: The graphical style is a suited high fantasy, think more stylized though than Lord of the Rings. The RTS system is in place, allowing very minor (only 6 building types at the time of writing) city building and army composition (3 unit types, militia, soldier and archer). The combat controls work as Mount and Blade when in first person. With F1 being attack, F2 follow, F3 guard etc. There is a wide range of spells planned, with a small amount in high detail available now (10~). The spells themselves are amazing to look at, vastly superior to that of say, The Elder Scrolls: Skyrim. The world seems vast already even in just a "small" starting zone, with multiple dungeons and quests to progress as well as 2 other factions. Dungeons themselves are present and look fine (except a perhaps over-use of resources, more on that later).
Mid-point: Re-use of resources and tile sets leave dungeons looking "samey" and sometimes confusing. Making the same 2 of 5 corridors looking almost identical from start to finish due to this. This isn't the intended final build of these dungeons but it's left a otherwise good looking dungeon set becoming confusing and repetitive. Combat is also neither good nor bad. With controls being clunky and melee not feeling weighty enough, at the moment it depends on the utter fantastic visuals of the magic to keep it afloat above "cons". Dodging is delayed and somewhat gimmicky, whilst archery is otherwise worthless at the current build. It is scheduled for regular improvements, so think in the lines of Skyrim for a final product.
Con: Lack of building variety. Resources take a large amount of time to generate forcing buildings to take a large amount of time to save up for. You'll also find a rapid snowball in resources once you've finish those initial buildings though, which leaves an inbalance rather than a enjoyable pace, given there is no new buildings to make. RTS controls are clunky and unfriendly at the moment as the UI is placeholder and not fully functional for unit control. Quests and other minor bugs are apparent, some annoying, many irritating and a rare few game breaking. At the time, there is only a handful of hours playable. Performance is the major kicker, with all but the most powerful systems struggling to maintain even 30 FPS. This issue has come and gone with every new update, and given the scale of the game. It's likely to last another month or 2, maybe even more from he time I'm writing this review.
Summary: The game has a lot of promise and Larkon has shown full ability and commitment to finishing and releasing a great game. The game's faults are ones that are commonly expected in a new EA title by a small indie studio, bugs and placeholder resources. Most of the faults being easily resolved as time progresses without major effort by the developers. At the moment, Early Access gives you a starting zone demonstrating mechanics and not much else. Something more like the first 10 mins of a Elder Scrolls game. My advice is buy it if you even like the concept of being able to press a button and turn into a fantasy styled hero amongst a Total War esque army. Especially Lord of the Rings fans. If you're on the fence, check out their forum and see how hard they've been working and how transparent they've been. At the moment, the game isn't much. In 3-4 months? It will be great. By the end of the EA period? It will be something, legendary.

Having very little experience of Warhammer 40,000 as a tabletop game, I am not going down the road of making any sort of analogy nor comparison. While it may be a strange idea to some, over the years I have had the constant barrage of "Oh, it's nothing like the tabletop game, you know." despite me not having claimed otherwise. Instead I will evaluate its merit as an RPG. I will note at this point that I have also played vanilla Dawn of War and the preceding expansions Winter Assault and Dark Crusade.
On first coming to this game I found it very easy to pick up. With most races simply having the two basic resources, requisition and power, it was easy enough to settle into the tempo of gameplay. Requisition is collected by taking and holding control points (so no messy resource gathering) and power by building generators anywhere you control. The races each have their own distinct styles of warfare, but when broken down to basics they all follow the same pattern with unit types consistent across all races, so understanding what to make when and how to attack/counterattack is simple. However, the technology trees make advancement slightly different, and tactics must be adapted. Some races have unique benefits and requirements, such as the Orks requiring you to fill the Waaaaaargh! meter to progressively increase the population cap and develop improvements, or the Dark Eldar who gain powers as they consume the souls of fallen enemy troops. The differences make gameplay refreshing when playing as or against the different races.
The battlefields themselves are well designed for balance (for skirmishes) or to challenge your leadership (for the campaign), with plenty of terrain variations that may help or hinder your troops advancement and survivability in a firefight. The environments too are well varied for visual and, to some extent, tactical enhancement with a healthy mix of wastelands, forests, swamps and cities from across the galaxy to whet your appetite. The campaign is reasonable, but not great, and sees you vying for control of a star system (I won't spoil it) against each of the other races. There are several tactical objectives that can even the odds before you invade a territory Risk-style should you take it. If you have played the Dark Crusade campaign then there's nothing much new with the cinematic-style endgame fights when you strike an enemy's capital, which are actually more structured scenarios than those of regular territory invasions, along with the obligatory cut-scenes.
There's a decent amount of customisation available throughout, with the in-built Army Painter allowing you to do virtually what would take hours of laborious armwork and make a mess of your room/shed/garage. It has to be said, there is a certain sense of accomplishment seeing your custom flag being raised as you capture a control point. What I do find to be absent is a map editor, so in that respect customisation is a tiny bit limited, and the skirmish maps are all pre-built with no randomisation beyond your starting position (which makes little difference on a symmetrical-ish map).
From a graphics standpoint the game is presented very well, with plenty of satisfying and beefy explosions, eerily beautiful plasma bolts and las beams flying around (The Baneblade in particular is especially good at showing these off) and, depending on your particular chipsets (mine not being too spectacular at the minute), the game is easily one of the prettier RTSs around, even now. The AI is decent, although bumbling on easier settings, and should provide a challenge to every skillset.
In short;
FOR : Simple to pick up, challenging to master. Custom armies. Good graphics, even by today's standards. Nice soundtrack.
AGAINST : Limited customisation. Pre-built arenas. Not very engaging campaign (compared to previous iterations).
Overall, despite its flaws, I would certainly reccomend you at least try this game. I find it to be enjoyable and quite addictive!

I remember playing the demo for this game over ten years ago so it was a pleasant surprise to find it on Steam. Not only is this a third person action game, it also contains a number of real time strategy features. As well as this there is stat management and an inventory system, although I'm not sure that this game could be classified as an RPG.
The combat is rather unsophisticated, but I found it enjoyable - it plays a lot like a Musou game, involving relatively large battles and combo-based attacks. That said, by modern standards the combat is a bit clunky, so if you can't stand old PC games, this might not be for you. Like many older games there is a lack of widescreen resolution options. There is a fix available, but I honestly had no problem just playing the game with the default settings, even if the aspect ratio was stretched from 4:3.
Aside from playing as Joan of Arc, you can switch to a number of other characters with different weapons and movesets. The later campaign missions also introduce an RTS mode, which allows you to command units from a bird's eye view. I found that this game was the most fun when ignoring your troops as much as possible and simply going through the levels solo. You can even fill your inventory with arrows and play the game like a first person shooter. Joan's kill count was well into the thousands by the time I finished the game.
One of this game's main strengths is its scale - levels are large and open with plenty of forts and towns to capture as well as sidequests. There is even a day and night cycle. Completing all eight campaign missions took me over sixteen hours, so there is plenty of value for money. That said, the later levels can start becoming repetitive and often take over two hours to complete, so you should pace yourself accordingly. I also found the real time strategy component to be a weaker part of this game, mostly due to poor pathfinding. In one of the campaign missions I almost had to restart because Joan and some soldiers got themselves stuck on a narrow staircase and couldn't move out. The RTS mode is also a relatively small part of gameplay as supporting units can fend for themselves fairly well. Comparisons to Mount and Blade are fairly fitting, but don't expect too much. This game is at its best when you are mowing down hordes of enemies and not thinking too much about strategy.
I'm very glad to have had the chance to revisit this game, but it may not hold up for some people today. If you can tolerate the simple graphics and don't care too much about historical accuracy I would suggest that you give this very underrated game a look.

Just finished DE:MD last night and here are my thoughts:
1. The ending sucked.  Straight up the worst part of the game.  It just ends.  What felt like a good mission towards the back-half of the campaign finished up the credits rolled.  It feels unfinished for a $60 product.  I couldn't even tell you what the story was and I read every email and watched every cutscene.  The ending bad guy was a side character from an earlier mission who was just a minion.
2. Graphics are pretty good.  The environments looks amazing and it all runs at a great framerate on my GTX 970 but the animations look stiff.  It's a farcry from the Tomb Raiders and GTA.  The futuristic artwork is the best part of the graphics.  From the street art, the city skylines, to the clothes and armor, it all looks great but it can't save it from crappy animations.
3. Level design is what you'd expect from a Deus Ex game (I've played them all).  Multiple ways to get to the end of the level.  You can sneak or you can shoot but you'll probably do a combination of both.  Lots of backtracking through Prague which was disappointing.  It all looks beautiful but it's repeated a lot.  No really big levels similar to the original which is still the best game in the series.
4. Gunplay is good but not great.  Still feels as clunky as it did in Human Revolution.  I avoided gun battles because it just didn't feel that good.
5. AI is super dumb.  They don't notice when you take their buddy out that they were just talking to.  If you slightly alert them (yellow suspicious) they'll walk over to your area without alert any other guards where you will take them out with cutscene takedown.
6. Hacking get's old quick.  Same minigame as Human Revolution.  Do something new.
Overall it's an ok game.  It looks amazing at first and some of the levels are truly awesome but an abrupt ending, confusing story, and just ok gunplay it's a 7/10 at best and probably a 6 to a non fan of the series or genre.

While Deus Ex: Mankind Divided offers great gameplay mechanics, inviting you to explore the world it grows even more apart in offering a meaningful story, a proper plot and actual people you care about.
The environment design is astonishing, the care for detail extraordinary. Due to the emphazising on exploration it even serves some purpose and was for me one major motiavation factor.
Aside from that though you meet rather generic characters on a technical animation level of some irrelevant indie game, which creates a tremendously huge gap between the "AAA" feeling of the general visuals and the bad implemetation of life into it.
That is crowned by a very forseeable storyline with no major turns, extremely boring characters and side quests, and still not even a remote match within the soundtrack the original DX offered. The soundtrack is forgettable as it was in HR. While the tones of DX still ring in my ears 2 decades later.
And then, of course, there is Adam Jensen. One of the worst VG characters ever due to his lack of character in both visual and VO representation of a "bad♥♥♥♥♥quot; who simply looks and even more sounds ridiculous after the third word when a dialogue has been triggered...
While DX:HR tried to be close to the original and failed in certain areas, DX:MD removes itself even further due to using the same recipie without actually telling a complete story nor delivering anything meaningful in the process.
It's okay, even great, from a few point of views such as art desing and exploration, but that has been just a part of the original Deus Ex. The game as an entirety is very disappointing and cuts off at the point where it just started to get somewhat interesting.
Given that this is kind of why DX actually was so interesting, I just have to give it a "negative" review. I did enjoy it quite a bit, but in comparison and in retrospective, DX:MD is just unfinished and rather shallow despite the effort put into giving it a great look.

Overall, is this game perfect? No, no it's not. Is it decent, playable and enjoyable? Yes, it is, just not at full price. I would highly reccomend giving this a try if you can get a good deal on it, especially because it has potential to be improved in the future with further patches, if Kalypso and Reborn do release more updates, but even if they don't it's a pretty decent game as is, a strong 7 out of 10.

As a lover of the Tropico series, I went against the reviews and bought the game on sale for around $10. Frankly, I think the game is not finished, but has some great ideas - I wouldn't ant to pay more for it than what I did.
Good Points:
- Like Tropico there is a great dynamic between different areas of the game (research in particular), many moving parts to manage and so many stats to sink your teeth into. The writing is in true Tropico comedic style, with a couple easter eggs thrown in!
- The politics work...okay. In principle (again), the idea is great and works well at times. In certain (repeated) scenarios though the game ties your hands with unworkable parties. I like the favour-appeal system though which does allow you to get around some tricky situations.
- The city builder is again...ok. It's clunky but does the job. It's fairly simple.

Bad Points:
- On that note: Finance. It's really hard to keep your finances up and often completely unclear as to why some districts perform well when others dont. You try to upgrade your districts within the slim margins you have but you inevitably end up sinking into the red. I will keep trying different ways and update on this.
- As mentioned above, the politics can get predictable and there's a particular scenario (far-right stronghold) that makes it really hard to get anything done. This impacts finance and city development a lot, wasting loads of time.
- It took me a while to work out that the special buildings (port, train, etc) are the only way to keep your bank balance afloat...for a bit.
- The game is buggy. It crashes a lot, which might explain the frequent autosave. Some actions don't correspond to the result and it's really unclear how certain decisions impact trade. Often you get 3 choices but can only see the results of 2 in advance (bug).
Tldr: If you liked Tropico, you might like this because it contains the same humour. It's a good idea as a game, I'd love to play a finished version one day. 5/10

"Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons" is a short and simple 3D adventure game with a truly beautiful art style. The intriguing control scheme adds some needed depth to gameplay that's otherwise fairly shallow, and the soundtrack is haunting and generally spectacular. It's unsurprising to me that this game is well regarded by so many people.
With all of that said, however, I thought the needlessly depressing 'narrative' (there's no dialogue) utterly ruined the experience. In aiming for some deep level of emotional impact, all the developers and writers actually managed to achieve was making the game feel remarkably pointless and unsatisfying. As the credits rolled after completing my playthrough, which takes at most a couple of hours (playing very slowly), the only thing really going through my mind was "this was a waste of time".
I had heard only spectacular reviews for this game, and this seems to be replicated in the Steam reviews here, so I was really hoping to love it. When it came down to actually playing it, though, I just really didn't.
As I said, the other reviews suggest that there's a good chance you'll love the game. Personally, the short length and flat narrative means I definitely wouldn't bother picking this up unless you're absolutely desperate to try it, and be sure to manage your expectations - perhaps if mine hadn't been so high, I would have enjoyed it rather more than I did.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a wonderful adventure game. It's mechanics are simple: you control two characters at once (each brother) while running through its beautifully crafted world solving simple puzzles and discovering a tale of life, adventure, splendor and tragedy.
What a unique game. Never played a game that you control 2 characters the whole time.

The game opens in a peaceful town in a magical land, and two brothers are compelled to leave their home to find a cure to save their dying father. While the premise is rather basic, the world that this game is in,  is not. I love the different places that you travel through, and I feel it is quite an immersive game, their is little combat,  and there isn't even an "attack button", but rather an "action button", which changes function depending on what you need to do. I would recommend this game to anyone,  it has great visuals and great themes

Hey guys, welcome to my review of Legends of Ellaria. I finally got to play this game after keeping up with it for a while. It's completely new, you can tell it needs some major polish, but I have amazingly high hopes for this game. It's trying to do what really needs to be done, give every type of gamer something to do in one game.
You can clearly tell the game isn't ready yet, but that is part of Early Access gaming and is a major part of what I love. I love watching a game being built, playing it one day only to find out things have changed drastically on the next update. As of right now, this game doesn't have an RPG Leveling System, it says that is coming soon on the loading page, which is one of the things I was talking about, Been playing it for a couple days, when the RPG Leveling System is introduced, it'll be a totally new game. Reinvigorate the game, new video to produce, and new content for fans.
There are several animations that could be updated, such as Jumping which seems to look weird, especially if you are running. The Magic Shield animation isn't amazing, and unless I'm messing up it only works against Magic like a fireball(no complaints there). Clipping isn't the greatest either, but we shouldn't expect trivial things such as your cloak going through your body or your face going through a wooden door when standing to close at this point in a game, that comes much later.
The greatest example I've found of graphics is the fireball, I absolutely love the way it looks when it explodes and I can't wait to see the rest of the spells are amazing too. I'm hoping the Ice spell won't be lame or bland like most games. I'd love to see it having an awesome effect, like being able to see the air around you or the enemy freezing instead of a blue/white fireball. Maybe if as it went towards the enemy you could literally see everything in a certain radius freeze, even the ground...see shards of ice fall to the ground as the moisture in the air freezes, something like that :D! Frost/Water is my favorite spell trees and I'd love to see them maximized!
Right now we seem to have keybinding issues, which you can see in my upcoming vids. Doesn't seem to be tied to which slot you put it in. For example, the Fireball can't be hotkeyed. No matter which slot you put it in, he will not equip the fireball and that hurts in the middle of combat. I've come across two or three things that can't be equipped in this fashion...but so far everything seems to be working out good...like the fights, hope they get more fluid!
Right now your followers don't come into the caves with you, as you travel alone when you load into them, and they don't seem to teleport with you when you use the portal. I do however love how you can walk around with your militia and watch your town grow as you are able to see workers building up your town to your every desire.
This review may sound like I'm pointing out flaws, but it's the exact opposite. This game isn't to the point of having flaws yet. It is still very early, and so many things are great about it, just the idea and art/graphics of the game make you feel like walking around for hours in the world. The grass and flowers are enthralling. I can't wait to see a world map, as I'd like to be able to see what they have in store for the rest of the world, and seeing as they are able to go to different universes using the Rift, it'd be nice to be able to explore that too...or use that as a way of integrating online kingdoms.
Thanks for taking the time to read, hope you guys enjoyed this. I'll update it as necessary  as I play and the game gets updated! Come back for more updates/vids and check out my Youtube at

This game is amazing. Both literally and metaphorically speaking. It would have you play a girl named Sarah, who is tripping on some meds, creating a beautiful and sometimes grimy world in her mind. The game wants you to explore. It gives you just the basic info and then you're on your own in this mad and surreal world. Where visuals go, music follows. The overall atmosphere is pretty thick and dreary. You might find the game is littered with the references too. And other than one bug and some wonky controls here and there, which you can neglect, I had a wonderful time playing this game. And for a minor price too. AND they give you music. My thanks to the devs.

I feel like the controls aren't AS fluid as other platformers. What I mean is, certain actions are stop. And go. Stop. And go. Which feels very video-gamey and has the potential to take you out of the experience; HOWEVER, This game was not attempting to be the next Super Meat Boy, so to pick at this one point and call it a bad game would be a slap to your face.
I will say this: the story is something unique, definitely crafted with love and affection. This is what keeps me playing. Not the controls, not the sometimes-annoying-to-figure-out-puzzles, and certainly not the amount of backtracking.
(About backtracking through the levels; the makers of this game made an insane amount of ways to get back to the spots you need to go. I strongly commend them for this design choice.)
But this is a solid game. You should buy it, ESPECIALLY if it's on sale, though, I would recommend it at full price. ($6.00 at the time of this review)
All in all, I feel like it completes everything it set out to do. I think a game I've played that is comparable to this is Home, but that one was a little more horror.

So, my thoughts on Mankind Divided, now that I've gone through all of it once, tried out some Breach Mode and got a feeling for all of it.
I'm of a mixed opinion. I will rate Deus Ex: Mankind Divided 7/10 on my personal scale, compared to a stunning Human Revolution (9/10).
Generally, it it much of the same - the combat, the mechanics, they all follow the formula established in Human Revolution. Controls had some minor changes I was not the biggest fan of (hiding behind cover being a toggle being an example), but they are still fine.
The main story, missions, everything feel like more of the same - which doesn't necessarily have to be bad, but it just feels like it's done with less love this time around. Level design always feels a little off, and dialogue sometimes feels..well, just loveless.
Keep in mind this is with Human revolution in mind - the design of the levels is still very good, it's just not on the same level.
Anyway, as for content:
There are a number of side missions available as well as places you can just explore for yourself if you want to mess around or feel completionist-y - you can sink many hours into the game. It feels a little bit lighter on the content-side (both in terms of side-quests as well as length of the main storyline) than Human Revolution, but I can't say that with any sort of authority.
The additional "Breach" mode I only looked into for about half an hour. It feels very...hectic and cyberspacy, but that's what it's going for, I suppose. It also includes online leaderboards and all that good stuff, so there's something added on for people who like speedrunning those kinds of things.
A major issue are the graphics requirements. It is very noticeable that Mankind Divided has been a console port, and was not properly optimised for PC. The graphics in the game, while being decent to good, do not justify the rather demanding hardware requirement for the game. (I got an AMD R9 380 just for Mankind Divided and even then, Medium/windowed or High/fullscreen is the best you could reasonably pick.)
The main problem with the game for most people seem to be microtransactions. They are not an issue - in fact, they are designed completely unintrusive and I played the game without even noticing the option for them. Additionally, the game is beatable (easily) without any sort of added-on benefits.
Conclusion:
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided feels like a step back compared to Human Revolution, but it is still a good game, and I feel it is worth the money I paid for it.
It does not fail to deliver a Deus-Ex-y feeling, even though it has its - mostly minor - flaws.

An excellent follow-on to DX:HR, and worthy of the name Deus Ex.
The most important thing for me in a game like DX is that I need to "fall into" the world. It has to look and feel complete, with details and compelling characters. DX:MD completely succeeds here. I can't say enough good things about the art direction and world design. The level of detail was at times overwhelming. I spent a good deal of time wandering, exploring Prague, listening to conversations (a remarkable number of unique ones), and just getting a feel for the world. When I first got to TF29, I spent at least an hour just exploring, reading email, and talking with everyone.
I thought the story was fine - compact and focused, yet with tendrils of the larger conspiracy. I didn't think the ending was abrupt. Perhaps that's because I was prepared for it, but I think the main reason is that I look at DX:MD as a serial. There are going to be more episodes, so it is appropriate that not every one is wrapped up neatly. I'm good with that; in fact, I was getting a little tired of the DX formula: the game ending with a conclusive, world-changing event in which the hero decides the outcome. I appreciate the change of pace in MD. Of course, I would have been even more happy with a longer game, but I don't feel cheated.
The side missions were one of the highlights of the game. Almost all were deep, complex, with fascinating characters and significant choices. The side missions added as much to the game as the overall story; that isn't an indication of the main story's weakness, but of the side mission's strengths. They completed the world. As did the other characters, each unique and with their own set of motivations.
Game play was solid - a little better than HR. Some of the new augs were pretty cool, but I didn't try them all as I was doing a mostly-stealthy run. Thus, my weapons experience was pretty limited too. The guard AI seemed reasonable.
Graphic performance was okay; I had to drop down some of the settings from High a bit to get a consistent 60 FPS on my system, which is basically a "Recommended" spec. That was disappointing, as was the lip sync (especially for minor characters). Minor complaints, but complaints just the same.
As for game length, I played 45 hours. I did all of the side missions, but I didn't explore every nook and cranny. I paid $45 for the game (pre-order on GMG), and considering I plan at least 2 more play-throughs, that is great value-for-money.

Now this is my first actual review so i'll keep it short and sweet and try not to drag on to long.
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is the 4th game in the Deus Ex franchise and the 2nd to feature Adam Jensen as the main protaginist. Now i hadnt even heard of this franchise until about 3 years ago when I played the xbox port of Deus Ex: Invisible War (often refered to as the worst out of them all.) and i honestly enjoyed it. then about a year later I played Human Revolution on the PS3 and I enjoyed it but at the time it was to hard for me so I gave up. recently after i got a gaming PC I decided to give HR another shot and i beat it (on the hardest dificulty i may add) and was getting hyped out of my mind for this game. I bought it day of release and saw that it had mixed reviews so I got kind of worried. I decided to read some of them and saw that it had performance problems and got even more worried but in the end this game in my honest opinion is the best of the series.
Here we go, First, the game never felt to drag which was a problem with Human Revolution to me. Second, It had more of what was good plus way better mechanics and controls (the aiming is so much better). Finally, It just felt better and had no problems with peformance and graphically appealing to the eye.
The story isn't that great but honestly neither is HR's story, It got the job though. Adam Jensen is still my new favorite protaginist and he's even overtook snake in my top 10 characters at this point.
To conclude, this game (to me) is ****ing amazing and definitly worth the 60 or 90 dollars if you want the deluxe version, it's a great edition to the franchise and i can't wait until they decide to make a sequel to this sequel.
P.S: the microtransactions are fine to me they're not obtrusive and you dont need to buy them, its just a thing for people who are lazy (i've never bought them but i understand if someone does)

I had high hopes for this game, maybe that's why I was so disappointed by it.
The concept sounds promising: Real cities don't exist in a vacuum and mayors aren't dictators, so why not introduce some political and historical elements into gameplay?
Unfortunately, the execution is flawed. In-game history pretty much follows a pre-determined path based on real-world European history: You have monarchy giving way to democracy, workers fighting for better working conditions, women's suffrage, etc. (Note: Some players apparently perceive this as 'leftist ideology', but I'd argue it's simply a representation of the developments during this period. European society at the time of the Industrial revolution was far more authoritarian and conservative than what we have today, so in order to get from there to here, things had to 'move to the left'.)
The problem is that this leads to repetitive gameplay. It may be realistic that a single mayor can't change the course of history, but it also means that you can't really explore alternative options but simply have to go with the flow. Public opinion will always shift a certain way around a certain time, and if you want to stay in office, you always have to adapt in the same ways. Basically, the political part is more about reacting to a pre-written script than about having any actual influence, and that just gets old really fast. Research is similarly restricted: Get certain techs for certain improvements, so you can do the things the script needs you to do at this time.
It's a pity, because there technical side of the game is perfectly fine for the genre. They just couldn't find a way to make the gameplay engaging for more than an hour or two. At full price (currently 45 EUR), it's definitely way too expensive. If you can pick it up for $10/ 10 Euros or less, it might be worth a look. Just don't expect more than a few hours of play time out of it.

Just seeing the first page reviews, I'm rather appalled that people think there is nothing to this game or that it is too hard or that it should be similar to Cities: Skylines. It is none of that. This is a different city sim altogether. You do not lay roads individually or place zones where you want them (although I wish you could for the zones at least), you build a city through the eyes of a politician through an old world council - or, more precisely, a European-based political cabinet. It's a different take and challenge and I welcome it. I am not debating its mechanics since I'm just starting out, but the first impression that it has been wrongly given. You cannot approach this game with the typical city sim mentality, at all. You have to carefully balance your budget, understand how to grow you city while also balancing party influence so that you can continue to build since (depending upon your political emphasis) people can vote you out if there is too much conflict from yours and other political parties. So it is challenging, but in a very good way.
This is one of those games, it seems like, that there are many paths you could take, but you're not going to be able to hit the gold mine and do everything and have the most 1337 city known to mankind. You have to make choices. So there is realism in this game.
It really makes me wonder the percentage of complaints below of "it's too hard because I want to play it like other city sims," and what the real rating for this game would actually be... Apparently it got a rough start, and that's an unfortunate hit, too.
***===============================================***
Update: I've played a game all the way through every stage to the point you get a victory. (This took 19hrs and it was my very first game - no redos.) In my case, I managed the victory of making it through every stage. (I wasn't paying too close of attention, since I continued onward with the game (I'm glad it gave me that option), but it appears you go to the year 2020.)
What's my impression? I love this game. It is very challenging and for a while there I wasn't sure I was going to make it, but got to Stage V and the economy was easier to manage. (My city was so poor and in the red for a long time that only a few districts had the privilege of running water and even fewer had electricity.) I definitely learned a few things about establishing an economy and am excited to try a whole new game to see what I can make happen.
I really like the storytelling aspect to it as you get to create a kind of history with your game that is rather faint (but left to your imagination) when I would play Civ games or the Total War games or any city sim game - this seemed more personal. I do wish when there were world conflicts (and possibly smaller ones that might affect you) that you felt it and had to make choices like you do any other time. (For example, since you do get the arms industry, I thought perhaps you might try to promote that industry during a war or have a political aspect that may involve a vote on helping another country out or something.) That would really make you feel like you're part of a bigger world instead of feeling closed in to the city that you're building. The game hints at some sort of economic hit, but that's all I could tell.
But it was exciting and frustrating in every regard that made this game interesting. It is a pitty that it had a rough start and it is a greater pity that a lot of people are not seeing this game at a different, and deserved, angle since there is potential to make this super interesting if the developers went deeper into this game. I'd say with the big upset, the devs have better time spent with something else...

Title: Dreaming Sarah
Developer: Andre Chagas Silva, Anthony Septim
Publisher: Andre Chagas Silva
Released For: PC (Windows, MAC OSX 10.6+, Linux Ubuntu 14.04+)
Reviewing: PC (Windows) version
DRM Versions Available
Released On: Mar, 12, 2015
MSRP: $5.99
Purchased Copy
Dreaming Sarah is a 2D retro-style adventure platformer with puzzle elements in the same vain as Yume Nikki.
In Dreaming Sarah, you’ll run around a series of different areas, collect items, solve puzzles, and platform your way to the end of the game. You play as Sarah, and you’re dreaming (get it? Dreaming Sarah?). Sarah begins dreaming after she gets into a car crash and is put into a coma. We’d say that’s a spoiler, but it’s in the description of the game on Steam…so yah.
The gameplay is inspired by Yume Nikki, but thankfully has some better gameplay elements, like plot. On your way of exploring this odd and bizarre little dream world, you’ll discover a colorful cast of characters, and explore odd but nicely detailed areas like a mansion, a lava world, and a never ending desert. You’ll start off in a forest section of the game, and slowly find more and more items along the way which help you get to other areas on other parts of the world. For example, you’ll find a magnifying glass which will help you get to other areas by shrinking yourself, or you’ll find glasses which let you see items you normally couldn’t see and so on. Some characters you come across also require certain items which will help you progress, while other characters are there simply for world building. One of the character we particularly found funny was a skeleton in the mansion area. During their text, we pictured them with voices similar to the Terry Pratchett animated movies. While some of the things you need for areas are obvious, it’s not entirely obvious or clear for others. For example, one character requires orange juice in order for the player to continue forward. However, it’s never really made clear the character needs orange juice. There’s also certain puzzles that we overthought in terms of complexity, when it was just one of those ‘we hadn’t done this, so that isn’t available yet’ types of puzzles. They’re in the game and annoying when they appear, but they’re not so annoying because you generally only find them when you’re about to or already have the required item. Some of the areas however you won’t need to access until a fair bit later into the game, like the Moon area. Despite this, exploring the areas and solving the puzzles was fun, and made the game fun to play as a way to winding down.
The game tries to play like a bizarre platformer like Yume Nikki, but it plays far better than Yume Nikki for the most part. It’s less bizarre than Yume Nikki as a result of this, but it’s also easier to actually play.
The only major parts of the gameplay to criticize is that there’s no real ‘dead’ stage to the game. You can fail at a puzzle or jump, but it never sets you back far enough to really consider it failing. There’s also the item problem where if you change into a fish and change back, all the items you previously had equipped you have to put on again. You also have a few items that you really don’t need to stop using except in certain situations. For example, you never have to really stop using the glasses you find or the magnifying glass to shrink you.
The game itself is short, but it’s as short as it needs to be. It took us around three hours to beat the game, but we also got stuck on a few of the puzzles, so it’s really more like a two hour game unless you have a brains like ours which contain string and some peanut shells.
Visually, it looks quite nice. Some of the character designs and inspired areas (ala the mansion is similar to the castle from Castlvania II) look nice, and everything somehow still flows visually, despite having very different looking areas. Sarah as a character looks a little too simple, but the extra animation on her hair when she jumps and moves is quite nice. We wish some characters had more dialogue with animations, but it’s nothing too substantial to really complain about. Visually, we wish they used higher quality visuals, but that’s it really. It looks ‘okay’ as is, but could be improved. The scene at the end with the sunset really looked low quality as well.
The music is also really well done. It was fun to listen to, and (since the OST is free on Steam) we listened to it while writing this review. Some of tracks feel a little too simple, and little too low quality in terms of audio playback, but it’s certainly not a bad soundtrack by any means. It’s not quite the ‘listen to this while you work on something’ soundtrack like something from say, Bioshock or Fallout 3, but it fit the game just fine.
The controls were also fine. Switching items is kind of a pain when you get more items, but it worked fine overall. The settings were also fine as is. The controls are rebindable, there are multiple graphics settings, audio settings, etc. It’s fairly basic, but we don’t think there’s much more it could have that it currently doesn’t. As for the game, it was fun, and we had fun. It was entertaining, and we got our $6.00 worth from the game. The puzzles are mostly older style adventure game early 90s style puzzles, but they weren’t nearly as frustrating as that, and mostly worked in a way you’d expect.
Overall, it’s a simple but fun 2D retro-style platformer with some fun and triply little elements. We wish some characters had more dialogue, and we wish the game has better visual quality, but it’s still a fun game. We did run into some glitches , but nothing that deterred us from playing or finishing the game. It’s a short little platformer that we enjoyed.
PROS
- Colorful cast of characters
- Well designed levels
- Good controls and platforming
CONS
- Low quality visuals and random low quality backdrops
Score: 7.9/10

Dreaming Sarah........What to say about it?
Dreaming Sarah is an exploration game that plays like a platformer.  You collect objects to get to your next destination with a puzzle scattered here and there.  The problem is, you aren't told what you are looking for or why.  The game begins, you wake up on a grassy floor, and off you go.  Why?  The game doesn't say.
There is no story here, and the game can be beaten in less than an hour.  Finding objects by just wandering opens up new areas along with the occasional puzzle I mentioned before.  It just doesn't make any sense as to where to go or what to do and why you are doing it.
I don't mind games that don't hold your hand, but I still want an explanation of some sort as to why the character is doing what he/she is doing.  Maybe you are to come to your own conclusion on that, it's hard to say.
All in all, with it's short game time, and confusion as to what exactly you are doing when you start, I cannot recommened this game.

It feels fantastic to walk in the world of Middle Earth. It's been my dream to fight alongside Aragorn, Legolas and Gimli, and with Lord of the Rings Online, that dream can come true. With some brilliant graphics, a wide range of characters, and a seemingly endless supply of quests, there's no doubt in LotRO being one of the best MMORPGs out there. It has a fantastic and friendly community, which you can interact with in Kinships, and team up with other players to battle enemies in fellowships.
One of the things that I don't really approve of is the fact that you have to buy access to some region quests, which, for someone like me who doesn't really have money to spare, will frankly slow down your levelling to a complete stop, forcing you to end participation in the Epic Quest route. Maybe it could come to that some of the regions become free to play around in, because I'm kinda sick of being stuck at level 44.
Overall 8.5/10, some areas need to be improved, but I'm frankly glad this game exists.

While perhaps not as highly regarded as Dark Crusade by some, DOW: Soulstorm creates an enjoyable RTS experence.  Each of the races has a different feel and lends itself to different types of strategy and yet each race also has the ability to overcome its weaknesses.  This extension of DOW adds flying units (except Nekrons) and two new races, of which I have found the Sisters of Battle particuarly fun tio play.  The flying units are nice but not a real powerhouse of the game.  On the downside, the map is a tad less dynamic than DC--I feel its predecessor had more options in its pathing, but the races balance better in Soulstorm.  The difficulty levels also offer greatly different game experiences.  The campaign is nice for an extended play, especially if you change races it can be like a new game.  The skirmish mode also allows for some quick, fun play.  The AI is ok--you might find yourself able to begin overunning the map in campaign mode once you have won a few victories in a row at times.  Overall, I recommend this game for its replayability and various levels of alien color.

Kill Englishmen as Joan of Arc, in this 100 years old war historic fiction game. Yes. Kill Englishmen.  They want the French throne, its the 1300's and using Joan, you single handedly get to thwart and kill them for trying. Relive battles from this epic war as akin to '' Dynesty Warriors'' to fight to level up your gear, your stats and gain a larger troops through 8 beefed up missions. I say ''beefed up'' because they start small, there are large maps and the sub quests are lengthy. Its not that quick and easy as you thought. WAR just isnt. The quests/ missions revolve around mainly The Basterd of Orleans and the defence of the French city and the villages around it. Use Joan or and other French commanders she befreinds to complete the missions. All have diffrent fighting styles and weapons to your choosing. ( I stuck with Joan as being a pretty solid one handed sword user with top commander stats) . With French like classical music, sound effects of clashing armor and swords with accents, the game is pretty solid. The graphics and game play remind me of old Nitendo 64 games and runs rather well. The combat style sometimes can get jumpy, but its not so harsh. Yes, you have to learn gameplay and easily can be cut down by muarading English swords or pikemen, but thats the skill part that needs to be learned. Overal a massive army hack and slash for you French, I think its a fun one to play along with Total war and other like games. Kinda of a Age of Empires first person thing going on...

I'd like to point out that I'm recommending this game on a whim. It was overall a fun experience but only when you hit the last half of the game. This game is VERY buggy, has HORRIBLE AI and has overall bad balancing with enemies, specifically generals and archers/crossbowmen. I tend to write long reviews but, well, that's how it is. It's my personal experiences typed out for you to consider.
First off, the story. It's quaint. It's basically the whole Joan of Arc story, but it ends with a happy-note.
It's 8 chapters/missions, the first two being short and the rest being 1-2 hours, at least. The story is well done and the ending is very satisfying. Definitely gives Joan of Arc the ending she deserved and it definitely makes Joan of Arc awesome, gameplay-wise. Probably one of the strongest generals in the game, other than Metz. More on that later.
Secondly, the music. The music in this game amazing. It has atmospheric sounds (e.g. dirt crunching beneeath feet, sound of metal armour hitting ground when moving, bird chirping, shouting and cheering sounds when fighting, etc.)that go very well with the game. The actual music itself has two side. The first side being the atmospheric-y non-combat music like this one, my personal favourite
Then there's the combat music like this, which is my personal favourite :
If you listen to the combat music, at around 0:25 ish is when it really hits it hard. It just has a great feel to it for what the game's theme and atmosphere is. It's especially amazing when fighting the enemy generals. Overall, the music is satisfying if you like music that really goes for the home-run and fits into where it's placed.
Enough drooling over the music. Here we go. The graphics. The inevitable paragraph. The graphics are actually pretty amazing for its time (2004) and at the same time they aren't particularly anything to freak out over. The graphics fit the game and it doesn't hurt my eyes. Good enough for me.
Of course! An inventory system! You basically have 5 types of items : Weapons(main weapon for the hero's preference, e.g. maces for La Hire or polearms for Duke), armour(both aesthetic and pretty useful for damage reduction late-game), food(basically potions for health / energy), misc. items ( keys for chests and doors, letters for mostly story but also a few sub-missions), and ammo(for the crossbow/bow). Weapons consists of Base Damage + X% and bonuses for each attack such as +40% Down Attack, for killing downed enemies. The ranged weaponry is literally there for being the ranged weaponry and should only be used for taking out distance ranged enemies. Other than that, the inventory system is pretty simplistic.
Finally, the gameplay! This is where the game shines but also falls quite a bit. This is also where the wall of text is introduced. First off, I'm not exactly a "pro gamer" type of person but I'm also not horrible. I'm mediocre. The gameplay in this game is similar to dynasty warriors. It's a slash-a-sword-through-a-group-of-enemies-with-combos game. You can do both a normal attack and a power attack. The power attack uses up, well, energy and is significantly more powerful than your normal attacks, regardless of what bonuses you get. You have combos as well but for the most part they're there for the sake of being there. See, you can upgrade each individual attack/combo. The max level of an attack is level 10. Upgrading combos changes the damage by a minimal amount, so the best you can do is upgrade two attacks that are by far the most important ones. The first is the rush attack, which is THE quintessential forward dash. It also makes you invulnerable while perform it and costs very low energy (1 EP with a specific ring). The second attack is the "energy attack" which is basically an ultimate. It costs both HP and EP but is a ridiculously good crowd-control ability, mostly because it makes you invulnerable for the duration of the attack, knocks down everyone, and you move while performing it. Simple. Upgrade those and you'll do well... Against the normal enemies. Here's where the biggest issue of the combat comes into play : Ranged and Generals. Now, the ranged aren't *that* bad but the issue with them is that they constantly move around, shoot at a moderately fast rate (even the crossbowmen) and they generally don't die in one hit, being as durable as light infantry units. They can also make you stop in your tracks with one hit and any subsequent attacks knock you down. So, yeah, they're annoying. Cool. What about the generals? Simple! They're invulnerable when using their power attacks(which they can do an infinite number of times and in repetition one after the other), they deal a ton of damage(1-hit killed one of my generals with 108 HP SEVERAL TIMES, and the hit didn't even connect) and you can only really get hits in when you down them with a rush attack or sneaking hits in *immedietally* after they finish their power attacks. The good thing about all of this is that blocking can, well, block anything. You can defeat any of the generals 1-on-1 if you block-and-hit. That being said, it's horrible unbalanced and can make for a bad time if you don't know that. Yeah, that's it. Unbalanced generals and annoying ranged units.
A second finally, I'll talk about the siege and RTS aspects of the game. RTS is, well, RTS. I don't know how to explain this but somehow RTS makes the game easier. I don't know if it's because the AI goes ham on the combos and attacks and just bruteforces the combat but it makes it easier and it's one reason why the final mission is ridiculously easy, considering it's required that you use it to move some units. The siege mechanics in this game requires you to use RTS to move the units onto a siege weapon and then to move the actual siege weapon. Cannons can attack both units and buildings but the other siege weapons can only attack the buildings. You can either capture your own siege weapons from the English or you can build them at resource spots, which only the Duke can do. You're not even required to use the siege weaponry since you can buy explosive ammo which can take down gates, and generals are pretty good on their own. You can effectively solo any siege if you have the food and ammo for it.
Final finally, I promised to talk about the generals you can play as, so here we go. Joan of Arc is your all-around general at first-glance but she tends to have the most powerful attacks and her ultimate weapon has 5 socketable items that buff it up pretty nicely. She's definitely the spotlight. There's Jean Metz, who is basically Luke Skywalker with his attack speed, movement speed, and capability for high ranged damage(he starts off with decent dexterity). His power attacks are also VERY quick. There's the Duke, a halberd-wielding general that is required to make siege weapons and has a more AoE set of attacks. There's La Hire who takes the role of "lovable human boulder". His attacks are more AoE, especially his ultimate attack. His power attacks are in a circular formation. There's two unplayable characters : ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of Orleans and Prince Charles. They are playable in RTS mode but that's not so much "playable" as it is moving them around. So, who do I suggest for the "most powerful"? Metz. He's ridiculously OP with his attack speed and movement speed.
Inevitably I missed a few things but they would be very small things and not worth mentioning. Overall, the game was pretty decent but there were a few issues with it, like bad AI and invincible generals. If you can get past the small issues that litter this game, it's a pretty good Joan-Of-Kick♥♥♥♥♥game.

When to by this game? Think of it as medieval total war as a combined RPG/RTS that you can switch to on the fly. And if you've seen the well-rated movie 'the messenger' with Milla Jovovich (thats right, the resident evil chick) as Joan of Arc, you will definitely encounter many similarities and even in-game scenarios that happened in the movie too.
On normal mode, the game is very easy to play. It's a typical old-school hack-n-slash revolving around using your left and right mouse buttons for combo's, and Q for blocking. Jumping and pressing C can be used for other powerful attacks. What makes the game enjoyable is the historically correct story (to my knowledge). Downside is the not optimally working collisions at times or some NPC's getting stuck (or even yourself, because NPC blocks path).
The castles and encampments in this game look great and you can decide to destroy them in RTS mode. The walls, towers and gates can actually break and be destroyed. Or you can decide to take it up close and personal and breach our way in and kill all the soldiers inside.
There's a few classes of troops to choose from from light infantry and crossbowmen to polemen and macemen. you can assign all of those to your controllable commanders (the main characters, same as historic equivalents) or to the occasionally appearing less significant NPC commanders which look the same as regular units except they're donning goldplated armour.  The configurations stays both in RTS as in RPG mode.
In the first few missions the RTS element isn't introduced yet which doesn't really matter as you will not have a lot of units under your command thus playing in RPG mode makes sense. Later on in the game, you'll be able to build more troops, buy more armor, weapons and food and even build siege weapons.
Despite all the positive goodness, here a list of things that may downgrade the gaming experience:
- the poor collision registrations when striking enemies who are down. Instead, just use a power attack, you'll hit anyone down and standing. problem solved!
- getting stuck. it's annoying when your fellow soldiers get stuck especially if thereby they block your path. the only place it happens a lot is at Tourelles. if you go up into that fortress to destro the arbalests, make sure you have not too many units following you. or it will be impossible to go back via the narrow stairs and you can't jump off the wall.
- food shortage. There is only so much food in the game. You have a special inventory for yourself and the main characters, and a separate inventory for troops following those characters. with 15 troops under your commmand, it's doable. If you've got like 50 of them and they're under fire from siege weapons and arrows, food disappears within a minute. The only ways of getting more food is slaying enemies, slashing crates or buying from the food store, and the food store's food is NOT infinite. ...
- The drag and drop interface. you can only move 1 item at a time. This becomes very problematic if youre in the heat of a battle and have to pause the game, to remove food items one by one to your troops inventory, to keep them alive -.-. Takes away from the gaming experience.
But yet, a game truly unique in its design with a nice story (you might learn something.) and oh yeah, checkout that movie joan of arc: the messenger with milla jovovich, you will recognize a LOT from that movie in this game.

is a deceptively simple puzzle platformer that has quite a bit going on under the covers. Its story is told almost entirely wordlessly, with a lot of little side excursions that paint a world of fairytales that is actually quite dark. Don't let the bright graphics and cartoony characters fool you -- while there are some funny and uplifting moments, this is not a feel good game. It's not deliberately out to depress you either, but it's more brothers Grimm than brothers Warner. I'm not saying you shouldn't let your kids play it, but I am saying you may want to look over their shoulder if they do.
Believe it or not, this is the game I bought a controller for. I borrowed one to see if the game was any good (it was) and then I completed it after buying one for myself. It's not easy to convince a hardcore mouse and keyboard guy to twiddle the sticks, so it deserves credit at least for that. It deserves some more credit for possibly being the very first game to use its control scheme to evoke an emotional response. I can't get into details (spoilers!) but you'll know it when you get there. It's beautifully done, and you'd need to have a heart of stone not to be at least a little bit affected. If you remember "press F to pay respects", this is pretty much the exact opposite of that.
The gameplay is just about right. It's not very challenging, but it's not a cakewalk between cutscenes either. The game does make the most of its controls, and coordinating two characters requires your full attention. Liberal use of checkpoints means you're not likely to get frustrated from having to replay bits, though. If the game was much longer the mechanics might wear thin, but its length works to its advantage here. My only gripe, if I can have one, is that one or two achievements are almost impossible to obtain without a guide, not because they require skill but because they require some very unintuitive actions. Still, this in no way detracts from the experience on your first playthrough, and the game allows you to replay chapters at will, so those who want the achievements can get them easily enough.
Whether you want to pay the full $15 for 4-5 hours of game is up to you, but even if you want to wait for a sale (or another bundle), this deserves to be in your library at some point or another. Two thumbs up, one big and one little.
