I've been following Larkons progress on Ellaria for a while now and am happy to see they finally released this Early Access. You can definitely see how much progress and time they have put into the game since the pre-alpha version. And even now, so much that they already released a significant update. So I am confident that they are commited to fixing errors and bugs and cannot wait to see how the game keeps evolving. It is not by any means perfect as of now, yet it has the potential to become something great. It still has a lot of bugs and it's missing simple features, but with feedback from the community and work from the devs these can be solved.
PROS
- Spells look and feel great.
- Switching between third-person and RTS view makes it feel unique, and is, in my opinion, it's most unique mechanic.
- Graphics look good and locations look distinct. It also has a nice atmosphere.
- It makes you want to explore.
- I thought the music was pretty good (when I could actually hear it).
- i think it's awesome that I can build my own kingdom from the ground up.
- The quests were pretty good, and the quest tracking system works great.
- Animations look good, even though they sometimes bug out.
MIDS
- The story was just kinda there for me, but i think it's decent.
- Movement needs polishing. (You keep moving a bit after you let go of the keys).
- It's missing some mechanics that sometimes make the game a bit annoying. (Can't move while using the bow, quest items are hard to see, weird character dialog faces, and more).
CONS
- No auto-save. (31/7/2017)
- Combat feels unfinished and just doesn't feel good, except for spells. I also found that using spells was the way to go, everything else was just weird or sort of useless.
- Enemy AI is bad and very easy to trick. For example, if you move far enough from enemies, they'll hit an invisible wall and you can hit them from far away (with Spells!). Enemies will also get stuck on walls and rock and such.
- The game is very dark sometimes, to the point where i couldn't really play because i couldn't see much. Not just caves, the overworld is also really dim at night (Fixed, although I think it would be pretty cool if you had a torch spell or something that you could use while exploring).
Overall, i'm happy with the game and will continue to play it and follow it's development.

Torchlight 2 is a game for those that enjoy playing with friends. I'm a sucker for beautiful game art, and T2 gave me
more than enough to take in. It's not over-done, so the creators found a great balance between art and game-play.
The magic system is immersive enough that I found myself feeling really smug whenever I broke out my big spells to
do in a whole room of monsters. It's colourful; the character design is detailed enough to become really fond of your character and be impressed by all the others; and the content-rich world is one that you can get really stuck into. So I would recommend this game to those who want to have some fun with friends, and just enjoy a gorgeous game of adventure, teamwork and amusingly mis-matched armour sets that still manage to make you badass anyway. Enjoy!

Torchlight's just awesome.  It's everything that Diablo 3 should have done, one of which being character customization.  And it's easier to find a build that works for you so it's more fun to experiment.  And exploding criticals.  How many other games blow you enemies to bits with just a critical?

Punch things
Cut things
Shoot things
Blast things
A nice lengthy story mode with randomly generated dungeons/maps
Four base classes, each with 3 sub-classes able to be levelled in MANY ways and styles
Each character you makes will have a pet that can be chosen alongside them, which can learn spells, equip things, etc
Up to six player co-op with the game scaling depending on how many people are playing
Multiple difficulty settings including a hardcore mode, meaning if you die, all you can do is weep and/or delete your character
Random dungeon generator at the end of the story, allowing you to continue playing your characters to your hearts content
AND THEN THERE'S NEW GAME PLUS
And if that wasnt enough
Easy to use mod support, with an extensive modding community.

All things said, you should get this game.

I bought this game on Halloween sale last year, and the only thing I regret is that I did not take the time to actually play it earlier than I did (which was pretty much yesterday).
For everyonen who has played Yume Nikki, this game will feel quite familiar, in visuals and sound, but without appearing like a total rip off. It certainly stands on it's own two feet (and I additionally enjoy that you are capable of discovering why Sarah ended up where she did).
Now, explorative puzzle platformers are not for everyone, but it is a nice game for those, that want to immerse themselves in it for a little while and just spent a bit of time relaxing and exploring.
Visuals and especially sound are really nice and I am super happy that the game comes with the OST, because Anthony Septim did a really great job at giving it the musical accompaniment it needed, to bring this familiar yet odd world to life.
Now, the game is quite short (albeit with a nice variety of settings), and the length is only buffed out by how quick you are able to find everything you need, as it is often with such games. It would have been great to get a bit more use out of the transformative items you aquire in this game, but that, again, is something I feel happens a lot in this genre.
Never the less, I consider it beautifuly crafted and if it is your cup of tea, I can heartily recommend it.

Dreaming Sarah is an excellent exploration game. The puzzles are mild and charming, although I was occasionally frustrated by the game's lack of direction. If you like exploration and have patience, Dreaming Sarah is fantastic. The environments made me feel like I was in a twisted, other dimension... kind of like a dream.

This is an exploration game into an dreamworld, inspired by games like Yume Nikki and LSD while being arguably a better experience. Between the overstuffed mechanics masquerading as emergent gameplay that makes a mockery of the original Deus Ex, the half-finished and half-baked main story, the Jensen Stories content that is obviously just main game content cut and repackaged as DLC, the unnecessary and bloated focus on side missions over the core experience, in addition to the the numerous and ongoing technical/graphical/gameplay glitches, AND not to mention microtransactions, Denuvo, requirement to "check-in" online regularly (for a single player game, seriously!?), intrusive surveillance masquearading as 'diagnostics,' and the inclusion of Breach instead of a full Deus Ex experience, it's now official: Square Enix has taken one of the greatest franchises in gaming history and absolutely butchered it. I would go so far as to say that its in worse condition than Adam Jensen at the end of Human Revolution's prologue -- but that would only be accurate if we assume that the series can be salavaged. Given what I've played and what both Eidos and SE representatives have said, I don't think that's possible.
Now, let me be clear that I have been playing the Deus Ex series since 2000. I have bought every game in the series, sometimes on multiple platforms. I have even written college essays and conference presentations on the series! I am, quite literally, an original fanboy. But this... this is completely unacceptable. This game is Deus Ex in name only -- the trappings are there, but the spirit has been sucked out of it (kind of like Adam Jensen, who skulks around the game barely seeming to care about much of anything).
So congratulations Square Enix. If I were wearing a hat, I would take it off to you. You have managed to both ruin one of the greatest intellectual properties in gaming history and alienate someone who should, for all intents and purposes, defend you at any cost so long as more Deus Ex is provided. But no. That's not the case here. In fact, I can tell you right now that I will never buy another product from you -- Deus Ex or otherwise.

Very old but catchy and interesting game. For the first time, I've played this game when I was a child, and it gave to me tons of hours of fun. Now I can remind to myself of these epic and positive moments.
What's the game like?
I can compare it with Dynasty Warriors with an actual story set in medieval times, with an inventory system and RTS elements. In simple words, it's like an RPG (but more or less linear) where you can select the character (not only Joan of Arc is available). The game has eight stages, and each stage has it's own huge battleground – an entire map where you can feel yourself free to explore every corner. It’ll take about 2-3 hours to finish it. There are even some sub-quests you can get from civilians. However, the main feature of the game is fighting and castle sieges. Command all your troops via RTS mode to besiege the castle or stronghold and switch your control to Joan of Arc to fight personally. Tons of enemies will try to separate your body from your head. You can lead your battle however you want: upgrade your main characters stats and lead an entire army to victory or fight alone 1vsDozens of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
On the other hand, the game will not impress you with its graphics but the story is still pretty nice and the soundtrack is great, and perfectly fits with the mood of the game. The sounds characters make, and the sounds of battle – everything is perfect.
It probably isn’t for everyone, but definitely one to give a go. I can recommend this.

This is one of my favourite games, These's something about starting out as a measly peasent and turning into the leader of a huge undefeatable army that is immenley satisfying.
Lets you aquire villagers from different regeons of the map and upgrade them into their own specialized units. You can become a vassal of a king of a warring faction or dominate the map as the king of your own emerging nation.
The game has a top down view of the map when you're out of battle, where different armies roam the large map of Calradia. When you run into an enemy army you get thrown into a fully fleshed-out battle simulator where you control your main character with the ability to give orders to your army such as "Follow me" or "Stand your ground".
The combat system is easy to use but hard to master. You click and drag back the mouse to simultaniously draw back your sword in the game. It feels fluid and getting a connect on an enemy while on horseback feels more real then if you were to just hit a button to swing your blade.
Overal this is a great game and you should buy this one (Warband) over the first Mount and Blade as this is the better more refined version.
TL;DR - Buy it.

PROS:
The main strength of this game, in its current state, is the atmosphere. Each location is distinctive, detailed and entertaining. It makes you want to explore and, from what I could tell, the world is large.
- Visuals: textures, models and dungeons look really good and the spells look amazing!
- Writing: the quests, after 2.5 hrs of playing, were still interesting and unique.
- Building: I only played long enough to create a single house, but placing it and then watching it get built was nice. You're also able to go inside of every building.
- Audio: I liked the background music and sound effects.
- Humor: Sometimes, a dying enemy screams, "no, my treasure!", which I think is quite funny.
MID:
- No map: I honestly liked exploring the large caves without a map. You feel like you could actually get lost in there, but I can see how some people might not like that.
- Day/night cycle: this seems like a useless feature atm. It might be cool for some quests, but there should be some way to sleep or light your way so that you don't have to explore in the darkness.
- Items/resources: you're able to find, pick up and carry different things. It's in a good state for an alpha. I couldn't figure out what I could do with the extra weapons that I found.
- Physics: there are some noticeable physics. For example, your fireball falls down over time.
CONS:
The main weakness of this game is the complete lack of immersion and fluidity. Even if you ignore all the (many) bugs, this game is still an example of choosing quantity over quality and form over function.
- Combat mechanics: if the devs remove ALL enemies and temporarily make this an exploration/building game, while they completely change these mechanics, then I would probably recommend the game. That's how BAD it is... Your bow is useless, the sword is great for swinging, but not for fighting or blocking. The fire spell aim is off. The only way to stay alive is to outrun your enemies (horrible AI), to wait for them to get stuck (horrible path finding), or to kill them from a distance with your fire spell. Oh and you can't loot them.
- Fluidity: Do you like constant loading screens and choppiness? Well, play this game because that's how you get both. The movement is choppy, the music stops and starts randomly and the FPS seems to take a dip as soon as you need to defend yourself. I can understand a loading screen when I enter/exit a cave, but not when entering every tiny building or when opening the options menu. This game is the reason that steam needs a "neutral" option for reviews.
I enjoyed this game, and I thought it had a bunch of new ideas that I would have loved to see in the base Half-life series. I loved the destructible buildings, I loved the object placement, and I loved the defensive arena-style fights. However, I just felt like the whole game could have been thought out better when being produced.
By far, the biggest reason that this game deserves a neutral rating is the creative new weapon. I really like the idea of what the new weapon does, and I think they were smart to balance its jumping ability by reducing fall damage and increasing the height requirement to even take damage. I thought that this gun would be overpowered, but it was actually balanced fairly well by way of its recharge timer. One large gripe I do have though is that one of this weapon's key features (clearing paths) seems to change the game's pace in a bad way. This is especially noticable early on, when the player is expected to figure out which doors, walls, and piles of crap are clearable and the correct way to go, and which aren't. I found that the extensive walks between points of interest were only elongated by this, and it lost its charm quickly. I was also disappointed that this superweapon capable of clearing waves of enemies at a time in a massive explosion could not be used to take down striders, which would have made for a very challenging and plesantly unique fight that the developers missed out on.
The game itself is pretty good as far as gameplay, but I really can't explain very well why it feels like a tired idea since it's pulled off so well. The game seems to have too many gaps between fights filled with walking and puzzles. Of course, these segments are spiced up with excellent area design, but it's not enough to make it completely better. There are several problems with the achievements in this game, as I was very early in the game awarded with the achievement for completing chapter three, and never received achievements for previous chapters. Other achievements also seem to fail to register, such as the garden gnome achievement.
So would I reccomend this game? No, but I'm not going to tell anyone that it's crap either. I much prefered Riot Act to this, even though it had less ambitious goals, and I preferred Minerva even though it was even less polished. This game is worth trying if you're dying for more Half-Life style gameplay, but otherwise is unremarkable aside from its unique machanics that could have been pulled off better.

After nearly 150 hours and two other reviews, I think I can finally say yes to recommending this game. But I also feel the need to organize my thoughts on the game.
-All microtransactions are purely cosmetic.
-The developers pay close attention to the community.
-There is just as much focus on balance as there is on new content.
-Blue Mammoth gives new players some room to learn naturally without holding their hand.
-Some of the lore is pretty damn entertaining.
-Added an extra casual game mode so people aren't playing the same thing over and over.
>gg button
-ELO system still feels sluggish.
-Ranked mode matching still placing players with large skill gaps together (though this has happened less and less as of late).
-Notable color and skin bias when in Free For All (I main Orion and go into a match with stock skin and color, get new players; put on my Harbinger skin and black color and immediately get paired with people who are immensely better than me).
-Most maps are either boring or annoying (Shipwreck Falls VS Thunderguard Pass), but that's pretty subjective.
-Existant transactions can easily be considered expensive when they're purely cosmetic.
-Blatant 'tiers'. Not sure if it can be helped because of the nature of the game, but when you come across nothing but Bodvars, Hattoris, and Teros..es in competitive matches, something has to be up, right?

-Optional detailed diagnostics window at end of each match (think Super Smash Bros. Damage dealt, projectile kills, et cetera).
-More casual modes to keep things interesting.
-Dynamic maps (again, think Smash Bros and the WarioWare maps).
-Perhaps a Steam Workshop interface could be a pretty cool feature later on into development. Allow community members to create their own skins for brawlers and maybe even add some of the higher quality ones into the game.
-Handicaps and special modifiers in private or local matches. It'd be pretty funny to see a highspeed fight where it only takes one hit to fly off the screen.
-Rewards for leveling up your profile beyond a few coins.
-Skins also change particle effects of attacks according to theme. Perhaps even color changes depending on the selected color as well.
TL;DR, keep up the good work Blue Mammoth. I've gotten a few of my friends to start playing it already, and they have a blast too.

Dreaming Sarah is a nice little platform adventure game.
You are Sarah who is in a coma and is dreaming of various locations from the normal to the totally surreal.
You awake in a field and are sent on your merry way.
There are no obvious pointers of where to go or what to do next.
Now sometimes, this can be a real problem but not here.
The game is small and you never truly get stuck.
For example, at the start, there is an uncross-able gap to the right so, you go left!
You find a brolly that lets you glide over gaps and that’s how one progresses.
Find a toy, access the new area with said toy to find more toys!
The game can be sprinted through in about half an hour but you are going to want to take your time exploring every area as the lovely pixel art combined with the atmospheric music makes for a nice relaxing gaming experience.
On your travels you will fly to space, traverse the innards of a grand father clock, buy alcohol with a fake id and make a tonsil inside a giant mouth sick!
If this was generic forest/castle areas all the way through, I get the feeling this would have felt like a chore but the diversity of locations held my interest.
While I really enjoyed the game, there were a couple of negatives.
The puzzles were rather arbitrary with a bit of random object x used in location y with no real link or context.
I did find myself after getting a new object, running back round all the locations to see if it done anything.
Not all the puzzles were like that.
Indeed some were decent logical puzzles where you knew exactly where to go next but some were just random.
To it’s credit, these are mostly for secrets and achievements.
The other issue is that the game can be quite buggy.
Several times I found hovering off the ground unable to move.
I also found my controls locked out after speaking to an NPC.
Clearly the controls were meant to reinstate after the conversation was over but I had to quit and re load my save.
Not good.
Despite the niggles however, I would recommend this, especially as it’s a budget game.
For the few quid it cost, I feel satisfied I got my money’s worth!

I generally like ARPGs a lot and loved the original Torchlight, but I do have a few concerns about Torchlight 2 that I'd like to address below.
First, let's start with the positives. The game is true to the genre and essentially capitalizes on the idea of loot gathering, character advancement and various builds based on 4 main characters. It plays well even on older computers and has all the necessary ARPG elements, including item customization and enhancements and even various scroll based spells that all characters can learn to add another level of power, such as summons of different type, resists and buffs. It doesn't unfortunately allow you to craft items, but there are plenty to find around anyway.
It also features decent soundtrack and sound effects, all created by the master who wrote the sound track for Diablo 1, which is both an excellent addition and in a sense a boon to the game's atmosphere (see below).
The game is also generally long and features tons of randomly generated dungeons set in at least 10 different settings with 4 major areas you go through (4 acts).
Gameplay wise, it's a stong contender with other ARPGs and offers a good variety of fact paced combat with tons of special effect.
Now let's talk about the concerning facts with T2.
First and foremost, the mismatch of the cartoony animations with the grim storyline and music. What worked so great in Diablo 1 and gave us an excellent understanding of a town in trouble haunted by demons and other evil, in Torchlight 2 is way out of place. The game looks too cartoony to be taken that seriously and should have gone with a more upbeat type of music as not only does the moody atmospheric tunes don't suit it, it may even make you more apathetic to what's happening in the game. It's sort of like taking a horror movie and turning it into a cheesy comedy. Which I personally think was a bad move.
Second, I think the game has WAY too many items, most of which are completely useless and even those that aren't, don't have that same oomph effect that items in other games like Diablo 2 or Titan Quest used to have. Finding that amazing sword of kickassery used to mean so much, but is unfortunately not that big of a deal in Torchlight 2 as you'll probably be showered with mediocre yet somehow useful items, inhancements and jewelery and will end up selling most through your subservient pet who will make quite a few trips to the town while you continue the items grind below.
Lastly, the level design, specifically the disjointed collection of maps connected through portals, rather than a seemless world like in Titan Quest and Diablo 2 is a bit of a disappointment as well. Although I like the idea of having tons of random maps, at the same time it doesn't make me feel like I'm going through a world and instead feels very "stagey". Every loadscreen shows the worldmap, yet it means nothing as not only do you never travel through the world itself, you generally just jump from one point to the other without any particular progression. This disjointed approach to level design is probably one of the bigger concerns I have for the game as it makes it feel more like the instance based MMO games of the late rather than a large living breathing world of older RPGs.
Nevertheless, for the price and the amount of content offered, you will be pleasantly satisfied for at least a few hours.
tl;dr
+large world
+lots of content
+many items
+Diablo 1 like music
+various character progressions
+randomly generated dungeons
-too disjointed
-way too many mediocre items
-no item crafting
-music doesn't suit the cartoony graphics
-storyline is not particularly exciting

It's a great game, but a bit of a letdown in terms of "Deus Ex Experience".
I'm not going to add to the plethora of reviews about the technical fidelity (which is state of the art) or the massively improved mechanics compared to its predecessors. Instead I'd like to address, that I understand why many players find themselves being disappointed by the game, but shouldn't really be.
- I bought the game for less than 40 EUR somewhere on the internet, which would give me more than ten EUR to spend on micro transactions to reach the usual price on steam; however, I never had the feeling to need any more praxis kits or whatever they offer in the shop. During the - absolutely amazing - sidequests there're more than enough experience points to gather so you'll never find yourself wishing for an easier experience
- the main story is underwhelming; yes, that's a good point and I agree. However, the game makes up for it by giving you by far the best sidequests you'll find in a modern computer game. No silly farming, no "bring me 5 of this", nothing. Just honest little stories which are fascinating and give you an experience that shines brighter than the main quest, which I only considered the topping on the cake at the end. The atmosphere is thick und uncomfortable, the dystopian world is a very tangible experience. After the incident that caused all the hatred and mistrust between the Augmented and Non-Augmented, the world makes total sense. The game is full of little details which give you more insight on how it must be to live in such a world and you'll find hints on many occurrences in the Deus Ex universe wherever you go and look.
Altogether, the expectations clearly were too high. After the brilliant CGI trailer they've released and the gameplay videos, as well as the deep and diverse predecessor, we were lead to believe this would be an even greater Deus Ex game. But its a different animal. You don't get to see many interesting locations, it's not that immersive roadtrip that we've become to expect from Deus Ex. Moreover, the choices you get during the development of the story are somewhat lackluster. However, it shines in different areas and it shines bright.
It's up to us to see the beauty of this game and I'm confident, it will be considered one of the greatest games in its time - if not now, then a few years later.

TLDR: It's bad when the publisher ♥♥♥♥s up a bad game even more, like EA did with Battlefront.
It's worse when the publisher ♥♥♥♥s up a really good game. Mankind Divided is a really good game. Buy it in 2 years when it has all the pieces available.
Review:
My opinion on this game is quite
. On one hand I am extremely impressed by the game's exposition of the world and environmental storytelling - superb, and the levels are some of the best I have ever seen in any game to this date. On another hand what was done to the rest of the game makes me loose faith in
.
Mankind Divided
an
cellent job at rewarding exploration. For an exploration fan like me, it is a joy to play. The gameplay is also solid and very varied, albeit really easy (played on Give me Deus Ex). Levels are extremely non-linear and sometimes truly vast in size, considering the level of detail. Enemies are also quite smart and the AI behaviour feels natural. They don't magically know where you are if they didn't see you, but neither do they ignore a gunshot because the "bar didn't fill up". Also I like the searching algorithm. It adapts to environment and is completely unscripted. You actually have to move your♥♥♥♥♥if they find evidence of your activity if you don't want to get caught. There's also a way to just shoot everything if you are a heathen like that.
Side quests are a jewel of this game, because unlike the main plot, they are actually complete and not cut into pieces to sell separately. They show that the team is very capable of producing good writing, good characters and good plots, which is why I have such a strong suspicion that most of this game's issues are caused by the publisher and not the development team.
That was it on the good bits. The bad bits: there are microtransactions in a SP game. Enough said.
...
...
NO THAT'S NOT ♥♥♥♥ING ENOUGH! There's also a vital story mission cut out for pre-order bonus - a mission that has TON of build up in the story, which never gets acted upon unless you pre-ordered, quit the main story at the right moment, launch the mission, complete it, then go back to main story, so it actually ♥♥♥♥ing makes sense. Disgraceful.
They also cut out the ending. I am willing to bet the game's price on the fact that we will see the proper ending for this game "just €19.99" or something like that in the near future. And you'll buy it, because ofc you will. In addition to all that, it seems like a lot of loose ends and good characters are left hanging for what seems like "DLC injection points". Because why make a good game AND good DLC, when you can make a good game, cut it into pieces and make DLC out of those?
I noticed one legitimate problem that is in the game by design though (i.e. couldn't have been caused by the publisher): people are right about lack of area variety. While existing levels are absolutely sublime, there aren't that many of them and they don't feel as different from each other as levels in Human Revolution were. The most interesting and different area that I was in was actually the last one - in London, with some nice mixing of off-limit and civil indoor areas, combining public places and office layouts. Prague is one of the best city hubs level-wise that I have ever seen, but I agree - it's just one. Perhaps it would have been better not to have such a big and detailed hub, but have multiple but in different parts of the world. Prague has multiple districts, but they all feel similar (ofc they do - they are in the same city).
Also it has dodgy optimization at times and 21:9 is not supported. It only crashed once for me though. Also there's some sort challenge mode with leaderboards? Why? Oh right: microtransactions. Gotta have some kind of motivator to buy items. And I HIGHLY doubt they did that mode just because they completed the game and still had some extra money left...
To have the gall to defile a Deus Ex game. And good Deus Ex game at that... This, Square Enix, I will never forgive. Not buying any of their games at full price ever again. No matter what they do (unless they release the rest of Mankind Divided as free updates). And I encourage you all to do the same. Get the Director's Cut of this game on sale later, you won't be disappointed: Edios Montreal are a VERY talented studio and they didn't loose their talent with this game that is clear to see.

Just beat my first playthrough and I generally enjoyed the experience. I would also highly recommend playing the previous game,
, before this one. Here are my thoughts:
Honestly these aren't as big a deal as they're made out to be. If you don't buy any of XP/weapon packs, the game is still perfectly balanced in my opinion. People have pointed out that they doubled the price of praxis kits (items that level you up) compared to the last game, but I really think that was a good move regardless of the microtransactions. I remember being able to buy two or three at a time in Human Revolution, while still having more than enough credits to afford everything else I needed. It makes more sense to have to give up buying weapons and supplies in order to buy XP. Anyways, it makes sense in universe too since you're technically buying them through the black market.
If you want to stick it to Square Enix, just don't spend money on the microtransactions. Buying the game and only the game will still mostly support Eidos Montreal and help them to keep producing works of love like this and
.
That whole "Augment Your Preorder" thing was stupid though. Glad they axed that.
At worst, it's more of the same from Human Revolution. They made a lot of improvements to the overall feel of the game. The guns feel a bit better to use. The cover system got a neat little upgrade making it a lot quicker to move between points of cover, though it can be a little finicky and difficult to use at times. This is apparently the year of the ledge grab, but for this game it really helps with some of the platforming and generally works the way you want it.
The new augmentations are cool, I guess. They could have explained the Remote Hacking aug a little better to make it clear that there are some things that can only be hacked with it, and that you can't hack computers and keypads with it.
They adjusted the energy system this time around so that you recharge more energy at a time, with your max rechargeable energy going down in slivers each time you activate an augmentation.
The in-game map is a little wonky. Doesn't really gel with mouse+kb all that well and locks you out of viewing zones ouside of the one you're currently in, which would have been useful.
The AI is still pretty stupid at times, even on Hard. During combat they generally do a good job of giving you a challenge, and while you're sneaking around they have pretty realistic lines of sight. That aside, it's still way too easy make the enemy bug out, or to find someplace to hide that the AI simply can't pathfind to. In
dlc from the last game, they did a good job of having guards adapt to your playstyle and would reward sneaky players with laxer security measures in the later portions of a level, but I'm not entirely sure that those features made their way to
which is a bummer.
You may have heard that there is only one hub world this time around, Prague. That's technically true, though you do still visit a variety of other locations such as Dubai, London, and Switzerland, and there's at least one other location in the game (Golem City) that I'm fairly certain was a more fleshed out hub zone in early drafts of the game but was cut. I think the main hub is fine enough, and has plenty of details and density.
There's officially only one boss on the game, which people complain about, but then I suppose that's an improvement considering that the boss fights from
were so heavily panned. But depending on how you look at it, there are technically more. There was one side quest that basically had a boss fight at the end, even if the boss could be KO'd in one hit. There are a lot of debate encounters which also act as boss fights in a way, and there's at least one major debate in the main story that I can recall, and then a couple more in the side quests. There more subtle but they serve the purpose of climatic encounters.
Overall, this is a very above average stealth-action game.
At first, the setup did seem kind of stupid to me. I still think that the racism analogy is a little bit forced, but the prejudice against Augs is actually very justified and believable in context. The story does a lot with this setup, and does manage to throw you a few moral curveballs at you to make you consider augmentations and transhumanism in ways you might not have before.
Along with this theme of discrimination, the game also plays at themes of conspiracy. The main conflict has to do with the Illuminati, and Adam Jensen's efforts to oncover them. I think this part of the story was a little less developed than it could have been, and it definitely doesn't account very much for player choice. A lot of it is developed through optional side missions or exploration, but the events of the main mission don't really account for the knowledge that Jensen might have at that point, which can be frustrating.
However, to the game's credit, in my experience of focusing on in-game leads and side missions, it really did put me in the conspiracy mindset. There was a point by the mid- to late- game where I was constantly over-examining my interactions with other characters and questioning their true allegiances. I was constantly scrutinizing my actions and movements under the assumption that Jensen could already be under survellience. Even though experience has tought me that something like that would be almost impossible to implement into a game, I loved the fantasy and immersion of it all.
On the subject of side missions, I don't think the name even does them justice. Most of them are very neatly integrated with the main events of the story and really fill in the cracks of the story.
Yes, the game does in fact have a quite sudden and unsatisfying ending. It doesn't necessarially leave anything unresolved, it's just that the execution of the ending is kind of bad and feels rushed. Ultimately, they're shooting for a trilogy here, so they had to leave plot threads open for the third game, but I also think they could have done a better job of framing the main conflict between Jensen and the main antagonist. But it's all about the journey, right?
was a pretty good journey to me.
I have a mostly mid-range build (Core i5 with a GTX 960) and this game definitely put a my rig through its paces. In isolated areas I could get the game to hit the 40-60 fps range on medium/high settings. If that was how the game always ran then it would be fine.
Unfortunately, the main hub suffers from horrible stuttering. High-end rigs can mitigate for this somewhat, but for me this meant single-digit framerates at times. It's sort of understandable, since the hub is really busy and there are absolutely no loading screens aside from the subway that you have to take to get from one section of the map to the other (though those loading screens can get pretty lengthy, but never more than a handful of minutes for me). There are also points in the story where major events happen in the hubs as you're going through them, which also might account for the dips. I haven't heard if this also occurs on consoles, so it might just be a port optimization issue.

One of the greatest games of all time. I suspect the developers made the ending first, found the best controls for that ending, then built the game backwards. This game explores concepts of death, suicide, war, and animal cruelty, but in a very mature and respectful way. It is a very well written story, and the game is designed to entertain, not frustrate and challenge.
Because of that last choice, there is not a lot of level repition. There isn't even much repitition in the gameplay, with each experience uniquely crafted to serve the experience. Because of this, the gameplay time is about 4 hours. So if you're expecting something to keep you busy over a month break, this is not what you're after. However, if you've a spare 4 hours and want to spend it experiencing an emotional rollercoaster ride, this is the game for you.

While this game looks good(Box art, so to say), it has many, many problems that have yet to be addressed by the developers Kalypso Media.
The first main problem is the communication this game has with the player. While you have a shiny tutorial which most games now-a-days gloss over, the way the game tells you waht is going on is not clear. Multiple typos appear regularly, and what you are changing at times through edicts/etc. is not clearly indicated to the player.
Another major problem with this game is the reset upon re-loading if you are able to even get your system to respond to the commands, especially in later eras.
The preformance of this game is pitiful, at best. Even if you do find a way to get it up and running on your system, expect major preformance issues, especially again, in later eras as your city continues to grow.
This game feels like it was pushed way to quickly through to the public, without taking simple steps to make it the best game that could of come onto the market, to us, the players. I can not recommend this game to anyone, especially for $39.99 USD as of time of posting. Even at a sale of 50%, I wouldn't touch this product. While fun, the bugs and preformance issues will give you buyers remorse for weeks.
Kalypso Media has many great games under their belt, the Tropico Series and Airline Tycoon 2 come to mind, but this game is not one of them, and brings to mind the EA-SimCityDisaster'13, and we all know how that turned out.

Just beat my first playthrough and I generally enjoyed the experience. I would also highly recommend playing the previous game,
, before this one. Here are my thoughts:
Honestly these aren't as big a deal as they're made out to be. If you don't buy any of XP/weapon packs, the game is still perfectly balanced in my opinion. People have pointed out that they doubled the price of praxis kits (items that level you up) compared to the last game, but I really think that was a good move regardless of the microtransactions. I remember being able to buy two or three at a time in Human Revolution, while still having more than enough credits to afford everything else I needed. It makes more sense to have to give up buying weapons and supplies in order to buy XP. Anyways, it makes sense in universe too since you're technically buying them through the black market.
If you want to stick it to Square Enix, just don't spend money on the microtransactions. Buying the game and only the game will still mostly support Eidos Montreal and help them to keep producing works of love like this and
.
That whole "Augment Your Preorder" thing was stupid though. Glad they axed that.
At worst, it's more of the same from Human Revolution. They made a lot of improvements to the overall feel of the game. The guns feel a bit better to use. The cover system got a neat little upgrade making it a lot quicker to move between points of cover, though it can be a little finicky and difficult to use at times. This is apparently the year of the ledge grab, but for this game it really helps with some of the platforming and generally works the way you want it.
The new augmentations are cool, I guess. They could have explained the Remote Hacking aug a little better to make it clear that there are some things that can only be hacked with it, and that you can't hack computers and keypads with it.
They adjusted the energy system this time around so that you recharge more energy at a time, with your max rechargeable energy going down in slivers each time you activate an augmentation.
The in-game map is a little wonky. Doesn't really gel with mouse+kb all that well and locks you out of viewing zones ouside of the one you're currently in, which would have been useful.
The AI is still pretty stupid at times, even on Hard. During combat they generally do a good job of giving you a challenge, and while you're sneaking around they have pretty realistic lines of sight. That aside, it's still way too easy make the enemy bug out, or to find someplace to hide that the AI simply can't pathfind to. In
dlc from the last game, they did a good job of having guards adapt to your playstyle and would reward sneaky players with laxer security measures in the later portions of a level, but I'm not entirely sure that those features made their way to
which is a bummer.
You may have heard that there is only one hub world this time around, Prague. That's technically true, though you do still visit a variety of other locations such as Dubai, London, and Switzerland, and there's at least one other location in the game (Golem City) that I'm fairly certain was a more fleshed out hub zone in early drafts of the game but was cut. I think the main hub is fine enough, and has plenty of details and density.
There's officially only one boss on the game, which people complain about, but then I suppose that's an improvement considering that the boss fights from
were so heavily panned. But depending on how you look at it, there are technically more. There was one side quest that basically had a boss fight at the end, even if the boss could be KO'd in one hit. There are a lot of debate encounters which also act as boss fights in a way, and there's at least one major debate in the main story that I can recall, and then a couple more in the side quests. There more subtle but they serve the purpose of climatic encounters.
Overall, this is a very above average stealth-action game.
At first, the setup did seem kind of stupid to me. I still think that the racism analogy is a little bit forced, but the prejudice against Augs is actually very justified and believable in context. The story does a lot with this setup, and does manage to throw you a few moral curveballs at you to make you consider augmentations and transhumanism in ways you might not have before.
Along with this theme of discrimination, the game also plays at themes of conspiracy. The main conflict has to do with the Illuminati, and Adam Jensen's efforts to oncover them. I think this part of the story was a little less developed than it could have been, and it definitely doesn't account very much for player choice. A lot of it is developed through optional side missions or exploration, but the events of the main mission don't really account for the knowledge that Jensen might have at that point, which can be frustrating.
However, to the game's credit, in my experience of focusing on in-game leads and side missions, it really did put me in the conspiracy mindset. There was a point by the mid- to late- game where I was constantly over-examining my interactions with other characters and questioning their true allegiances. I was constantly scrutinizing my actions and movements under the assumption that Jensen could already be under survellience. Even though experience has tought me that something like that would be almost impossible to implement into a game, I loved the fantasy and immersion of it all.
On the subject of side missions, I don't think the name even does them justice. Most of them are very neatly integrated with the main events of the story and really fill in the cracks of the story.
Yes, the game does in fact have a quite sudden and unsatisfying ending. It doesn't necessarially leave anything unresolved, it's just that the execution of the ending is kind of bad and feels rushed. Ultimately, they're shooting for a trilogy here, so they had to leave plot threads open for the third game, but I also think they could have done a better job of framing the main conflict between Jensen and the main antagonist. But it's all about the journey, right?
was a pretty good journey to me.
I have a mostly mid-range build (Core i5 with a GTX 960) and this game definitely put a my rig through its paces. In isolated areas I could get the game to hit the 40-60 fps range on medium/high settings. If that was how the game always ran then it would be fine.
Unfortunately, the main hub suffers from horrible stuttering. High-end rigs can mitigate for this somewhat, but for me this meant single-digit framerates at times. It's sort of understandable, since the hub is really busy and there are absolutely no loading screens aside from the subway that you have to take to get from one section of the map to the other (though those loading screens can get pretty lengthy, but never more than a handful of minutes for me). There are also points in the story where major events happen in the hubs as you're going through them, which also might account for the dips. I haven't heard if this also occurs on consoles, so it might just be a port optimization issue.
I enjoyed this game at full price, and I'd say it's a no brainer if it's on sale. The microtransactions aren't a big deal and can easily be ignored. Gameplay's great. The story has pretty awesome moments.

It's disappointing.
DE games were always about:
1) Gameplay choices, different approaches to the problem (present here)
2) Story full of dark, global illuminati plots (absent here. Not only the story is unintriguing this time around, it ends with a cliffhanger. There is a good chance there will be no remedy in DLC's either. It smells like a huge bet on a sequel).
3) Distinctive locations all around the globe. (barely here)
As you can see, this game struggles quite hard to justify its DE name.
Gameplay-wise it's a polished version of DE:HR, which was polished enough in its own right. And while there is nothing wrong with such gameplay per se, I personally have a gripe with difficulty. Yes, they've added an Iron Man mode, but that's a different kind of beast meant for second+ playthroughs. What I mean is that when I play on hardest available difficulty, I expect the game to be at least somewhat challenging. Addition of new augments made the game extremely trivial. If let's say in HR, in order to non-lethaly clear a room with 4 targets while avoding the alarm you had to resort to gas grenades/mines and grouping your enemies in some way, here you've got a no-brainer augment that locks onto all 4 targets from across the room and quietly puts them to simultaneous sleep. So the only way to create challenge is to artificially limit yourself in augemt choices. No dash, no cloak, no tesla, no x-ray vision - this sort of non-lethal playthrough might actually be entertaining. Sadly I'll never know, because game leaves zero reason to play through it again.
Story is a complete mess. It gets interesting for a very short period of time when "double-agent" action is being introduced, but sadly, it leads absolutely nowhere. Not to spoil anything story-wise, the biggest problem in narrative department is probably Adam Jensen himself. Unlike DE:HR, here he has zero character development. His motivation is nonexistant. In first game dude was brought back from the brink of death, lost his girlfriend, was struggling with getting used to his new augmented self, had a strong motivation to pursue the attackers, as it was him, head of security at Sarif, who failed at his job of protecting the facility. After finding out that Megan was alive, stakes went even higher for Adam. All that drive is in the past. In MD Adam literally just wakes up in the morning and goes to job. He also has this side job thing going on, that sometimes interferes with his actual work. And that's about it. Regardless of decisions you make throughout the game, Adam in the end of MD will be exactly the same person he was in the beginning of MD.
Finally - the location diversity. In DE:MD we've got one opening mission in unfinished hotel building in Dubai, one in the slums of the "Golem City" on the outskirts of Prague, one in the powerplant\research facility\military camp in Swiss Alps, and one in the most-generic-skyscraper-ever in London. That's it. 4 missions outside of the main hub. 2 of these missions are quite short, 2 have a more respectable duration. Rest (read the majority) of the action takes place in Prague, which they did not manage to sew into one location, so you'll enjoy quite a few loading screens while exploring the city. Not only this lack of diversity makes game less memorable, it also makes it incredibly short. My 42 hours in game include non-lethat approach, avoiding any alarms, turning every stone I could find (reading every email/newspaper/pocket secretary) while also spending around 4-5 hours in breach mode. A regular, relaxed playthrough with minimum save-loads on normal difficulty should take around 20 hours.
Speaking of breach mode - it's surprisingly well built for a side-activity. While I found artstyle quite uninspiring, I suppose quite a few people might enjoy the ability to test out whole weapon\cybernetic arsenal (somewhat expanded compared to the main game even !) in non-story driven environment.
Preorder mission that you can't access during the campaign using your actual character - is just a spit in customers face. You have to start it from main menu. You're given "fresh" Jensen, set amount of praxis kits, couple of tools, and off you go. Lasts for another hour tops, takes place (surpise!) yet again in Prague. I'd take any bet arguing that this mission was originally just a regular sidequest that some genius in marketing department decided to gut from the main experience and use as a tool to boost their preorder sales.
All-in-all, this would be a good game if it weren't for DE name. Hell, it could almost be a decent DE game if not for what HR managed to achieve. But HR showed us that DE is not dead, so naturally, we wanted more and we wanted (at the very least) the same quality. Sadly, Eidos failed to deliver both.

Well, to be honest, it was an enjoable ride, but a lot of things inside this game made it very difficult to me, to give it a positive review, but I should start from the beginning.
First and maybe most important to everyone who didn't play Human Revolution; you get a "short" (circa 17 minutes) summary of all the events during the story of Human Revolution, so you can play Makind Divided without playing the predecessor.
Interesting sidenote for all the other players, who played Human Revolution: During this video, there are no hints, which of the free choices you have during the storyline, is used to tell the story of Makind Divided.
An Example: You get no information of what happened to Jensens former pilot Faridah Malik.
Another Example: You won't find out, which of the endings caused the storyline of Mankind Divided.
You only get hints during the story, and you have to think for yourself, to find out.
This was at first a strange occurance, but still, I was eager to play.
After the summary, you get a short cutscene in a VTOL-Aircraft and you land in Dubai, to invstigate a case there.
In that Cutscene you don't get a clue, why Jensen is sitting in a VTOL with soldiers.
You only get a cliché briefing from your "chief" and you get the classic options of lethal/non lethal, short/long range combat, which players of Human Revloution already knew.
this mission is used as a tutorial and I really needed it, because they changed the controls, which is, in fact, another negative point.
I really had problems to aim at enemies, and during the whole game, I rarely tried to use the Rambo way, because of that controls.
The mouse sensitivity, when aiming was just awful and you have to keep pressing the right mouse button to hold the sights.
I never found the switch in the controls, that it stays when just clicking the right mouse button once.
This and some other controls were just badly choosen, so I decided to set everything back to Human Revloution, so I, at least get a little bit used to everything.
So, I finished the Dubai Mission and you promptly get to Prague.
Prague looked beautiful and even though I just played with "High" settings, the graphics there were shwon at it's best.
Sure, it still had flaws, especially with face animations, but I come back to that later.
All in all, from a graphics point of view, I had no problems and I am using a Geforce GTX 970.
I just lowered the graphics and some other parameters like shadows and anti aliasing, which just devours a lot of power.
So, I walked across Prague and get used to the new kind of open-world they offered.
You get some side missions which were pretty good, I think.
One mission contained a murder case, another one of finding things, another one of stealing or breaking into something, a lot of investigation and dialogue based mechanics, but still, satisfying when completing one of them, but nothing special.
And here I find another netagive point: You just get too distracted with all the side missions, that you almost completly forget the main story.
I had this with Metal Gear Solid V and Assassin's Creed IV, where you just have a huge open-world, which gives you a lot of freedom, but also the danger of forgetting the main plot.
This game is another good example.
I just found myself, walking from A to B, to complete the side mission and this almost took 2 Hours.
Later when I completed 3 or 4 of them I scracthed my head and thought "okay, where do I have to go on next and what happened before that?"
So, open the inventory, looking at the main mission bar, and then heading back to the main plot.
Oh yes, and I almost forgot to mention: During your free exploration you have two areas in prague, both of them are seperated in two different levels, connected with a subway-system.
The loading time is just awful long when travelling between these two points.
I, just measured the time once, and came almost to 3 Minutes!
For a 2016 open-world game, this is an awful long time period, and the sad thing is, the areas aren't even that big!
Sure, there is a lot to explore and find, but still, this is no excuse for such loading times!
I also had to get used to the new kind of art style in the inventory.
It is darker and a little bit more convoluted.
Sometimes, I haven't found things as fast as in Human Revolution, but with some time I got used to it.
The main story is pretty short and the ending was cunfusing and dissapointing at the same time.
You litterally have just ONE boss fight, sorry for the small spoiler, but I realy have to mention this.
After that Bossfight the epilogue cutscene starts, answers some questions and then the credits is coming next, with a short cutsene in between, so you should stay on it (well, and because you can't skip it, and have to stare at all the names circa 15 minutes long).
The cheeky thing is, not all of the questions raised during Mankind Divided will be answered and you get left alone, with the questions in your mind, so, you are forced to buy following DLC's, Expansion packs or successors.
They really should have took the time, to give the fans at least a good and satisfying ending, and not just a part of it.
During that cutscene they also mention some of your completed side missions, but if they get mentioned or not, is not very important, nor does it satisfy you, when Eliza Cassan reports them.
She just summarize them, and then goes on with the next topic, that's all you get.
When you expect, that your decisions have some sort of greater impact, well, you get dissapointed.
Also the location variety is ridiculously low.
[Small Spoiler]
The Loctations are:
- Dubai
- Prague
- Golem City
- Prague
- Switzerland
- Prague
- London
Golem City and Prague were the only locations worthy to be mentioned, but all other consisted of small areas, which were disapointingly empty and somehow heartless made.
Even though Human Revlolution had smaller areas, but they had more flaire and athmosphere in it, than these.
I thought I got to see some other places during these dystopian times, but also here, I gut dissapointed.
During that main story you get to a few "crossings" where you have to choose, which path you take.
There aren't many of great impact for the storyline. You just get some other sort of dialogue, when you choose otherwise.
ALso, as mentioned before, the facial animations aren't very convincing.
Only if you get to an imporatant storyline dialogue [small spoiler] like Talos Rucker later, for example), the facial expressions are far more convincing, but during side missions you get over gesticualting NPC's whose facial expressions are ridiculously B-Movie styled and just look awful.
Only the voice acting made it bearable.
I should mention the sound/music.
These are, with the graphics and the athmosphere one of the best things in Human Revolution.
The Voice cast does their Job perfectly.
Specifically the voice acting from Adam Jensen, Talos Rucker, Victor Marchenko, and Alex.
Musically you get orchestral masterpieces mixed with electronic elements from Michal McCann, who also did an awesome job with the Human Revolution Soundtrack.
So, I really should focus on a result.
A lot of people are asking now, why does he still recomend this game after he criticises it more, than praising it?
Simple:
Steam just has a recommend and not recomend button, and this game is still too good to be not recommended.
Sure, it has major flaws, like the controls, the very short and not satisfying ending (where the Human Revolution endings were better made, with a clearer message), the loading times, the smaller variety of loctaions and more, but still, you get an enjoyable ride with tons of side missions and things which just keeps you playing for hours.
Also the athmosphere is great, mixed with the awesom soundtrack and voice acting you get a unique gaming experience.
So, I still can recommend the game.

I have been looking forward to Mankind Divided since before I even knew it was in production. After the credits rolled on Human Revolution for the third time, I couldn't wait for the next game in this new series. Now it's here, I've played through it to completion one time, and I have little to no desire to go back and I am going to outline why. First, let's start with the positives.
+ The gameplay is polished to a shine, a true refinement over what made Human Revolution so fun to play.
+ Levels are vast and filled with things to see and do, places to explore and secrets to find. Though there are fewer levels than in HR, their size and scope has been greatly increased.
+ The weapons are all fantastic, and my favorite from the first game--the stun gun--now looks like a pistol making it much more fun to use.
+ The new augs, while largely pointless overall, add a new level onto the gameplay, especially remote hacking. They aren't necessary to beat the game, but they are fun to use.
+ It is a decent PC port. I was able to turn most settings to max on my new GTX 1070 and the game played flawlessly for the most part.
Now, onto the negatives.
- Lip sync is terrible in most cutscenes, characters practically look like puppets when they talk
- The story is a truncated shadow of what Human Revolution delivers and it ends on a wet fart. It's very clear to me that this game was cut in order to sell the rest to us later. They might as well have splashed "Please buy the season pass" after the credits rolled.
- Enemies seem to be placed much closer together, so it's hard to kill/knock out without instantly being seen by everyone else. And of course, as soon as one person sees you everyone in the area instantly knows your exact location.
- This game is very short in comparison to Human Revolution. There are a fraction of the side missions we saw in HR and maybe half the story locations. In addition, there's only one hub area which you will spend the majority of the game schlepping back and forth across.
- Towards the end of the game, the hub city goes on lockdown, and you have to spend time stealthing around in order to get places. It wasn't fun, it was padding, and it just made it take longer for no good reason.
All this being said, I would still recommend Mankind Divided to fans of Human Revolution. There is a 12 minute video new fans can watch to get all caught up and which does an admirable job of hitting all the major plot points. If you are a newcomer, maybe wait for a Steam sale. Most of my nitpicks are for people who were expecting more from a sequel coming 5 years down the line. It's still a great game and well worth playing.

: Transmissions: Element 120
: 8/10
: A great little experience if you're a fan of the Half-life series, although the brief length of the game hinders the full potential of all the elements and new ideas the game brings to the table.
: Let me first say, the game certainly was a great addition to the source engine's vast library of success. It utilized all of its assets and created an experience that was well worth enjoying. Power to the developer for making such an interesting little mod for a near-forgotten universe. Although, I'd like to give (hopefully) constructive criticisms where I see them fit.
- What I mean when I say this is, you are presented on multiple occasions with an interesting new mechanic that aids in solving a couple of puzzles, though thereafter it's merely tossed to the wind. A primary example of this is manuevering in the dark amidst zombies. There was so much potential for further utilizing this type of puzzle, though after only a one time use it was never used again at any point in the game.
The gravity gun in many respects also falls under this critique, as it had the potential for so much more, yet met its peak of use mere moments after having acquired it.
- Aside from recognizing that you are in a city infested with zombies and that there are combine soldiers patrolling the streets, there isn't much to tell. While there are notes that further elaborate on the situation, they too left me wondering 'What happens next?'. It's good to have ambiguity in stories such as these, though without any form of revelation, I feel as if the premise falls flat.
But, aside from my opinions, the game itself is certainly a more than enjoyable experience if you're looking to kill an hour or two. So, with that said, I would definitely recommend picking this little diddy up!

I'll start with the bad things first because everyone else is actually pretty darn good!
The combat could be more fluid. You see, combos rely on locking on, so does dodging. The problem is that while locked on, you move extremely slowly. Constant locking on and off is more a nuisance than enjoyment. Furthermore, the dodging system is made only for that, dodging. You can't dodge towards an enemy to close distance quickly.
Next problem, platforming. I don't hate platforming, but the fixed camera angles are very annoying. Extremely annoying. And having the camera switch into your face when you enter somewhere means that you quit right where you entered most of the time.
That aside, the game is fantastic. While I couldn't care less for the DMC lore, the gameplay is a blast. The whole "God of War"-genre is often called "spectacle fighters" and there is a true spectacle to be had here. With some finger dexterity, you can unleash torrents of strikes and dismantle enemies in spectacular ways.
Level design suffers from invisible walls, but the actual combat arenas look good, platforming is mostly good and what especially intrigues me is that you can spend several missions in one big area, unlocking parts of it un a non-linear fashion, almost like a Metrovania. Thumbs up!
Due to the not-so-dynamic combat, I would recommed thos one AFTER Bayonetta & DmC (5). But after you've beaten those and enjoyed them, you really can't go wrong with this one. I have to add though that this one has a huge mileage. Really huge. So if you're going to buy one game, get this one!

Plastic soldiers you say? Well, why not, it's not like this is the first time game used those. Suddenly an onslaught of soldiers looks kind of cute, instead of severed limbs you get shattered plastic and there is no blood. So apart from the theme, what is this all about? The Mean Greens - Plastic Warfare is a multiplayer third person shooter in which two sides of plastic soldiers, greens and tans, fight on a variety of über cute maps with their plastic arsenal.
Each side can have five soldiers at most and while you cannot pick different types of little warriors, you can pick from a variety of weapons to use. Each soldier carries an M4, sniper riflle, shotgun, rocket launcher and flamethrower from which you can choose on the go. Have you used all your sniper rifle ammo? No problem, take out your shot gun and run around for a moment while your ammo gets automatically replenished, that is if you live long enough. I would say that neither of these weapons is weaker than others maybe apart from rocket launcher; which however can fire just one rocket before having to replenish ammo. The gun handling itself is far from being unique as it is very arcade like, fitting with the theme of the game I would say. If you are a fan of realism... well, you would not be even reading this review so whatever.
Soldiers can duke it out on an astounding number of 10 maps (hi SW) each equipped with a different mode ranging from typical deatch match and capture the flag to candle lighting on a birthday party. The theme of the game let the devs to come up with some really unique arenas for the soldiers to fight in which is in my opinion the biggest perk of the game. Who would not enjoy a ride on a toy train around a christmas tree or an onslaught inside a Foosball. When you are riding a little gummy duck inside a bathtub you won't even care that the graphics are not exactly perfect and some textures could use a little more work which brings me to the next part of this review, graphics.
As I have said, the game is not the "bestest" looker on the market, devs of The Mean Greens tried to bring us a fully 3D experience and as many small indie studios kinda struggle with the delivery; However for what it is, the game is pleasant to look at. It is very colorful and one will forgive it the sometimes too rough edges and blurry textures. From a technical standpoint the game runs fine and I did not notice any major hiccups on an upper mid-end desktop. In settings there are plenty of options to fiddle with while trying to get a better performance from a lower end machine.
All in all, The Mean Greens - Plastic Warfare is a pretty decent game which cannot, and in my opinuon should not, compete with the popular shooters like CS:GO or Overwatch; However in itself can bring a lot of joy if you are a fan of arcade shooting in an unique arenas while listening to a pretty neat soundtrack. The main question will be whether it can keep the servers running and populated and for how long. So should you buy it? For 10 bucks it is not a bad deal whether you are bored of competitive shooters and want to relax or want a not so brutal game for your young ones so feel free to grab it, it works and it's fun!

Very nice adventure game, beautifully made. Was worth buying and playing.
A side note: the game is best played by two players together. It is possible to go through alone, but controlling the two brothers simultaneously is quite a work at times.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a game developed by Starbreeze Studios, the same people behind The Chronicles of Riddick series and the Payday series and published by 505 Games
The game follows two brothers who find out that there father is sick with an unknown plague, they must venture into the beyond to find the tree that holds regeneration powers, over their journeys they will encounter obstacles, danger and friends that will aid them on their journey
The game's story, although relatively short, is well written and the character development, especially between the two brothers is really good. The game manages the two brothers really well when it comes to gampelay with the use of the controller (which is they only way to play the game), the left analogue stick controls the big brother whereas the right analogue stick controls the little brother
Through puzzles and obstacles they must complete their journey to the tree. The whole game is spoken in an unknown language or gibberish (whichever you prefer) and although I found this weird at first, the way the game handles it with the emotions and movement of the characters, there was no need of any 'spoken' dialogue at all
The music and sound effects are spectacular as well as the graphics and environments. Running on the Unreal 3 engine, the game manages and nails the atmosphere correctly for each part that you with the two brothers roam to. I did encounter some dips in framerate, but that was most probably to load the rest of the environment. Overall, I encountered no bugs or glitches
The only complaint I would have about this game is the controller. People without a controller can either give this game a miss, go and buy and controller then play it (which is what I did) or try and play the game with a keyboard, which sadly won't work. I can understand why they chose to use a controller, but it does kick a lot of people out from trying the game
The game is short, clocking in at around two to three hours long which you can play this game in one whole sitting (which is what I did), I personally have no complaints about the length, however, I would only recommend this game if the game was cheaper or on sale
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a magnificent game which shows us that with the miminal amount of dialogue and no story explained whatsoever, we can imagine and form our own version of the story and bond with the two brothers on their adventure to heal their dying father

Not worth the money. Nearly everyone else is saying it but it can't hurt to add to the cacophony because they are right in nearly every count that I've seen. I love city and political simulators so this game could not fit my tastes more but unfortunately this game is lackluster in nearly everyway. Once you gone through one playthrough (which will take you maybe 3-4 hours) you have seen all you are gonna see. I can't tell if the economy is too hidden are so simple that you can frequently run on auto-pilot but it is barely a factor. The political game quickly turns into automatically passing 9/10 votes and then seeing if you want to bother pushing through a few of the other 1/10, mostly for RP reasons that do not really seem to effect the gameplay. In short, the economic mechanics are shallow and the political mechanics are shallow and that really is all there is to the game. They try to add a cool story element but tying your playthrough to the story and personalities of your ruling family, which is cool, but it has little impact and the decisions you make don't vary substantially. If this ever drops down to $5-$7, these simulator games are already your niche and you don't have anything else to play then pick this up and you'll burn a decent few hours getting the hang of the game. After that the most satisfying thing to do is making your districts look nice on the map.

Ohh man, what can I say about this game... Don't be fooled by my "low" play time. I probably have close to 500 hours in Mount and Blade Warband since the game itself doesnt rely on the Steam DRM and you can launch the game without Steam. I remember saying to myself why so many medieval games have magic in them and how cool it would be to have a game that tried to be a bit more historical with its medievalness and even let you screw around as a peasant or farmer and just be more grounded in reality and I searched through forums and someone wrote that a game like that exists and is called Mount and Blade: Warband. I looked at trailers and gameplay and thought to myself, "This game looks like garbo, its looks so damn old and dated." But I saw it had a crap ton of positive reviews and I ended up grabbing it during a sale with an attitude of, "Meh it aint costing me much even if it is garbo." Man, do I regret getting it in a sale. Yes, the visuals are absolutely dated and the tutorial to be honest is hella lacking and the game doesnt even fully explain the mechanics of what you are supposed to do and what you can do at all. It just thrusts you into the game, which is a sandbox-style game and you either sink or swim and I imagine some people just put in a few hours and get bored and wondered what the hell they are supposed to do and stopped playing. But if you are curious and inquisitive and stick with the game, you'll realize how absolutely deep the game can get. Basically, you need to make yourself emperor (or empress) of Calradia... or not, you can just be a trader making money or just kill off bandits harassing peasants without pledging allegiance to any of the factions present, or you can be a bandit yourself. There is legit soo much to this game that you can do and its depth runs so deep, that I would have to legit write an essay on how this game is so goddam great and all the mechanics in it but I dont like making long♥♥♥♥♥reviews. And thats just the vanilla game... With modding the game really shines and theres even a mod that puts MnB:W in feudal Japan, let alone the DLC like Napoleonic Wars. All I can say is if you like historical games, you'll absolutely love Warband, and its eventual sequel Bannerlord is currently my most anticpated game.
P.S. I personally recommend the Floris Mod, its pretty good : )

A brilliant 2D brawler. I usually don't like 2D brawlers because of their iffy hit/hurtboxes, but this one feels as tight as you can get. The characters and weapons are constantly buffed/nerfed to the tides of the community as the devs release their weekly updates. This ensures that the tier list is very balanced. Common advice is to learn whoever looks cool to you, as you can truly be great with everyone. The paid DLC is all cosmetic. There is nothing that you can buy that will give you any advantage at all, or even adjust anything but the looks. This is how DLC should be done in a F2P game. To top it all off, a new character is added every month.
I highly recommend this game for anyone who enjoys Smash Bros, and even many who don't.
Comparing it to Smash Bros:
The characters are much floatier. Air combat plays a huge part in this game, and there is almost no reason for you to fall of the stage. 3 jumps (2 if you jumped from the ground instead of walked off), a recovery, and an up dodge should rescue you from positions that would be hopeless in Smash.
The devs are also working on distancing themselves from the Smash series, even going so far as to reject technicalities that are similar to Smash, such as grabbing and wave dashing. They instead focus on features that Smash doesn't have. The dodging system is currently amazing. You can dodge in all 8 cardinal directions for an extra boost. They just added chase dodging, which allows you to pull of an amazing combo, send your opponent flying, then zip towards him. This, combined with dodge-canceling allows for the chaining of chains.
There is also a technique called gravity canceling. This involved spot dodging in the air, then immediately attacking. It allows you to perform ground attacks in the air.
Further separating this game from Smash is the focus on weapons. In Smash, unarmed combat is the default. In Brawlhalla, armed combat is the preferred method.
