I love this game! It's alot of fun, and for someone who is playing it for the first time without much knowledge of it, it's tremedously easy to understand. The basics are like any other MMO or RPG. I really enjoyed playing as my engineer, Skie, with her wolf, FireHeart, but all that came to an end with a simple problem.
I had just logged onto Steam and was about to play Torchlight II, when it asked me which file i'd like to save it to- Drive or Cloud. Old or new.
Of course, I chose my Drive, as I always did, but something different happened this time!
It wouldn't load! It crashed about ten seconds after that, and the Crash Reporter screen popped up.
I told them what happened, and went to my Steam Files to try and figure it out. I deleted all the crash bugs  I saw, and prepared to launch the game again.
It worked! I was so happy...
...Until I saw that it did not save my game. I was at a high rank, and for that not to save made me very frustreated. I logged into Runic Games to see if that would make the "Continue" button pop up, but no such luck.
I went back to my library to see that if I hovered over the Torchlight II game, it would bring up a list of what I could do.
Around the middle, it read:
"Backup game"
I knew the cause for the loss of my character was because I didn't back up my game onto my hard drive! I would have normally thought that the game automatically backs up for you! I am now currently trying to get back to my rank with a new character, very dissapointed. In files, I only deleted crash bugs, not my character files! I do not know how this happened, and I am deeply upset. I love Torchlight II, one of the best games I've ever bought. I honestly hope Runic Games could possibly shed light on my issue of loss of character, but I know for certain-
ALWAYS BACK UP GAMES.
I have learned that now, upset that the mistake had to be on my most favorite game of all time.
This is a very fun game, but always remember to back up your character the first time you get it, and from then on, it's your choice to back it up. I love the graphics and the story line. It's great for ages around 10+, and you can also turn off blood and such. I recommend this game to you! It's very unique and exciting!

Right, so I have just completed the game and decided to share my toughts.
First thing first. Yes, there are microtransactions there. Does the game asked me or forced me to buy anything using this system at any point? No it did not. Therefore, I do not care that much since I have managed to max out all augmentations that I wanted to use in my playstyle (stealth) - mind the sentence: not ALL but all that I wanted to use. And still after obtaining these I have started to randomly distribute points to Augs secondary and tertiary from my perspective, which means that there is a significant number of Praxis to gather during playthrough.
Gameplay - this is improved Human Revolution. That's what it is. Finaly I was able to perform a takedown from around the corner or from behind cover. Awesome. Shooting is also very good. You can actually feel the power behind assault rifle.
Story (main plot) - not as good as Human Revolution, yet still I was engaged and wanted to bring it to the end.
Story (side quests) - purely awesome. There was only one side quest that I did not like (out of 12).
Story/Universe (exploration/Points of Interst) - this part I have enjoyed very much. Some places, computers, books, notepads are there to add to the main story - which makes it more interesting - while some are there to add to the world - which makes you wonder whether it will really look that way within next 13 years.
Last but not least, performance. I do not posses a PC that would cover recommended specs and yet I have managed to run the game on 50 fps - average - with settings being a combinatoin of Very High and Ultra. I have to be honest though: all the fancy graphical effects were turned off. Despite that, game looks really good and plays without a single issue. Loading times between sections of the Hub - each time I managed to go and grab a cup of tea or coffee while waiting.
All in all, on a scale of 10, this game - in my books - is a solid 8.

Sarah is left trapped in a dreamlike world with no directions nor explanations: it's up to you to guide her, to find a way out by exploring and putting the items you find to good use.
What follows is a pretty casual and short game that mixes exploration, puzzles and some light platforming: despite its simplicity Dreaming Sarah manages to impress with its interesting gameplay and great atmosphere.
-while extremely simple the graphics have a certain charm
-great soundtrack
-a dreamlike and changing world that is very interesting to explore
-tight controls
-interesting puzzles
-some cryptic clues can leave you stuck
-while it is intended, there are times where the lack of direction can get frustrating
-quite short overall
Dreaming Sarah is, I'd say, part game part experience, the actual gameplay is very simple and basically boils down to exploring, making sense of the clues you find scattered around, finding items to bypass obstacles and ultimately unlock new areas. While this is all quite plain it also is quite satisfying as the world has a dreamlike quality that makes moving through it very pleasing: the lack of direction can indeed be frustrating if you find yourself wandering aimlessly, but it also gives a sense of wonder that helps the game shine.
The areas you travel through are often weird, sometimes disturbing and all'd feel right at home inside a dream, or a nightmare: this paired with the truly excellent soundtrack give the game a truly bizarre, "trippy" atmosphere that makes it an experience worth having.
Dreaming Sarah might be a bit limited in terms of content and actual mechanics, but it's truly a small gem of a game due to how well it works and the sense of marvel it can evoke: I had a blast playing it and heartily recommend it.

My first negative review on Steam; that alone says a lot about how much I didn't like this game, I think.
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is very pretentious and serious about itself, it touches some sensitive matters like death, love, fear, friendship and treachery. But it presents all this things so bad, it isn't even funny. It's like a low-grade TV soap opera with really bad actors. Just painful to watch and play.
Characters are not likeable and don't evoke any sympathy. Gameplay is repetitive. Controlling two characters at a time is somewhat interesting idea, but puzzles built around that are trivial.
It boggles me how much positive reviews this game has! How is this possible!? I wouldn't have written this review in the first place if it wasn't for the fact that it seems everyone on the Internet thinks the game is great and wonderful.
I played to the end, hoping to find even the slightest thing that would touch me and make me like this game, but I didn't find anything. The only things I _really_ liked were beautiful scenery and architecture.
In the end I think that overall pretentioussness and cheesiness killed the game for me. I would have even tolerated the not very interesting but good enough gameplay. But the plot and the characters are the core part of this game and you can't ignore them.
I suppose developers worked hard on this game and tried to make it good, but, sorry, I just can't recommend it to anyone.

Having spent more money on this game than any other - indeed somewhere in excess of fourteen times as most of my purchases I'm - disappointed.  Firstly it has either not crashed at all or only crashed once on a Windows 10 machine with virtually every extra installed (I went for it in last Steam sale).  But...
1)  The towns now feel completely depopulated.  Particularly difficult in the nightlife city where every second NPC is a celeb and your interactions are limited with them.  Neighbours just don't run or pass by as much, colleagues from work don't come home, and the time clock moves so quickly that you can rarely interact with anyone long enough to have an impact.
2)  The moving to real time now messes badly with character development.  In Sims 2 when you left your house time effectively froze so when you came back it was the same time you left, no matter how long you were away.  This enabled you to have 30 - 40 hours in a day - and far easier to get stuff done.  Here it is real time throughout - but punitively slow.    Showering, going to the toilet, and cooking and eating some waffles now takes two hours.  There simply aren't enough hours in the day - even with shortened work hours.
3)  Building anything is a complete pain in the butt.  In the Sims 2 you'd simply select a lot and then place the pre made building there.  Having a task for my Sim to go to a bar and there not being a bar in my Sim's world (and they can no longer transfer - major downer) I tried to build one. And tried.  And tried.  Even after searching the internet I was no wiser.
4) Everything is very expensive.  You have to rise high in your career before you can do much more than cover your taxes.
5)  Loading is even more ponderous than Sims 2 although the spot an object game (flawed) helps the time pass.
6)  After spending a LARGE amount of money on the game it was disappointing to see so many items still shut off behind a Pay Wall.
This is not a bad game.  More hours in I might appreciate it more.  But it is A game, no matter how thinly E.A. slice it.  At 75% off in the sale I spent more on Sims 3 than a brand new AAA game.  And it's not as good as Skyrim which I bought for £5.00.  Few games are but still - E.A. charge VERY HEAVILY INDEED for this game.  For the money they are taking this should be an unalloyed joy... and it isn't.
E.A. seem far more focussed on gouging ever more cash from their customers than giving them great gaming experiences.  After this I wouldn't buy Sims 4 at 90% off.

◾2 teaspoons active yeast
◾2 teaspoons caster sugar

◾5 cups highgrade flour

◾75g butter, melted
◾1 size 7 egg
◾1/3 cup caster sugar
◾2 teaspoons mixed spice
◾1 tablespoon cinnamon
◾100g mixed peel
◾1/2 cup flour
◾4 tablespoons water
◾2 tablespoons apricot jam
◾2 tablespoons water
◾1 tablespoon sugar
Method
Place the fruit in a bowl, pour over 1/2 cup boiling water and set aside for 20 minutes.
Combine yeast, 2 teaspoons sugar and warm milk in a large bowl and set aside for 5 minutes. The mixture should start to foam.
Place the flour, sugar and salt in a bowl and make a well in the centre. Pour in the milk mixture, butter and egg.
Mix to combine. Turn dough out to a floured board and knead for 5 minutes. Drain the fruit well and then mix with the peel, cinnamon and mixed spice. Work the fruit into the dough and continue to knead for a further 5 minutes or until the dough feels smooth and elastic.
Place the dough in an oiled bowl and cover. Place in a warm spot and leave
for 30 minutes or until doubled in bulk.
Turn out dough and lightly knead.
Divide dough into 12 balls and place in a greased large square cake or roasting dish.
Cover and sit in a warm place until doubled in size.
Preheat oven to 200 C Mix together the flour and water for crosses and place in a piping bag or plastic bag with the corner snipped. Pipe crosses on buns. Place in oven and bake for 20 minutes or until golden and springy to touch.
Meanwhile, place the jam, water and sugar in a small saucepan and stir over medium heat
for a couple of minutes. Brush hot buns with the apricot glaze.

Deus Ex Mankind Divided is set in a cyber punk future and is primarily focused around stealth in an RPG fashion, the main protagonist is Adam Jensen who also starred in Human Revolution.
Mankind Divided is set 2 years AFTER the events that unravelled in Human Revolution and is a prequel to the original Deus Ex Game. If you played Human Revolution you’ll be glad to be told that the game plays out quite similar, but this time with more augments, a better control scheme and overall better gun play, many of the games characters’ have a unique personality and feel to them. I personally felt more attachment and cared more for the characters in Mankind Divided compared to the characters of Human Revolution (except for Pritchard, no one’s going to top that gorgeous hacking man) due to the sense that you actually feel like they evolve and develop with Jensen as the story progresses. Speaking of Jensen, it really does seem like he has distinct emotions and feelings for everything that happens around him. For someone that is stuck in the middle of the games plot, and is literally “1 in a billion” as he puts it, he cares for those that are suffering around him and will try make change with the best of abilities (or dare I say … Augments)
The game is mainly based in Prague, which is the capital of the Czech Republic. Prague does well in serving as the main hub of the game and in my opinion has a better feel and look to it than Detroit from Human Revolution, its dividedness (no pun intended) with “naturals” (non-augmented humans like you and I) and Augs (People who are Augmented, commonly referred as “clanks” to discriminate against them) also really makes it that more memorable, small things like the Augmented having to go through their own SEPARATE lines in order to do daily tasks like taking a train really puts an eerie feeling into the game and really sets the mood well for it. The other hubs are also beautiful and I fell in love with the colour scheme and design that were used throughout all of them. Eidos Montreal really hit the nail on the head in terms of locations and overall design.
The gameplay is focused on creating the Adam Jensen that YOU want to be, and delivers this through the way of using upgradable Augmentations using Praxis Kits (which can be earned, sold, and found throughout the game very easily, they really are accessible) the same way as Human Revolution did it. If you have a couple of Praxis Kits you have a couple of new cyborg upgrades you can work with in your journey throughout the game. This time Jensen is equipped with a few entirely new Augmentations that can be unlocked at any time of the game, the PEPS gun knocks people back non–lethally (I’m not sure if this actually knocks people out as I did not use it in the 35-hour stealth non–lethal play though as it did not appeal to me.) The Tesla gun can knock multiple enemies out (non–lethally of course) when fully upgraded. The Nano Blade serves as the opposite as the Tesla Gun, it is the lethal alternative and can kill either 1 person quietly, or multiple people loudly with the upgraded explosive blades that can be unlocked via augmentation. My personal favourite was defiantly the Remote Hacking Augment that allows for (as you should’ve expected) Remotely Hack just about anything in the game, TVs, security drones, turrets, mines, laser grid and most importantly cameras all can be either permanently disabled or temporarily depending on the object that you are hacking. The other 3 new augments include a small instant blink/dash, a Red Dead Redemption / GTA V slow down time and aim really well because you’re a f****** Augmented freak of nature activation Augmentation (which is actually VERY useful if you intend to approach the game with a lethal mindset) and finally a temporary “tough as nails” skin / armour augmentation that raises your defensive capabilities drastically.
The game is set in a few playstyles that I have briefly mentioned, those being non-lethal, and lethal. I found that non-lethal did not have enough weapons and I would’ve gladly taken 1 or to more for my journey, or perhaps a sort of non-lethal ammunition for guns such as the pistol (maybe they could contain just enough venom that could put the body into shock and into a deep sleep, maybe just even tranquilizer rounds that are rare/costly? This game is set in the future let me have my idea). Whereas the lethal group of guns were fantastic! 35 hours into the game I was still finding guns that I had not come across earlier such as the Lancer Rifle, and the on the fly customisation is fantastic. Finally, the 3 different types of ammunition at your disposal are fantastic and open up a lot of different paths and opportunities in the game, the Sniper Rifle, Combat Rifles and Battle Rifles pack even more punch with the armour piercing rounds that can be found in the game, while EMP rounds are fantastic for disabling turrets and security drones that reek the streets of Prague later on in the game. On the fly magnification/scope changes are fantastic and really make getting kills that bit more satisfying. One thing that I was a bit disappointed in was the lack off take down animations, I thought there would’ve been plenty more and was annoyed when I discovered I’ve seen all animations early on in the game.
Finally, the main story admittedly is a bit hard to / strange to follow, Mankind Divided is a game where you should replay it (with the new inclusion of New Game+ this helps in encouraging you to do so) to FULLY understand everything that is happening and why you’re doing something. In loading times there are short little readable texts that come up and reinforce what’s happened in the story and any stage of the game can be re-read, maybe it’s just because I did almost every single available mission (minus The Rave side mission) and that’s why I forget about why what I’m doing is relevant at all.
Overall Mankind Divided is a beautiful game and is a successful follow up to Human Revolution and the other Deus Ex games as a whole, although it has a bit of controversy surrounding the game with the ability to buy Praxis Kits with real life money (which is completely unnecessary and not needed at all) it is defiantly worth the full price if you are an avid lover of stealth/RPG/cyberpunk themed games. It’s a step in the right direction (in terms of gameplay and graphics) for the franchise and will serve well for many play throughs to come.
Overall a solid 8.75 /10.

I have to say, this game is pretty great. Not as bad as some people have said. And not the best game ever, as some others have said.
The one thing that stands out to me about it, besides the main story and setting. Are the side missions. The side missions in this game are some of the most interesting and engaging side missions I have ever played. They give this world so much more depth and realism to it.
The main story is interesting enough, but a bit short. As previously stated, the side missions are truly where this game shines. If you don't go out of your way to play them. you'll have a fun an interesting experience in a cool city. But if you take the time to read emails, and go exploring to find secrets, and hidden events/missions. This game will give you one hell of an exmerience.
The gameplay is improved in almost every aspect from Human Revolution. Making it much more fun to go in on the hardest difficulty, and try to survive. gun fights are more engaging and fun. The CASIE Aug actually works this time, making it much easier to read someone. Unlike Human Revolution where you might as well not even try to use it. The AI from my experience is more intellegent. Though from time to time, It did fall short. For example: I was in this restricted zone, and a guard was right in front of the enterence. But because his line of sight was only on the area outside of the restricted zone. I was able to walk out of it, in clear view of the gueard, but he only saw me out of the zone, so he didn't even care.
Now, here are some things that are really bad: the loading times are atrocious. I don't have an SSD, so it will be much faster with one, but it can take several minutes for the game to load a new area, or start up. The lip syncing is practically non existent, especially during ingame cutscenes.
Here's just a nitpick; Jensen's collar is too small for his face. What do I mean by that? If he moves his head just a little bit to the side, it clips through the collar on his coat. The collar doesn't move, but his jace goes right through it.
Now, would I recomend this game? Yes. But only if you are willing to deal with having a monster rig chug at tmes running it. The gameplay is fun, and will keep you on your toes no matter how you play it. And only if you plan on doing the sidemissions.

Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon is the most unabashedly fun games I have ever had the pleasure of playing.
Because the gameplay was pretty much already created for FC3, the brunt of the effort could go into the art design - and it shows. Biehn turns in an inspired performance as the robo-armed Cyber-Commando Rex Power Colt, spewing obscenities, pop-culture references, and deliciously bad one-liners ("Send for a medic... so I can kill him too.") while mowing down waves of cyber-soldiers. The monstrous Colonel Ike Sloan and the sexy Dr. Elizabeth Darling round out the cast with clever dialogue. The metallic neon glow of this fantastical world and the badass synth soundtrack by Power Glove builds a wonderful world to play in. Flavor text for weapons, enemies, notes, and VHS tapes (yes, that's right) add more hilarious charm.
Every gameplay decision seems to be based around "What would be the most fun?"
Sergeant Colt can sprint forever, hold his breath underwater indefinitely, and does not take fall damage; the only holdover from modern action games is holding your breath to snipe. I was reminded of the classic Doomguy as I ripped and tore my way through foes. This comes in handy as you explore the island on foot, jeep, boat, zipline, and hang-glider; allowing you to really get around and take place in confrontations in many ways.
Gunplay is excellent as well - the upgrades and sidegrades provide more ways to fight your way through compounds and enemies. Will you get in close and blow 'em away with your a quadruple-barrelled shotgun firing incendiary darts, fry them with your laser Fazertron, blow them up with your explosive sniper rifle, silently dispatch with a neon bow and arrow, or stab them with knives and shuriken?
This game isn't without its flaws, though. Although a wide variety of sidequests kept me interested (there are plenty of things to track down, plus mini-missions to unlock upgrades), the compound raids began getting a bit repetitive. There are only about four or five different enemy types (there are also cyber-animals, and the titular dragons), and you don't really need to switch up your tactics much for them (apart from the incredibly annoying zombie enemies). But just when you're starting to get bored, a new mission or setting will come up and keep you invested. If this game was a full-sized adventure these flaws would be more apparent, but as it is now the size and complexity go hand-in-hand.
Health is usually pretty good, but there are some poor parts there as well. Rex does not regenerate health, but he can heal via stimpacks or by patching himself up. However, you can only carry a measly three stimpacks and I often found myself running out while in the wild. In addition, the "use health" button is the same key used to put out fires and I would often hit it too soon or too late for the flames, wasting a stimpack on one or two hit points.
In addition, I encountered an annoying glitch with the cutscenes. Pre-rendered in the limited color palette and animation style of 8- or 16-bit cutscenes, they should have worked just fine. However, they lagged incredibly hard for me - there would be a 2-5 second gap between lines and shots when they should have been around 1 second or less. The soundtrack didn't sync up, and the delay made sentences stilted and awkward. I ended up having to skip the cutscenes in-game and watch them on YouTube later.
If you like '80s music, action movies, classic FPS games, or just having fun, definitely pick this bad boy up.

As far as RTS's go, I dont like them. Too many of them do their systems too incorrectly, or just dont plain make any logical sense, or reason. Dawn of War (all the expansion packs, consider this a recommendation for Dawn of War + all of the expansions), does some critical things right, which makes it stand out from the crowd.
First, it actually focuses on strategy for the most part. Instead of spamming 1000 tanks at your enemy (im looking at you Ruse), you actually have chose a limited number of units to bring into battle. Meaning, every man, tank, and resourse is valuble, and losing any of the above can cost you the battle. This tension, and balencing on the brink of death keeps tension high, as players must constantly have to outdo their opponent on a mental capacity, not necessarily on a quanitative capacity. This conbined with some rather unique in game mechanics, such as morale, means interesting strategies can arise, when those similar would fall flat in other RTS's.
And secondly, the game is able to keep a consistent feeling, tone, and atmosphere. Even for a strategy game, this is important, nothing takes you out of a game more than an interface, so even immersing the mission select screen in 40k does its job. Everything is plastered with 40k jargon and logic, a dark universe of war, death, and betrayal. As well, the game itself feels fitting, with you not taking resources, just getting requisition points to send in more troops, as you are successful in conquest, just as an example of many different things the game does right.
The game is fitting, and is able to keep a consistent feel to gameplay and atmosphere. For this, I must heartily recommend Dawn of War to RTS fans, you will not be let down.

The Dawn of War series (The original, Winter Assault, Dark Crusade, and Soulstorm) is one of the most incredible RTSes out there. It has fluid action, unit counters that force tactical play, and it even allows one of the rarest options in any RTS. . Persistant corpses. You can actually count (or lose count of) the number of bodies that litter a battlefield. Oddly, this is a feature I wish more RTSes had. I guess I'm just twisted that way.
Resources are simple: You take requisition points to steadily generate requisition (the main resource) and you build generators to produce power (the secondary resource). There's good unit variety among a total of 9 factions in all if you own all of the expansions.
Note that buying Soulstorm will NOT let you play factions in multiplayer which were released prior to it without CD keys for those races. You need to own a copy of each respective game to play its races in a multiplayer mode. The only gripe I have is its lack of backward compatibility with its prior games, which is a shame since you need to own those games to play those races.
For example, I have been unable to get a game going with my friend because he has Dark Crusade but not Soulstorm. His game does not recognize the Soulstorm races, and we had no luck finding a patch for it. This is -very bad- for this kind of expansion style. You can however play any race in skirmish mode regardless of having prior expansions, which I also find to be a little odd, but at least you can try the races in single player.
Besides my gripe on the expansions, if you want an RTS that is phenominal, I give Dawn of War two thumbs up. It currently comes with all prior expansions in one Steam pack, and Soulstorm as a seperate game. This is a must play if you are an RTS fanatic.

Oh my gosh!!! I've logged over 3,000 hours on this game!!  Can you say "addict"?  LOL
Not everyone will enjoy this game as much as I do; but you'll never know until you try it.  Some folks writing reviews say it's not fast-paced enough for them.  Personally I like the pace.  The graphics are great.  In fact, some of the scenery is breathtaking and a close friend I met in LOTRO loves to just sit with me in pretty places and talk at times.  He loves to say that there's more to LOTRO than just questing.  That's very true!  I've met some great people here!
There's a great deal of emphasis on team work in LOTRO which makes it hard to play alone at times.  So you are actually forced in some circumstances to meet and play with others (unless you just want to run around and kill stuff haphazardly like one of my friends).  That can be a good thing or a bad thing, depending on how you look at it.  I think this might be the norm for other MMOs but I don't really have that much experience with other games.  I've played some other games, like Shaiya (which I really didn't like due to all the morons I encountered who loved to steal my kills) and I also tried Everquest 2 and RIFT (which I'm also not fond of as they were very confusing at times).  I like playing with other people though.  After all... isn't that what an MMO is for??  :p
You will also need to buy the various areas other than the four free ones:  Ered Luin, The Shire, Breeland and Lonelands.  That will provide you with free-to-play questing only up to about level 30 tops.  Any other areas must be purchased with turbine points (TP).  You can still kill stuff and gather crafting materials and even level; but you can't quest without buying the areas and that's where a lot of the fun is, right?  You can only earn just so much TP in the free areas too.  You can't earn TP in the areas you have to pay for unless you buy the area first.  So if you're looking for TOTALLY F2P then this will give you quite a few hours in the free areas but then you'll get bored after that unless you buy stuff. That means either spending realy money or grinding for TP.  I've met some people who haven't spent a penny of real money on this game -- they grind for the TP to buy stuff.  However that takes a lot of time.  If you're patient and don't mind grinding then that's not an issue for you.  You can max out your toon(s) by earning TP in-game.  I started out with that plan in mind but... well.... I have to admit I've dropped a fair amount of change on this game because I'm impatient.  LOL
It's also much harder to play with only the three inventory bags you start with.  If you want more bags you have to buy them.  It's also harder to play unless you have shared storage between your toons.  You have to buy that too.  They've changed the housing now as well; so even though you can expand the storage on a single house now it costs a lot of gold to buy extra space.  They're also pushing you to buy mithril now which you can't get in-game (except for some rare times when you get it for gifts to tease you into buying more).  You have to pay money for that.
So LOTRO (like any other game) has it's ups and downs.  I would still definitely recommend this game but.... as I said.... it's not for everyone.  You won't know for sure though if it's for you until you try it.  Just be prepared for addiction!    :D

First of all - don't get fooled by my playtime, I just stopped using the steam launcher a few thousand hours ago. I haven't been through the whole thing as most of the reviewers have and that's partly the reason I wanted to write this review now, because the only reviews I saw were either people who just got into the game or people who are lvl 105 and waiting eagerly for every update.
I love this game, but I don't love it for its gameplay. I love it because of the atmosphere, community, immersion, soundtrack... basically everything that makes it feel like you actually are in Middle-Earth. It's amazing how with everything so out of date (pretty sure the engine was out of date even when it came out and the game turns 10 this year) the game still manages to pull you in. Even through the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics, terrible combat system and other stuff that will annoy you throughout.
The game is free but it's more worth it to get a job and buy the expansions than to waste time grinding in-game money (in my opinion). Grinding it takes way too much time and is extremely repetitive (so it's just like a job but paying worse), and if you buy the currency when there's a triple bonus points event or something and use the sales to buy regions, the price gets as low as four bucks per region (absolutely amazing value for money if you ask me, a region is hours of fun).
The game's age is really showing in the mechanics of fast-travel, in the game interface and generally in everything, but it kinda makes the game feel more personal and unique. I don't even want the graphics to be better at this point, cos I got so used to it that it would ruin the game for me if they upgraded them (and they can't because they'd need a new engine and ergo a completely new game to do that). And I didn't even play the game long enough to get to the latest region, I'm about halfway through...
And the community. Every minute or so someone will write FREE [X] and the X can be a very valuable item, a nice cosmetic or perhaps a nice painting to put above your wall (the housing system is awesome too and they added a new housing region in the cape of Belfalas... my heart was melting when I was first strolling through that town hearing all the seagulls). If you ask something, people answer you, even multiple times and even questions you didn't ask, and all nicely. Since players are glad to not be adventuring alone, they're happy to help you with your problems, teleport you where you want or kill that one boss with you.
And lastly, for the achievement hunters out there - this is a game for you. Tons of locations to explore to get the explorer deeds, tons of slayer deeds when you kill enough of something (spiders, wolves, skeletons - you name it) and every region has its own. The rewards for completing those deeds is not too bad either, as this is how you farm the in-game currency (it becomes tedious after you do it with your first toon).
Overall if you like or don't mind the concept of MMO questing (fetch that, kill that, deliver a message) and are a fan of Tolkien and his works, give this thing a try. It's a bit old for an MMO but it ages extremely well and the devs keep adding regions, god knows when they'll stop. They'll be adding Mordor in August so you better get questing :)

Finely created game, but if I really thought about it, I would probably steer my friends elsewhere.
I would imagine that this game would have a greater impact on me if I had a close experience with death. I'm lucky to have dodged that bullet so far, but it made this game emotionally distant for me. With that in mind, here's my review:
Brothers leans heavily on emotional drama. The controls, while innovative, do little more than frustrate an endless series of simple parkour-like puzzles. By the end of the game, I still couldn't quite master the controls. The game ends up becoming an obstacle to get to the story. Brilliant graphics and stunning environmental visuals help break the monotany of the endless puzzles, but you can't help but escape that 'mouse in a maze' feeling: You have to beat each obstacle in the same way each time, and the simplicity of each obstacle makes them feel meaningless. There's no learning or progression, or hard thinking beyond the first half hour or so. Just use the 'do' button.
The lack of any ability to explore, given the incredible visual landscapes you're presented with, is particularly disappointing.
The story is shallow in approach, and attachment between characters is established solely as familial. There's no special overarching story: just Mom, Dad, Brother, etc. The game expects you to project your emotions and feelings onto these characters to give them meaning. If you're able to do that, it may be a very compelling play.
The reality of death is the main plot driver, but because there was no special connection established, it felt hollow. Performing the tasks of the game felt less like a herioc, charitable voyage, and more like a frustrating, overly extermely exercise of child duty to parents.
There are moments which are powerful, but only if you've emotionally 'bought in'. Otherwise, the whole thing feels hollow.

I dislike Dejobaan games, very much. They feel cheap and ill-maintained, as well as little consideration to practical functionality.
On the other hand, that can all be overlooked with this one. Sure, the menu system is terrible, sure it takes too much effort to organize - but what a fun little game!
The objective is basically to hug buildings, survive and land well; in that order. Hugging buildings is very fun - it can get tricky at times but that's the challenge really. The levels are a little short and I haven't unlocked the bigger, harder (?) ones - but for now i'm satisfied.
Surviving is however easy to make it for yourself; those high points only come from kissing/hugging buildings (their terminology, I promise you). It takes some practice and a few quick-thinking moments but you can rack up those numbers. There's even 'bonus' things to smash.
Lastly is landing safely; relatively easy to get it into the landing area.
In summary - a great little mini-game, lazy developers.

Dreaming Sarah is a puzzle adventure game set in a surreal, varied world. Every item you find along the way allows you to explore further across paths that were previously accessible. While the core concept of the storyline is a serious subject, this game doesn't really delve too deep; it is all in all relatively lighthearted, focusing mostly on the strange and surreal.
Concerning the puzzle aspect, this game is quite straightforward (I personally finished it in one sitting one afternoon). I imagine seasoned players of adventure games will not find much of a challenge in this game. Nevertheless, it was interesting enough to keep me going; the environments and characters were very colorful, the items were interesting, and the achievements were fun.
I would
recommend this to everyone who's new to these types of games (puzzle/adventure/exploration), it serves as a great introduction. Review:
Let me start by saying I was, when the game released a HUGE fan. It WAS one of the funnest games ever. I must now tell you to not purchase from Rockstar or Take Two. In fact stay away from anything Rockstar after GTA IV. This is a developer that does not care about its community or the quality of games it realeases. Rockstar and Take Two are now of the same ideaology as EA.
When I first got into the game I was really excited, GTA IV was and is one of the best games of all time and the multiplayer was insanely fun. When the videos and articles came out for GTA V I was so pumped - what an epic looking game! The game came out and I had it the first week on the PS3. The multiplayer was amazing and a ton of fun. I waited for what felt like forever until the Rockstar team got their heads out of their butts and put it on the PC because I knew the adventure would be so much better on hardware that could properly create the world Rockstar envisioned.. I probably had 200 - 300 PS3 hours, 20-30 on PS4, as well as the 232 you can see on my Steam account as well after being banned I have put another 100 hours into a brand new account I had to purchase. Combined with purchasing the game for my wife as well I have put a cpmbined amount of $240 and some tax into this game, I put a lot of time into this game, and for quite some time I was very satisfied with it. I really enjoyed it until Rockstar began their massive attempt to scam players - queue the Shark Card, maybe the worst attempt to rip off players from a AAA dev team in history.
I honestly believe that cheating was spawned from Rockstars decision to create Shark Cards and and attempting to scam the living daylights out of players. Having to pay in game insurance, losing money when dying, barely making anything after hundreds of missions, the game just "losing" your money, and then everything good costs over a mil is a huge waste of time. Rockstars constant updates to the vehicles and buildings with the tiniest of changes costing millions of in game currency and nothing new or exciting yet costing what equals hundreds in real currency for each updates new cars or buildings is complete crap.
So after all the crap the community started making the game fun again via exploit kits. Taking advantage of Script Hook initially This allowed players to spawn any manner of in game items, make themselves invincible, and even use the single player animations. It's really a freaking hilarious sight to see an alien running down the street slaughtering the whole server. The irony is this is also out of Rockstars laziness and cheap attempt at bypassing real static servers, by making the game a mesh P2P Rockstar could save money and have half or less infrastructure to support MP. In the end this allowed for players to in real time issue commands that all the other clients would recognize.
Rockstar at first didn't seem to care at all about the rampant hacking. All was good in their mind since it didn't initially cut into their shark card profits massively. As time went on though I believe it affected the bottom line because no one gave a crap about buying over priced fake money for a video game (after all this isn't clas of clans is it.... is i?). Then Rockstar started to notice that people were no longer having fun and spending money on their game. First they tried to rectify this with small ban waves and little content updates. As it became more noticable Rockstar cared less and less about the players and more about their bottom line (free cash cow right?) the ban waves affected people not even cheating, I personally lost my account from players "gifting" me money. This happened to hundreds if not thousands of players. Rockstar knew you had illegitemate money and they were going to punish you for it - no matter how you got it. I know I have attempted to explain this to their staff but their new system makes the second ban a perma ban according to their staff...
So now we have a new update every few months and a ban wave. Except back again to Rockstar's laziness the game still has rampant cheaters. Now I can tell you that there was a mod that would have likely fixed the rampant cheating called Five M. A mod being worked on allowed players to host private server, which would have allowed admins, passwords, and overall better security in the end. Rockstar like a shark card smelling dollar bills in the water immediatly went into a frenzy sending immediate cease and decist letters - how dare the Shark Cards be threatened. I do honestly believe though this would have resolved a large part of the issues with hacking as people would be drawn to other places and the community would continue to provide multiplayer mods for years to come. Now I must make it known that Rockstar not only wants to affect how the multiplayer modding community exists but also remove single player modding entirely. This is the final straw. Literally every negative review for this game is either because of a disagreement with the developer's business practices, or just a bunch of made up garbage to hide the fact that it's being reviewed negatively for a reason other than the game itself.
It has everything human revolution had and more. The story is great, the characters are pretty interesting, and the gameplay is like human revolution's but greatly improved.  You can tell the devs put countless hours of work into developing the backstory alone, because everywhere you go there are emails, pocket secretaries, ebooks, and npc conversations that help detail the world and the overall tone. I fail to see how the story is bad in any way.
The gameplay is a lot of fun, you can basically do everything you could do in human revolution, only with more augments, more weapons, and a more interesting way of handling weapon mods. Hacking is pretty much the same, which is good because it was good the way it was in HR.
I somehow have 51 hours already, and I'm still in the Utulek Complex, which is like the 2nd or 3rd mission.  I doubt I've actually been playing all that time, but still, most of it has been spent exploring, finding rare items, or doing side quests, and I haven't been bored for a second of it.
People are saying this game isn't worth $60. It's more than worth $60. It's definitely worth the $40 I paid for it.  Gamers nowadays are entitled and think that games aren't worth all that money.  For $60 they think games should be 300 hours long, make you coffee, and tickle your balls too.  That's just not gonna happen.  Games are getting even harder to make as technology advances, not that they aren't hard to make already.  They literally take every moment of the years they stay in development, because it is extremely hard work.  Support devs, support games, pay for games you like, and don't complain about stupid things like microtransactions.  That's what it's come to these days.. Devs simply don't make enough, so what's wrong with an optional thing like microtransactions to supplement their income?
So in conclusion, this game is great, just as good as HR at least, and the devs deserve your money.  They also deserve good reviews, but I guess that just isn't gonna happen.

Tried to like it again, as I enjoy the topics of cyberpunk and some of the designs. But it is not much of an improvement over the previous game and its add-on (that is, if you liked the old Deus Ex games (DX, DX2, DX3) and prefer PC controls and game mechanics).
It's basically a cover shooter. The first person controls and gameplay experience does not work well. The first person controls feel weird and restricted (can't really strafe while moving forward?).
Other than that, the surroundings are well designed and it has nice references to cyberpunk topics and past and present politics.
Still, the sneak through air duct gameplay already became boring in the previous game. They really should improve there.
Some level design elements just feel too cube like to me. Does not feel believable. Everything is too shiny somehow. Everything is too much designed for sneak-cover-sneak gameplay. I prefer the old Deus Ex games' mechanics. Some reviews lead me to believe that it improved into that direction.
Feels too much like console gameplay to me. Also the menu controls are terrible on the PC (inventory, hacking). Should've done a real PC port with decent mouse controls.
Graphics are good and bad. A mix of great elements (hair), some nice effects, great models and textures and some really cheapish looking reflection effects that hurt in my opinion and make everything shiny.
If you look closely there is some weird shader noise effect on some objects that apparently can't be disabled.
I don't understand how the energy mechanic has improved, its still crippling. No Ghost in the Shell feeling comes up if you can run five meters in cloak before the battery runs out (if in the low empty state). And recharging kits are too limited in my opinion. I think it should allow a bit of action even if you are low on energy. But I guess this type of game is a pain to balance right. A bit more into dynamic gameplay would be nice though. Seems to punish that a bit. Probably because of the console type gamepad compatible game design. Remember the large outside areas of the old DX games? Missing this here so far, the gameplay just does not support that well.
Probably just not my type of game. Darnit, I wished they brought it closer to the old games or shooters like Neo Tokyo.

Lots of promise, although I didn't have many of the graphical issues that are being presented in a lot of these reviews, the game just fell short in a lot of other ways.  I can appreciate obfuscating some of the raw numbers driving certain game mechanics, but the economy is nearly impossible to manage in any meaningful way.  Upgrades to townships don't seem to have the kind of impact you'd expect.  You can be in the late game, with huge swaths of your townships still working on gas lighting and unimproved streets and no one seems to care.
Additionally, while I can appreciate that one political ideology may be favored by the developers, and its success influenced by their own ideologies, but the other political spectrums should at least be viable, which they are not.  This is a game afterall, and viability of the other paths would increase replayability.  The political system was a unique spin on the city building genre, at least that was my take on it in the beginning.  However, it quickly becomes tedious and as mentioned above, shoehorns you down a specific political path.
With the lack of updates and fixes that came from the developer post launch, I'm definitely suffering from buyer's remorse.  A real missed opportunity here.  I would not recommend this without a deep, deep discount.

If you expect a very long game that can entertain you for hours on end or a game that has a happy ending: Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons isn't it. In fact I'd say that Brothers is decently short and can be beaten in one sitting if you are up to it, however this doesn't mean it's a bad game!
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons, is the Tale of two brothers going on an adventure to find a cure for their sick father. During the game you control both sons at once, using the left analong stick to steer the older and the right analog stick to steer the younger brother, using LT to perform actions with the older and RT to perform actions with the younger. This setup can take some time to get used to, but it is worth it. The Artwork of the game is - with a few exceptions - very good and the enviroments stunningly beautiful, just like the lighting. The story itself seems a bit bland if you look at it seperately from the game, but it is convey very well - without the use of text or voice-overs, only through the actions in the game itself. The puzzles in the game are not "Portal-Quality" hard, but more on the light side.
Would I recommend others to play the game? Yes. Will I play it again? Sadly, no, at least not in a couple of months. Not because the game is bad... It's just the ending, ugh, the ending is something I can only experience only once in a while, even though it is pretty good.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is my favorite game of all time. A simple masterpiece. It shows what an imaginitive and talented group of people can come up with. The AMAZING (and, I mean AMAZING) kulning in this game helps set the atmosphere so well, and the graphics are very well made. I found myself sitting at just about every bench taking a screenshot. The platforming isn't very challenging, yet very fun. I cannot recommend this piece of art enough.

Brothers - A tale of Two Sons was...
pretty good. Not bad, not fantastic, just pretty good.
The game has pretty good graphics, amazing sceneries and astonishing music. The music is really, really great. The story didn't leave anything to desire too. Can be quite an emotional ride for some, but I just thought it was good. Something that really is a great addition to the game is that the way it's played is intertwined with the story and the characters themselves. I think it's kinda hard to explain, it's something you should experience.
But the controls... I get what they were trying to do, but I didn't really get the "Two Sons" experience. Sure, the gameplay actually adds a lot to the story but it didn't work for me. To explain: in the game, you follow the story of two brothers and by doing that you control both characters at the same time. For most of the time, I had issues with controlling both protoganists  using my keyboard. You use the WASD buttons and spacebar for the one, directional buttons and lctrl for the other. It probably would have been a lot better if I had someone to play this with, because controlling them both was quite a pain. You can however, use a controller. I figure it would have been a lot better this way but, for some reason, my game has serious framerate issues when I plug in my controller. I couldn't find anything about it online, so I was forced to use the keyboard.
The game can be finished in one sitting, about 2 to 3 hours long. To get all the achievements, you'll probably need to do a second playthrough because I only got half of the achievements on my first, and I really went looking for everything.
tldr; the game is very beautiful, with great music. The story is interesting too but keyboard controls are not the best. Short game, achievements not too hard. Still worth a buy.

Dreams are an important part of who we are. It is through them that we solve daily problems, face our fears and, sometimes, come to understand ourselves.
accomplishes exactly that: in a pixelated and rich platforming scenario we dwell into Sarah's mind to find out what exactly is bothering her. But it isn't as simple as that. The story starts off unassuming, mascarading itself as just another adventure platformer with nothing new to add to the genre. That's just meant to fool you, for as the story develops one is quick to grasp that, just like dreams, the game offers so much more behind what can be seen at first.
The game is creative and confusing, eye catching and trippy – all whilst maintaining coherence between Sarah, "random" NPCs and inventory items. You will never get to know Sarah just by looking at what she does or the little she herself sometimes reveals. Her dreams scream of her identity, what she caries of her needs and desires, and who she envisions in her dreams of her past, her fears and her story.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is the direct sequel to the reboot/prequel of one of my favorite games ever made, the original Deus Ex (confusing, I know). How does it hold up compared to Human Revolution, and does it hold a candle at all to the original game?
Kind of, I guess… That’s the disappointing, honest truth. It’s on one hand one of the most dense and detailed cyberpunk video game worlds I’ve ever seen, but on the other hand a disappointingly unresolved story that feels more like an expansion pack to a real, full length game. On one hand a game with levels that have been impeccably designed and were made with a lot of love and care, but also a game with the stink of Publisher interference sprinkled throughout, despicable in the presence of obvious cut content and micro transactions in the form of consumable items, basically pay a few bucks and unlock cheats for yourself. It’s a game that’s desperately trying to shine out of mediocrity muckiness despite the corporate dredge board of directors trying to hold it back from being all it can be, kind of ironic considering the game’s storyline.
The game takes place two years after the end of Human Revolution. Basically at the climax of that game, augmented people lose control briefly and attacked everyone around them in a blind rage due to an Illuminati plot, and as a result in the past two years it seems as if there is a slow but steady marginalization of people with robot arms and stuff. They are forced to sit at the back of the bus, as well as forced to use different drinking fountains, and there are even massive dystopian ghettos that they are being shepherded into like cattle. The clear parallels between this cyberpunk future world and our current world in terms of racial identity and prejudice is shoved into your face constantly. It would have worked better if they writers were more subtle at it, but I found the general storyline compelling and interesting enough, despite them shoving it down your throat like, “GET IT YOU GUYS, IT’S LIKE RACISM/ JEWS DURING THE HOLOCAUST GET IT??” I understand they felt as if the general demographic of gamers might not “get it” but it’s so obvious it’s painful at times. I personally don’t have any issues with the basic storyline though, it makes a lot of sense to me. For example, there are people in this country who think Muslims should all get the ♥♥♥♥ out of our country and get banned from entering because of the actions of a minority of the religion. Now imagine if ALL Muslims lost control and started attacking random people, killing a bunch of them. Wouldn’t our response in this world be similar?
Adam Jensen returns, now working for Interpol, trying to track down Terrorist threats, namely ones by augmented coalitions springing up due to their marginalization. He is also a double agent (for some reason, never really explained well) for the edgy hacker group, the Juggernaut Collective or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ Jensen needs to pierce the veil of these large, world spanning conspiracies and find the truth behind these shadowy groups in a complex web of intrigue where nobody can be trusted! Or so that’s what was promised, and what was badly, badly undelivered… The main storyline of this game is a huge, huge disappointment, honestly nothing of importance happens until near the end of the game, and the game ends abruptly. I’ve read the reviews, I was prepared for the abrupt ending, but MAN does it come out of nowhere. Like seriously in the middle of a ♥♥♥♥ing conversation. Jensen says something and the screen cuts to black, and I saw the little Steam Achievement pop up for completing the game. Huh?
Imagine if the ENTIRE Lord of the Rings trilogy ended after the Battle of Helms Deep. It’s a cool, exciting battle sequence, but you knew while watching it this was just a middle chapter, an “Act 2”, the halfway point between the beginning and the epic conclusion. Mankind Divided is like that, basically you see the boring main story start to pick up some steam and boom. Game is over. This is by far my biggest complaint of this game, at least Human Revolution had a nice resolving climax and a tying up of story elements, but Mankind Divided doesn’t bother. I’m sure this is just stuff to fill in with DLC content and/or the next game in the series, but seeing this stuff get cut up was annoying. There is a difference between a sequel hook and blatant cut content, and this definitely falls in the latter category.
I don’t know what’s going on with Square Enix, but it seems like they are taking small, iterative steps and stumbling nonetheless. Like Rise of the Tomb Raider, Mankind Divided is a near copy of the previous game (also rebooted) and takes a few steps forward, but also a couple steps back. This is fine, of course, but I’m afraid that we are no longer going to see anything new and exciting from this company, just small iterative steps. I had my issues with Rise of the Tomb Raider, but in that game’s storyline, however stupid, resolved itself in the end. Mankind Divided, unfortunately, has a stupid story that ALSO fails to resolve itself…
Regardless of the issues I had with the main campaign. I still recommend this game, definitely if it was discounted to around $30. I had a lot of fun exploring the city of Prague, and the game is a graphically stunning piece of art, as well as nicely tweaked gameplay elements. It’s still a fantastic game, a testament to the love and attention the developers put into it, despite Squeenix meddling.
Microtransactions. Do you want to break the game and make your character overpowered? Instead of just entering cheat codes, why not pay Squeenix more money for some Praxis points? Honestly I hate this kind of stuff, and it’s almost made me not recommend the game based on it, but I’m truly, dearly hoping Square Enix makes like $10 off of this ridiculous business endeavor. Just don’t buy them, just ignore them. The game is balanced as it is, I was pretty overpowered near the end and you shouldn’t shell out any more cash for this game. Don’t even buy the season pass, see what kind of stuff they give out. If it’s just more Praxis points and really really short story levels, would not be worth it in my opinion.
All in all, Mankind Divided is a flawed, somewhat claustrophobic experience that nonetheless as brief flashes of brilliance throughout. If you were a fan of Human Revolution, you will most definitely enjoy this game for what it is but be disappointed in its story. The gameplay is superb, the world is very detailed, and the side quests are incredible, just don’t expect anything in the main quest to blow you away. I would probably pick this game up on a sale, knowing Square Enix’s policy, they’ll probably sell the game for cheap soon enough, citing disappointing sales figures despite selling like a million copies.
I wish this game was better than it was, but it is still good. Unfortunately that’s all I can say, Mankind Divided is good, but not great.

I also really enjoyed the control scheme, where you control one of the two brothers with the left analog stick and trigger and the other one with the right stick and trigger.

One final positive thing I like to add are the achievements. They're all optional stuff and earning them feels a lot more rewarding then to get achievements just by doing what you're asked/following the basic story!
The puzzles themselves I found rather easy, which I think is neither bad nor good, since I didn't really buy it for the puzzles and I'd advise others to do the same.
However the game's supposed strong point, the story, didn't resonate with me that much. I think it is often tonally too different from what I believe it wants the player to feel or experience.
The moments of suspense or joy, which are placed throughout the game and journey of the two protagonists, did connect with me, but the sadder parts didn't, which, as I've said, I think the game wants to pronounce more to the player.
In the end I still very much enjoyed my time with the game. While maybe the ending isn't everyone's cup of tea, the rest of the game certainly had the feeling of adventure and for me, just looking at the world of
was fulfilling enough.
However for anyone skeptical I'd advise waiting for the next sale.

INCOMING REVIEWER!
Ah yes, the Incoming series. Awful shame it had to die off so long ago. The original Incoming was one of the first PC games I ever played, utilizing a Real3D StarFighter graphics card, and a whopping 400MB of RAM! I had fond memories about this game; how graphically impresive it was for the late 90's. But two questions remain; Does the Incoming bundle hold up today, and is it worth buying? The short answer for these questions is Yes and No, so please allow me to explain.
It's safe to say that Incoming and Incoming Forces do not hold up by their own selves today. With our PC's always upgrading with maximum stats, combined with how old these games are, it should come to no surprise that the games are heavily outdated, and poorly optimized. In the original Incoming, I found many of the models to be incorrectly rendered, enabling you to see through them. I am also aware that Incoming cannot be correctly played on Windows 8.1 and 10 machines, so unless you have Windows 7 at latest, you may want to pass this game; you're not missing much.
On the other hand, Incoming Forces is a much more optimized piece of software, but is not really a "great" game per-se. In retrospect, the plot is silly, and for a 2002 game, I've seen much better-looking games. Gameplay is also a bit lackluster, so I would recommend the consumer to purchase the product mainly for the original Incoming; Incoming Forces feels like an unnecessary pack-in, so I'd consider it as a form of bonus game.
Now, is this product worth buying? For me, it was a simple "yes," because I obtained it during a sale. I had fond memories of this game, and I wanted to return to see what I was missing all these years. As for the average consumer, I would recommend this game only if they are a hardcore fan of vehicular combat, combined with space-like arcade railshooting. If you are into that "futuristic" techno vibe, look no further than the original Incoming's soundtrack. While small, the songs are rather catchy, and the game is definitely worth playing to at least hear these songs.
All in all, Incoming and Incoming Forces isnt too bad of a product to invest in. I feel that the price may be a bit much for these rather obscure titles, but hey, you're getting a dual-pack that was originally valued along the lines of $40 dollars in the day. It's ultimately your choice whether or not you want these games.
Ratings:
Incoming: 7/10
Incoming Forces: 5/10

Dreaming Sarah delves into the dreams of the comatose Sarah. Within, you'll find things you'd only find in dreams - magical beans that can make upward drafts, mansions with things that can only be seen with special glasses, and the ability to turn into a fish. You'll only receive small snippets of story as you explore the area.
The platforming in Dreaming Sarah is pretty well done. While playing on controller it felt pretty responsive. Switching around items can be a pain at times, and you may often find yourself deactivating your parasol when you accidentally open the menu. There is a large amount of backtracking to do in the game, but it does generally push you along in the right direction.
While I do highly recommend Dreaming Sarah to those who like puzzle platformers, I only give that high recommendation if you can get it on sale. At full price the game just feels too short.

A surreal little side scrolling adventure platformer, with minimal platforming elements and lots of exploration through weird but well made and definitely dream-like 16bit imagery.
I'm slowly realizing that I'm bad at these exploration type games. There is a certain amount of patience required to get lost in its weird maps that go all over the place, in two directions or even looping onto themselves, and that require you to revisit them after finding certain items to see whether something new has unlocked. I'm apparently also not great at solving a couple of its slightly more abstract, lateral-thinking-required puzzles, so yes, a walkthrough was consulted. However, the game is good at creating a sense of controlled bewilderment that makes the exploration interesting, most of the puzzles do seem to resolve themselves after a bit of exploration or trial and error, and the different locations were distinct enough to keep fascinating even after getting lost in them for the n-th time. It helps that the game isn't particularly long (about 2-3 hours, depending on how lost you get), so frustration is kept at a minimum.
I will avoid spoiling any of the discoveries you can make within its fragmentary (and admittedly not super original or particularly deep) story, because it includes some really interesting/shocking moments that carry the minimal, up-for-interpretation narrative forward. But I can say that Dreaming Sarah never got boring, because wandering through these dream sequences manages to stay refreshing throughout, with a new little surprise around every corner. The beautiful soundtrack also elevated the experience, and if you like this type of ambient, dreamy music, you will enjoy it.
If you are even mildly curious about this game, and if you have the patience to get lost within its interesting surreal world, then Dreaming Sarah is definitely a game I would recommend. Despite not being the main target audience, I enjoyed myself. If you're still unsure about it, the Brazilian Indie Developer Asteristic is offering a downloadable demo at their website
.

Nice and short Brazilian platform-puzzle with multiple possible interpretations that will surprise you for its narrative’s randomness. Be prepared for walking in circles and running through its multiple scenarios quite a few times before figuring out what to do, as there is no map available. Could have been a downside, but it turns out to enhance the experience, for the game world is under constant minor transformations, and you never know for sure what you’ll stumble upon.
The soundtrack is both smooth and mysterious, fitting perfectly with the overall surrealistic atmosphere. Pixel-art is well-made, although not outstanding. Total runtime shouldn’t exceed three hours, so I'd recommend playing it in one just sitting: some serious immersion will make this game all the more interesting (it’s supposed to be an one-night dream, after all).

So, for the game.  I am part way through, so don't want to comment on the story, but so far it's been the standard affair, which is not to say bad, just cliché.  It's what I wanted though, so I am very happy with the result.
The gameplay is fine.  That said, for the first time in a while, I had to turn the graphics down and not even to very high...  It is graphically intensive, though I suspect this is not purely down to optimisation, but the hardware I am currently using.
This happens to be: AMD 8350, 16GB RAM and an MSi 970.  To say the least, on high settings it still looks damned nice.
Ultimately, this looks, feels and plays like a Deus Ex game and contrary to others, I feel the single hub works in its favour, much in the same way I found with DA2.  It allows more focus on the creation of that city, rather than it appearing an empty shell you go to purely to sell things.
As such, I can only recommend the game.

Brawlhalla is a stylish 2-D fighting game in the same gameplay-style vein of the Nintendo Super Smash Bros, series. It’s a free-to-play early access title, and it carries with it the usual nonsense often stuck to games in this category (limited characters you’re allowed to choose from with the rest locked behind a time-wall where you’re forced to wait for the potential of characters being in the week’s rotation of six fighters (legends) or a pay-wall, unbalanced characters, sloppily planned-out maps, easy-to-scumbag weapon gimmick, ineffectual dodge-mechanic that harkens back to the days of SSB Melee. etc.).
Brawlhalla is technically well planned out, but undermined and destroyed with horrible balancing and the aforementioned points; especially the broken balancing among the characters. The most notable of these broken “legends” is Azuri. I viciously dislike this character because she is arguably the most broken character of the roster with several fast and effective attacks that seem to completely ignore all other oncoming attacks. Many others characters have this issue (I’m looking at you in particular, Hattori), but it’s most prevalent with Azuri. Furthermore, one of my friends almost always plays as her, so there’s no escape from her horrifying onslaught. I honestly should have this game mastered by now; after all, Brawlhalla plays very similarly to Smash Bros, (a game I am rather efficient with). However, after TWENTY hours of dedicated play with this game, I still get served on a silver platter no matter who I pick (or, rather, who of the limited few I’m allowed to pick that week’s rotation). I’m not an expert, but I have a strong reason to believe this is a problem with the game’s balancing and not a problem with me.
In conclusion, Brawlhalla can honestly give you a good time, it really can (I have 20 hours on record for a reason), but you can very easily find yourself having a bad time due to my points listed above. If the game significantly improves, I may revoke my review, but until then, I simply cannot recommend Brawlhalla. It’s simply given me more noteable bad times than notable good.

This is a lovely casual game that tells a touching tale of two determined brothers on a journey in search of a cure for their sick father. While the premise sounds simple enough, the journey takes you on a sweet adventure, at times meandering, all the while staying true to the objective.
The artistic style of the game is gorgeous and the gameplay is very relaxing. It will also help to prove the excellent point of exactly how non-ambidextrous you may be. In fact, it's wonderfully frustrating trying to navigate the world of these two brothers simultaneously, keeping within distance, while navigating small challenges and puzzles. I should also mention that I played using just my keyboard and assume it would certainly be easier with a controller; however in the end, it was quite manageable.
As others have mentioned, it is quite a short game and there are a few hidden achievements to pay attention to (if you're interested in them). Some of the creatures that you encounter are especially endearing and I do believe you may feel a tug or two on your heartstrings. Enjoy!!!

A lot of classic games either skimped on discussing any plot or simply didn't have the technology to incorporate a complex storyline. By reducing voiced character interaction to a minimum and having them speak in a foreign language, the player is left to interpret the story; a compelling and central aspect to this indie contender.
I've been told that this is one of the very finest games ever made and while I understand the appeal and certainly agree its worth your time, I don't think it belongs on the pedastal so many critics have garnished it with.
Despite clocking in at three hours, the game felt much shorter as it seemed to just fly by. Every blink I took was accompanied by a huge transition in location. Before I knew it I was adventuring in a completely different place, each one bearing its own set of rules and all goverened by the same overarching objective (venture forth and get your sick dad some medicine).
You'll never feel stressed and even dying won't set you back more than a few moments. Progress is blocked by a handful of simple, contextual puzzles. This is the perfect game for relaxing with one day.
Perhaps the strongest point and what makes this game so unique is that like Mario and Luigi RPGs you'll be controlling two characters (who can't typically sepraate far from one another). The way they both interact with the expansive world made everything come to life. One brother would kneel down to pet a sheep and the other would pick it up and carry it with him. One would admire the caged bird and the other set him free.
This game's been on sale before so try to pick it up on the cheap. I snagged it for about three bucks. You'd have to enjoy a AAA game for sixty dollars proportionately if you wanted that sort of value.

A lot of people know Soulstorm by "SPESS MEHREENS", "METAL BAWKSES" and such. And in all fairness, if there was one thing I would critique Soulstorm for other than lack of polish, it is occasionally train-wreck level off-kilter VA work.
However, occasional VA disaster aside, I would consider Soulstorm a flawed, yet still highly interesting gem. The campaign system, while no larger than Dark Crusade's, is deeper from the introduction of Webway travel and a better slew of racial bonuses on the campaign map (no more Necrons with Fury nonsense  on Turn 1, looking at you, DC) and both the new races are at the least of a different variety to the others in the game with viable differing strategies. The introduction of flyers adds at least in part another element of power-play to the game by acting as an extra combat element on the attack and the defence.
Would I recommend Soulstorm for £40? No. But for the asking price offered, I would absolutely encourage people to round out the DoW 1 collection and see what Soulstorm has to offer. You might be as surprised as me.

First of all, many of the reviews for this game are EXTREMELY unfair. I have played up to the 3rd Era with each family, and through the 5th Era with the von Pfilzen family & the Shuskys. I have enjoyed EACH of my playthroughs enough to say that I would recommend this game.
The main criticisms of this game seem to be shutdowns, errors, and similar issues. I am speaking as someone with a Dell Latitude E6410 laptop I got for free from my old job that was donating them to a local school. I have played hours upon hours with NO issues whatsoever. Granted, this is at the lowest settings, but if you have a crap computer then don't expect brand new games to work like your playing on your PS4.
Most of the ACTUAL gameplay criticisms are in regard to the politics. I find the politics to be a bit...odd. I mostly enjoy the politics, but it seems a bit disconnected. If the political party likes you, they will always like you IF you dont annoy them all the time. If a party does NOT like you, there is nothing you can do. HOWEVER, once you get used to how the political side of the game works, it becomes no more annoying than any other thing in any other game.
My only other criticisms are the lack of a good tutorial, only having 3 maps to choose from, and being forced to watch my conservative aristocratic family turn into a radical liberal family.
All of that being said, I recommend this game because it is pretty much exactly as advertised. You do NOT have 100% control over every building, every citizen, every law, etc. You may PROPOSE the building of new districts, however you will have to get the various parties to vote in your favor. You may get that new district built, however it will be up to your citizens to build the various buildings. Then again, they may not build new buildings...perhaps due to heavy taxation, or whatever. When new buildings are built, they may be profitable...or they may go bankrupt. The world is NOT your oyster. You are a Mayor, not "El Presidente" Dictator.
This game does NOT deserve the terrible rating it has been given. This is a VERY niche game, but it isnt terrible for what it is and what it is trying to be. Is it worth $40 (USD)? Heck no, but if you are eyeballing this game and see it on sale...get it. Get it, and enjoy it for what it is...a new niche take on a classic game archetype.
UPDATE: Just purchased a much newer computer with all the bells and whisles. When it arrives, I will be redownloading and replaying this game to compare, and will update this review if needed.
