Urban Empire is a game developed by Reborn Games and published by Kalypso Media Digital. I love city building games. I love politics. I love running a city when it comes to politics, so technically, I should love Urban Empire...
When it was first announced, I was incredibly excited, however, I started to reduce my hype when I found out Kalypso Media Digital was publishing it after their bad track record with other games except maybe the Tropico games and the high price point, nearly 45 EUR! Thankfully, I waited for a sale and bought it on Humble Bundle for only 20 EUR
Urban Empire starts wonderfully exciting. To start, it has open territory to place your districts, a council to influence, and support from the emperor to get you going. The game remains fun while you create and grow your first couple of districts and through the entire first era. As the game goes on each era becomes more and more repetitive, and the errors in and problems with the game become more apparent
What I like from Urban Empire is the premise of growing a city through political wrangling with the option of the families; though I wish there were a few more of them from which to choose and the politics of the council and the parties
What I don't like from Urban Empire and there are loads... Firstly, the decision tool tips: in many cases there aren't any tool tips and fluff/story-based decisions out or order
Replayability is severely lacking. In my experience: progressive agenda issue (for the era) proposed multiple times, even if vote fails or overruled. Conservative policies (for the era) are one-and-done. Both the council and the populous should be a bit more randomized every play though. This would allow for more replayability
All families should be able to win based on their ideals. Populist or Liberal Western ideals shouldn't be the only path to victory
There is loads of lag nearing the endgame. This game is horribly optimized, if my PC can play The Witcher 3 on Ultra, then it should play Urban Empire with no problems, yet it doesn't
Whether it's on the city map or even in the city council starting in Era IV the game becomes very, very laggy. There's no point in even moving the camera over my city unless fully paused, and waiting 3-5 seconds for a button click to register is not ideal
Urban Empire has bad spelling grammar which I'm not too worried about this, and I'm by no means perfect, but it should be noted that they could use a better English editor to fix the numerous spelling and grammar errors
Based on price and experience, for now, I have to give this game a thumbs down. However, it is my sincerest hope that mods and patching will really improve both the primary experience and the replayability of Urban Empire
I want to love the game, and I think I can if they take a good hard look at what city building combined with politics can fully offer. But it seems like Reborn Games and Kalypso Media Digital have completely thrown Urban Empire out of the door and left it to rot...

I'd rather make this review neutral than negative, but I suppose I tip slightly on the negative side.
The good:
The game has generally pleasing music and visuals. The different zones were vivid and interesting.
There were a few genuinely interesting/disturbing moments that were very much in the spirit of Yume Nikki.
The bad:
The creator acknowledges the inspiration was Yume Nikki. It borrows the plot, the tone, the protagonist, the gameplay. While the experience may seem fresh to those who haven't played, I found Dreaming Sarah akin to a mainstream recreation of Yume Nikki.
Dreaming Sarah attempts to be artsy and mysterious while still having a simple, happy ending. Before the player starts the game, they've probably read the two-sentence blurb explaining that the protagonist is a girl trying to wake up from a coma. This was a hideous mistake that provides two major spoilers: the game is a dream sequence, and you'll probably wake up. I get why the creator wanted to do this: so "normal" gamers would play past the first five minutes. And yet this both spoils the ending and removes the dream world's mystique. If we know it's all dreamscape before even installing the game, we can write off all the imagery as a little girl's nightmare.
Lastly, the protagonist was flat. Yume Nikki's protagonist was interesting because the player could probe her psyche and question her sanity as they navigated her dark dreams. Sarah took a more passive and indirect role. She never fights, breaks, or opposes anything. She silently accepts the plot coupons NPCs drop into her hands. She barely interacts with her own dreams, and never gives us reason to doubt her sanity.
If you want a short, easy, tour through Wonderland that will leave you with your feet on firm ground, this game may be worth your while. Otherwise, there are games out there that do the artsy and psychological aspects a bit better. Check out Yume Nikki, Dear Esther, and Year Walk.

Brawlhalla is a 2D fighting game that's easy to learn, but hard to master. You choose a character, each with a variety of moves unique to only that character, and battle it out in a variety of maps and gamemodes.
Fighting:
This game has an near-perfect fighting system. Perhaps the best bit of it is the fact that you can't just spam-click to victory, and you actually have to use a bit of strategy. Every character has their own set of moves, giving them different strengths of weaknesses. Since each character can be used in a variety of different ways, this means your often forced to find ways to counter your enemies in different ways. There's also a small array of weapon-types, which basically serves as a way to generalize each character's strengths. Bows have a longer reach but require more precision; Swords have quick attacks; Hammers generally have attacks with heavy knockback, but are slow, etc. I say its near-perfect because there's one thing that bugs me (Though I don't really know how it could be balanced), and that's the fact that bows and guns don't actually have "ranged" attacks, just melee attacks with a decent reach.
Replay-ability:
The game is a good way to settle scores or disputes you have with your friends in a fair way, and gameplay is generally fun, but its pretty easy to get bored of the game if you play it too much. It's not one of those games that's really good to play once, but it isn't a game you'll dedicate weeks into either.
Learning Curve:
Brawlhalla is very user-friendly all-around. In about half-an-hour, I was able to figure out the gist of pretty much any character I tried. However, this doesn't really make the game that easy, as everyone is now on an even playing-field, which is the exact setting you want when playing a fast-paced game like Brawlhalla.
Character Creation:
This is one of Brawlhalla's few downfalls, in my opinion. Though there are a fair amount of characters, they can't really be customized in a gameplay perspective. Every character is locked to a specific pair of weapons. Brawlhalla does have "stances", though they only slightly adjust the 4 main stats (Strength, Dexterity, Armor, and Speed), and don't really change the overall game.
Arena Variety:
Brawlhalla has a lot of maps, but they aren't really "unique". With a few exceptions, the maps are mostly static, and generally don't have very much to offer. However, the variety of arenas isn't a particularly pressing issue in a game like this, and the amount of maps themselves is enough to keep games fresh.
Pace:
Overall, with the game's combat and variety of characters, the game has achieved a near-perfect balance. There isn't a single character that will cause a game to end really quickly, and no character particularly poor at fighting.

The Mean Greens is a simple shooter with some incredibly fun and unique maps.
The fact that you play as toys in this game allows for some really imaginitve objectives and maps.
For example, a kitchen map has you zipline in by a string attached to plastic cups. You battle in between gigantic doughnuts, bubbles from a sink, and your mission is to knock over the enemy cup so that they can't zipline into the level anymore. There are so many creative objectives placed on colourful and alive maps. It's a nice breath of fresh air in the shooter genre.
The gameplay itself is quite simple. You sprint, jump, shoot and roll. The combat at the moment isn't very in-depth. There are no weapon pick-ups, you just have all 5 on you at once. That's really all there is to say.
Overall, simple gameplay but the fun variety of objectives and maps keeps the game fresh!

This game has so many minor flaws that I struggled to enjoy my first playthrough. Yet, only after it could I appreciate it.
- The map allows unnecessary backtracking
so you can return almost to the beginning even in later stages. This, combined with some difficulty identifying where the correct path has opened up, lead me more than once backwards, assuming it was the right way, but eventually ending up in a dead end, wasting plenty of time and losing motivation.
Fortunately, there is an upgrade which allows quick-running outside of combat, as well as a map that shows where you have been, but not where you need to go.
- Getting into the combat system was fairly infuriating at first, when getting used to the controls (Which took me to the final few stages to find comfort with). The enemies and bosses can, and will step outside of melee-range on purpose, which leaves you open for attacks from other targets while recovering from your own move, that you missed. Some attacks requires lock-on on a target to be performed. And these attacks usually toss the enemy out of range. Meaning you'll have to get into range again. The flaw is that these moves are activated by the joystick used for moving. So more often than not, you'll end up with such an attack instead of the basic slashing.
- Coming from the newer "DMC: Devil May Cry" before I played this game, The ability to make combos is almost nonexistent, as you only have a few moves, and later on a few weapons, which can barely be used together. The trick for style-rank is instead to not get hit, while dishing out random damage. Not to look cool while doing so.
The different handling in DMC4 forced a different approach in playstyle.
Trying to make use out of every ability/weapon I have is just a personal, preferred playstyle.
- The camera is locked, or semi-restricted in some areas which requires the lock-on feature to be used in combat. Enemies can often stand outside the camera's view, preparing a sudden ranged attack.
The dodge-ability requires lock-on active. Though its invincibility-frames seems shorter than the animation. So before the animation is over, before you can perform another move, you can still take damage and get stunned.
- The few soundtracks I got to hear while playing through this game did not redeem the game, but rather fuelled my fire.
The entire game featured one single track while in battle with common enemies. One somewhat monotone track, which often only last a few moments. Most, if not all bosses featured their own tracks fortunately. And are considerably better.
The ambient background-tracks were different for each "area" but got old really quickly, hearing the start over and over, as area-transitions restarted the track.
- The bosses all had very diverse abilities/playstyles each and that really shines a positive on this game. Though due to your own clunky abilities, It was all more of a dull grind to chip off damage while they backed out of range, and not have time to back away yourself due to their attacks rarely showing a visible build-up.
- The game features 5 different characters (2+2+1) in their own playthrough. And by playthrough, It's the exact same stages and bosses as the main story but without cutscenes. (Just one introductory cutscene).
Yet, there is one word to nullify most of this: GAMESENSE
Once you're able to avoid triggering the lock-on moves while locked on a target, things will go much smoother.
You'll be able to understand what to do during bossfights, when to retreat from incoming attacks.
Closure from finishing the main story was a pretty big deal. Especially with the hardships of trying to get used to the controls/abilities.
I would not call this game satisfying or worth getting. But it's not hopeless, and can be a fun experience
. Learning its mechanics is the replay-value of this game.

Virtual Basement’s (Ark- Survival Evolved) latest game, The Mean Greens, does what a number of bigger games fail to do. While it may sound like some kind of Vegan juice drink, The Mean Greens is charming title that showcases vast amount of potential from a young developer.
The core concept is the classic battle between Green and Tan toy soldiers. Those little pieces of plastic, vaguely human shaped, that has entertained generation after generation. In this case, we’re no longer using imagination to act our play wars, we’re directly playing. From the outside, The Mean Greens looks like a cookie cutter third person shooter, and that’s partly right. The true star of show is not the gameplay, but the maps.
The Mean Greens is about as accessible as you can get. Simple third person shooting, no classes or perks. Variation comes in the form of different weapon types, allowing players to engage from what ever range they wish. It all works well, even if it can lead to some slight sense of repetition creeping in.
Virtual Basement have a clear vision of what they waned to The Mean Greens to be. Map design and concepts reflect the exact vision and themes that were desired. Each map is set in various parts of a typical house. Kitchens, table tops, bath rooms and even the fish tank. It’s nice little throwback to all the typical places we’d wage plastic warfare as children.
Each map has it’s own unique objective, from the classic to the crazy. Be it Free-for-all deathmatch or capture the flag, The Mean Greens puts a twist on it. The most notably of twists comes in the shape of the bubble bath battle for flags. Players are tasked with collecting flags dotted around a bath tub full of floating rubber duckies, with a giant octopus occupying the centre of the tub.
There’s also a play on foosball table in which players battle to push the ball into the opposition goal. Each and every map oozes with character and charm. It’s the little touches that go along way. From the popping of bubbles in the sink, to the haunting yet oddly catchy rendition of Operation Birthday’s ‘Birthday Cake’ song, it’s hard no to smirk when playing.
Presentation forms a key part of the experience. In order to get that true feel of playing with toy soldiers, the visuals have to be on point. It’s a testament to the craftsmanship and care shown by Virtual Basement that the game looks beautiful. The soldiers look amazing, almost to the point you swear you could pick them out of the screen. Environments blend real life elements and colour pallets similar to films like Toy Story, resulting in some brilliant imagery. Each maps has it’s own distinct look, feeding into the concept that this is what you used to think of when you were a child, army men in hand.
The Mean Greens only real issues come in the shape or some sever connection issues and the odd bit of balancing. Within a period of 4 hours, a number of disconnections from sever occurred once the match had ended. This issue was mentioned a few times in the in-game chat, suggesting it’s far from isolated cases. A minor niggle comes in the shape of hit detection and satisfaction. There’s times in which weapons feel like they should be hitting the target. Headshots tend to feel part luck more than skill. It gives the gunplay a touch of being rather floaty instead of satisfying.
Weapon balancing could use some work. One of the six weapons, the bazooka, is hugely overused by nearly every player in the game. The overuse of the weapon results in a number of modes becoming nothing but bazookafest, rendering other weapons slightly pointless. Additional weapons may be on cool down, but the regularity of death and respawns means you’ll be a victim of a rocket extra 30 seconds.
As a whole package, The Mean Greens is an admirable release. With 10 modes, 10 maps, 6 weapons and voice chat, it puts EA’s Star Wars: Battlefront to shame. Code Virtual Basement can be proud of what they’ve produced. It may not be packing all the fancy tricks and frills of other multiplayer titles, but it sure is packed with charm and sheer enjoyment. For less than £12, it’s hard not to recommend The Mean Greens, even more so as a nifty Steam stocking filler for Christmas.

But it's not about length, it's about the heart, awesomeness, and the sheer cyborg balls that made this game. If you have a good sense of humor, and an itch for anarchy and violence, play this game!
.. Did I mention you get to ride a Blood Dragon that shoots lazers out of its eyes? Yeah, that happens (albeit in just one mission).

This game is  a Joke. Yep, a really, really good joke. The Ubisoft folk sure know when to take a joke's seriously, and they have the evidence to back it up. Far Cry 3 - Blood Dragon is an epitome of the parodic genre. A parody indeed. Set with the unforgetable post appocalyptic 80's version of the future, the game slaps movie refferences on the face. Far Cry 3 - Blood Dragon takes the player in for one hell of a ride, putting you inside the boots of an♥♥♥♥♥kicking, cyborg-killing and ruthless war machine; Sergeant Rex Powercolt. Although part of the experience may feel like an overused capture-the-fort mechanic on a massive reskin of the original Far Cry 3, the idea of being an invincible Cyber-commando is more than good. Who cares about repetition and lack of variety when there is plenty to be had with the Blood Dragon enemies and the amazing armory upgrades that make up for the previous. Sure to be said that the overpowered neonlights theme and the sounds of Powerglove's score/soundtrack  provide a superb setting for this explosive, radioactively unstable, laser-shot-filled adventure.

This game left me with so mixed feelings about it it is hard to describe. Nothing about Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is black and white; it is not good, nor is it bad. And it all burns down to a simple question: what are
expectations?
As a huge fan of the Human Revolution I expected DE: Mankind Devided to be at least on par with the previous game. Instead it has only offered a slightly more refined gameplay. That's it. The rest of the game is mediocre for my taste: story is terribly underdeveloped and ends with no conclusion what so ever, screaming for a few DLC and a sequel or two. Consequences of player's decisions are very minor and have no affect on state of the game world.
Existing locations are well designed and it is pretty fun to go on exploring everything for the first time, but excitement doesn't last long as there are so few of them: most of the time Adam spends in Prague, the hub-area, and its' sub-levels doing hack-this-fetch-that sort of quests. Hub-area is mostly flat, no roof parkour or anything of that sort. And practically no need to stealth either, untill the very last visit - just run around. Traveling through sewers instead of going up top is a so-so idea because the in-game map is bad and doesn't let you see streets when underground and vise versa, making navigation a plain pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Besides there is no point in doing so anyway.

As a hardcore fan of the original Deus Ex, one of the best games I've ever played and which I've finished many times I must admitt that I was worried about the outcome of the newest franchise. My doubts where based upon Human revolution which wasn't a bad game (especially the music was stunning) but it lacked something for me, it had many flaws which I didn't liked (ex. boss fights). So I was waiting for Mankind Divided with a lot of reserve.
Fortunately the game turned out to be really good, not perfect but IMO way better than Human revolution. I prefer stealth kind of a gameplay and I like to explore every nook and cranny, read notes, messages, and other lore included in the game. So finishing it on a hardest difficulty level (I do not mean new game+here) took me about 50 hours including additional "Jensen Stories" mission , and without touching Breach. It was way longer that I thought it will take me, especially after reading reviews of other people.

Don't get me wrong the game has it's flaws. For example going trough it guns blazing IMO would be pretty frustrating, cause feeling the of weapons isn't very good in open battle. There is just something about them that feels uncomfortable. And so I used mainly silenced pistol, stun gun, and tranqulizer rifle :)
I wasn't encouraged to use other tools as well, like mines, or grenades. There just wasn't any situation I couldn't resolve without them. It's really cool that You can go trough the entire game without killing anyone, but at the same time those gadgets are reduced to toys, which You can choose to use when You wanna have some fun, cause You really do not have any other reason to.
There can be a lot of hacking, and after some time it becomes boring. Because of this i regret that game developers decided to not include lockpicking or some other mechanics which could be nice alternative for hacking.

Graphics could be better, some textures desperately need higher resolution, and character animation is really weak for most time. But those aren't things of most importance to me.
There are some other bugs and glitches as well, but I haven't encountered much of them, and they seem to be patched quite regularly.
What I reallly liked about the game was good stealth mechanics, nice story with interesting plot and dialogues (which is pretty rare nowadays) cool augmentations, good music, and a lot of those little things that reminded me of original Deus Ex game.
So in my opinion Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is solid 8/10 and really worth playing for anyone who liked previous parts of the series.
Cheers :)

First of all, let's get the whole microtransaction salt out of the way: if you don't like them- don't buy them! Simple! You'll find that most things in life work this way. Is the game bad because of the microtransactions? No, so it isn't fair to give the game a bad review for it. Most people don't even know it has microtransactions, and I finished the game with 48 unused praxis points, 30k credits and maxed out on everything I could carry, though I like to play minimalistically the first time. Now, onto actually reviewing the game, as you're supposed to do in these comments, instead of complaining about microtransactions.
Pros: In most ways the game has improved. The city hubs are bigger and have much more depth, tons of ministories, even more exploration, many ways of getting around. There are many more sidequests and they are much better than in HR (btw it'd be nice if they carried over to the next game). There are also many interesting unique interactions with characters you can find depending on where you are in the story. The new augs are fun, especially the blink (Icarus Dash), although I don't get the point of the overheating system. There is more "vertical" exploration now(roofs, apartments, floors, etc.), but it would've been even better if you could travel on as many roofs as in Dishonored with blink. It's also nice that you can finally take down enemies leaning on something from behind. The atmosphere is still great too, music is good, though fewer tracks that really stand out as opposed to the previous game. Graphics are great for those that can run it, but I didn't notice any optimization issues on the low settings I used for my crappy laptop, it ran about as well as I expected. They also clearly heard the complaints of pacifist not being an option in HR. Setting-wise the story is great as always, however, (onto cons)
Cons: The single biggest issue is, unfortunately, the main story line. It's not bad, it's still probably better than in most games, but it's much more predictable and straighforward than in the previous game, and some things didn't make a lot of sense. Major spoilers:
It also feels like not much progress was made, and the story was cut short. Minor spoilers:
I realize cliffhangers are great, but there were too many cliffhangers. Also, (fairly minor spoiler):
There are a few more minor story issues but this review is long enough already.
Lesser cons: Although you can do takedowns behind cover now, in some infrequent cases you still can't do it, e.g. if they're leaning on something rectangular like a bed, so you still have to walk up to them from the side which is risky.
Also, there are less interesting weapons, for example no laser or plasma rifles like in the previous game.
And with the new hacking look, the icons overlap and I often click the wrong thing.
TL;DR overall a very good game, a lot of work clearly went into the depth of the environment, but the main story, while not bad, isn't as good as in HR, and I think the side missions were actually better.

Dreaming Sarah is an odd little indie platformer.
It’s very hard to figure out exactly what’s going on in the game or what the premise is from the in-game content, but if you read the description, the game is about a woman in a coma named Sarah. You wander dream realms in an attempt to help her wake up.
Alright, fair enough. So what exactly do you do in this game? You start out in a forest area and ‘wake up,’ though you have no real idea as to which way you’re supposed to be going. Pick right or left and start running. That’s pretty much it except for the jumping.
Dreaming Sarah is a surreal game. The levels are connected to each other in strange and bizarre ways, but there’s no real rhyme or reason as to what they are or why you go to them. The gameplay is fairly freeform. Run around until you reach some obstacle you can’t get past and then find some way around it.
As you play you collect various items, some of which are pretty darn cool. There’s an umbrella which slows your falling speed, a paint can which changes your outfit colors, a magnifying glass to shrink you down to tiny size to get through little tunnels, and even an item which transforms you into a fish so you can access an underwater level.
In addition to all the useful items, there are a bunch of items which don’t do anything and whose significance to the plot is largely mysterious. Basically just collectibles, but strange ones. I have no idea why I was getting them or what the point of any of them are. Supposedly if you get all of them it makes the ending slightly different, but I took a look at the comparison between the two endings and it’s hardly worth it if you don’t collect everything.
The main joy of the game is the atmosphere. The music is great and the artwork is retro styled, but very pretty. The levels loop back in on themselves, so if you go far enough right or left or even down, you’ll end up back where you started. There are NPC’s, but they don’t have much to say. Talking to them can be kind of neat and some of them have collectibles you can get from them.
On the whole, Dreaming Sarah was an enjoyable experience for me. It is very short though. It only took me about three hours to beat it and collect every item and secret, almost all of which I found myself with no help. It’s not very difficult for a platformer and there are only a few ways to actually die, after which you instantly respawn, so it’s not for those looking for a challenge. The gameplay isn’t really the point though. It’s functional and there are some neat things you can do with the useable items.
An atmospheric, enjoyable experience overall. I’d definitely recommend it if you have a few bucks and you want something neat.

This is a really fun game with some beautiful and imaginative maps to play around in. Most maps have their own special game mode that puts a twist on the standard FPS modes like FFA, CTF, ARENA, OBJECTIVES, ETC. The game has really good potential, but there are just a few lingering issues  that keep it from being great (yet).
Positives:
-Amazing graphics
-Fun maps that put you into a miniature world
-Nice optimization and runs smoothly
-Good music
-Original and interesting game modes
-Quickly switch between roles (sniper, assult, defend, objective) just by switching guns (no classes)
-Limited ammo and health per life means less camping
Negatives:
-Game needs VOIP ASAP! (at the time of this writing there was an option in game, but not working yet)
-Could use more guns and customization
-Needs more visual and sound feedback on hitting and getting hit. Needs feedback when shooting as well like recoil, screen shaking and the like.
-Games often end in a stalemate because game objectives are too difficult with fast and close respawns
-Rocket launcher and 'nades need balancing
-Need to be able to shoot in the air on the underwater level
-I would like to be able to rebind ALL keys
Overall it's a fun game to play and for sure worth the low price tag! If the devs make some improvements it's going to be an even better deal.

Jeez i have never found the need to write a serious review for a game but it's rare to find something in EARLY ACCESS no less that feels so polished, mechanically intensive, clever, and elegant. The selection of items ("gizmos" henceforth) is small, balanced, and all of them revolve around creating interesting counterplay. The weapons all feel good (even the ones I hate to fight!), and every character, despite sharing weapon styles and light attacks with other characters all have extremely unique and varied signature skills . Recovery is a minigame in and of itself in a way that SSB only wishes it could be, and fighting inside the shenanigan spot in Thundergard is one of the more tense feelings I've ever gotten from a game. And did I mention that I've never seen a flash-animated and rigged game that looked prettier?
Like I said, y'all. I really don't do this often, but this game deserves so much love. It's beautiful, it's polished, it's got a great skill ceiling, its's fun competitive or with your buddies on a friday after work, and best of all it's free. There's nothing about this game i could even think of badmouthing. It's really that amazing. 10/10, would play forever.

For those of you who played Smash Bros. then you'll love this game. Brawlhalla is a 2D cartoonish video game where you can brawl against other Legends. Couch Party, where you can play offline with friends on the same screen using game controllers. Tournament, where you battle other AI Legends moving from bracket to bracket to acheive the highest score possible. Versus BOTs, where you can fully customize your match settings and battle against AI Legneds. Online, where you can choose a Legend and join a 4-player free-for-all match. Ranked is where the most experienced players play in a 1v1 or 2v2 match. Custom, where you can join or host a custom game with the settings chosen by the host.

Okay, I believe I owe the game of giving it a proper recommendation instead of just writing "BUY. THIS." Even if it demands sacrileges, like telling you to forget everything you know about it – noramlly one would urge a responsible customer to factor in every information one has got about the product from reliable sources –, or drop all of your expectations – one should have at least some, reasonable expectations towards a product.
So here I am, telling you to do exactly that: forget everything you know about Brothers and drop all expectations. Instead, do yourself a favour , buy this game, free 3-4 hours for yourself on a weekend evening and play it whole with short brakes, with facebook closed and steam in offline mode. No, seriously, the length of this game is intenional and chosen with great care, specifically so that one could complete the game, from start to finish in one sitting. Why, you ask?
Because this game is... a magic trick.
Hence another heretical thought I must emphasize: you can only appreciate this game if you played it (PLAYED, not watched someone else to play it) from beginning to end. And no, NOOO, HEY! NNNNO! Don't go ahead now and play this game thinking 'oh, so the ending is what matters! Better rush ahead to find out about that epic closing of a game!' NNNNO. BAD PLAYER! BAD! I said, the WHOLE game is, what matters and its so hard to explain why, without ruining the game for you. But here's my final advice: after you finished the game, stand up from your computer and just... go, be somewhere else where you can have a few minutes of undisturbed thinking, and then think about what the game did to you and how it achieved that.
Your mind will be blown.

Like many others I picked up Diablo 3 with my friends on day one with much excitement. A week later I noticed my friends weren't playing anymore and I was the last one holding out. I remember the exact moment I put down Diablo 3, it was kiting yet another champion pack and after hitting them like a million times I started to ask myself if I was playing a Diablo series hack and slash or World of Warcraft in isometric view? I remember in Diablo 2 that when I cast Ice Storm, things DIED! It wasn't regulated to be used simply as a tool to slow and tickle champions that required over a trillion hits and two bottles of No-Doze to kill! Then I looked at my items and then I realized this WAS just World of Warcraft in isometric view. Disgusted I logged out and never returned.
In Diablo 3's defense that was the early days and maybe they fixed the issues (for me the snore-fest gameplay) I don't know because I never returned. The only newsletter I got from them was something about the Auction House which I didn't care about, I only cared about the boring items and taking five minutes to kill high level champions. I figured why bother when there is now a game which resolves all of those problems from go...
In steps Torchlight 2. From the moment I started playing Torchlight 2 every problem I encountered in Diablo 3 that I thought killed the series (for me) was gone instantly. Fast and FUN gameplay, items with interesting effects, even the music and atmosphere… Torchlight 2 nails it. I also have to note that this game sports one of the most fun classes I think I ever played in a hack and slash game. The mage class in this game is so fun and really customizable. I created my mage which seems to play more like a 75% mage mixed in with 25% necromancer and I have a blast with that character.
My only regret is playing Diablo 3 and I don’t say that because I felt jaded. I only say that because it burned me out a bit on hack and slash after that experience so when this came out soon after I didn’t poor a thousand hours into this like it deserves. I am positive I can get 1000 hours out of this game, I have no doubt about it.
The one bad thing about this game though in my experience with it is no dedicated server and I only mention that because I started to run into more and more players in multiplayer that had modified weapons and cheats. It got to a point where I was required to play solo more often than not especially in NG+ modes. Solo mode was balanced perfectly so it's not THAT big of a deal.
In short, if you’re a fan of the original Diablo and Diablo 2 games, this is the game for you. If you want to experience the golden age of hack and slash, this is it. In my opinion, this is the genre’s torchbearer now.
*Disclaimer Diablo 3*
Not everything in Diablo 3 was a completely bad experience for me and I’m not so much as bashing Diablo 3 as I’m trying to convey my disappointment in it. To be up front, I was one of the players that made their money back for the game on the Auction House selling their unused items so it wasn’t all a loss for me. In a twist of irony though, the only newsletter I ever got from Blizzard regarding Diablo 3 was an announcement they were doing away with the AH… the only good experience I had with the game that I can recall.

Classic arcade flight/combat game for PC (then Dreamcast, THEN arcade systems funnily enough). It looks great for its time and it is still satisfying as hell to play. In arcade mode, pick a plane/heli/ship of your choice and blow other ships up for as long as it takes them to blow you up. Periodically upgrades get dropped for you to collect, so depending on how good you are, arcade runs can go for a surprisingly long time.
What really stands out, however, is the campaign mode. It's maybe a little repetitive but the various scenarios you're placed in get challenging, like defending a runway from an onslaught of bombers. Story-wise, it's a game of its time. It features just about EVERY 90s alien movie trope imaginable:
Arctic-based invaders with no clearly-defined motive ✓
Man comes together around the world to get rid of the evil aliens ✓
Hilariously incapable military equipment somehow beats back well-equipped aliens through sheer will (and lasers) ✓
A sudden horrifying realisation that the scale of the problem is worse than first thought ✓
There's also a tactics mode but I've barely touched it since I'm not a strategy kind of guy. Sure it's fun though.
There's a fairly decent variety of maps, most of which are set on Earth but a couple are extra-terrestrial, and a LOT of craft to choose from. There's a good few attack helicopters, several real American fighters and bombers, a Russian MiG, and some pretty imaginative spacecraft drawing from both 50s and 90s alien motifs. Oh, and
.

Do you like Super Smash Bros.?  Well, did you an entire sub-genre is building around the basic concept?  Yep!  That's right, kids, and they're called Platform Fighters.  Brawlhalla is one of the best games to come out of it.
Pros:
- Four-player local and online multiplayer (your couch buddies can play online with you too!)
- Generally well-balanced
- Ranked and Unranked lobbies
- Silly custom gamemodes for when you want to mess around with friends
- In-depth training mode allows all characters to be tested and many stats seen (hitboxes, hurtboxes, damage, stun times...)
- The beginning of a competative scene (Devs holding $50,000 dollar tournament!)
- Keyboards are a viable control option
Cons:
- Some players may find the characters a bit bland compared to Smash
- Netcode is unforgiving towards bad Wi-Fi connections and (rarely) gets quite wonky
-Some players may find attack spam frustrating and hard to deal with
-Music is just... there.  Luckily it can be turned down so you can have your own in the background.
Yep, Brawlhalla is free to play.  That being said, it uses the only FTP model worth using.  All characters (or "Legends" as Brawlhalla calls them) are availible for free through in-game currency.  It doesn't even take much to collect in-game currency, either- just play the game and rack in the cash.  I was able to purchase my first new character for 3900 coins after a little under 10 hours.  Some of those hours were spent in the training room, so you could cut that down to less.  Speaking of the training room, all characters are availible to test there, so you can make sure you know you're making a good purchase.
You'll be fine.  Most people playing Brawlhalla have little to no experience playing Smash,  as all the good players are... playing Smash Bros.  Brawlhalla's mechanics are in no way a copy of those in Smash, anyways, though the basic idea is the same.  This genre is designed to be simple and fun to pick up and play while still containing the mindgames of more complex fighting games and combos for those who can learn them.
Your goal in Brawlhalla is to knock your opponent off of the stage.  Brawlhalla uses something of a reverse HP bar- it tracks how much damage a player has accumulated.  The more damage you've taken, the farther you fly when you're hit.  There is a great deal of arial combat in Brawlhalla, either due to knocking each other into the air or an agressor leaping right off of the stage to ensure his enemy can't get back.
Brawlhalla is primarily weapon based.  The weapon your character is holding is more important than the character itself.  Each character has two weapons they can equip out of a total of eight weapons.  The only things uniuqe to a character are their ground special attacks and their stats (Strength, Dexterity, Defense and Speed).
The weapons of Brawlhalla (eight currently) offer a nice diversity in playstyles.  Some, like the axe, swing in big arcs, making attacks easy to aim.  Others (the bow, for instance) have fairly odd hitboxes for some attacks that make practice key for simply connecting with the opponent on a regular basis.  The Lance is based entirely around punishing enemy mistakes.  Others, like the Daggers (or unarmed attacks) are very combo-heavy.
You're in for a shock.  There are no shields, and no grabs of any kind (including ledgegrabs).  Everyone can walljump.  Items are allowed in competetive play.  Characters will seem... bland.  As much as I love Brawlhalla, it's lacking the depth of Smash by a longshot- but in my opinion it's more balenced as a result.

First of all, let's get the whole microtransaction salt out of the way: if you don't like them- don't buy them! Simple! You'll find that most things in life work this way. Is the game bad because of the microtransactions? No, so it isn't fair to give the game a bad review for it. Most people don't even know it has microtransactions, and I finished the game with 48 unused praxis points, 30k credits and maxed out on everything I could carry, though I like to play minimalistically the first time. Now, onto actually reviewing the game, as you're supposed to do in these comments, instead of complaining about microtransactions.
Pros: In most ways the game has improved. The city hubs are bigger and have much more depth, tons of ministories, even more exploration, many ways of getting around. There are many more sidequests and they are much better than in HR (btw it'd be nice if they carried over to the next game). There are also many interesting unique interactions with characters you can find depending on where you are in the story. The new augs are fun, especially the blink (Icarus Dash), although I don't get the point of the overheating system. There is more "vertical" exploration now(roofs, apartments, floors, etc.), but it would've been even better if you could travel on as many roofs as in Dishonored with blink. It's also nice that you can finally take down enemies leaning on something from behind. The atmosphere is still great too, music is good, though fewer tracks that really stand out as opposed to the previous game. Graphics are great for those that can run it, but I didn't notice any optimization issues on the low settings I used for my crappy laptop, it ran about as well as I expected. They also clearly heard the complaints of pacifist not being an option in HR. Setting-wise the story is great as always, however, (onto cons)
Cons: The single biggest issue is, unfortunately, the main story line. It's not bad, it's still probably better than in most games, but it's much more predictable and straighforward than in the previous game, and some things didn't make a lot of sense. Major spoilers:
It also feels like not much progress was made, and the story was cut short. Minor spoilers:
I realize cliffhangers are great, but there were too many cliffhangers. Also, (fairly minor spoiler):
There are a few more minor story issues but this review is long enough already.
Lesser cons: Although you can do takedowns behind cover now, in some infrequent cases you still can't do it, e.g. if they're leaning on something rectangular like a bed, so you still have to walk up to them from the side which is risky.
Also, there are less interesting weapons, for example no laser or plasma rifles like in the previous game.
And with the new hacking look, the icons overlap and I often click the wrong thing.
TL;DR overall a very good game, a lot of work clearly went into the depth of the environment, but the main story, while not bad, isn't as good as in HR, and I think the side missions were actually better.

An interesting shooter RPG. The game provides you the tools to play however you want, and there are usually at least 3 or 4 discreet ways of accomplishing your objectives. The NPCs in the game react appropirately to the choices you make in your gameplay. The game does sort of funnel the player into a stealthy, less violent approach in many cases, at least in terms of encounter design.
The game looks very good, with stellar environment and art design, it is very clear a lot of care and attention went into crafting the world. The main characters are acted and emote well, but less important characters feel a bit stilted in their performance. Story is a bit lackluster but passable; however, many threads are left dangling at the end, likely in service of a sequel.
As of this writing, many of the technical issues and bugs have been solved for me but your experience may vary greatly. The game in its current state also requires a powerful modern GPU and lots of memory to run with any sort of eye candy on.
Microtransactions are in the game, but are very easy to ignore, and the game is clearly balanced around their non-existence. The game becomes quite easy if you attempt to min-max your character, but the game rewards a more considered, roleplaying approach; the gamne will let you play it like a video game, but it's more enjoyable if you attempt to roleplay.
Not a perfect game by any means, but I wholly enjoyed this cyberpunk adventure.

In all honesty, this is a really fun game.
The gameplay you expect from Deus Ex is here, and indeed it is refined to a spit-shine polish. There are many ways to tackle objectives, and many tools to assist you in attempting those methods - and, of course, there are backup methods for tackling whatever problems occur should you mess up in your endeavors. :P
Perhaps the most standout of the positives this game has to offer are its sidequests: I do not wish to say much in case of spoilers, but they're important, they're plentiful, they're unique, and importantly they're fun.
On the other side, the storyline does cut itself quite short. The game will likely take as long to complete as any other mainline entry in the Deus Ex franchise, but this is due to the massive (but singular) hub world and time spent exploring it and the sidequests within. I'm honestly okay with this, given the rest the game has to offer, but it would've been nice for the storyline to be more complete.
As of writing, I have not tackled Breach Mode or the Jensen Stories, nor have I touched anything to do with microtransactions.
And, yes, the game does have microtransactions - and they're appalling. You do not need me to add my voice singing their evils here: by the time you read this you've already had an earful.
That said, the game is properly balanced WITHOUT needing to purchase any DLC or microtransactions - they were apparently added quite late in the game's development at the behest of the producers, after the game had already been balanced.
I do recommend this game. While its story may not be as strong as it should, the environments are amazing, the sidequests powerful, and the gameplay has never shined brighter.
Just be sure never to touch the microtransactions, and if you're asked it might be wise to state you're against them. It's a disgusting business practice bordered over an excellent game: make it clear you're buying for the game, not for Square Enix's extremely poor attempts to milk fans of Eidos' work.

Pros:
+ Just as beautiful as the last game, and Graphically it is far better. Hair looks good, cloth looks real... very nice.
+ Gameplay is great, better in many ways. Combat feels quicker. Mechanics like energy usage are more manageable.
+ Exploration is rewarding, with loads of little nooks and crannies to find.
+ Dialogue, animation, and cutscene quality GREATLY improved.
+ You WILL get your money's worth. 33 hours of content for myself after trying to explore every nook and cranny, and I'm convinced I missed some things as well.
+ Very well optimized for PC.
Cons:
- Story was a massive let down. Very very interesting themes were displayed, but nothing substantial was done with them. A good deal of the characters felt flat and uninteresting, and the few that ARE interesting are given no room for learning about. Even worse...
- The ending. Jesus. Let's just say the people who say it "ended abruptly" are NOT kidding. Several large questions are hinted at... and not answered. No story resolution whatsoever in a game that promised we'd "go after" the people responsible. There is also a severe lacking of choice -- only two major choices are given to you, and only one actually changes much.
Questions not answered:
* Who are the people that are taking part in this conspiracy? We get names of a few, but encounter none of them personally.
* What EXACTLY happened to Jensen? Who is responsible for his AUGs? Hinted at heavily in the cliffhanger, but despite doing thorough investigation we learn nothing.
* Who is your partner really, and what about the Juggernaut Collective/Janus?
* ???? THE CLIFFHANGER SCENE ???? WHY WAS SHE INVOLVED AND WHY DID WE NOT CONFRONT HER???
- While the new augmentations are fun to use, the unfortunate side effect is that you're either super overpowered for fights, or the enemies make you feel like fights are a drag. This is ESPECIALLY true with the "Titan Armor" aug and the "Reflective Camo" stealth aug. I ended up avoiding these augs and fights that involved them.
- ONE BOSS FIGHT. ONE. No, I don't count the side missions or the minor enemy fights. ONE BOSS FIGHT. And it was SUPER anticlimactic.
- Prague was the only major city visited, which felt almost misleading due to how it was advertised, and downright unfaithful to how expansive the first Deus Ex was. While Prague felt enormous, the overall scale was honestly not too much larger, and I would've gladly given Prague up for new areas if given the choice.
- Controls are very clunky on PC, especially using Augmentations.
Overall:
I went between "Yes" and "No" on this one a lot. On the one hand, for both new players and Deus Ex fans, this is a very fun ride while it lasts. I believe the company should be praised for where it succeeded in improving upon the Deus Ex namesake. On the other hand, I've never felt this betrayed by a company I was SURE could do no wrong. There is no excuse for how this game's story progressed. I feel like I got a taste of the actual experience I wanted. And, at the end of the day, the "No" makes more sense, at least as a warning.
By all means, buy the game, but buy it knowing your heart is going to be torn out, especially if you liked the last game.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of The Mean Greens - Plastic Warfare. The Mean Greens - Plastic Warfare is a Team-Based Multiplayer, Third-Person Shooter that was released on Steam December 8th, 2015 by Publisher/Developer Virtual Basement LLC and Developer Code Headquarters LLC.
(NOTE: This game was reviewed using a key provided by the Developer and/or Publisher)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Fun little multiplayer shooter. Solid graphics and awesome sound. Just needs the community to grow!
3.5/5 Pick it up for that $10 it's at now or you'll regret it later.
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
The Mean Greens - Plastic Warfare is very much like the old Army Men game series, I think I had played it on the N64. It's essentially a really fun twist on your basic Team Based Multiplayer, Third-Person Shooter game. You are those little green army men that you see in toy stores all the time. You can cycle through any of the multiple weapon types available to your soldier (M-16, Shotgun, Sniper Rifle, Bazooka, Flamethrower) and go to war!! Now, I have not yet been able to get in a game on each map. Unfortunately, with it being so new, there are not as many players online as one would hope. Surely with time, that will change. As is, the game is absolutely gorgeous and really brings the scenes to life. You do get the feeling that you are just a little toy running around the house. The graphics are really good. The music is superb and really gets you in the mood to march to battle. There are several maps and each of these maps appear to have a different objective, aside from just the basic "kill the other team" approach. For example, in our Kitchen Run, we had to try and push the other Team's cup off the ledge. It really is your standard squad-based shooter, but with some really fun twists. A lot of the players I played with were into the nostalgia kick, as this game does call back to that Army Men series. I think as newer players pick this up, it's community will grow and make this a keeper. On release day, even with the frustration of waiting to get into games and finding enough people, I have enjoyed it enough to give a 3.5/5 as the graphics, sound and gameplay certainly warrant that and it just needs it's community to grow some to be able to stand out some more.
Happy Gaming!!!

Devil May Cry 4 felt like a flawless DMC game, until you progressed through the middle section and then you basically had to play the same levels all over again, in reverse order and battle the same bosses. I think this was because they rushed to publish it and thus ended up with half a game. Apart from this, everything else is great about it. Combat feels amazing, the story is what you would expect from DMC (slightly downgraded from 3, though), the characters are cool, entertaining and fun. Nero is a fresh new playable character, looking somewhat simple, but definitely has a steep lurning curve, Dante reigning chaos with his arsenal of devilish weapons, as well as his flexible style switching, which of course requires a bit of time and effort to master.
With the 2015's Special Edition  they've added new stuff, including 3 new playable characters (OP Vergil), but it's still the same repetitive game with no new levels whatsoever.
Overall, this is my all time favorite game of the genre, since it offers a remarkable balance of difficulty and fun, with a smooth and intrigue combat system, which is super rewarding once mastered, while at the same time playing as your favorite characters of the franchise.
I definitely recommend this game to anyone new to the Devil May Cry series, or even new to the action/hack n' slash genre, as well as to anyone who has played any of the other DMC games.

Soulstorm is pretty much a carbon copy of Dark Crusade. It's a standalone expansion to Dawn of War that adds two new races and using the new non-linear Grand Strategy style campaign map that THQ have grown so fond of.
Like in Dark Crusade there is really no learning curve for new players. You are thrown directly into the fray with no introduction to the gameplay, units or technologies and just have to wing it as best you can. Also like in Dark Crusade you can only use the new races in multi-player unless you already own the previous Dawn of War games which is really a bummer for anyone that buys this with the intention to play with friends.
The single-player is the continued development of Dark Crusade and the campaign works much the same way. The introduction of two new factions have made the map a bit bigger and this doesn't help as it only adds more grind. Playing through the single-player is essentially a progression of skirmish maps and it becomes boring, very fast. The stronghold maps are quite entertaining but they are the only fun thing in the campaign so you'll often find yourself dreading going into battle against yet another pointless incursion into your territory.
The new factions introduced in Soulstorm aren't quite as interesting as the ones introduced in Dark Crusade either. Firstly you have the Sisters of Battle which are essentially the super fanatical military arm of the "Ordo Hereticus" in the Empire of Man. Essentially they are the people you send when it's time to massacre your own people in great numbers. They have no remorse and will willing sacrifice anyone in the name of the Emperor. In game they play much like the Space Marines, in fact they are eerily similar in terms of unit composition to the regular Space Marines, only with a somewhat disturbing tendency towards pyromania.
The second new faction are the Dark Eldar which are what the Chaos Space Marines to the Eldar. Unfortunately they are not nearly as cool or as interesting. They feel like some Eldar went and smoked some Chaos but forgot to inhale. In terms of gameplay they are little more interesting than the Sisters of Battle with their fast moving units but they don't really add too much to the formula.
Both factions read really well in the WH40K universe but their implementation in the Dawn of War franchise feels really poor. They just lose so much of their personality when they don't have any proper campaigns, you never feel the fanaticism of the sisters or the sadomasochism of the Dark Eldar.
Sound and graphics are solid as always but as nothing new is being added it's beginning to feel a little stale.
Although this installment maintains that special WH40K feel that I enjoy so much it, much like the rest of the game, has begun to feel a little stale. No new story or interesting characters have been introduced since Winter Assault and there really isn't much left.
Soulstorm feels like a last attempt at squeaking out the last bit of money from Dawn of War before THQ moves on to making a proper sequel.

Felt like experiencing a movie actively, rather than passively. This game should be a case study on how to tell a story well through gameplay alone.
Controlling the 2 brothers is used masterfully in a way that lets you experience their relationship to one another and to other NPCs, moving beyond just showing these to you. Also, even though there is no (intelligible) dialog, you always know what is being said by interpreting gestures and tone.  Having to understand what everyone is saying by feeling and reacting to it yourself is another clever way of involving you in the story.
I thought controlling 2 characters at the same time would be complicated, but the game makes it easy.  Mostly this is because the only other thing you can do besides moving is a context-specific interaction with objects and characters.  The puzzles aren't hard either, and are mainly just obstacles that serve to convey the relationship between the 2 brothers and keep the game fun. You'll never get stuck, which is appropriate for this game - the journey is meant to flow.  That flow isn't impeded by the achievements either - they are mostly rewards for observing things not far off the main path, and none are missable because of chapter select.  Thus, completionists can sit back and enjoy the game, and return later to 100% it with minimal backtracking.  The game length is short, but exactly right - it took me 4.5 hours to finish w/ 9 achievements, and about 10 more minutes to return to a few places and 100%.
The scenery and music (ambient mostly) are beautiful and contribute to feeling like you're on an adventure.  Some spots were so nice that I ended up stopping and taking a screenshot.  The tone gets slightly dark in a few places, which didn't really bother me, but came as a surprise based on my initial expectations.  It's not really a kids game.  The story is a bit sad, but not in a manipulative way, more in a way that reveals that you played something you cared about.
Bottom line - set aside a few hours and play Brothers if you can appreciate a good story and don't always need fast-paced action or high-intensity puzzle solving.

Quick Summary: Short puzzle platformer focused on “show, don’t tell” plot, with controls that take some getting used to. You can finish the game in a few hours, and it will take close to that long to get used to controlling the two brothers.
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons has a fairly generic plot, where two brothers are going on a quest to save an injured family member, but nothing is really spelled out for you because the game uses a made up language and there are no subtitles. You literally don’t know what anyone is saying for the entire game. However, you can pretty much guess what’s going on from the context of each conversation. Your ultimate goal is to get to a magical tree and return with a healing potion.
First of all, as the game’s Steam page tells you Brothers requires a controller to play. In this case an Xbox 360 controller worked for me, and I read somewhere that Playstation controllers may have trouble. The reason for the controller requirement is that you’re controlling two characters at the same time with 2 different joysticks. This is not like Trine where you switch between controllable characters, you actually need to control both brothers on the screen simultaneously. If you’re a keyboard + mouse person like me you’ll have some trouble getting used to the control scheme, especially in the portions later on with simultaneous swinging/platforming.
Pros:
+Interesting concept of dual controls. Maybe I just haven’t played as many games as some people but I’ve never seen this before.
+The game’s puzzles are pretty intuitive, and you probably won’t need much in the way of hints to solve most of them.
+A touching story, despite not understanding any dialogue.
Cons:
-A very short game, with very little replay value. I beat it in about 3 hours and will probably never play it again now that I’ve experienced the story.
Overall the game is a fun, short diversion. The Steam score of “overwhelmingly positive” is probably due to everyone giving it thumbs for being “worth playing.” It isn’t the greatest game ever, but it’s a nice diversion for an afternoon.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is an story-based adventure game, developed by Starbreeze Studios and released in 2013. Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a game where you play as two sons who are sent to retrieve a cure for their very ill father. ...And that's the "elevator speech" version of it, read on for mechanics and my experience playing the game with a keyboard and mouse (It's definitely better with a controller, but doable with a keyboard).
I don't dare go into greater detail for the story of this game. You control both brothers throughout the game to get past obstacles. The character express themselves with physical gestures, and the tone of their voices, but they speak in a fictional language
. The game starts up very light heartedly, and then progressively grows more grim as you journey across the fairy tail land.
So as I said in my introduction, I played through this game completely with a keyboard and mouse... and my short summary is this: Don't. If there is ANY way for you to play this with a controller of any type, you should do that. Heck, maybe you can plug in a Joystick if you still have one of those laying around
.
The game controls very well, but ONLY if you're controlling one brother at a time. My keyboard starts to hang up if I try to move both. But I'm getting ahead of myself! You control the younger brother with
and the
, While the older brother is controlled with my old friend
and
.
For the first few levels of the game I realized my coordination wasn't nearly as good as it should have been, I kinda felt like I was playing a two player game by myself!
Then I came across a problem when I was trying to use the brothers to rotate an object, I had to press two keys with the older brother: WD, and hold the space bar. And hit two keys with the younger brother: Up Arrow, right Arrow... AND hold the CTRL key!
Now some of you out there already know what went wrong, but I went blissfully through my life not knowing I ever needed to press more keys at once then to write face rolling text: awkernhflkajnfaadf. The problem? "N-Key Rollover count"
. I can only hit so many keys on my cheap plastic input device, before my keyboard is like "nah, that's enough, don't be greedy".
Some people with mechanical keyboards with anti-ghosting or high N-Key Rollover won't notice anything, and then your only problem will be if your brain can process what you're trying to do.
. If you want to know if your computer will have problems with N-Key Roll over or ghosting, Microsoft has this nifty little website you can test it on:
Okay, as far as the puzzles themselves go... They're not particularly tricky, I did over think a few of them, but that's my own fault.
As a whole the game mechanics aren't revolutionary, sometimes challenging, but they're introduced quite well and are quite appropriate for the story, and they feel very good and you learn how to use both hands in a very different way from most puzzle games.
If you're reached it this far, you're probably either angry that I haven't really praised Brothers: A Tale of Two sons very much in this review, or you're thinking
Simple answer: This game is an experience.
I feel like I should slap myself for a cheap cop out, but that's the best answer I think I can give. Coming into this game I had heard some very high praise for the game, many people heralding it as one of the best games of 2013, many also saying it's their favorite game.
I had high expectations, but I wasn't quite sure what to expect... I didn't expect to laugh, and then feel chilling fear, then dread, then to burst into tears, regain composure, then to weep. Damn it my eyes are watering just writing this much. Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a fantastic game and I highly recommend to anyone.
It connects and hits strongest to people who have brothers and sisters. At a certain age it becomes even more effective... Being the eldest. I have two younger brothers, and I empathized most with the older brother, but I think it doesn't make much difference which age in your family you are, regardless of whom you identify with, the story will move you, and I've said enough.

An awesome game if you can get a friend or two to play it with. These kinds of games, to me, are only fun when you have others to play with. If not, they seem kind of empty and dull. One of my friends that I bought a copy for stopped playing after a short while and never got through the first half of Act 2. I played for a bit, but lost interest shortly after because of it. Online multiplayer is a coin toss as servers hosted are either private, specific mod enabled, or cheatery.
However, the game itself is great. I played by myself for a bit and got to Act 3. There's a good variety of mobs and bosses. Also, the replay value of the game is decent too. The layout changes when you create a new character or re-roll the world making it seem pretty new. New landmarks appear or move around a bit. The items and shops are great in-game. The balance is pretty reasonable but can be broken by using certain items together. I had a lower level 20-ish ranged class with dual pistols that would roll over anything up until around the 40's because of certain sockets that were stacked thanks to being able to transfer items between characters. Hardcore mode and mods from the steam workshop fix this up pretty quick.
If you don't mind playing solo, this game is great. It can be compared to Diablo 2 styled gameplay. The graphics are a bit more colorful and less grim, but the feeling is there. If you have some reliable friends to play with, you'd probably have a much better time and get to the fun bits that really start happening around the end of Act 2 and into Act 3.

To put in in short, MD feels a bit brighter than HR in terms of surroundings and ambiance, but it has lots of story to balance it out.
If you play to complete the game in a short timeframe, i can understand somewhat that people feel it´s too short, but it´s another thing if you roeplay it and play it on a higher difficulty setting. Sprinting everywhere and using the mechanics as a "game" will just shorten it for you, so take it slow and the story gets deeper and more rewarding.
Pros:
- Upgraded visuals and sounds + much more story than in HR.
- More fluid combat.
- A big controll improvement.
- Bigger playfield and progression options.
- Upgraded Augs and ways to use them
- A game system that actually makes you consider both weapsons and stealth alterations.
Cons:
- Even with RP playstyle and completing as much as possible, it is still "a bit" on the short side.

Deus Ex Mankind Divided, was one of my most anticipated games of 2016. I love Deus Ex Human Revolution, played it at least 5 or so times. Mankind Divided certainly improves on many aspects of Human Revolution, but unfortuneately doesn't do everything right.
The gameplay is the most improved feature of this title, as you can truly be a augmented pacifist, or an augmented sociopath, as you see fit. Any situation can be tackled as you want to, to fit your playstyle. Environments and missions reflect this, with open and varied layouts, that promote the exploration that is synonmous with the Deus Ex series. Tackling things quietly is incredibly rewarding, however I will mention that the gunplay has significantly improved, so that combat feels rewarding and versatile. Mankind Divided also never penalises you for your choices, whether you are ghosting through entire areas, or killing anything in sight, you never feel like the developers push you into the "right" decision. However, there just isn't enough gameplay. There aren't enough missions. I finished this game feeling like half was cut, that either DLC will be released, or a sequel sometime in the next few years.
The story in Mankind Divided, was marketed as a massive conspiracy, that we as the player would take apart. When in reality, we only really solve one of the issues, and don't really have any conclusive answers to the story. This is what has most dissappointed me, that the story could of been so good, when you get to the final area of the game, if that had been a new hub, I would of been thrilled. But when the credits rolled I just felt, underwhelmed. This isn't to say the story of Mankind Divided is bad, it just, it could of been so much more. I wish it had another 20 hours of story content, but I suppose we will see whether it is a DLC release in the next few months.
Does this game deserve your time and money? If you're a fan of Human Revolution, then gameplay wise, it greatly improves on the previous itteration. But the story is lacking. It needs more. The main story needs to be a conspiracy tale, filled with twists and turns, deceit and betrayl...not DLC or cliffhangers for future titles. I won't complain about the microtransactions, as personally, I didn't find them intrusive, I could never have noticed, but I will concede, that I wish that the developer had put more effort into the story. Perhapns my best recommendation is this: wait for a sale. If you truly want to play it, you will enjoy it. But for what is here, as good as it is, Deus Ex Mankind Divided feels like half a game. A really good half of a game, but a half none the less.

This is a game that makes itself difficult to recommend.
If you've gone through other reviews, you probably know the graphics are great, the gameplay is solid. On an ATI card I had no crashing or game-stopping problems as of 9/12. A lot of people are upset about the microtransactions, and while on principle we can make hay out of this all day, it has zero impact on the meat of the game - I wouldn't know it existed if I hadn't read about it.
Having said that, what ultimately soured me on the game was the multitude of minor and thoughtless, but ultimately endless, fumbles on execution.
Acceptable gameplay hours, but the story doesn't possess the scope or heights of previous entries. They're obviously aiming for an arc, but it leaves what is presumably the first part of it fairly mundane and disappointing. In their favor, the side missions are far more fleshed out than previous ones, but their success only serves to underscore the mediocrity of the primary plot.
Having only a single hub leaves you running into later areas early and looting them dry. I couldn't count the number of times I had to go back to a building with enemies who seem not at all surprised about every door and computer being unlocked, every security system being disabled, and a pile of discarded items in the middle of the floor.
Gameplay achievements can be broken by storyline choices. If you're going for a no-alert run, google GARM and foxiest of the hounds or you'll wind up with 25 hours of wasted effort. Further story and endgame achievements are locked behind a mandatory credit roll that otherwise has to be task killed to stop - to make it worse, it's nothing but arrogant pictures of the devs being drunk and/or stupid.
Tons of lazy bugs. Dumpsters that go flying when you brush against them. Knocked out enemies that continue to groan and contort minutes after being knocked out. AI that's confused on when it should and shouldn't be upset.
Overall, it's a sophmore effort. Worth $30 at most, I have hopes that the devs will learn some humility from this and try harder on the next installment.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided (DE:MD) - TL;DR: 6/10. I'm disappointed, really, *really* disappointed.
A game I was exceptionally excited for, having greatly enjoyed Human Revolution (DE:HR) in 2011.  It began with a reasonably enjoyable (but fairly linear) excursion mission to Dubai, but if I'm honest I was underwhelmed, very very underwhelmed.
Admittedly I had defrosted a bit a few hours into the game and then I fell into the true ebb and flow of Deus Ex, stealthily ninja'ing my way through environments, hiding unconscious meatbags in ventilation systems, and generally embracing the Cyberpunk thematic.  Then it ended, just like that.
Perhaps I've been spoiled by the narrative epics of games like The Witcher 3, and perhaps games have just evolved that little bit more since DE:HR's release in 2011.  Either way, I was exceedingly upset when the credits rolled, and my main thought was: Is that it?  Is that the best you can do?  It felt exactly like a game that had been cut in half for either upcoming DLC or for the almost inevitable "sequel" (i.e. other half).
Without entering into spoiler territory, the main plot lines converge into a sort-of melting pot of mediocre stew, and all of those delicious side missions plot lines that had seemed important, weren't or were never seen to conclusion.  Cue anger and disbelief.
By the end I couldn't shake the nagging feeling that this is a 2011 game released in 2016 with a lick of polish and paint, and I kept hoping that things would improve as the game went on.  I truly believed that I was about to enter the Rabbit Hole into a whole new world, but it turns out that there isn't a hole, there isn't even a rabbit.
Despite enjoying the mechanical aspects of the game, it would be really difficult to fully recommend DE:MD at its full asking price.  Like me you'll likely still enjoy the mechanics of the game, and yes the world of Deus Ex is still fascinating, despite its unfulfilled form in this iteration.
If you think it's going to get better, it isn't.  If you think it's going to get deeper, it won't.  Take it at face value and don't be a sucker like me. Buy it when it is discounted.
6/10.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is going to be a very appropriate name for this game, but not for the reasons Sqeenix thinks.
So here's my thing, I love all the Deus Ex series. I don't hate the original though I haven't been able to bring myself to play through it just because of it's age. I love the idea though, the whole super future cyborg guy being all sneaky or going in guns blazing, having multiple paths to different solutions. So where I'm going to be coming from is someone who is probably going to buy anything Deus Ex related, regardless of how much of a cheap cash grab it is as long as there's that central story and those game elements I love. The visuals in this are top notch, the sound, every single scene is jam packed wall to wall with absolutely incredible detail. This is Deus Ex.
Now as for this game, you may hear it's less gameplay than Human Revolution. The story isn't as over the top illuminati style grab-your-tinfoil-hat. There's a lot of side areas and things that aren't integral to the main plot. I'd say all of these things are true. None of that is nessesarily bad and as for actual game length? I have a hard time telling for sure. It took me about 2 days with HR and about 2 days with MD. The game isn't divided up by minibosses or as many areas so it may seem shorter.
One thing though that certainly is evident in this game though, the ending isn't the ending. No spoilers here but it's clear this is the first chapter of something. I notice this is the first game to have the 'Deus Ex Universe' tag on it, implying there is going to be more to come. Yearly releases with more parts of the story? DLC for the clearly missing additional chapters? Squeenix, you play a very dangerous game here, clearly not learning from the backlash over Day 1 DLC they already dealt with. I do not worry for the sake of Squeenix or Eidios or even the players. I worry for the future of my Deus Ex!
I likely would eat up a yearly or even biannual release of continued story. I would buy it and play it. It's better than what most companies do with DLC, tacking on 10 more levels and asking you to play the same game again. It could work if each game was as solid as this one actually is. The problem is I know most players won't do this and most players will raise absolute hell when they feel a single game is chopped into pieces and resold piecemeal, which is exactly what Sqeenix is stupidly and blindly doing.
tl;dr I can't wait to play Chapter II of Mankind Divided.
