What I like:
(1) Interface - one of the easier ones to learn. (2) Tutorial - it could be more clear, but for the most part, it's straightforward if you're paying attention. (3) The general idea - as a long-time fan of the Tropico franchise, it was nice to see Kalypso trying something similar, yet new. (4) Politics - having to work the game's political system to stay in power and pass legislation requires cunning and strategy, making it easily the best part of the game next to building stuff.
What I don't like:
(1) Game crashes - that speaks for itself, except to say they're mercifully infrequent. (2) Financial aspect - it seems the only way to increase revenue is to up the tax rate, putting your city at a 70% or higher rate by the end of the game. Income seems unaffected by population, and when switching a district to medium or high density, the revenue almost never outweighs the costs, regardless of the demand for new space, which is almost a new problem itself with how the zoning demand meters never seem consistent or accurate. (3) Slow - due to the issue with how finances run, progressing and upgrading the city go very slowly. I've completed several campaigns with different families, but I never once had the revenue to risk paying for high density. If there's a way to do it consistently without following a strict strategy, someone please tell me and I'll try it out and edit this review accordingly. Otherwise, there's something seriously wrong with the financial aspect of this game. Comparitively, (4) the political consequences always seem a bit too easy, and fixing it would not be a simple matter of making things harder. There should be more options to really make it the complex challenge the game suggests it is (more details within the available options also wouldn't hurt).
Bottom line: If the developers fixed zoning demand, political consequences and options, revenue/cost issues, and the crashes, it would be a much more playable/replayable game. Until then, I've played about as much as I'm interested in playing it, and at 15 hours of play, I can't say it's worth buying.

The best way to summarise this game would be "good but repetitive" and that applies not only to the combat, which is the best thing this game has to offer, but to the whole thing.
The story is repetitive since you basically play through the same missions twice from slightly different perspectives.
The music (Nero's fight theme specially), even though i thought it was pretty good, soon became repetitive since it's reused for every battle.
The gameplay is repetitive because even though the combat is very deep, the difficulty and enemies make it trivial.
To top all this, the level design is pretty bland, the camera is annoying when trying to exit/enter a room or corridor, the characters are ok and the story itself is uninteresting, in many of these ways DMC 3 was better, but DMC 4 makes up for it by improving the combat, which is really fun once you figure how each character handles before slowly becoming tedious once you are satisfied.
Overall, i still feel i can safely recommend this game. Buy it on sale and it's an excellent time killer, but i believe the people who will enjoy this game the most is those who play games to master new systems and increase their own skills at it in order to feel satisfied, those who prioritise gameplay above all else. If you are one of them then this game will have great potential, and that is the reason i nominated this game to the “CRY HAVOC AND LET SLIP THE DOGS OF WAR” award for the Steam Awards 2017 (i know the game released in 2015 but i played it this year so shut up).

To be honest the only reason I bought this game was because it was 59 cents on sale and I had 60 cents, but boy it sure surprised me.
First off the music was rather surprising. It has kind of a grim undertone while still being lighthearted, pretty hard to pull off but it's done well and fits the game perfectly. Huge credit to Anthony Septim. My favorite was the Manor song, and for such a small Indie game i'm quite (happily) surprised the soundtrack was so nice and peaceful.
For a pixelated game it's pretty well done graphically. I guess "picturesque" is the only way to describe it. It's fun to look at most of the time, and there's a looooooot of weird stuff thrown into the mix.
The game itself is fun, and it keeps throwing new things at you every few minutes. It keeps a really nice pace, the puzzles aren't incredibly hard and finding new areas isn't too much of a challenge, but at the same time you're going to have to search. Your curiousity is going to get you lost a few times. As I played along I would notice a new item that wasn't there before and say "ooo whats this" and click it, only to get thrown in a completely new area that I didn't want to go to. It's the perfect balance of being long enough for you to appreciate each area, while also not boring you to death.
If I had to compare it to other games, try and think of a mixture between Limbo and Pixeljunk Eden. That doesn't really paint a good picture but that's because this game is unique.
If you're looking for a logical game with puzzles and enemies, this game isn't for you. It's more for the aesthetic and strangeness, and that's why it's fun to play. Some people call this art, some call it stupid. We all have our opinions. I, for one, enjoyed every moment, and I added 5$ to my steam account so I can buy this for a few of my friends who I know will enjoy it.
Is it worth 6$? Maybe not since it's so short, but for 59 cents, it's worth every penny.

First I will mention the bundled Incoming game, the parent of Incoming Forces. It was an amazing game at the time when it came out and was lots of fun. You play as a human soldier defending Earth from aliens. However it aged pretty badly, not only in the graphics sector but in OS compatibility. While I was able to run the game I always had some upper bar or other obstruction over the top of the game screen. On top of that the controls are terribly clunky especially with mouse so just go full keyboard control instead. So perhaps try it out but move on to the much better sequel Incoming Forces where this time you are in control of an alien pilot. The story is not complex but somewhat cute and quite enjoyable. The range of vehicles expands, you get to control turrets, tanks, artillery and a range of air fighters. Missions are replayable separately and have a High Score system. The transition between vehicles is really smooth and controls are great. The graphics are a bit clunky but that does not matter in this case. However only 16 (mostly short) missions is not that much. Overall a fun shooter with a big range of vehicles and nice (although cheesy) story. Recommended.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided (DE:MD) - TL;DR: 6/10. I'm disappointed, really, *really* disappointed.
A game I was exceptionally excited for, having greatly enjoyed Human Revolution (DE:HR) in 2011.  It began with a reasonably enjoyable (but fairly linear) excursion mission to Dubai, but if I'm honest I was underwhelmed, very very underwhelmed.
Admittedly I had defrosted a bit a few hours into the game and then I fell into the true ebb and flow of Deus Ex, stealthily ninja'ing my way through environments, hiding unconscious meatbags in ventilation systems, and generally embracing the Cyberpunk thematic.  Then it ended, just like that.
Perhaps I've been spoiled by the narrative epics of games like The Witcher 3, and perhaps games have just evolved that little bit more since DE:HR's release in 2011.  Either way, I was exceedingly upset when the credits rolled, and my main thought was: Is that it?  Is that the best you can do?  It felt exactly like a game that had been cut in half for either upcoming DLC or for the almost inevitable "sequel" (i.e. other half).
Without entering into spoiler territory, the main plot lines converge into a sort-of melting pot of mediocre stew, and all of those delicious side missions plot lines that had seemed important, weren't or were never seen to conclusion.  Cue anger and disbelief.
By the end I couldn't shake the nagging feeling that this is a 2011 game released in 2016 with a lick of polish and paint, and I kept hoping that things would improve as the game went on.  I truly believed that I was about to enter the Rabbit Hole into a whole new world, but it turns out that there isn't a hole, there isn't even a rabbit.
Despite enjoying the mechanical aspects of the game, it would be really difficult to fully recommend DE:MD at its full asking price.  Like me you'll likely still enjoy the mechanics of the game, and yes the world of Deus Ex is still fascinating, despite its unfulfilled form in this iteration.
If you think it's going to get better, it isn't.  If you think it's going to get deeper, it won't.  Take it at face value and don't be a sucker like me. Buy it when it is discounted.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is going to be a very appropriate name for this game, but not for the reasons Sqeenix thinks.
So here's my thing, I love all the Deus Ex series. I don't hate the original though I haven't been able to bring myself to play through it just because of it's age. I love the idea though, the whole super future cyborg guy being all sneaky or going in guns blazing, having multiple paths to different solutions. So where I'm going to be coming from is someone who is probably going to buy anything Deus Ex related, regardless of how much of a cheap cash grab it is as long as there's that central story and those game elements I love. The visuals in this are top notch, the sound, every single scene is jam packed wall to wall with absolutely incredible detail. This is Deus Ex.
Now as for this game, you may hear it's less gameplay than Human Revolution. The story isn't as over the top illuminati style grab-your-tinfoil-hat. There's a lot of side areas and things that aren't integral to the main plot. I'd say all of these things are true. None of that is nessesarily bad and as for actual game length? I have a hard time telling for sure. It took me about 2 days with HR and about 2 days with MD. The game isn't divided up by minibosses or as many areas so it may seem shorter.
One thing though that certainly is evident in this game though, the ending isn't the ending. No spoilers here but it's clear this is the first chapter of something. I notice this is the first game to have the 'Deus Ex Universe' tag on it, implying there is going to be more to come. Yearly releases with more parts of the story? DLC for the clearly missing additional chapters? Squeenix, you play a very dangerous game here, clearly not learning from the backlash over Day 1 DLC they already dealt with. I do not worry for the sake of Squeenix or Eidios or even the players. I worry for the future of my Deus Ex!
I likely would eat up a yearly or even biannual release of continued story. I would buy it and play it. It's better than what most companies do with DLC, tacking on 10 more levels and asking you to play the same game again. It could work if each game was as solid as this one actually is. The problem is I know most players won't do this and most players will raise absolute hell when they feel a single game is chopped into pieces and resold piecemeal, which is exactly what Sqeenix is stupidly and blindly doing.
tl;dr I can't wait to play Chapter II of Mankind Divided.

For the most part, they succeeded. It really is a pretty game, Prague is nicely done (albeit more Russian than Czech at times - wtf), the hub is a joy to wander through and explore, Jensen is truly a one-man army at this point, especially in New Game+, the possibility to complete an objective in a handful of ways is still here..BUT..
I did say the game was pretty, but I do not understand how it is possible to release a game with a six month delay (for improving it, nevertheless!!), and for it to still be buggy and unoptimized. Now mind you, it wasn´t that bad for me, I was actually more pleasantly surprised than I expected, but for others..read the reviews.This is simply unacceptable. Look at Mad Max for a butter smooth launch (for most people). That´s how you ship a game!
Secondly, the story, while fun and intriguing, leaves more questions than answers and ends rather..abruptly at the end. I mean I get it if the Jensen saga is meant to be a trilogy (is it?), but seriously, was stuff cut out just for insta-sequel purposes? I felt I had more closure in Human Revolution, to be honest.
Thirdly, F*UCK you, Square Enix, just F*UCK you..Microtransactions in Deus Ex? You spit in the face of fans, who are with the series since day one. I don´t care that they are not neccessary (at all, actually), but they ARE THERE. Breach? In essence, pointless..Competing scores with others in a Deus Ex game??Season Pass - one time consumables? Are you re*arded? The 2 stories for Jensen better be good (I did not purchase the Season Pass, btw).
To sum up: Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a great game, make no mistake about that. It begs to be played repeatedly and differently, encourages experimentation and rewards the player. That is what I wanted, to play an improvement of an allready exceptional game (Human Revolution). I got that. So hats off to the developer team. But a BIG F*CK you to the publisher. **YOU DO NOT NEED A CONTROLLER TO PLAY THIS** (I noticed the main page's warning that you did-- I played entirely on keyboard quite succesfully.)
I am moved to leave my first Steam review after playing this :) Brothers - A tale of two sons is short, but doesn't overstay its welcome. I played alone on keyboard, and it was strange at first controlling two characters. This, however, immerses you fully in the brothers' experience-- while it could easily be a two player game (via keyboard or controller (s)), I felt connected with both characters as we sometimes struggled our way through the innovative platforming. This ultimately made for a much more impactful story, I feel.
It's an "easy" game-- paths are fairly straightforward, boss fights are briefly memorable even if they sometimes rely on tropes, and any LOTR fan might roll their eyes towards a scene at the very end-- but poignant. At times dark, at turns fanciful, this game continually filled me with a sense of childlike wonder at the environments and creative "two-player" controls. It's very linear, but worth a replay for any achievements you may have missed, if like me, you weren't quite sure what path to travel but found yourself too caught up in the next scene to go back. All the achievements are tucked away off the main path, though not hard to find.
There is story to spoil, so I won't touch on plot. The theme is vaguely Norse, and artfully rendered throughout. The dialogue is unsubtitled gibberish, but that only adds to the character. Overall, Brothers is an evocative, adventurous title that is worth picking up on sale (if only for the short runtime).

Having played Torchlight I I decided to give Torchlight II a chance.
While the games are basically the same, Torchlight II has many improvements and additions that make the game bigger and better not only than Torchlight I but better than Diablo III.
Unlike the original game, Torchlight II features 4 classes: Embermage, Outlander, Berserker and Engineer. The first 2 (Embermage and Outlander) are basically Alchemist and Vanquisher from the original game but with a better, bigger and a more complex skill tree and more interesting attributes, while the last 2 are both a fork of the original Destroyer but with different specializations.
Generally speaking, the gameplay remained the same the most important changes being triggered by the fact that every character now has a more complex skill system (every class has 3 skill trees that can be combined any way you want), allowing you to make different builds and adding something that was missing from the original game: replay value.
Another big change is fact that Torchlight II, unlike Torchlight I, is open world. You can go everywhere in the given world and, once you've discovered an area on the map, you can teleport there any time you want.
This feeling of a bigger, open world game is also given by the bright and cheerful colors used and the different music style, as opposed to the dark, self-contained yet peaceful artistic direction, level design and themes used in the original game.
The use of Steam Workshop also adds a lot to the game and offers a big selections of mods that are one click away and ready to change the way you play the game.
In conclusion, Torchlight II looks refined and polished and offers many hours of gameplay and replay value.
The only downside I could find is that all that cozy self-contained small town yet dark feeling is gone but I guess you cannot have a cozy self-contained open world game.

Torchlight 2 is a fast-paced action multiplayer role playing game, similar to diablo 3. It has a colourful art style with smooth animations and 'click to move' movement. Torchlight 2 greatly improves on its predecessor Torchlight 1 through more gameplay options and content however still has some problems such as the lack of endgame due to the improved but still few build paths.
In Torchlight 2, the aim is to stop 'the alchemist' from taking over the land in which you must complete a series of 'acts' which all include a large amount of dungeons and maps which are randomnly generated. The story however will only take a few hours to complete on easy difficulty but will be increasingly challenging the higher the difficulty. After you complete the story you are given the option to replay it at a higher difficulty or enter the 'clockwork' which is like a HUB where you choose various dungeons to clear and recieve rarer and stronger loot to upgrade your character. Overall the story is interesting and gives a sense of urgency to the player and will provide entertainment for a couple of hours until you complete it.
However in Torchlight 2 the story is not its main focus, but rather its combat and rewards for completing dungeons. Torchlights combat is smooth, flashy and makes grinding fun due to its fast-paces and simple design. 3 Skills builds exist for all classes in which you can only undo up to your 5th choice making choosing your skills an important decision. Stat build also exist which improve your general strength. Rewards are recieved by killing monsters  which will drop gold, potions and items. Items come in various rarities with rarer items being stronger which you can upgrade by inserting gems (also dropped by monsters). The mentioned drops can also be found in chests found across the maps. In total the combat system is great and but lacks variety and the items dropped dont have much of a power up feel.
Overall Torchlight 2 is a fun game to play while it lasts due to its great combat and beautiful artstyle. This is also supported by its multiplayer compatability and various skill options allowing for customisation of your character. This however does not last long due to its lacklustre end game which grows full and boring relatively quickly (yes, there are mods available but even they dont last very long and gameplay is in all intents and purposes the same). I have mixed feelings about this game. The game was enjoyable at first, but quickly became a rehashed hack-and-slash rpg without a compelling story or interesting combat system.
There was pretty good mod support from the community in making new content like different classes and such, and the games style had a very diablo-esque feeling to it. The animation was pretty and fun, but not overly cartoony. Most of the time whenenver you're moving through an area you're fighting a horde or something. However, I have no idea what the story is about. At all. For all the time I spent playing it, I never could care less about the actual world around me. It never really tried to draw me in. It just kind of existed. The quests were rather boring and the gameplay was really repetitive. The item system basically just spawned junk constantly on drops, and most of the time even if i got a 'good' weapon, it had very similar stats to a lower tier weapon. After a while it just felt like I was farming for bad items to sell, and everytime you go back to your safe zone to buy/sell, all the monster zones reset, so you have to grind your way through them again. Boss battles were fun, though, and a bit challenging, so that was good. After a while I just stopped because I felt like I was playing this game to grind for levels and items because I didn't care about the story progression at all.
Pros:
-Good class ranges
-Constant fighting when walking around areas
-Good modding community
-Boss battles were enjoyable
-Abilities use is fluid and there seemed to be decent diversity in ability paths
Neutra:
-Game art was simpler, not necessarily to be cute or cartoony or crisp and serious.
-Dungeons and plain areas were somewhat varied and had diversity, but the environment wasn't very egnaging.
Cons:
-Story was very dry and unengaging
-Items all felt the same despite strenghts. Stat boosts and abilities felt lackluster
-Very repetitive fighting
-Boring quests to go along with a boring story line
-Too much farming for exp and items
Overall: 6.3/10
And that's being generous. If you want to get this game I would wait for a steam sale. It's fun at first but quickly gets old, and I think there are other games that did a better job at accomplishing what this game tried to do.

Dreaming Sarah is an adventure/exploration game that is short enough to play in an evening while simultaneously delivering a fragmented (but by no means boring) storyline highly up for interpretation.  Inspired by Japanese psychological/horror indie game Yume Nikki, it has a similar feel. Other than the obvious being that they are both exploration games taking place in a dream world, both have surreal music, at times disturbing art choices in character design, and a female protagonist with no dialogue. Also, both have artifact collection, with the game ending basically when you finish collecting all of them.
Whereas I enjoyed this game, I did feel as though it was just a lighter, more simplified, version of Yume Nikki in a lot of ways. Although they share many characteristics, Dreaming Sarah lacked the same amount of depth, and did not do much in adding to the genre.
That being said, the creator is upfront about it being a major source of inspiration for him, and there is at least one easter egg of Madotsuki's shirt's symbol on a bulletin board in one of the locations (there might be more, but I was giddy to find this one).
For the price it's being sold at, I would recommend this game. It's fun, doesn't have any boring tutorials, and most of all is an experience in surrealism that toys with your psyche.

Of the series, I've only played Mortal Kombat 9 prior to this, on the PC. I loved it. The story, the feel of the combat, Johnny Cage. So I was pretty pumped to hear that MKX was on its way.
At release and for the next year and a half, there were issues with netcode and performance on middle of the range computers. There was a recent patch that really fixed a lot of the performance drops I was noticing. I am running what would now be classed as a low end machine, and it can still run the game at 1920x1080 on low with some spikes here and there, where as before I had to lower the resolution significantly. Apparently the netcode is much better, but I'm in Australia, so no amount of software wizardry will help our small population and crap internet.
As for the combat, it is so damn smooth. I loved 9 because I thought it felt great, but now that feels slow and clunky. Everything just flows. You will need to play to understand what I mean, as I won't be able to get it across in words. The characters are quite varied, allowing for all manner of play styles. Each character has 3 variations (and one has an extra secret one you can go and hunt down if you are interested), which really allows you to tailor a character to your needs. The DLC characters are quite expensive, but they are good fun. Kombat Pack 2 is especially good. Try to nab them on special, but really they are not crucial; the game will still be very satisfying without them, and you won't feel underpowered against people using them.
The story is good, but didn't feel as good as 9 for some reason. The cut scenes were done really well, and bridged into combat nicely. The living towers are a good addition, but it is a bit of a shame that the Challenge Tower has been removed. Another feature I miss is having tag teams so that you could coop. Otherwise everything else in this game has just been made bigger and better.
Graphically, the game is incredible. Even on low settings it looks really good. The environments are really detailed, and the particle effects have some really nice qualities to them, such as their patterns, lighting, etc. The Fatalities and the X-Ray moves are all pretty full on, and the Brutalities are nice to have back. The animations during combat are really smooth as well, a lot of time was clearly put in to making them feel good.
Overall, for fighting fans, definitely grab the game, especially now that it has been fixed up. If you are interested in getting into fighting games, this is a good place to start I think, as it can be a bit more forgiving on combos than other fighters. If you aren't interested in fighters, don't get this game, it will offer nothing you want.

I'm a beta tester for The Mean Greens (this includes testing future content), if that matters at all.
I'm a person who doesn't really like shooters at all. There were a few exceptions for me (Halo 2, Army Men: Sarge's Heroes 1 and 2), but I couldn't get into any of them. The Mean Greens, however, tapped into the part of me that remembers the aforementioned 3D0 Army Men Sarge's Heroes games [and just to be clear, I played the PlayStation versions of those games; I hated the N64 versions...), and reminded me that these games don't have to be all doom-and-gloom, ultra-realistic, or boring and gritty-looking.
Aesthetically, the game looks gorgeous, running at a full 1080p 60FPS [when on max settings]. The environments are just like the ones you'd find 2-inch tall plastic toys playing in. The kitchen, a bathtub, a living room, a table, a fish tank, a refridgerator... it's all here and accounted for. They're all full of wackiness and creativity, and I loved every single map.
Gameplay-wise, it reminded me so much of (you know the games by now). There's new stuff like sprinting, an admittedly better aiming system (simply hold down the right mouse button), and it controls very, very nicely. I was playing with both a controller (a PS4/DualShock 4 controller) and a mouse and a keyboard. While I personally prefer the latter, using a controller, at least a DS4 one, feels very natural for this game, and it works as well as any other shooter.
The online itself was fun, fast and frantic. The maps are small (or, um, a little smaller than big? Not that small but still big? How to word this... but they're by no means super small or compact) but that doesn't make them any less fun. Plus, in each map, there's a different objective. In one map, you have your average "slayer", but in another, you'll be having to thaw out a dinosaur frozen in ice (using a flamethrower) before your opposing team thaws theirs first. Every map doesn't have the same mode, which is really refreshing for a genre like this. The different modes were all fun to play and I didn't really have complaints with any of them.
But at this point this may all seem like blind praise, but these are the words I'm sticking to. Obviously, I may have a small nostalgic bias because of how much this game reminded me of my beloved Sarge's Heroes games, but nevertheless, The Mean Greens delivers in all aspects of fun, entertainment, action, and everything it's trying to achieve.
I had an awesome time playing the game and I hope a lot of other people will, too.
Seriously, just go play it. This really isn't something you want to miss out on.

Holy Mother of God. What a game...
As many others, I started playing without expecting too much. I always liked games where you have a companion on your journeys, though (as ICO, the unfairly bashed Prince of Persia 2008 and, for those old enough to remember it, Bermuda Syndrome, among the others). I almost immediately found myself immersed in the world, and growing fonder with the two main characters.
The game starts with the very sad image of a kid still mourning his dead mother, who died drowning without the kid being able to save her. Without a single spoken word (or at least, without one you can understand) you soon find out that his father is very ill as well, when the kid's brother rushes him out and asks for your help to bring him to a doctor. There you discover that the only way to save him is to find a miracle cure somewhere in the land.
This is the beginning of the game and introduces the mechanics: a ICO-like game where you actually control both characters at the same time, in order to have them proceed together. The young and older brothers have different skills. which you'll have to take into account to solve the puzzles along the way. And the journey itself (and the choice of words here is not random: it DID remind me of Journey at times, especially the gorgeous views and the spectacular soundtrack) is amazing. Funny, exciting, charming, melancholic: every emotion is out there, in a turmoil that won't leave you until the very end.
I won't tell you a single thing of what happens: other reviews do, and I believe they can spoil the experience for you. Just go ahead and play it. It's short, not very hard, but rewarding, and you'll definitely remember it for a long time when it ends.

- Leaving a poor review because of micro transactions and a cut short story -
The new Jew Sex is really quite good gameplay-wise, but the story is weaker than anticipated and the narrative is slightly more convoluted (despite ultimately having a pretty simple premise). It's like the writers came up with a really basic idea for how the game's story would play out, and just spend a lot of time throwing transparent misinformation at you to make it seem more deep.
The hub was also a bit boring, and the poor lip syncing really did make a lot of cutscenes very hard to concentrate on.
That said, the gameplay has been improved since Human Reproduction and is pretty spot-on and does a good job of distracting you from the dulcit story line. I just wish they'd concentrate on making a solid title that sells well rather than stuffing it full of micro transactions to the point that it has a negative impact on everything.
A good 30-40 hours of fun though (I spent around 25 hours playing the story/side quests - not Breech - but accidentally didn't close the game one night when I went to bed) if you go out of your way to do everything (story is probably about 10-15 hours long if you take it at a gradual pace). I just can't endorse some of the financial decisions made and hope (probably in vain) that at some point some executive somewhere is shown the reviews and takes heed.
This is a good game in its own right, but not a good successor to Human Revolution and the fact that it's clearly cut short is why it deserves poor reviews like this one.

Deus Ex 1, the original one, is one of the greatest games I've ever played. It's also really old and low-fi. But that's the pedigree. Deus Ex 2 was an absolute monstrosity that most people try not to think about too much. DX:HR (the first of the new series) was an absolute masterpiece. Everyone recognized it and it was widely adored. DX:MD (this game) is not as bad as Deus Ex 2, not at all, but it's also not quite as good as DX:HR. Read on for more.
DX:HR was a sprawling, multifaceted game. This game comes with a "catch me up to the plot" video which takes 12 minutes to summarize the plot of DX:HR. That's how in-depth and crazy it was. Some of it was good, some of it was great, some wasn't. It wasn't as wide-reaching as the original Deus Ex, but it was well-written and interesting, if a bit anonymous-feeling.
DX:MD feels more personal. It's smaller scale -- there's one major city hub and that's it. No more traipsing around the world in this one. It's centered on Prague and it shows. The city hub is beautiful (all the graphics are) and the voice acting is strong. The plot is much more individual person-centric than shadow organization-centric. There are, as there shoudl be, a huge number of choices in how you proceed and you can almost never do something the game hasn't anticipated as possible.
But the game is a little smaller in its scope and it shows. This is more a sophomore effort following the heights of DX:HR. If you're okay with a smaller game with a more focused story, you will love this game. If you need your games to all be huge scale with massive shadow conspiracies then you'll be disappointed.
And the DLC nonsense is a non-issue. It's stupid, it shouldn't be in the game, but it's not necessary. Not a big deal.

This was the first game I bought when I got a Steam account. This game is blast with friends, but I've also spent a significant amount of time soloing and it's still very fun. There are so many good features. The gameplay isn't groundbreaking, but it is executed in a marvelous manner.
I love the fact that, in multiplayer, all people get their own loot so you don't have to worry about other people stealing your hard-earned treasure. You also don't need to go through the awkward process of trading with yourself since all characters you create have access to the shared inventory.
I also have a weakness for games with pets, but I hate it when pets are only for aesthetics and they just sit there looking cute. In Torchlight II, they fight with you, cast spells, and sell and buy things for you. They are anything but useless.
The game has a lot of replay value as well. Since each class has three skill trees, you can make many different characters and they will all have unique play styles. I have also spent an embarrassing amount of time fishing.
The biggest disappointment was in the character customization. Each character has about 2-4 options for their face, hair, etc. However, that is not the game's biggest flaw. In my personal opinion, there are not enough inventory spaces. I like to collect rare armor/weapons as well as complete armor sets. After you play the game for as long as I have, you'll find there is not enough space for everything. Also, the shared inventory does not get bigger, even if you've created multiple characters. I also found I had a constant lack of gold in the game since buying things, enchanting things, and saving/destroying gems all take gold.
Despite some minor flaws, Torchlight II really shines. Whether you play it with friends or you just want to relax by yourself, Torchlight II is a great game that you should definitely add to your game library.

Once upon a time, there was a game Called Trine 2.
It was the sequel of (you guessed it), Trine 1, a beautiful puzzle/plataformer game which managed to pull some hours of fun with a beautiful graphics.
But Trine 2, being as it was a sequel, needed to be bigger, longer and better than the first part to avoid the curse of being a sequel.
Trine 2 pulled even better and more beautiful graphics than its predecesor: Everything was bright, and colorful, and full of virtual life. There was forests, and dungeons, and castles, all beautifully made. Even the evil goblins looked great with the new engine.
Trine 2 was longer. And with its DLC/expansion, even more than the original. More puzzles to solve, more secrets to find, more goblins to fight. Its history was told in the same nice fairy tale style that used the first game, and it was a pleasant one to see unfolding as the heroes advanced.
But, after playing for a long time, you realize... that Trine 2 was just Trine 1 disguised!
Being the same characters with almost the same skills was just the first step. The developers just added some new elements (like water streams that you have to redirect) to the already over used pool of elements for the puzzles, mix them up and start pulling again permutations of the same stuff. It felt cheap, and it felt repetitive after solving few puzzles. Of course, the progression was the same: Get into a "section" of the level which is blocked by a door, solve puzzle, open door, get into next section. The same pacing in every level, together with a fairly unoriginal and small amount of elements to create the puzzles leads to boredom really quick.
But the DLC came to the rescue, with a new story, powers and some new interesting puzzles and elements. Sadly, at least in my experience, it came too late, as I was already tired of the same puzzles to be bothered with more difficult stuff. I want to revisit them, though, but "in the future."
In the end, Trine 2 (Complete Story) was a mediocre game, with LOT of downs and some ups, and before the game realized that it had to include something REALLY new and challenging, it gets boring and repetitive.

Purchased this title on sale on a whim since it is co-op and it sat untouched in my library for a year(the Steam curse).  I finally got around to trying it out with a friend and I regret not trying it sooner.
Pros:
-Artwork is really stunning.
-Puzzles are fun without being frustrating
-Variety in the characters makes for a unique experience
-Variety in level design with hidden areas abound.  Was very surprised at the level of exploration given the game's nature.
-Co-op players aren't "screen-locked" to each other so you are free to explore above, below, and beyond your other mates.
Cons:
-Puzzles lean towards simplistic however working co-op with someone on them makes them enjoyable none-the-less
-Controls are "okay".  At some points they are crisp and responsive but there are a few motions/jumps that feel a bit wonky.  While occasionally frustrating, not a deal breaker.  Have not tried with a gamepad, that might be part of the issue.
-While there is no "screen-lock", if another player reaches a checkpoint bubble, you will be teleported to them no matter what you are doing.  Once realized it is fairly simple to avoid but some puzzles do not allow you to double back after being ported out.
Trine 2 is a solid buy, particularly if you have friends to run co-op with.  The environment, story, and stunning artwork combined with crisp and exciting gameplay make it one of the best co-op platformers I have ever played.

Brawlhalla is a fighting game commonly equated to Smash, and on the surface, there's a ton of similarties. From the stages to the way attacks work with a sort of light/heavy/air moveset, there's a lot that can be compared. Also like Smash, maybe a bit more so, Brawlhalla recites the motto of "easy to learn, hard to master."
Each character, or Legend, is unique. They're based around having two weapons, each with its own light and air attack moveset, and the Legend's unique heavy attacks, called signatures, that are different for each of the two weapons they wield. In addition to the weapon, each Legend has different stats (strength/attackSpeed/Defense/Speed) that heavily influence their playstyle. For example, a legend with Blasters and low attack speed would play somewhat more defensively, whereas a legend with the blasters and higher attack speed would tend to be more aggressive.
The game gets a patch every Wednesday, with new skins, changes to how the game works, bugfixes, balancing, and etc.
Also, you never have to spend a cent on the game! With each patch, there's a new rotation of free Legends to play, and you can buy any legend you want from the store (the Mallhalla) for Gold, earned through just playing the game. The gold gain is very quick, and especially if you want to play one specific legend, you could have enough gold in 2-3 days of casual playtime, depending on the cost of the legend. Also free are alternate color palettes for every Legend, unlocked by leveling up. There are, so far, 5 color palettes unavailable to be earned through leveling up a legend: White, purchased with gold after level 10. Black, purchased with gold after level 25. Holiday/Valentines, only purchasable with gold during those events, and Community Colors, which are earned through giveaways and winning tournaments.
All in all, the game is great, and if you're a fan of Smash, you might want to give Brawlhalla a try. Afterall, it's free, so there's really no harm in trying. c:

Dreaming Sarah is unfortunately a disappointment. The visuals and music are both quite pleasing, but they're attached to an essentially mediocre puzzle platformer. The puzzles themselves are generally simple to solve, but are throttled by tedious back-tracking and slow-paced exploration. The platforming itself is a chore with no challenge. At under 2 hours for completing all achievements, there isn't a whole lot here, but unfortunately by the end it already felt too long. Most of that time was spent running back and forth through the same areas, which lost much of their charm in the process. There are shortcuts revealed throughout, as well as an item that can teleport you back to the start, but even with that, traversing the small map areas becomes tedious. There's not much story to get involved in; the dibs and drabs of text that come out are largely disjointed and don't form any sort of narrative. Given that the game is a dream sequence that could be forgiven; if there were more to the game itself then the lack of story or character development wouldn't be an issue. Some older reviews mentioned technical issues. I didn't find any in my play through. I would like to point out that there is an umbrella in the game that lets you float around, which is needed for some puzzles but can be used everywhere. It's a pretty enjoyable enjoyable mechanic, and jumping and floating through each stage is the one nice break from the tedium.
As I said before, the art and sound are both nice, and are what initially got me to make the purchase. But nice visual design and soundtrack can't make up for the flaws in the actual game. I bought it on sale for under $3, but unfortunately even if it were free I would have been displeased, as the time spent was not really worth it.

A bit short and obtuse at times, Dreaming Sarah does have a few flaws.
However, the game itself is fun as it's full of character and its main focus, exploring the world, is engaging and rewarding.

If Dreaming Mary and Yumme Nikki had a baby this game would be it. It had me hooked, giving little in the way of help, forcing me to figure out what I needed and when. The game itself is light on story, but heavy on satisfying gameplay and immersion. I would definitely recommend it if you need somethinng to really sink your teeth into and figure out.

It may be a short game, but it's a wonderful experience. The $6 price is definitely worth the short experience and the amazing soundtrack.
Not to mention it's on sale for $2.39 until the 22nd of June, 2015. So if you think $6 is too steep for a 1-2 hour game and soundtrack, the 60% off hopefully changes your mind.

From the music to the smokey ambiance, Dreaming Sarah is one of those games that manages to find common ground and really draw the audience in. To anyone who ever played Earthbound/Mother 2, you'll know exactly what I'm talking about.

I really want to love this game, Army Men needs to be a thing again and the maps are all quite cool. The graphics are nice and it runs well. I give the devs credit for the creative objectives and gimmicks in each map, such as the foosball map which plays out like a shooter version of Rocket League and the freezer map where you have to use flamethrowers to melt the giant ice block containing your team's T-Rex before the other team can. But the execution is ultimately, and sadly, quite poor. The shooting mechanics are not good, there's bad hit detection and possibly bad netcode that makes killing enemies needlessly unreliable and leads to a lot of questionable deaths and frustration. It just doesn't feel satisfying to play, and that's not good. Perhaps one of the biggest problems for me though is that the maps which I find quite fun and endearing, are unfortunately also far, far too large for the 5v5 player limit. This needs to be bumped up to at least 10v10 badly. There's just too much downtime spent running across the maps, not seeing any enemies, for a fast paced game like this to work. Additionally, and this is perhaps personal preference, I don't like that everyone has every weapon by default instead of picking things up on the map. Ammo for them all is also on a cooldown, so once you use your 1 allocated rocket or 6 sniper rounds, you have to wait. It's an odd mechanic to say the least, though I suppose not necessarily unbalanced. The shotgun seems to be everyone's go to at the moment though because it is ridiculously powerful. Right now, as it stands, I can't really recommend this and I'm currently on the fence about refunding it. $10 isn't much, but I feel it could be better spent elsewhere. I genuinely hope the devs improve the game because I've been waiting for another game like this for the better part of the past 15 years, but until that time, I may just have to get out my N64 and Sarge's Heroes again to get the experience I was hoping to have here.

Hey guys! Big fan of the Deus Ex franchise here, so keep in mind that my vision on this game is indeed very subjective but maybe it will still be helpful for some of you guys.
To start things of , a quick summary for those of you who don't want to read through a wall of text.
But now for a more in-depth review.
The graphics of the game look gorgeous. Even with my outdated hardware it looks just great, there are probably other games out there with even better graphics (Witcher 3?) but it's really up to date.
The weapons and animations just look well designed and I didn't have any graphical bugs occuring to me.
Walking through Prague at night has a nice athmosphere thanks to the light effects implemented in to the game.
Special graphic options include also realistic clothing physic, which I didn't really notice though.
Not much to say about the sound design. I didn't attract my attention in any way. No major flaws, no big improvements compared to Human Revolution. But one thing that was lacking this time was....
The music score. Even Human Revolution couldn't capture the epic score of the first Deus Ex, but had an ambient score that was very fitting, the main theme Icarus had a nice implanation in the ending as well.
In Mankind Divided I never noticed the music as something outstandig, which is kinda sad because the trailers did have good music in them, never caught my attention though in my playthrough.
Now the probably biggest improvement, compared to it's precursor HR.
They didn't make any big changes, which is reasonable because Human Revolution already had polished gameplay, but they added little mechanics in to the game.
The crafting itself is a very weak system as it stands right now that feels just slapped on.
It's not bad in any way but it's also not a great aspect of the game. You go around, find some junk              here and there and then you either craft something or upgrade your weapons. For the weapons you can craft new fire modes and upgrade the stats of your guns. While the craftable objects are consumable things like the energy cells or ammunition for your augmentations.
They included new augs that really can affect the gameplay more than some other augs did previously.
Especially remote hacking is a very useful and funny tool that you should acquire during your playthrough.
Now you can change your weapons directly during the heat of the battle or while walking down the streets of Prague. Now you can revert mods on your weapons. You can put the silencer on your weapon and take it off, change through different types of scopes, etc. You should make use of it in harder difficulties, since the silencer for example really gives your weapon a big damage penalty.
While in the previous game, Adam Jensen could only move in cover and change corners in a 90° angle,
you now have a much broader variety of movement. You can jump over an obstacle to get to another piece      of cover etc. Can be helpful, I personally never made big use of it and sticked to the old mechanic.
While the gameplay has been updated, they have serious problems with the story.
The beginnig looks promising, after a while it falls flat, then it starts again and falls flat again, same happens towards the end AGAIN.
Compared to the achviements you've made in Human Revolution or Deus Ex 1, the story here just looks laughable. You pretty much are only solving one terrorist attack and slowly are starting to learn about a conspirancy. But you don't even scratch the tip of the iceberg during the mainstory line.
Also, new characters get introduced way to fast (Alex Vega) so you can't even build up sympathy for them or trust them, which can be pretty important in quests where you have to take decisions that change the outcome later in the game. Old characters get introduced very oddly, while some of the important characters from Human Revolution only appear in quests that are optional.
Also , big SPOILER!!! ahead....
But, what they did so very well are the
I'm not even joking when I tell you that I guess that most of the sidequests even take longer to complete than the majority of the mainstory quests.
Almost every single sidequests has a unique and well written story, and sometimes even change the pace of the game. There's for example a quest which let's Jensen back into his old role as a police officer and you have to find clues etc. to solve a crime. This quest kinda hooked me more in than most of it's mainstory. Sad.
Last point I wanna scratch fast.
Yes this game has an in-game shop where you can buy Praxiskits/Credits for real money.
It also features DLC packs where you can get a Weapon with a unique firemode+ammo+1 praxiskit+one pre-determined augmentation unlocked. Please keep in mind that, apart from the weapon I think, everything is ONE TIME USE ONLY. That's right you can only use the praxis kit ONCE in your save. Start a new game and you need to buy it again.
These kind of microtransactions are just stupid in a game like Deus Ex Mankind Divided. I didn't even notice the store until the very end of the game out of curiosity.
You don't need anything of their DLC's /Microtransactions to beat the game, which of course SHOULD be like that. Every weapon you can buy for money is still in the game, they even feature the same stats, just that the money-version has some unique firemode like 3-burst or something like that.
Soooo...

I really wanted to like Mankind Divided but there were just too many slow missions and poorly designed levels that I ended up getting really bored or frustrated more often that I would have liked. I understand that not all parts of a game can be 10/10 but now that I have beaten it the parts that I remember are not when I was having fun but when I felt the game was being unfair or the levels were just horribly designed and seemed to shoehorn me into doing them in ways that I wouldn't have expected from a Deus Ex game.
It is quite possible that I am remembering Human Revolution with rose coloured glasses but after finishing this I see Human Revolution as the vastly superior game and would recommend people play that instead.

If you liked Human Revolution you'll like Mankind Divided it has similiar game-play but its more fleshed out and has more Augments to play around with, my favorite new one being the Remote Hacking Augment because it makes stealh playthroughs easier. Also the level design has seen a step up too and there is a lot of different approaches to take for each mission. The game mostly takes place in Prague but its a really interesting hub to explore and gets more interesting to explore as the game progresses.
The main story is average at best and has a few interesting points to it but overall falls flat and ends rather abruptly. I assume Square Enix is saving some extra content for DLC or the game was released before it was completed, story-wise at least because the gameplay feels complete. Were the game really shines is in the side missions, which are some of the best I've experienced in an RPG since the Witcher 3. The side missions are usually multi-part and take place across the span of the main story, most of them have really good payoffs story-wise.
The Graphics are good and it runs really well on medium settings on my AMD Radeon R9 390X 8GB, I could probaly play the game on High settings just fine but I hold off on that due to my CPU's heat output. Also the music is as amazing as you expect, which makes sense since the music in Human Revolution was good too.
So Overall Mankind Divided is a good game that could have been close to perfect if the story was more fleshed out and there was more than one hub world to explore. If you liked Human Revolution and want to play more of that but with more interesting augments to play around with than give Mankind Divided a buy.

Abrupt ending aside, Mankind Divided is truly a worthy successor to Human Revolution.

Dreams are a rare occurance for me. Going to sleep usually causes me to fall into complete emptiness, or hover just between alert and unconscious as I struggle not to wake myself up. When I do dream though, it’s because something is wrong. When I’m feeling scared, or guilty, or anxious, these feelings manifest themselves in vividly internalized strangeness that often cause me to wake suddenly in a sweat, and then just as quickly slip away as I attempt to recall what happened.
Dreams are not fun excursions into my imagination the way they seem to be for many, but torturous self examinations without the constraints of logic and reality. I become my own worst enemy, helpless to suppress the ideas twisting themselves into things I can’t begin to describe even to myself as I wait and hope it will soon be over. My dreams have been this way for as long as I can remember, at some points during my childhood becoming so bad my religious family began to think I was possessed and mentally unstable.
It has been a long time since I’ve had anything quite so graphic as when I was a child, but that didn’t stop me revisiting these moments I had thought I’d forgotten as I journeyed through Dreaming Sarah and its protagonist’s equally bizarre and terrifying visions. Dreams are common fodder for media, but Dreaming Sarah is one of the first I’ve experienced that so perfectly illustrates the merging of reality and the surreal, and the petrifying helplessness within it that has been haunting me all these years. It exists at the point just between a dream and consciousness, where you can’t be sure of what is real and what isn’t; where your experiences and trauma come to life in ways you can’t control or understand, but are forced to make sense of or else allow them to swallow you whole.
Dreaming Sarah is excels at taking something conventional and warping it just enough to feel unusual yet still recognizable. Its artwork and soundtrack becomes continually more twisted as you travel deeper into Sarah’s subconscious, but always with a tinge of the familiar that only serves to put you more on edge. Gathering and using items feels traditional and expected, yet for what actual purpose I was collecting them I couldn’t say. Everything is so very ordinary but also alien, like you’ve been here before only now it’s changed and you aren’t sure how. Something is so clearly wrong, but you’re the only one that seems to notice.
I wouldn’t describe Dreaming Sarah as terrifying so much as it is haunting and unsettling. There is never any real danger and I knew this the whole time, but as is always the case in dreams what I knew became irrelevant. This was a world of my character’s own creation but which plays by its own rules, leaving me in a state of disarray as I attempt to rationalize the impossible. I wanted to get out, but the only way to do so was to find a way to understand this dream and trace it back to where it came from.
Looking at the dreams of someone else, whether they be but the creation of an artist or drawn from actual experiences, I was able to more easily see how they reflected some portion of reality. As I was helping to piece together Sarah’s psyche, it felt as if I was also in some way beginning to reconcile some of the inexplicable terrors I had conjured up over the years. It was clear that Sarah wasn’t insane, but that she had suffered and was hurting, and these dreams were the only way left for her to compartmentalize and begin to move past her trouble. Perhaps then my nightmares can similarly teach me something about myself, and help heal the subconscious wounds still eating away at me at night.
It seems likely to me that there will be people who don’t “get” Dreaming Sarah, who perhaps enjoy it on a mechanical and artistic level, but who see any deeper meaning as being fabricated or pretentious. Perhaps that is true to a point, but it also seems to say something about how we often view dreams as only that, rather than an extension of our real life experiences and potentially even a coping mechanism. I want to believe the horrors I’m inflicting upon myself are there for a reason, and that there is an ending in which I’m no longer tearing myself apart from deepest corners of my mind. At the very least, it would seem I’m not the only one.

M&B:Warband is a pretty good game. It's sort of like an Open World (The map is kind of an overworld) in which you can roam around in between different Nations/Empires, as well as hire soldiers from villages and city taverns, and buy supplies, weapons, and armor. The combat is unique in the sense that you get to participate in battle and lead your army against the enemy. There are also RPG elements as well, namely being the stats and skills you put points into when you level up, and weapon proficiencies. You can become a vassal to a King and get land (Namely a village, which you can upgrade), or if you want, you can attempt to take over land yourself and form your own Empire. I'd give this game a 8/10, it's an excellent game but the graphics haven't aged that well (Although the new sequel M&B:Bannerlord looks much better)
Oh, it's also kind of fun to keep playing "When The Winged Hussars Arrived" in this game too, in addition to screaming Deus Vult when you invade the Sarranid Sultanate.

Take the world of Far Cry 3, replace it by a 80s cheesy saturday morning cartoon post-apocalyptic universe that doesn't take itself seriously, that frequently breaks the fourth wall and mocks it, add an awesome 80s soundtrack by Power Glove, and a ton of other fun gimmicks... and you've got Blood Dragon.
Only two complaints with this game: it's short (but well, it's a cheaply-priced spinoff made for the hell of it), and the cutscenes are mostly static images sliding around. But beyond that, the production value of this game is definitely AAA... and I would not mind seeing some sort of sequel to this game, because it's a bit of a transgression towards the traditional triple-A manshooter values that needs to happen more often.

I absolutely loved FC3, and I ♥♥♥♥ing love the 80s.  Infact, I'm going to go ahead and get my small complaints out of the way early so I can spend the rest of this review going balls deep:  It sucks that there are so few weapons.  You get new attachements, and they can really alter the way the weapon works, but there are only actually a handful of death implements.  This bothers me  because  A.) The sheer amount of guns there are in Fc3, and B.) Because of how ♥♥♥♥ing cool potential weapons could have been.  The guns that are in the game are simply common archetypes - there's a shotty, sniper, AR, etc.  That's not necessarily an issue, but given how creative the rest of the game is, I can't help but hold it to a high standard.
Now on to the good stuff.
I'm going to tell you the very moment I fell in love with this game.  I had just loaded it up, watched a truly sick cutscene and sprayed down a bunch of future cyberninjas with a helicopter mounted minigun.  The helicopter lands, and I receive a comm message informing me that the tutorial is starting. Without missing a beat, my character screams " I ♥♥♥♥ING HATE TUTORIALS ".
Hilarious though it was, this moment is also very significant.  It's Blood Dragon's way of letting you know exactly what it is, and what to expect, right as the game starts.  It is a fun spinoff of a popular game franchise.  It is not DLC.  It is not an expansion pack.  It is a stand alone experience that doesn't take itself to seriously.  It is a love letter to the movies, stories and games that many of us grew up on. It is charming, it is gorgeous, and it is incredibly engaging.
You take control of a cybernetic super soldier tasked with unraveling the defection of your former superiour officer.  The story itself is pretty cookie cutter, but the way it is told is anything but.  Cutscenes are an anachronistic fusion between the 8-bit era and modern flair.  Though the story failed to captivate me, the dialogue was frequently a highlight.  Blood Dragon thrives on it's unique brand of tongue-in-cheek humor.
Storywise - zero carry over from anything Far Cry, but there are quite a few similarities in the gameplay.  There are animals to hunt, there are unlockables to find and missions often play out exactly like clearing a compound in Far Cry 3.  The bones of it are the same, but not quite as deep (understandable, given the games bargain price point).  Aiming is almost exactly the same as FC3 - there is still that kind of "floaty" element to it which usually necessitates aiming down the sights to hit a shot.   There are not as many weapons to unlock, but the level of upgrades available for your arsenal per weapon is much improved.  Your relationship with your weaponry is a lot more intimate, and doing missions to earn these upgrades will be where you'll spend a lot of your time.
As a gamer, the thing that I find most appealing is atmosphere.  This isn't something that can be quantified, nor is it the result of any one thing.  It is the pervasive feeling you have while playing the game.  Blood Dragon has a very unique and powerful atmosphere.  The neon juxtaposed by the darkness of the island itself is amazing.  Running in terror from the eponymous Blood Dragon's (or alternatively using them as attack dogs) is a thrill.  Using your cyber ninja stars/samurai sword for stealth kill combos just feels right.  Watching a cyber ninja's head explode in electric sparks after a perfect headshot is satisfaction squared.  All of these things contribute to atmosphere, but they are only parts of the whole.
The thing that I love most about Blood Dragon is that it exists.  That a triple-a game studio like Ubisoft let their employees run wild and create something that was fun to them is incredible to me.  It isn't a (true) sequel, it isn't made to nickel and dime you, it was a bunch of people creating something cool for the joy of it.  This more than anything speaks to the feel of the game.  The soul of fun and creativity is apparent in literally every part and every moment of FarCry3: Blood Dragon.  I cannot recommend it enough, and I hope that we see more of its kind.

Honestly if there was a way to leave a "~" review, I'd do that. DX:MD feautres incredible gameplay that truly feels like a fusion of the original Deus Ex, and HR. Unfortunately the story driving it is weak in comparison to both those earlier titles. I haven't finished the game yet at the time of writing, and I'm not feeling inspired to work toward it either. There are some enjoyable moments, but ultimately the game lacks the pacing and sense of urgency that HR had, and you quickly begin to loose interest in what's happening with the story. It's a far cry above Invisible War where the gameplay suffered just as much as the story, but ultimately it's still a low compared to the series high standards.
It's like MGSV: The Phantom Pain in a lot of ways. Excellent gameplay with a poor story and a real sense of descalation compared to what came before. But while TPP can be sumarized with that explanation, fullstop, DXMD also has a load of corprate ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ttery that nobody asked for. Microtransactions in singleplayer are annoying, but having terrible performance and unecessary DRM is inexcusable on publisher Square Enix's part. I honestly feel that if the devs at Eidos Montreal (who clearly care for the franchise and didn't appreciate having to bow down to corprate) had been left to their own devices, we'd have gotten a better game.
So should you buy it? I'd say no. Not now anyway. There's a genuinely amazing game in here somewhere, but just the fact that I can more readily name off more bad than good shows MD is a step down as a package from HR. Wait for a GOTY or Director's Cut edition or something, and then wait for a sale for that around $10-15. If you got it as a gift or something though, you should definitely give it a go sometime.

A game that's developed by Rooster Teeth, the same company that produced a ton of Halo machinimas in the past with the help of the now late Mounty Oum. The latter introduced an
spell that gave us RWBY. Whether or not RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is indeed what people wanted lies really much on personal experience.
You wouldn't know nothing about the game nor any basic details unless you've watched the web series yourself. So do your best to avoid this game unless you've watched the first two volumes of RWBY yourself. That said, let's back to reviewing.
You start with four (
) characters, sent out from your Academy to investigate a certain situation that may put a threat on Vale and the rest of the World of Remnant (
), only to see that everyone's favorite monsters being the Grimm starts to wreck havoc on areas that you are sent to. From the forest that looks unusually similar to the trials, to a city ruins that was once a place for a radical Faunus organization, to an island that hosts a generic evil laboratory and an evil villian.
Obviously the gameplay. A hack and slash type, pretty much the basic type of it's genre and having four/eight characters at your control each have their own types of attacks, combos, semblance and ultimates. You pretty much have your light and heavy attacks, combos to rack up like in Ninja Gaiden or Arkham, and ultimates that are rather set from close impact, to support buffs to a crowd-ending mess. Sounds pretty similar to other types of hack and slash games right? So why bother buying this game?
And if that's not the reason, then they'd probably buy the game for a new type of hack and slash, even though it has little difference of anything. Just ask a RWBY fan whoever they want to be, and the most likely answer is either Ruby or Nora. The biggest factor of the game comes with coop/multiplayer mode. You can certainly beat the game solo, but where's the fun with RWBY if you don't have three more players with you to play their part? Heck, you can execute team attacks which is fun. While playing, each of the characters usually taunt or talk about what they see, face, interact or attack. An example is the few but ridiculous cringeworthy puns of Yang, and Nora's *explosive* personality spewing out words of gullible and hyperactive expressions.
Now for the graphics, visuals and environment, it certainly looks pretty though not as beautiful as it presents itself to be. The forest and mine levels are something to take note about, as they certainly have been the common, generic stages for every hack and slash games in the book. Though the new places like the laboratory that we know nothing of from a random island, and the fact that Mountain Glenn looks depressing is enough to put a charm of quality and content in a game that doesn't really tell that much story. Can't really say anything bad about the visuals, other that the locations feels generic and bland.
The enemies on the game are totally forgivable as to how you approach them, but the mini-bosses are best fought with teammates rather than solo especially if you set the game to Eclipse difficulty. Well you can play solo in Eclipse difficulty, but the Grimm count may overwhelm you if you are not used to such horde size. It also gets annoying to face some mini-bosses, with two of them having a ridiculous amount of health should you face such enemies alone.
Replayability on this game seems to drain down fast. Really fast. Starting from Square one or go from Point A to Point B doesn't satisfy the fans or people interested to keep going. And such replayability is also threatened caused by frequent, technical difficulities even on a powerful computer. If RT wants to get this game played more, they need a new roster of characters for us to play with, extend the campaign, or just make a new game that's basically a tournament fighter type, which I personally think suits RWBY better on that. Extra contents like the DLCs out there, with JNPR included shouldn't be just paid with extra money, it should be free.
This is not going to be the last time RT is gonna pull an attempt of making a video game based on RWBY. I certainly did enjoy playing the game so far, and having to
people to play with me adds the feel that playing as one of the characters in RWBY is certainly an honor.
The asking price doesn't seem to be fitting for me
but when the game is struck with a 50% discount, don't hesitate to buy it alongside the JNPR DLC.
If they are going to make another RWBY game, a tournament based fighting game is the safe, swet spot for them. I would love to play as the antagonists or anti-heroes of the series. If they want a second chance with the same genre, they have to get PlatinumGames to make them borrow the license and give us a worthy hack and slash game.

"Dreaming Sarah" is an adorable (and somewhat trippy) side-scrolling exploration game in which you play a young woman trying to wake up from a coma. Naturally this involves being harangued by a pirate in the middle of a desert, falling through the inside of a giant grandfather clock, and accidentally causing a massacre in a nightclub populated by aliens. (At times "Dreaming Sarah" almost plays like a journey through a magic-mushroom fiend's dream journal).
There's no real plot to speak of, other than the coma thing, which is spoiled in the Steam description of the game and not really integral to the game experience anyway (hence the lack of an alert in this review). The joy of "Dreaming Sarah" comes not from the sliver of a story but rather from the little throw-away surprises in its short, stream-of-consciousness levels (what is UP with that happily undead manor-keeper anyway?), the charm of the 2-D retro graphics, and above all from the excellent musical score by Anthony Septim (included with the game). The modern vibe of Septim's ambient/trip-hop score provides a nice counterpoint to the old-school graphics and gameplay (one button to jump, one button to choose an inventory item), and dispels any hint of tedium from the game's central exploration mechanic.
"Dreaming Sarah" runs about 2-3 hours, depending on how lucky you are in finding hidden objects and doors. I used it as a way to chill out after playing through heavier stuff (again, the music played a big part in that). It's fun, cheap, creative, has a great soundtrack, and comes with trading cards -- what more do you want for six bucks?

An absolutely fantastic game dripping with atmosphere and adventure.  Despite there being no understandable dialogue or written text, Brothers manages to tell an emotionally charged story not through nuanced exposition, but through the bond formed through a long and arduous journey that the brothers endure in order to seek out the cure for their ailing father.  This game is a perfect example of how to successfully incorporate the narrative technique "Show, don't tell".
While the controls take a while to get used to (and never quite lose their inherent clunkiness), the game has a few tricks up its sleeve that make the investment worth it (there is a clever twist where the controls play into the narrative perfectly in a way no other game I have played has done).  While it can be argued that a majority of the game's challenge comes from wrestling with the controls rather than any gameplay puzzle, I never felt as though the game dragged on to the point it became a chore to play.  The stunning visuals and variety of settings the two brothers explore compelled me to push forward, and each one felt as though it had its own place in a believable, lore rich world.  All-in-all, Brothers is a game in which the gameplay takes a backseat to the narrative and wonder of adventure.
The game itself is relatively short and lacking in challenge, but the excellent soundtrack and fairytale like narrative make it one of the most memorable games I have had the pleasure of playing.

Too many game-breaking bugs.
Instantly lose fights as you spawn, making it impossible to defend against attackers, pillage villages, conquer castles and towns, or helping allies.
AI spawning underground and hitting you and your allies, forcing you to retreat and lose 90% of your troops, then hopefully be able to outrun them.
Savefiles being corrupted if you save before fights, sieges and tournaments (For some reason this does not happen on "realistic" mode where there is only 1 savefile and you can not quit without saving*).
Game crashes if you buy items above 5000 cash.
Arrows going through enemies if they are not facing you (Still hits teammates though).
Tournament is basically a game of luck, you get random weapons, enemies might have bow&arrow and you have a horse and a sword with no shield, or they might have a sword and shield and you have a lance but no horse. If the latter happens, then you can't win the tournament because the AI will eventually be within 1 meter distance of you, and when he does, you cannot hit him because you are using a huge and slow lance.
A normal army for a vassal to have is between 50-150 troops, and for kings 150-300 troops. This is usually the amount of enemies you will attack mid-game unless more vassals are in the immediate vicinity of the one you are attacking or defending against (This can make the enemy have up to 500-550 troops). This seems fine until you realize that 1 single group of bandits can have up to 4000 troops in mid- end-game. If they outrun you and you are forced to fight them, 1 of 2 things will happen:
-You lose.
-The game crashes because the game for some reason tries to load what looks like all of the 4000 troops, even though it is only supposed to load a maximum of 150 troops depending on how many you have chosen in the settings.
I hope that the developers take their time with Bannerlord and do not publish the game too early, and that they at least fix the game-breaking bugs before release.

Great promises, but disappointing.
Politics as a new focus in a city builder/manager? Great! - I love city-simulators, played them for 20+ years...
I will refrain from listing any pros, as the cons far outweigh any pros and until fixed, I would strongly recommend your money to be spent elsewhere!
Summary:
Lack of control
Tedious and repetitive political mechanics
Abysmal performance issues
Waiting and frustration guaranteed - for the majority of the time.
Elaborating the cons:
1. Political part is tiresome and repetitive:
Sadly the game is poorly executed, as every action requires a vote, however realistic that might be, it means that changes takes ages: All your city districts takes a vote to change, which quickly becomes tiresome and repetitive. Imagine you want to roll out electrical grids in your entire city, before you are done you will have spent 20 years tediously modifying a district, waiting on the vote and repeat.
My recommendation:
Perhaps some unlockable ability that a mayor can modify within certain thresholds before it triggering a vote or a similar mechanic, or at least removing the constriction that only one "modify district" vote can be active at a time. Perhaps increase political interaction, such as more access to voting groups, ability to do campaigning (both for mayor elections and city council) and the ability to choose a political party, as well as interaction with other cities such as trade or infrastructural connections - not just the horrible "twin cities" mechanic that is currently the only inter-city interaction available.
2. Info and theory crafting in this game is so bad it hurts:
You can, if you look into city statistics get info about traffic congestion, but the consequences of traffic congestion are not apparent. Need for certain zoning such as industry or housing seems important but after 15+ hours I still havent worked out exactly hot to satisfy it, perhaps because changes happen so slow that I have moved on to trying alternatives before the initial attempts effects kick in. Similarly it is not clear what exactly the different citizen parameters do to the game, health, security and happiness etc. all seem important, but as long as they stay in the green they don’t have apparent modifiers to the city.. (?) I would love some percentages and modifiers show here and there.
3. Performance issues are by far the worst I have ever experienced:
I just upgraded my graphics card, and even on lowest settings, speed 2 (out of 3 speed settings) still lagged - I spent about 10 hours on one play through, which was a pain. Granted, I maxed out my city size, but that should really not be an issue. If you want to avoid performance issues, try keeping your city at 1/4 of max size or so (Fun isn't it?).
4. Combined with the above, the lack of control and info and the bad performance, the game just becomes painfully boring and frustrating. The last 100 years of gameplay was, for me, just setting to the max speed and answering every vote that showed up until the game was over.

Let me start off by saying I've spent hundred of hours and dollars on thie game, across console and PC, and would be even more money had the DLC not been free. That sounds like the start to a stellar review, but unfortunately is nothing close.
Mods and modder's resources, such as OpenIV, Nexus, etc., play a vital role in games, like another popular game that start with "Sky" and ends with "Rim" in which mods effectively saved that title from being lost behind its much-better predecessors, and is similar to the situation here. Mods are not "breaking" your game, they are adding hours (hell, even weeks) of playtime to a dying game. Take the mods, modding community, (and why not cross "fun" off the list too?) and you're left with what you had before: a dying game.
Yes, we know you've had trouble with mods in the past (sex animations accidentally being left on the disc with San Andreas) but once again, you shot *yourself* in the foot there, and apparently like how that feels enough to do it again. Enjoy your "pure" game, while 90% of the community moves on to better things.
Oh and if Red Dead 2 doesn't make it to PC then everything I said in this review counts as double.
