Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is very hard for me to rate. Why? I am a huge Deus Ex fan and had been looking forward to this for a long time, so much so that I preordered (I generally never preorder games). Having said that, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided falls short of a few of my expectations while delivering on some others. May be it was my lofty expectations that let me down, but here they are:
Pros:
1. Gameplay: Gameplay is excellent. The fluidity of the whole FPS made the game very thrilling. I am still not a big fan of 3rd person cover system, but hey, not everything us perfect. Shooting and new Augs were seamlessly woevn into the new game mechanics.
2. Graphics: Stunning. Well, you shouldn't expect anything less. Even at low settings (not the most powerful system), it looks stunning. I can just imagine it at its fullest.
3.Backdrop: While I was disappointed at only one major hub area, Prague has been designed magnificently. All its sub-hub areas are well made too. The setting is as grim as possible, but still with hope in it, if you get what I mean.
4. Side-Quests: Without spoiling anything, I have to say that the side-quests are well placed within the game and help the main-story and the backdrop quite a bit. In fact, some of the side-quests were way more fun than the main story at some points.
Cons:
1. Story: My biggest pet-peeve. I love all the gameplay and stuff. but Deus Ex games have always been about story for me. The whole Cyberpunk, dystopian world of Deus ex is what I fell in love in the first place. And as good as the game's beginning and middle part is, there is no actual epilogue. The game just abruptly ends with a lot of unanswered questions. I understand the old cliche of leaving the audience wanting more, but the story here did not give any closure to any part of the game itself. I just hope the DLCs coming next expand upon the story and add to that ending.
2. Lack of hubs: Deus Ex games have had some amazing explorable hubs ever since the first one. This one though doesn't have beyond one. The open ended world seemed pretty limited due to that. I hope we'll get to explore more worlds as the series progresses.
Overall, I'll recommend this title to the hardcore fans of the series, but by no means is this game anywhere close to perfect. A solid 7/10.

I'm kind of mixed. I really loved MK9, but I'm not sure this is really an improvement. Sure the graphics are much nicer, but I feel like the whole gimmick behind this game is that you get LESS. In MK9 you selected a character and had access to all of their special moves and kombos, you just had to memorize them like any other fighting game. In MKX, you get to choose your character's fighting style, giving you access to (approximately) 1/3 of their move set. Why would I want to only be able to have access to a third of my moves at a time? Also kombat is much slower in this game compared to MK9. MK9 was fast-paced with kombos being key. Kombat in MKX is much slower, with clunky movement. It is much more important in MKX to focus on movement than your ability to kombo, taking a liking to the importance of footwork in boxing. That's cool and all, but that's just not the same vibe of previous Mortal Kombat games, and it just feels too slow to me.

This game is very enjoyable. It is unique because you simultaneously control both brothers and use each according to their specific strength and weaknesses to travel on. It is so much fun and the obstacles are so creative! You don't have to figure anything out on your own really as  you follow a direct path really. The scenery is breathtaking and calming, with a great soundtrack adding to the atmosphere.  It was a pleasure to take everything in. Another unique aspect to this game is that there isn't a dialogue... which I enjoyed, leaving the playing to focus on body language, tone, and emotion. It gives you some freedom to fill story in yourself. At least I did, even though what was going on was quite simple and apparent, but I like that the option for extra imagination is there. This game will make you feel things.

Brothers a Tale of Two Sons is an adventure game which uses innovative controls and lite puzzle elements to progress the story. Despite the fact that the game possesses no audible dialogue its plot is still gripping due to fantastic art and world design. The game is beatable in a single sitting which in no way detracts from its quality. It plays out like a folk tale come to life, with beautiful scenery, and strange foes and friends, to meet along the way. You are also accompanied by a beautiful soundtrack during your journey.  Brothers has 12 achievements all of which can be obtained in a single play through with ease. Its graphics are not too extensive and benefit from strong art design meaning most machines should run the game with ease. Just be sure to take the store page seriously and abstain from purchasing unless you have a controller of some type, as mouse and keyboard are not fun at all.
Pros:
Controls
Puzzles
Art design
Soundtrack
Length
Characters
Cons:
Controller required
8.5/10

Ok, so, the game was marketed as fufilling the following.
The first was that it was a decent city building strategy game.
The second was that it would require you to manipulate the political parties.
The third was that it had a branching plot related to multiple generations that would
tell the story of the growth of both the city and the family you pick.
However, the game doesn't do any of these things well enough.
1) The Mechanics of the City Building Part are neither interesting nor challenging.
The game is not difficult enough for hardcore strategy players. I mean, once you figure out that you don't actually need to improve anything, the game becomes pretty basic. Just slap down districts and a couple schools for brainpower. Rely on institutions and edicts to raise stats.
You don't need to build anything else unless it's in the hard negatives.
The political management means very little other than "you can't do unpopular things' with damned little (if any) way of making things unpopular/popular. it's not like you can forge alliances against other parties or try and play people off against one another, and even if you did, it's not like you have to for 99% of the edicts you could pass.
Combined, this means that the game is not an interesting enough strategic challenge. You'll figure out what you need to do, you'll do it, and there's no changes to that strategy and no challenges to it.
2) The User Experience is Awful
There are a ton of controls and fiddly bits of the district but you can safely ignore them most of the time. That's good, becuase the tutorial and user interface are so opaque that I have no idea what the advatnage or costs are for doing anything.  Do you need to have residenital with your commercial zone to make it work? Maybe? It doesn't tell you. Commerical zones seem to populate when you build straight commercial districts.
Gas, electricity and water raise the efficency of companies in the district. How much? How much will it cost in maintenence? Dunno, probably not. Increasing roads reduces traffic, buying public transport increases "transit points". What do they do? I have no idea! There's like 30 seperate submenus for each district.
If this was something like a difficulty curve, it would be one thing, but a lot of these mechanics genuinely doesn't seem to matter at all. It's not just that these are hidden, opaque mechanics, they are hidden and useless mechanics. For example, the bonusesfrom sister cities don't seem to do anything worth mentioning. It's just another tech that provides a tiny, pointless bonus that won't matter all that much.
This makes the late game really, painful once you start unlocking stuff in age 2-3. Say you want to upgrade a district. You have to make all your changes in a single pass, because you can only alter one district at a time. This involves muliple submenus with a variety of options, a ton of optional buildings to place down, zoning sliders, and you doing this over 20-30 districts. Did I mention you can only change one district at a time because it requires a vote?
This adds up to make the game REALLLLLy slow when it gets big. Which is that...
2B) The game slows to a crawl late game.
I mean, not just in the mechanics, but the game LITERALLY moves very slowly, with no way to increase the rate beyond the barely adequate max speed from earlier eras.
There's were some serious optimization issues here.  The game just grounds to a halt once you get into era 3 ish, with max speed running like normal speed in the earlier eras. Combined with the aforementioned problems with district micromanagement, this makes the later eras feel like you are trying to pull yourself through quicksand.
* Note - This was on early builds in 2017. It may have changed.
3) The Game has no story and it's world isn't compelling, which fails to pull you in.
The game sucks at telling a story, and does a poor job of making me feel like my character matters, my family matters, or the city matters.
Ok, the first two might not sound like a big deal in a sandbox city sim, but Urban Empire SPECIFICALLY MARKETED itself as a gigantic generation spanning epic with a branching story. That was one of it's major selling points, and it just doesn't do that.
The actual decision points are rare and far between, and decisions have little narrative impact. Even major historical events barely qualifying as an an afterthought or a newspaper article.
Example:  Oh look, the empire has rebelled and is now a republic. Oh look, it's WWI. Oh look, it's WWII.  You don't interact with the other families or personalities in the city. You don't pick whether you side with the Axis or Allies. You don't have any big event trees to worry about. The only thing the choices seem to do is give you a few different character traits that mean very little. Woohoo?
The parties are hilariously random and fickle. I've had hard-right Christians support abortion, Communists deny worker rights, and Pacifists support violent nationalists. There's usually no reason or sense behind their decisions.
The whole thing ends up taking away any idea that the game takes place in a world. I don't mind game mechanics breaking a narrative immersion or being unrealistic, but this level of failure represents a basic lack of effort on the part of the designers to deliver any kind of emotional impact to the game.
4) Nothing really matters.
The main points combine to create a game that makes me feel that nothing I do has any meanigful impact. I had researched video games shortly after the 1900's, apparently somehow running in a city that had a power plant but no actual electrical grid.
Nothing looks different at any point, the game doesn't really feel very different from Era 1 to Era 3 (as far as I got). Nothing in the game feels impactful, at all. The story just sort of shows up as a multiple choice question that will affect a few character states, but I don't feel any sort of control over the narrative, nor does it in any way feel like a naturally evolving story with compelling characters (there aren't really any characters).
And these factors really reduces the idea of a Dynasty.
Fun Factor
There are a lot of heavily flawed games that are actualy kind of fun (hell, this is why Kalypso is still in business), but the thing is that at the end of the day, this game lacks an Exigence: a reason to exist.
There's no real story (despite that being a touted feature).
The game's not immersive enough to suck you in.
The game's not challenging enough to make you think about it very deeply for very long.
There are no campaigns to finish beyond the first, and I couldn't even bring myself to do that, because the game had slowed itself to a crawl by the time I was hitting the modern era.
In short, for strategy fans, I'd only buy this at a VERY deep discount. There are many strategy games that are cheaper and better than this from other independent companies. It's not a total disaster, but every aspect of the game is mediocre (at best) with no outstanding features somehow making it less than a sum of it's parts.
If you thought about buying this game for the political manipulation, watching a city grow over time and affecting it's outcome or playing a story, then avoid buying this game, period.
In short, this game was sold as an an city and political dynasty simulator, and ended up being a crappy city simulator and utterly failing to simulate the political or dynasty part.
No content in it, no interaction from the player even needed, no replayability. A 44.99€ price tag is infuriating, just a rip-off from "developpers" who have apparently never played a good game.

So after 100%ing this game and finding absolutely everything that you can do in 2 hours (would be under that if I didn't have issues with bugs, as the game just came out yesterday) I'm going to go ahead and recommend it but tell you a bunch of reasons why you shouldn't buy it if you're on the fence. Hang on while I explain.
I personally think this game is well made. I had a prepaid mastercard with 5 dollars left on it, and I looked at "recently released adventure games" and saw this. Being a fan of Yume Nikki and other games like it (because honestly, it's become a subgenre at this point) I decided to take the plunge. Usually I wouldn't put money down on a Yume Nikki fangame type thing because they're usually uninspired and involve a lot of bad game design, but this looked well made based on the screenshots and sold me with the trailer music. It was 3 dollars on sale, so I figured at the worst I could sell the trading cards and make back ~50% of what I spent on it.
First off: If you've played a Yume Nikki game before, this follows the formula to an almost funny extent.
Dreams? ☑
Looping levels? ☑
Weird Alien things? ☑
☑
☑
Creepy Eye Motif? ☑
☑
☑
However, if you haven't or the above doesn't bother you by being sort of done before (and I was ok with it, because it was done fairly well) then prepare for a weird platformer with great music and colourful graphics.
Going to get the thing that might change out of the way: The game is horribly buggy. This is semi-excusable because I'm guessing this is this developer's first major release, and I'm making this review a day after it came out. The developer is in the discussion boards taking bug requests and trying to fix them, so this might change in the short future- but if you're buying this game at this very moment... Be aware!
Dreaming Sarah is about a girl in a coma (which should be the game's only spoiler, but isn't considering it's both in the banner ad AND the description for the game) who is exploring her dreaming state. You walk around areas and find powerups to either help you, interact with other characters, or just to have for completionist's sake. The graphics are very pretty, the controls are fluent and simple (but not really instructed in game- I had to just guess what keys did what which only took a few seconds) and the music is relaxing and at times a bit haunting. As shown by my 2 hour play time and 100% achievement completion, the game is really short. Is it worth the money? Well, for almost 4 dollars you can't go wrong, but for 6? Ehhhhhh...
Most games like this are free downloadable titles or flash games you can play, and if Dreaming Sarah was free, I'd be ridiculously impressed and recommend people to play it a bit more. But for more than 3 dollars? It's a fun experience, and if this is the developer's first game released, it's pretty great for what it is. But my main complaint with Dreaming Sarah is that it
There's nothing to find, no quirky secrets or easter eggs that have a 1/64 chance of happening (there are secrets in the game, but all of them are so close to the path you have to follow that I'd put money on you finding at least 80% of them without trying), and no real "wow I can't believe how crazy this was!" moments that is usually what makes playing exploration based walking simulators like this interesting. It plays it very very safe, and while it's enjoyable to sit down and relax with, it's not worth 6 dollars to play a game through to 100% for an hour and never touch it again.
Take
for example. It's 15 dollars on PSN, but it's an hour long. But many people claim it to be a great game for the price. Why? Because there's so much to explore and discover, and even when you're done with that you can meet people and have new experiences every time. With Yume Nikki, the gimmick is that while playing you always feel like there's something new that's happening- something weird that just randomly decided to show up. This game feels like an on-rails shooter in comparison, and while the atmosphere is very good, there's just nothing bringing me back.
So all this being said, why am I recommending Dreaming Sarah? Well, on sale it's definitely worth it just for the experience, and I think the developer has a lot of potential in the future. The graphics are very eye pleasing (no pun intended) and the OST is pretty dang good (and you get it for free with purchase of the game) and if worst comes to worst you can sell the steam trading cards or keep them for a cool looking emoticon or background (most of them being well made, I'm wearing one on my profile at time of writing).
Overall: 6.8/10

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is very hard for me to rate. Why? I am a huge Deus Ex fan and had been looking forward to this for a long time, so much so that I preordered (I generally never preorder games). Having said that, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided falls short of a few of my expectations while delivering on some others. May be it was my lofty expectations that let me down, but here they are:
Pros:
1. Gameplay: Gameplay is excellent. The fluidity of the whole FPS made the game very thrilling. I am still not a big fan of 3rd person cover system, but hey, not everything us perfect. Shooting and new Augs were seamlessly woevn into the new game mechanics.
2. Graphics: Stunning. Well, you shouldn't expect anything less. Even at low settings (not the most powerful system), it looks stunning. I can just imagine it at its fullest.
3.Backdrop: While I was disappointed at only one major hub area, Prague has been designed magnificently. All its sub-hub areas are well made too. The setting is as grim as possible, but still with hope in it, if you get what I mean.
4. Side-Quests: Without spoiling anything, I have to say that the side-quests are well placed within the game and help the main-story and the backdrop quite a bit. In fact, some of the side-quests were way more fun than the main story at some points.
Cons:
1. Story: My biggest pet-peeve. I love all the gameplay and stuff. but Deus Ex games have always been about story for me. The whole Cyberpunk, dystopian world of Deus ex is what I fell in love in the first place. And as good as the game's beginning and middle part is, there is no actual epilogue. The game just abruptly ends with a lot of unanswered questions. I understand the old cliche of leaving the audience wanting more, but the story here did not give any closure to any part of the game itself. I just hope the DLCs coming next expand upon the story and add to that ending.
2. Lack of hubs: Deus Ex games have had some amazing explorable hubs ever since the first one. This one though doesn't have beyond one. The open ended world seemed pretty limited due to that. I hope we'll get to explore more worlds as the series progresses.
Overall, I'll recommend this title to the hardcore fans of the series, but by no means is this game anywhere close to perfect. A solid 7/10.

Disappointing. Game started great and was seemingly building up to a very promising progression and mind blowing ending that would resolve all the mysterious story lines and connect the new Deus Ex world with that from the first game. Instead it ended unexpectedly and worst of all anticlimactically. Very, very disappointing and dissatisfying.
A huge blow to the face for a DX fan such as myself. Because as soon as the game ended I realized what the developers and publishers are doing. They've come up with a story (could be good, could be bad) and they're going to stretch it into as many games as they can. Thus, there's a huge disbalance in this game between visual content and storytelling.
The game is 46 GBs, so the levels are very detailed and well structured. The music is fantastic. The gameplay is a huge improvement over that from Human Revolution, which I already thought was perfect. But as far as storytelling goes, this game only offers a tiny fraction of what the previous entries delivered.
I'm very sorry to say that Mankind Divided is just a cashgrab. The content it delivers is not enough to justify the price. It's not a complete game, it's a setup for future games, that tells a pathetically small fraction of the full story. Should have been called Deus Ex Mankind Divided Part 1/5 and priced accordingly. Wait till it goes on sale and buy it then, keeping in mind that it's not a complete game, then it won't be such a disappointing buy... maybe.
Edit:
I am changing my review to 'recommended', because although I don't forgive the developers for almost ripping me off, I do have to admit that this game is a unique experience and does an outstanding job at creating that classic Deus Ex atmosphere. Kudos to the devs for everything but the story length and depth.

But.....I felt like this game was rushed and didn't have a lot of time put into it. To me Human Revolution felt like a major step forward for the Deus Ex franchise, where as Mankind Divided seemed like a small step back.
Human Revolution had better immersion with the different open areas. Prague was very cool and detailed, as well as Golem City. But to me Detroit and Hengsha were way better places to do things in. Hengsha was so amazing to look at and it was very detailed.
The character models in Mankind Divided were good and detailed but the lipsync was off and the voice overs were okay but they could have been better. The takedown system seemed more fluid and faster in HR than Mankind Divided. The takedowns took a little longer than they should have and didn't look as cool like they did in HR.
As I said the game was good and I enjoyed every minute that I played. I think Eidos and Nixxes did a good job and I hope to see another game to tie in better to the Original Deus Ex game.

EXCELLENT GAME HELD BACK BY MONEY GRAB.  DO NOT PAY FULL PRICE.
This game is good.  Great, even.  It's got a beautful engine that takes advantage of the latest hardware, great mechanics, level design, voice acting and art direction.  The problem is the publisher has done some really obvious things to squeeze extra money out of players and I find that offensive.  Praxis kits, very affordable items in Deus Ex: Human Revolution now cost an obscene about of game money because you can buy them single-use with real money.  Leveling also feels incredibly slow on Give Me Deus Ex and there are a tonne of upgrades that used to come for free, perhaps for the same reasons.  Pre-order items are single-use so the infamous Pay2Win is now something you only get to use once, meaning I haven't used ANY of them out of disgust.  Content was obviously cut for Season Pass DLC and though I haven't finished the game yet everyone agrees the story is unfinished.
Gameplay-wise there have been a few steps back.  Conversation battles are now completely non-random and easy enough to brute-force, whereas in Human Revolution they were properly challenging even with the CASIE aug.  I'm disappointed this was done to appease the lowest common denominator.  Multiple ammo types were introduced for no real benefit to gameplay and suppressors unfairly cripple your damage output on larger guns.  Still, all of these are design choices that you can argue about.  The publisher greed is black and white.
Deus Ex is my favourite franchise in all of gaming and Square Enix has made it really hard to recommend its latest installment due to practises I don't want to encourage.  Great game, but don't pay full price.

Now with the MKXL update, MKX has finally recieved the support and attention it has needed for so long.  Much better optimizations in graphical rendering make it more stable frame-rate wise and the improved connection makes playing online far easier.
Combining the frantic break-neck speed or more slower defensive styles, you can easily mix-and-match your characters tactics and styles to create unique strategies that will confuse your foes and consolidate victory.  The characters feel less like the caricatures they were in MK9, now feeling more fully fleshed out both in personality and in their models and move-sets, with their own animation quirks and brutal attacks.
The gameplay feels a lot smoother than MK9 where it's easier to land combo's (though the game isn't so centered around simply combing), traverse the stage, and also take advantage of using pokes/jabs and naked strikes.
The roster contains a bevy of newcomers, some with completely new concepts to the game, such as Erron Black, and others that many players will find recognizable and interesting.
With fatalities, stage fatalities, and pit fatalities, the permanent blood pools on the stage, and the dynamic damage models on characters, the game is as violent as ever.  With the addition of the new brutality system which allows one to combo into a gruesome finisher, it truly lends somewhat of a new gameplay strategy to the game as well.
It's well worth the purchase price that it stands at now, and if you're interested in exploring even more of its content, there's a XL bundle with 8 extra characters in store for you and plenty of different costumes.  In my eyes, this is one of the top Mortal Kombat games.  MKX, MK2, and MK3 are all worthy of being mentioned in the same sentence, even the same breath as one another.

My feeling on the gameplay: You know the thing that makes people enjoy Super Smash Brothers? The thing where everyone can enjoy it and it still takes learning and skill to play the game? You do? Then take that aspect away, make all the "Legends" (AKA characters) play nearly identical.

I had Trine 2 originally on Xbox, but since the Goblin Menace expansion isn't available on XBLA, I had to open a Steam account to get it. In a nut shell Trine 2 is a fantasy platformer with a heavy emphasis on physics-based puzzle solving and a lot of combat in between. It's a mechanically two-dimensional game in a three-dimensional space.
As a product it feels extremely complete and well-rounded across the board. The obvious thing is the graphics which is just unbelievable; even more so in the DLC. When I first saw the game I just wanted to strip naked and rub it all over my nipples. That's not a figure of speech. The game is visually absolutely top notch both artistically as well as technically. The level design is varied with some really cool set pieces.
But other than that, every aspect of the game seems very polished: the soundtrack is solid, if unspectacular, the animations are by and large smooth. The sheer number of different ways to solve the puzzles in the game is impressive and really is testament to the consistence of the physics and variety of tools at your disposal.
Gameplay is super fluid and interaction with other players in co-op (played only on XB) is seamless and tons of fun. I somewhat struggled with PC controls after having got used to Xbox's gamepad, but from what I gather, that's at least partly down to my laptop not being quite powerful enough to run the game smoothly.
The storyline is not incredibly cerebral, though one might argue that in the light of the fairy tale setting, it is fitting. The voice acting, the characters as well as narrator, is done superbly.
Again, Trine 2 feels like a very complete entertainment product, but if there's one flaw, it must be the camera. Since you can't control it, which is to be expected, of course, in a platformer, it can, at times, act against your wishes. I find this rare, however.
At any rate, in terms of production values, this is a triple A game; at launch in 2012 there would have been little real reason not to charge the full retail price, had it included the DLC already back then, but at €16.99 the game is a steal.

Devil May Cry 4 is an enjoyable action game, let down by problems clearly caused by a rushed development. The game has 20 missions, just like its predecessor, but many of them are simple retreads of earlier levels, complete with the same bosses. While backtracking occured in DMC 3, it was handled much better than this. Thankfully, the developers know what they're doing, and have done their best to try and revitalise these old levels, but what was really needed was more time in development, not a rushed product.
The other main issue the game has is the bosses. While still enjoyable to fight and well designed, the majority of bosses can't hold a candle to the bosses of DMC 3 (excluding 3's Gigapede), and the two that can are some of the only bosses not repeated in the game. This repeating can make fighting some of the bosses for the second or third time tedious as a result, whereas repeating the other two would likely not have been: fighting Vergil three times was fun in 3, Angelo Credo would surely have also been fun to fight more than once.
That being said, this game still gets a recommend. The combat is as polished as ever, with new character Nero serving as a good introduction to the system for newcomers to Devil May Cry, and Dante now being able to switch between styles and all weapons on the fly, allowing for large amounts of player expression. On top of this, the Special Addition includes Vergil, Lady, and Trish as playable characters, who are also fun to play as (especially Vergil).
The enemies still attack you in swarms, and there are some very well designed enemies here, the standout being the Blitz enemy, a teleporting, electric abomination that can take and dish out a lot of pain. The stronger enemies outclass Devil May Cry 3's Fallen and Abyss enemies, although 3's fodder is better than the indistinguishable scarecrow enemies on display here. These aggressive enemies are a large part of why DMC's combat works so well, and the strength of this combat is what gets the game recommended.
Devil May Cry 3 is one of the kings of the action genre, and although its younger brother lacks a fully realised set of levels, it still comes close to taking the crown.

DISCLAIMER: Due to the evolving nature of MMO's, the described content may have changed by the time you, the reader, see this.
LotRO... well.
To start of, I've spent more time on this game than I ever thought I would spend on a single game, be it MMO or not.
(I started playing LotRO through the confines of Steam only recently, the game hours I speak of can be found on my
under "Most Played")
The short description which I can think of would be that 'iIt's a "Hotkey-MMO" similar to Everquest 2, RIFT and World of Warcraft which focuses more on a player storyline that goes through-out your leveling experience. Don't be fooled by that last bit as it's not a 100% in-a-line story RPG experience in a Massively Multiplayer world. There will be level gaps where you'll take time off from the story and do the good ol' MMO questing.
Aside the basic questing and the Story-line, known as the "Epic", we also have:
- Some scalable to a chosen level your level, for which the lowest level it can be scaled to tends to be the level you unlock the instance on.
- Others with a fixed level
- Same as instance type A, but generally a smaller experience/more compact experience.
- Same as instances, but bigger scale. (Kinda)
- Starts around lvl 10ish. Scales to cap. (Iffily or so I've heard)
The F2P model. Well this is something that rubs a lot of people the wrong way. To be frank, no one likes that a game, advertised as free, has the cash-shop surprise. However one should keep in mind that there's a difference between Free to Play and Freeware games.
It's better than most, but then again, all F2P games should be taken with caution.
The flat out free content includes the majority of the classes (with the exception of Rune Keeper, Warden and Beorning), all the starting zones (The Shire, Ered Luin and Bree Land) and 1 post-start zone, Lone Lands, which ends around level 32.
No level limitations aside the actual level cap. (
)
3 bags out of 6. (Static 15 slot bags)
All crafting tiers are available, but you only have access to the first 2 reputation tiers in a crafting guild. (Or something like that.)
Gold (100c = 1s, 1000s=1g) is capped at 2.
You have 2 character slots on each server.
Each character has 2 free virtue and race trait slots out of 7 and access to the Class Specialization tree, but not the specialization bonuses (an extra bonus per 5 points in the chosen "main" specialization tree).
is unlocked/free up untill the start of Helms Deep (Roughly around lvl 90).
Well, yes and no. You are able to gather the cash-shop currency through gameplay. There are deeds, which are the equivalent to achievements. Majority of the deeds reward the player with the cash-shop currency known as TP (Turbine Points) allowing players to unlock further content for just playing the game. In my time on LotRO I have ran into more than a few players who have been unlocking their way through the game via just that. At times it does feel like a grind, but it is a viable way for a Free player to expand their experience.
I have no interest in PvP. (It's Raid PvP and people complain on General. Though to be fair everyone complain about PvP always any way)
Well, LotRO focuses mainly (but not only) on PvE and the Epic questline. In that regard, I have not seen a single thing on the VIP features list, nor the cash-shop that would indicate that this is a P2Win game. Yes, it has PvMP (Player versus Monster Player) meaning PvP is in the game which in its essence is endgame Raid PvP and not your standard Arena PvP. Even there I don't see it being P2Win in any way.
This is my point of view on this, opinions may vary. (Opinions are like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and all that good stuff.)
It feels like an extended trial, infact it has enough content to be considered as something more than just a trial. I haven't seen a lot of games with a F2P model as fair as LotRO has. Which is partly why I've stuck with the game.
My experience so far:
I started playing a few weeks after LotRO went F2P.
To be entirely honest. Not as much as one would expect. I've never been a fast leveler. I like to explore a lot and alt-oholism takes its toll. Which is why I generally prefer to work on deeds for TP, instead of throwing money at Turbine. My highest level character is capped at 100 (provided there hasn't been a sneaky cap increase I'm unaware of [Yes there has. Multiple even.]), I have a total of 10 character slots and various convenience upgrades, most of which I've unlocked via Deeds rather than real money.
Premium. The status between VIP and Free. The player who has spent some money on the game, but isn't sitting on a subscription.
Yes, a lot. I'm a LotR fan and so far I have not been disappointed in this presentation of Middle-Earth.
It's possible. I am quite surprised I've been with it for so long. However I do believe that this is highly unlikely and if I recall correctly the Epic questlines goal is to reach Mordor which is something I would love to personally witness.
It's F2P, try it. If you don't like it then at least you have experienced something different and are that much wiser.

The concept of this game is great - the execution is lacking.
I wanted a game that focussed on the politics of running a city - playing factions against each other, ensuring that you had a plurality of support even if upset some groups. This is not that game. The march of progress is predetermined, and your actions have a negligible impact on it. More to the point, your prior actions count for nothing - council elections ignore your impact on the city, and there is not even the prospect of asking for a quid-pro-quo from an ally to get something you want - if their initial inclination is to oppose a proposal your only option is to beg, taunt or threaten them into submission, at the expense of your previous months of friendship.
The game has many, many numbers...but no feedback. If your city is making a loss, there is no indication why, and the city-builder-lite approach means that you have no practical way of solving the deficit anyway, short of exploiting a glitch in the game's logic.
I suspect a very large percentage of players are like me - they played once, got the "End of the Line" achievement, and have no desire to play again. Which is a shame - this promised to be the game this niche was waiting for, but failed to deliver.

This is an endearing and heatfelt tale that isn't afraid to stick to its guns and put the players through the story that the creators envisioned. While this may look like a children's game, it handles rather mature subject matter, and throws some curveballs along the way.
Pros:
- Beautiful environments
- Nice soundtrack
- Surprisingly manageable controls for two characters simultaneously
- Moving themes
Cons:
- Begging for a two-controller multiplayer
- A few clunky moments that can result in annoying deaths (but nothing incredibly annoying)
- Language might take some people out of the game (they don't speak a real language, it's more like Simglish)
Overall, this was a strong game that is very nice to look at, very relaxing to play (definitely helps me cool down after a frustrating session of Chivalry: MW, for example), and tells a compelling story about two bonded brothers.

Overall, it's the best cricket sim on the market. It's also a big step up from the Don Bradman series, and with Big Ant getting the licensing for the Ashes, I'm full of promise for the future of the game!
Positives:
- Great graphics, particularly the bowling and batting (fielding can be wonky).
- Brilliant controls (having the option of the classic or standard is perfect).
- Career mode is heaps of fun.
- Lots of modes to keep your interest (mini games, series, tournaments, career, one off matches).
Negatives:
- The commentary is the glaring bug, and it's a wonder it made it past QA, because it's a complete mess. Having Michael Slater commentate would be great, if it weren't for the fact 50% of the time he says something that is completely wrong/unrelated to the events that have occurred. Or missing audio: "Great work by... " And then silence.
- Some bugs. The biggest is the stumping/leaving the ball bug. Basically only applies to batters when playing spin, but if you press the button to leave the ball, the animation will take your player out of the crease and you will be stumped 9/10. Massive bug, but I'm sure it'll be fixed soon!
I really recommend this one. Sure, it's a bit rough and has some bugs. But overall it's great, and small developers need support. So pick it up and give it a crack!

If you are a fan of the series then this game is okay.  It's very shallow and not well thought out, but it does accomplish the very basics of a hack and slash game.
The game is unoptimized, a now all too common trend amongst developers.  It's simplistic graphics and want to be flashy combat leave much to be desired and stills manages to work your hardware beyond what is admittedly necessary to run the game at max settings.  To better understand this, I can run Witcher 3 at 4k on max settings and maintain 50 fps. GPU temps never go over 47 degrees on water.  RWBY, 4k, max settings which aren't much, my temps run 47-51.  Witcher 3 and RWBY.   Yeah no.  Just no.  Optimize the code people.
The combat is fun, but like I said, and much like the story (which is almost none existent) combat is shallow.  The skill tree is laughable at best and I personally feel there is great opportunity to make something of this part of the game mechanic but it just hasen't been done.  Bring in some Dynasty Warriors type action and give each character their own extensive skill trees and then we can have something to smile about.
Level design is not great but I guess it works.  Okay, really, it just seems boring.  There is literally nothing going on and no interaction with the game world aside from the occasional barrel or box or vase to destroy for very little to no reason at all.
Voice is pretty good for playable characters.  Not great but good enough.  All other voice acting sucks.
Overall, on a scale from 1 to 10 I'd give this game a 4.  It was a good try but there are just too many shortcomings to to give an honest recommendation for this title.

After playing 4.6 hours of this game, I have grown tired of it. Though the early experience wasn't stunning, it was fun while new enemy types continued to be introduced. However, this falls appart toward the end-game enemies. Several of the normal end-game enemies are simply faster than you are with attacks that can't be interupted likes your attacks, and there are multiple of them so you don't really have any time inbetween attack combos to hit them. Also towards the end of the game, the same groups of enemies get thrown at you in almost identical patterns rather than varying from one encounter to the next. For example, I would rather fight two mini-bosses at once sometimes rather than fight two in a row in five seperate encounters.
Then there is the final boss. The final boss appeared interesting but has many flaws and felt uninspired in terms of mechanics. It also has several issues such as causing damage instances in its pre-burrowing position while unburrowing as well as being able to pop up underneath you and instantly killing you. As there are no checkpoints, this will end your run of the last level imediately if you are attempting to play single-player. Also, as you progress through the battle, there is an add that continually spawns, presumably to prevent players from beting the boss by saying in the edge of the room and shooting the boss to death. I would rather the boss be improved so that this add does not need to be spawned than to let this add to remain. A simple volley of ranged attacks for the boss that is fired every 15-25 seconds at the player(s) could replace this add entirely, and would feel a lot less lazy.
I liked the game to begin with and I would love to come back to enjoy the game further but at least some of these issues need to be fixed before I will be able to enjoy the game again.

Before you start commenting and hate my review due to fanboyism. I for one, have been a fan of RWBY since day one.
As much as I love the RWBY franchise, I can't recommend this game to anyone except Anime fans, RWBY fans and players that are well into action or Hack n Slash games for that matter.
Let's start off with the cons:
- Replayability is garbage
- Difficulty is alright (in terms of fair play) but somewhat broken (in terms of balance)

- New character designs look like clay and it doesn't suit the characters of RWBY (Older ones were better)

- Story is meh
- Buttons and combos are very basic (A five year old can master at combos and that's a fact.)
- Main antagonist is bad
- Game updates (It's lacking new things. I presume RT have abadoned this game.)
- Occasionally the bugs can freeze the game especially if it's your first time playing it
- Incomplete game
Moving onto the indifferences:
- Game is fun for a while but falls short
- Graphics are nice but the character/monster designs prevent from being a pro
- Maxing characters levels will take you a long time if you go to prestige (Whatever it's called)
- Music is good but I feel there are times where it doesn't match the atmosphere (Except for 1-2 songs)
Moving onto the pros:
- RWBY Characters are awesome as always
- Level designs are nice to look at despite budget issues
- Multiplayer is fun to play (Especially with friends)
- Skill set is basic and very easy to understand
- RWBY vibes
Overall rating: 3.5/10

Now with the MKXL update, MKX has finally recieved the support and attention it has needed for so long.  Much better optimizations in graphical rendering make it more stable frame-rate wise and the improved connection makes playing online far easier.
Combining the frantic break-neck speed or more slower defensive styles, you can easily mix-and-match your characters tactics and styles to create unique strategies that will confuse your foes and consolidate victory.  The characters feel less like the caricatures they were in MK9, now feeling more fully fleshed out both in personality and in their models and move-sets, with their own animation quirks and brutal attacks.
The gameplay feels a lot smoother than MK9 where it's easier to land combo's (though the game isn't so centered around simply combing), traverse the stage, and also take advantage of using pokes/jabs and naked strikes.
The roster contains a bevy of newcomers, some with completely new concepts to the game, such as Erron Black, and others that many players will find recognizable and interesting.
With fatalities, stage fatalities, and pit fatalities, the permanent blood pools on the stage, and the dynamic damage models on characters, the game is as violent as ever.  With the addition of the new brutality system which allows one to combo into a gruesome finisher, it truly lends somewhat of a new gameplay strategy to the game as well.
It's well worth the purchase price that it stands at now, and if you're interested in exploring even more of its content, there's a XL bundle with 8 extra characters in store for you and plenty of different costumes.  In my eyes, this is one of the top Mortal Kombat games.  MKX, MK2, and MK3 are all worthy of being mentioned in the same sentence, even the same breath as one another.

Before I truly begin I’ve read a few of the negative reviews of this game and apparently it’s a rip off of some other game. Unfortunately I don’t know the other game so i’m incapable of judging this game as a rip off.
Revolution Ace is a total rip off! It’s just like every other SHMUPP! Har har har. All joke(s) aside the gameplay for Revolution Ace is most certainly no revolution. Luckily I don’t find this gameplay style boring and RA adds a few things in to spice up the flying and shooting.  There are all sorts of powerups to gather during active gameplay, they appear from “corpses” of enemies or destroyed buildings. In between missions there is an weapon upgrade and unlock system plus an xp based leveling system.  This game is very simple but that isn’t inherently a bad thing.  The few good things that Revolution Ace has, it does well.  The combat is a hectic bullet hell and standard SHMUPP experience.  The weapons I wield against my foes are satisfying and varied enough not to disappoint. Finishing each level is also far more satisfying than a standard SHMUPP; not only is there a point tally but you also gain xp from which to level. The points you gain are also the upgrade currency so they feel more satisfying that regular points.  Yeah obviously RA isn’t all that special, but, for a basic game it has the needed flavor to fill out the experience into something complete. It’s a well rounded snack of a game.
Pros:
-SHMUPP
-Solid Controls both in & out of play
-Customization & Leveling
-Varied Weapons
-Not Immediately Repetitive
-Snack Food(good in short bursts)
Cons:
-SHMUPP
-Repetitive
-Meh Visuals
-Meh Music
-Frequent utterances of “Meh”
-Snack Food (too quickly full and over it)
I liked Revolution Ace.  Playing it was enjoyable enough for a SHMUPP. I like the added “complexity” of the leveling and weapon placements/upgrades. The controls are responsive, they didn’t frustrate me or get blamed for any deaths. The things that let this game down do so not because they are bad necessarily, it’s more that they’re very meh.  The Graphics and Music are the most obvious examples of the mehness; they are not offensive they’re just alright and not distinctive.  This game is fun for sure, but it’s not worth $4.99.  I can’t remember what I paid for it but if I paid more than $0.99 then I’m F*ucking stupid. Thanks for reading. :D

2/22 edit: The image of this game sums it up. "See all these buildings? That's what Cities: Skyline's has. As for me? Ehh..." He's doing some sort of given up expression. It sums up my thoughts on this game entirely.
Man, where do I even begin with this game?
I wanted to love it so much after watching Youtube videos and playthroughs; this game looked amazing after watching several hours of them. Sadly, I don't think I've ever been burned as hard as I have been with this game more than any other game I've ever preordered in my entire life, including Spore. Yes. Including Spore.  I've tried to give this game some breaks, but...
Let's bulletpoint this.
1: Any resolution other than your native monitor resolution and the game will dull the colors immensely. Also, forget trying to play this game at anything above 1080p, because you'll get graphical errors that make all of your buildings white and blue. Also, kiss any framerate stability out the window, despite owning a GTX 1080. It's been three weeks since release, and no fix. Unexcuseable.
2. You feel like you have no control over anything, that everything you do doesn't matter, and by the end, you stop caring. You can see there's this whole economy ticking behind your industries and businessess, but you can't decide to help paper or barbershops directly or anything of the sort. You just place huge districts down and hope things work out. City council edicts are just passive boosts to your entire city that you just idly click on to make things easier.
3. I really must stress the lack of control. What does heavy traffic do to harm your city? Don't know, because unlike Cities Skylines it just gives you vague 'maximum traffic usage' numbers. How does it damage my economy? What can I do to make lumber or movies a better industry in my town? No idea! A lot of the time you're just waiting months to do minor adjustments to districts for... boredoms sake?
4. Your city looks boring as heck. Roads? All grids. Industries? I guess film industries, car factories, and lumber mills all look the same and I just didn't know about it. Don't you remember when film studios had smoke stacks? I sure don't! So forget having any major control on how your city looks, or putting it on a hill, or anything of the sort. It's just flat land. Remember Germany being flat? Guess we're in the Netherlands now.
You know, I could go on, and on, and on. About how the music repeats every ten minutes; how you really have to zoom in on max settings to even see people walk about; how despite the cool as heck technology tree is broken because you can be 30, 40, 50 years ahead of modern tech if you abuse it. This game made me not care about my city, what I was doing, and why I was doing it. That's the nail in the coffin for any simulator. I just don't see anything they could do to fix this game. It's just... not fun. And it depresses me saying that.
I wouldn't recommend this game, even if it went on sale from 40 dollars to 5 dollars. It just feels... like some major spark is missing. Cities Skylines absolutely destroys this game, and still stands as the best city builder to date. Go get that, and like two hundred mods, and watch a day pass by. Oh, and they aren't even sure this game will get modshop support now. Heck, Tropico 5 is still an excellent choice for those who want something more local and flavorful. To me, I should have bought the new Skyrim instead of this. This is literally, the biggest disappoint in gaming in years to me. I wanted to love this game... but I can't. The concept screamed epic, the execution... souless.

Dreaming Sarah is an adventure platformer with puzzle elements, set in a whimsical but often eerie set of dreamscapes. You play as Sarah, a young girl in a coma, with the hope of finding your way out of the dream and waking up.
There are a handful or two of other characters to meet in your journey, from a plant-like creature to an old man staring wistfully. Sometimes these characters will require help, such as finding something that has been lost, or other times, they will help you, gifting you strange and sometimes baffling items.
While the movement is rather stiff (there is no inertia), platforming is easy and enjoyable enough. There is only one hectic platforming moment (and this is only due to a time constraint), and Sarah controlled fluidly enough to get through it without a hitch.
All of the puzzles are easy enough to figure out, but not to the point of ridiculousness. It was entertaining to take notes here and there, and to eventually put all the pieces together. The puzzles and platforming definitely take a backseat to the exploration, but I was more than happy to traverse through this world, whether I was running through it for the first time, or backtracking for a final achievement.
It was fun to jump and float with Sarah’s umbrella, and to wear magical seeing glasses that revealed hidden platforms (among other, sometimes terrifying, things). The only complaint I have with items is that many of them are currently useless (it is, however, early access), and that my compass didn’t work (despite that I saw it works quite clearly on Youtube).
The art style is beautiful to say the least, with the environments conveying a sense of both wonder and yet loneliness. Sarah’s animations are lovely, with a clear distinction between her walking, standing, running, finding a wall, sitting, swimming, et cetera. The same goes for the few NPCs of the world. To perfectly fit this world, a completely atmospheric soundtrack plays, but there is one area without sound at all.
I can’t really judge this game properly yet, as it is still unfinished, but I can definitely recommend it. It captivated me for three hours, and I only stopped because, after being stuck for some time, I realised I’d probably reached the end of the game as it currently exists*. If the second half of the game is as decent as the first, then it will be my absolute pleasure to play again.
*I got to the road with the skeletal ducks, and then the grandfather clock with some unhelpful balloons. Has anyone made it further?

Mankind Divided is a cyberpunk-themed role-playing stealth game and a direct sequel to Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
Story
You play as Adam Jensen, an augmented Interpol agent working with a special Interpol unit to capture a terrorist group of augmented humans. He is also secretly working for the Juggernaut Collective, a hacker group out to stop the Illuminati.
You are a double agent. The main story is about 10h long.
Gameplay
You can approach each situation the way YOU prefer. You can use combat, stealth, hacking or...talking.
The game itself is presented with a first-person perspective, with a third-person cover system.
If you prefer combat over sneaking then you're in luck because you have a pretty wide arsenal of "tools". You can do lethal and none-lethal melee takedowns, unlock augments that can kill an entire groups of enemies. You can also loot, buy and upgrade weapons. There are assault rifles, shotguns, sniper rifles, pistols, different grenades and more. All firearms are customisable.
If you prefer stealth then well, you're also in luck. You can sneak around in ventilation shafts, look for alternative routes and use cloaking augmentations that let you go unnoticed for a certain period of time. You can also hack doors, cameras, turrets and drones.
You can also persuade people into doing what you want. For that you need common sense and a social augmentation. The game uses a conversation wheel similar to Mass Effect. I think it's pretty self explanatory.

I'm giving this game a recommendation with reluctance.
But before I get started I need to add a disclaimer that Human Revolution made me a fanboy of the Deus Ex series and novel(s)
So, why a recommendation?
IT’S DEUS EX!
This game takes everything that was brilliant in Human Revolution (HR), polishes, adds neat twists and then spits it back out into the hub city of Prague. My first thought of Prague was that it felt empty very much like my first feeling in HR, honestly I don’t know what I was expecting, the rain soaked and densely populated streets from Blade Runner? Yeah I probably was……but there’s just this nagging feeling that the devs stopped short of doing exactly this. Maybe because each person you come across has their own individual animation and voice acting and to replicate this across hundreds of characters would take forever, maybe so.
The main missions keep the story ticking along at a nice pace but this is where the game fails for me, the main missions. By the time I started the final act I JUST DIDN’T CARE, nothing in these missions and the story overall made me care about anything that was going on in this part of Deus Ex Universe. Yes there were nice nods to the original game and some nice character reveals or name drops so you knew what other unseen characters were doing but by the time the credits had rolled I JUST DIDN’T CARE. There was no hook for you to grab hold of, no “human” story as such to hit you in the feels and that was the biggest failure of this game. They had a chance to really progress with this, really give us more of the story that the original Deus Ex game started and that HR progressed via the beginnings of the back story but alas no, I feel the devs were given a direction by Square Enix to wring as much as they could out of this to create a franchise universe that could be cashed in on and trust me as a fan of the Deus Ex game and lore that’s the only thing that hit me in the feels.
The side missions were for me the standout feature, spending the best part of an hour escorting a golden penguin, smashing a drugs ring, helping a mafia boss and being the greatest detective in the world (yeah that’s right Batman, come and get me!)
Also I need to add that when the final credits roll and you can’t exit from them don’t leave your seat, there’s a mid-credits marvel type cut scene that draws you right back into the game. For all my complaining above this single cut scene has intrigued me as to what will happen in the next Deus Ex instalment.
Finally before I do the obligatory Pros and Cons I need to mention the shop side of the game. This doesn’t sit right with me at all, it’s not pay to win as such but more pay to boost, not once during the game did I feel that I needed to buy some extra credits or praxis packs. If anyone buys these, which is a blatant attempt by Square Enix to again milk this series you’re saying “Hay I’m cool with you doing this, I’m happy for you to add more things like this to your next game” NO! There’s no need for these type of things in game and no need for publishers in general to add real money boosts, this is a cash grab plain and simple, it fu%*s my right off to see this in a Deus Ex game.
Pros
+ Side missions - I found these more fun and interesting then the main mission
+ Everything that was brought over from HR and improved on. Shooting, cover, stealth, weapon mods, loadout building
+ The ability to build the Adam Jenson that you want to play as
+ Voice acting – whilst the lip syncing on the characters is shaky at best there are some great actors in this game and most of them are to be found in the side missions.
+ Funny moments – See the penguin mission in the game for further details or throwing items at NPC’s with zero reaction “Hugh? Was that a giant garbage can that hit me in the head?”
+ On the fly weapon and ammo modifications
+ The ability to complete boss missions in any way you see fit
+ Mid end credits cut scene which draws you directly back into the game
Cons
- The real money shop, yes it’s optional but if you buy from it the publishers will see this as a green light to do it again and again.
- Main Story, painful and not engaging. The mid-credits cut scene draws you back into the story in 30 seconds. Why couldn’t they do that through the entire game?
- Clearly a game split into two pieces so that we have a trilogy. We could have had a 60 hour blast but instead we get a 30 hour wet lettuce. Square Enix, take a look at CD Project and come back to us with something better
Final Score 6.5/10 Must try harder

GunZ 2 is a solid team arena fighting game.  It's one of the few that manage to blend melee fighting (sword, bat, dagger, greatshield, whip, etc.) with gunfighting (smg, pistol, sniper, shotty, RPG, etc.) and keep both of the two useful.  Sharp things are deadly up close, and shooty things are devastating if you can manage to land your shots without getting caught in melee range.  Everyone's super mobile.  The skill cap is pretty high, but there aren't that many people who are up there.  You're able to learn the basics in like five minutes (if that), and you'll be useful from that point onward, so long as you back up your teammates and don't try to solo a group of dudes on a fair field.  If the idea of running up walls, dashing through the air, slicing a dude up, getting knocked on the floor, and watching a guy unload a whole clip of a SMG into your face all within 0.02 seconds sounds like your gig, then you should give the game a shot.
GunZ 2 should satisfy your GunZ nostalgia (or it does the trick for me, anyway).  It
a different game, however.  At least two things are significantly different - the skill curve and the melee mechanics (melee staggers hard now).  Someone who's played for a week can compete with most people who've played for months.  There are still the guys who will pound your face into the pavement for hours on end though, so don't give up hope there.  Working toward skill cap on GunZ 1 was more about managing meta - weapon swapping/dashing to eliminate cooldowns, becoming more proficient at the kstyle/butterfly button combos, setting macros, etc..  In GunZ 2, it's more about managing your (and your teammates') positions, landing your hits/shots, and in-the-moment strategic improvisation improvements, because there are a few small cooldowns and staggers that you can't completely eliminate, and you can get caught in a melee stagger combo if you slip up.  That's not to say you can't still do meta things like juggle a dude indefinitely in a stun lock if you're willing to put in the time to learn how to do it, but in contrast to GunZ 1, GunZ 2 seems as though you're playing the game the way it was meant to be played, rather than as though you're learning to break it better than the other guy.  Whether that's a pro or a con is up to you.  The PVE in the first GunZ was hands-down superior though.  I wouldn't play GunZ 2 for the PVE element.  It's bad.  The cash shop is super reasonable in GunZ 2.  Much moreso than it was in the first game.  I really wish they'd implement the VIP/assassination gametype from GunZ 1, and the game could use some promoting, but it looks like development is stopped for the time being :(
The only thing this game really
is more people to play it.  The community's small right now, so it can take a while to find a match sometimes (especially during odd hours), but it's plenty worth it when you do.  If it suits your style, it's just pure fun.

One of the most beautiful,touching and relaxing video games out there.Brothers-A Tale of Two Sons is a co-op adventure game wich is played by a single person,simultaneously controlling the two characters.The game itself is not very long,but it's totally worth it.
Here are the things I liked the most about the game.

An amazing journey that's more like an interactive, albeit silent, movie than a computer game.  It's also kind of like 'Limbo done right'.
Although the ending is almost as disappointing as Limbo, everything else about is similar but in colour and just plain better.  Some of how they are similar:
* intriguing world
* beautiful scenes
* ghastly and/or creepy and/or mysterious at times
* a story told more through gameplay than text and cutscenes (but the cutscenes do help and are *nice*)
* physics based puzzles
How Brothers' differs:
* it stays puzzle based (Limbo ends up being about 'can you time the jump just right' and leaves the puzzles behind; Brothers sticks with the puzzles till the end - they just get different and/or are used in different combinations)
* wide range of environments (from lush forests to ice; from haunting to battlefield remains; lots of variety and the mood seems to follow)
* you control two characters at once - it's unique and it's handled exceptionally well both in the fluidity of the controls and in the different ways they choose to exploit it at different points in the game
As with any game, it's not without it's flaws.  It's well and truly worth it despite them, but for openness, here are three I feel it has:
* A near-game-ending bug at the end of chapter 2.  It wouldn't progress past a certain gate right at the end of the chapter.  Replaying from a checkpoint didn't resolve the bug; replaying right from the beginning of the chapter did.  (If it happens to you, the game is more than worth the one chapter replay).
* A disappointing ending.  It caters to a particular group of people, so some people will love it.  To me it feels like it ends that way *just* to cater to that group, so some people will be disappointed by it.  That said, everything else is just so amazing that the ending is ultimately just a drop in the ocean.
* It's relatively short time-wise.  (But story and location/environment-wise it still feels huge.  Treat it like an interactive movie and it's a whole trilogy worth).

Alright, yet another of my SG wins is officially done and dusted. It took less than an hour to complete the game and I thought since I need to let the game idle for another hour+ to get the remaining cheevos which are all playtime based that I'd go ahead and write up a brief review on Far Space Halloween Edition.
So, Far Space actually exceeded my expectations a bit. That said, I had really low expectations going in.
The story is obviously basic. You are one of three astronauts stuck on a space station that's been attacked by some alien robotic species. You simply need to escape and get back to Earth while avoiding or destroying said aliens.
Gameplay is a mix of super simple point and click with choices made by simply hovering over your choice of available decisions for a couple seconds. You do move almost insanely slow during these sequences. These sections alternate with some lite-shmup sections that feature pretty terrible aim mechanics. However, despite the game's best efforts, you will still get past these sections with relative ease. That is basically everything there is to it.
You will fight the camera a bit during the point and click sections, which can be annoying.
Load times are nominal, which was nice.
The graphics in Far Space are actually quite nice. This was easily the developer's focus as far as this game goes. With the exception of the actual astronauts themselves, everything looked nice and was fairly well detailed.
Oh...also....because it is the Halloween Edition, the astronauts are all Jack-o-lanterns.
The music track in Far Space is suitable to the game. It sounds like something you would expect to hear in a game like this.
The voice over was hilariously bad as was the actual dialogue, such as it is. In fact, it's fairly well meme worthy several times over. I'm pretty certain it wasn't meant to be funny, but it was.
Far Space wasn't a terrible way to spend less than an hour. It is by no means a good game, but as far as bad games go, this could be considered a decent "B" movie type adventure.
Overall, I would give this a 4.5-5 out of 10, but I'm going to go ahead and loosely recommend it regardless, as a decent little time killer with easy 100% achievements.

There are definite improvements here over the past Big Ant releases.  I preferred DBC 14 over DBC 17, but this probably  trumps both.  If you are familar with the DBC series, it won't take long to sort this one out.  To date I've only played a handful of hours, but here are a few things I've noticed:
Pro:
•	You now have a choice as to assign buttons on the controller in one of two ways.  You can leave it in the traditional Big Ant style - footwork with left stick, bat with right - or go with a different, updated setup.  It doesn’t look like individual button assignments can be done, however.
•	When batting, there are now "dashboard lights" to indicate the quality of footwork, timing, and shot choice (i.e., "Poor", "OK", "Ideal").  They stay visible much longer than the indicators in DBC 17 were on screen.  If you've had trouble in past DBC games sorting out where you've gone wrong, these will probably be a big help.  Similar “dashboard” indicators also exist for bowling: jump and release indicators for pace; spin input and release for spinners.
•	No longer necessary is it to hit left toggle to view the fielders while batting.  An indication pops up on screen when fielding adjustments have been made.  A radar graphic also has been added to the upper right of the screen to show existing field placement.
•	4 bowling lengths are now differentiated – short, good, full, and Yorker.  This allows for more precision.  I do like that it’s no longer necessary to give the ball a rub to make it swing.  I found that a nuisance in the past.
•	TV Replay:  Maybe it's just me, but in DBC 14 I never, ever had a TV replay come up with a "Not Out" on the big screen.  I can say for certain that it happens here.  The TV replays seem more relevant also; with DBC 14 they always looked the same to me (i.e., bat just at the line).
•	It seemed like in DBC 14 the bowler was a cross between an octopus and Superman - nothing went by.  I've had a few shots off a straight bat that have sneaked by the bowler here in the Ashes.
•	With DBC 14, when bowling against the AI I came to expect an “obligatory” boundary off the last ball of the over.  I’m still getting used to bowling in the Ashes game, but I don’t see that predictability here.  Main point being – the AI seems to have been updated quite a bit.
•	Team, player creation – I haven’t mucked about with it too much yet, but I do see the ability to create team logos, different bats, fields.  Female players can now specifically be created.
•	Graphics –I’m not writing about the artwork here, I’m referring to the manner in which the action is portrayed on the field.  It is good, a much more realistic depiction of cricket.  Too often in DBC 14, I would see fielders make diving, one-handed over-the-shoulder catches that would make Jonty Rhodes look like a paraplegic.  I haven’t witnessed that in Ashes.  AI players seem to be well set for the plays they make, run at human speeds, and mannerisms are accurate.  For another example, in DBC 14 all too often I would see fielders at Deep Square Leg, for instance, peg a runner side-on from about 50 meters out.  With the Ashes, now at least the ball goes to the keeper and he'll swipe at the bails.  Much more realistic.
EDIT:  After playing a bit more, I see them running like gazelles to cover gaps and diving like Chinese acrobats again for outstreched grabs.  Pretty disappointing, that.
Catching:    The catching controls are improved.  There is a slowed-down look at the play that you would need to react properly to for a catch to happen.
Con:
•	I've spent a lot of money on my gaming setup, and trust me, it can run anything.  Still, I've had some stuttering, especially with spinners bowling to me.  I've had to back off on the screen WxH, Crowd detail…  Things work well now.
•	Windows 10 – my mouse cursor doesn’t disappear while playing the game.  I have to move it off to the side of the screen so it doesn’t distract me.  I don’t know why.
•	Commentary – They don’t finish sentences, and even if they did it’s still not worth a listen. Shambolic to say the least.
•	Bowling – I haven’t spent too much time bowling, but I’m having trouble so far with adjusting to the new plant-and-release setup.  The indicators and controls are different from what I’ve become accustomed to.  It seems really sensitive and I don't see a way to adjust that.
•	Too many wides called.  I’ve misplayed some deliveries across the line, and the delivery has gone where I was standing.  Not a wide by any stretch, but so called.
•	Stupid run outs.  I’ve made dives, and have seen the replays with almost my entire body beyond the crease.  Yet, for whatever reason the bat is far from grounded.  Out.  In other cases, I've pushed the button to ground the bat, but the runner hasn't, instead he stupidly steps just short of the crease.
•	Fielding –   As with past games, when looking at my screen, the non-striker end is in the foreground, while the striker end is further back and upwards on the screen.  It seems to me that throwing to the non-striker end should be the “A” button on the controller because it is down, closer to me.  Conversely, throwing to the keeper should be the “B”, up on the controller.  Probably it’s just me, but I continue to get that backwards.  I wish I could re-assign that.
EDIT:  Removed comment about simulation - it exists in some modes.
•	Yes, a bit pricey.
EDIT:  It is said that the price includes ongoing support.  I hope so.  I understand it can't be easy for a small company to make such a specialist game and survive.
In all, there are big improvements to the series here, and not just cosmetic.  If you held off on DBC 17, this one could be worth jumping on.  The Ashes contains weighty, meaningful advancements over past Big Ant games.  This is the best of the lot.

If you seriously haven't played this game yet, get this version.  It is the definitive edition of the game despite some weird removals.  Multiple save files have been removed as well as a more stable performance for all hardware.  Now it's stable for most hardware and a bit more demanding.
This original game was rushed.  If you play it, it's pretty clear that Capcom slashed their budget and rushed them when they were halfway done with the game.  The second character you play as through the story does not have their own levels(Not counting Vergil who goes through the whole game himself).  That means that the first half and all bosses were built with Nero in mind and only him.  These bosses are all great, especially a certain rival fight which might be one of the greatest brawls in video game history.  However, they were technically only meant to be fought with Nero.  You could beat them with other characters no problem, but you miss out on certain animations and combos which aren't possible without Nero.  Guess what though, you have to refight almost every boss twice with that second character.  This is the biggest and most fundamental misstep this game had, but I blame Capcom more than I do the developers.  A lot of games around that time that they were making were notoriously rushed.
I'm rambling.  What does the special edition add?  3 new characters.  It doesn't have any of the cut levels, bosses or costumes that were missing.  These 3 new characters are great, don't get me wrong but I would have preferred more to the original single player for Nero and Dante.

I was very excited about this game coming out since it seemed to take away my least favorite part of City-Builder gameplay: laying down every single street and water pipe and powerlines etc... In this regard the game delivered on this expectation very well. Urban Empire is aimed at the political side of managing a city and hence it allows you to be the mayor and relieves you of the burden of also being the town engineer, subcontractor, and surveyor. This is a big plus for me and I enjoy how easy it is to build new districts and have control of the contruction of the city without being bothered by many small details.
However, I cannot recommend this game primarily for three reasons:
Firstly, most of the edicts, proposals, and laws that are voted on by the City Council are rather one sided. With rare exception, most of the laws/edicts only have good benefits for your city and no negative consequences (sometime not even with any monetary expense either). The edicts that do have a negative consequences often are very minimal negative effects and are greatly outweighted by the positive effects.
This leads to the political gameplay feeling very linear: Its like you are an omniscient mayor who knows that all of your ideas are great and they will all have good outcomes and your task is simply to get these nitwits on the city council to realize how good all these edicts and laws are for everyone and vote for them. I find that this leaves the feeling that the gameplay and strategic element is lacking. I would much rather have stronger positives and negatives for each edict. This will greatly improve this aspect of our city but it will also cause equally big problems in this other regard. I think it would also lead to the city feeling more specialized and have a uniqueness to it from one playthrough to the next.
Secondly, this games lacks a good guide to the numbers behind the game and understanding why money or happiness is climbing or falling is often not clear and so making strategic decisions becomes frustrating because unseen variables appear to be affecting your city in unpredictable ways.
Thirdly, you lose goodwill with politcal parties most anytime you encourage or cajole or persuade them how to vote on a particular issue. But apart from some random events, there isn't any consistent way to gain their goodwill. So when your goodwill is low, the only solution is to just talking to the parties until the goodwill rises back up to a normal level. My problem with this is that it ignores the whole deal-making and compromising side of politics. While its true political parties often become strongly divided from each and will not have much goodwill for the other party. At other times two rather different parties will come to an agreement to work together towards some mutual goal and will build up mutual goodwill to build up a stronger political bloc. If this game had some element of negotiating between parties or building up goodwill through consessions and compromise, then it would feel like an accurate political simulation.
Overall, Urban Empire successfully delivers a macro-level city building experience free of all the messy and frustrating detail work that most other city builders require. Unfortunately, the onesidedness of most of the edicts and laws as well as the inablility to cooperate and build up goodwill with political parties makes the game feel scripted and most cities feel the same as the last city you built.

Actually an interesting game to play, just a bit difficult, although after playing it for a couple of hours, I can finally say that the learning curve is not too steep as I previously thought.  You can pick and research technologies which may unlock edicts and certain services to improve the city life for your civilians, becareful, it can be incredibly easy to go into debt and eventually be voted out by other political parties, use your 'good will'' wisely ,use it too much, will make them hate you and will be impossible for you to pass your edicts and laws.
