A match-3 game with lots of cool little extras added to keep it interesting.
Enemies approach your town and you match runes on the same row as that enemy to fire an attack towards them. Your town gathers resources over time which you can use to upgrade buildings or buy spells, tools and minions to help during battle. You also get real-time "quests" as you play like 'make 3 fire matches' which will give you extra loot. To be honest there's so much it can sometimes be overwhelming remembering everything.
A nice addition is that after each story mission, you get to make decisions about your town's future. E.g. you may be asked what you want to do with the boss you just defeated - behead them and present them at the gates as a deterrent, use their body for science to help your research, or rehabilitate and release them.
The only issue is that sometimes the shape of the grid you play on can cause a lot of difficulties. E.g. on a diamond shape map, the top and bottom rows will only have 2 or 3 squares in, making it very difficult to make a match in those squares when an enemy is approaching on that lane. You end up just having to play that level over and over until you can overcome it.

This is a great little game. I have had lots of fun playing it.
You get to manage a town, collect resources, and battle to protect your town from invading monsters.
The battle system is a classic match-3 style game, but when you make a match, it fires elemental bolts at the approaching enemies.
So Match-3 + Tower defense sorta.
You get money and resources from fighting, and you collect resources in town, upgrade your town buildings, manage your citizens, and make decisions on how to run things.
The decisions you make affect your playthrough and can give you hidden bonuses (like I have moved my culture enough toward favoring magical research that I just received a "discount" on casting spells).
Overall, very fun game. It's a good game to pick up, play a few rounds and put down, or you can easily play it for hours.
Definitely recommend!

I'm writing this review for anyone that might be on the fence - give it a try.  I'll qualify by saying that I don't think I would have paid $15 for it, but if you can get it on sale or in a bundle, it's a good little game.
What you will have to do is go into it without high expectations.  The graphics aren't outstanding and it's not going to break any ground in the match-3 space, but I've found it challenging enough to keep my interest.
The short version of the gameplay is that you match symbols which then allow you to attack rows of incoming enemies.  Sounds easy, but it's more difficult than it sounds.  I died more than I thought I would, which is actually OK because the gameplay is fast-paced and doesn't feel like a chore to play a level again.
The city-building isn't spectacular but it's simple enough and gives a good little break in-between the core game.  And the decision making aspect is amusing enough.
Overall - give it a shot, it will grow on you.

Very touching story and beautiful art style. One of the few games that really takes storytelling in video games to another level.
The plot focuses two brothers in an quest to find a cure for their dying father. The story is told without a single line of dialogue (mostly done through vocalization in a fictional language and gestures) which makes it all the more impressive.
The world is beautiful and filled with mystical creatures from classic European mythology.
You will need a controller to play this game properly but that works out for the best. Both characters are controlled simultaneously, one analog stick and a trigger assigned to each. It takes some getting used to but should not challenge you too much.
Only con I'd say is that the platforming feels a little off sometimes and the camera controls can be a little sticky.
Overall definitely worth playing once.

This is gaming storytelling at it's best. Pure hart and soul was put into this game and it shows. The pacing of the game is excellent, the enviorments enchanting. This game is avalible in every language there is, yet there is no text or perceivable dialogue. The game features movie like storytelling. I feel there is so much unused potential in term of videogame storytelling. It is games like Brothers that tap into that potential. And it is with these kinds of games i feel this medium truly shines and offers something diffrent to other plattforms.
Sure i will not play this game of thousands of hours, but unlike my most played games i can actually take away something , like a great book or movie. This game has deep meaning behind it.

Mini Review: Better gameplay than Deus Ex Human Revolution in every way, somewhat lackluster story in comparison.

Any fan of the Deus Ex series is likely going to love the game despite the flaws.  I put about 40+ hours into my first playthrough and the conspiracy theory laden storyline holds up and keeps things exciting throughout.  The world of MD is a little less humorous than some of the earlier games in the series and the tone throughout is darker, but the action (and lack of action in some places) seem weighted appropriately.  For people new to the series, try out the previous games before getting into this one.  Not only are they inexpensive at this point and brilliant, they provide a great foundation for where the series is today.  And much of the storyline in MD references previously known characters and ideas from the series that will enrich your MD experience.

Overall not as good as Human Revolution but still a worthwhile entry in the series. The story is a step down from the predecessor and ends shortly after it starts getting interesting. The ending feels more like the end of a second act in a story. On the other hand the gameplay, world/level design is fantastic and a step up from the previous game. Prague is a great setting with it's mix of old-world architecture and the futuristic cyberpunk style that the series is known for, it's chock full of atmosphere and a total blast to explore.
The side quests are great and the little stories they tell are more enjoyable than the main story. The new augs and abilities are a lot of fun to use and the game plays very smoothly. My entire run was as a stealthy pacifist and sneaking/hacking my way through it was quite enjoyable (a little too easy on the normal difficulty setting though). The music is once again very memorable but the voice acting and animations feel like a step backwards.
All things considered, Mankind Divided is a great Deus Ex game that every fan should play. I'll definitely give it another go on NG+.

Short Version: If you had an erection for Deus Ex: Human Revolution, this game will be your climax. If you thought Human Revolution was good, this game will be very enjoyable. If you didn't like Human Revolution, you won't like this one at all.
LOOOOOOOOOOOONG Version:
I wasn't super excited for this game, but I did want another Human Revolution. This game is the good kind of sequel, having more of the same except enhanced. However, there are some problems here and there which stand out.
THE GOODS
+This game takes everything from the stealth to combat from Human Revolution and improves on it. More weapons and weapon mods, more augs of all kinds. Better hacking mini-game. Controls are improved and aiming down the sight doesn't feel tacted on. Now, I typically have a list for the "Goods" but all I really have to say is: Think Human Revolution, but better gameplay wise.
+This make be a token like but nVidia's 3d Vision looks amazing in this game since the 3d is build into the game.
+The side-missions are good!
THE MIXED
+/-The main plot is entertaining but it just ends. The plot is okay, and you really do want to know what happens next..... But it just ends! The story has a climatic build up to a cliffhanger. Now, I really want to do MORE of this game, but it's obvious this game is the middle-child of a trilogy.
+/-The graphics look bloody amazing but the game has a steep systems requirement. My 1080 can run a stable framerate of 70~120fps at 1440p with High details. Remember that 3d I mentioned? Unless you are running a stealth, non-combat character, you will never want to use 3d since the FPS dies. Just dies.
THE BAD
-Your actions in the first game did not matter whatsoever, and, unfortunately, I think all your actions in this game mean nothing as well. Without spoiling too much, the end of the game says "HEY YOU WON!" but Picus news is spinning it their way in the background. Just.... It feels like, even though I 'saved the world', so to speak, nothing has changed. Status Quo is back to normal.
CONCLUSION:
I got the game for $35.99 and, at that price, I'd recommend this game. Anything more is a tad much, but, since I have a job, anything about $40 better be solid gold. This game is a shiney, nearly-gold silver.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a blend of the first person shooter, stealth and role-playing game genres developed by the company Eidos Montreal. It represents the fifth game in the Deus Ex series.
+ The game offers a more varied world and realistic environment than the prior titles.
+ Obsessive attention to detail regarding level and room design give an authentic impression how a dystopian future may look like.
+ Synthetic music perfectly matches the futuristic aesthetics.
+ Excellent overall locational sounds.
+ Large amount of readable lore and numerous side quests provide useful background information.
- Poor optimization of the PC version leads to performance problems in form of irregular slowdowns and framerate drops.
- Inclusion of one-time micro transactions into the singleplayer campaign.
+ Basic gameplay mechanics and A.I. behaviour are solid and reliable.
+ Previously introduced augmentation system is further extended, allowing for an individual development of character that changes gameplay and unlock new ways in approaching certain situations.
+ Broad spectrum of weapons with extensive customization options offer several ways of trouble shooting.
+ Robust stealth mechanics and multiple paths through each level support a non-combat playstyle.
o The game does not feature any boss battles that appeared in Human Revolution, and remains purely as a series of increasingly challenging infiltration and investigation scenarios.
- Towards the end of the game the difficulty level falls flat.
+ Movie-like presentation of the narration and top-notch voice acting enhance the immersion into the game.
+ Dynamic and realistic conversation trees at key points during game are well done.
+ Multiple outcomes from dialogue with important characters.
- The story is cut short and leaves a lot of questions unanswered. As if the game was cut in half.
- None of the supporting casts or villains are interesting or memorable.
- Lip synchronisation is a train wreck. You want to look away but your morbid fascination gets the better part of you.
Mankind Divided does a great job of maintaining the Deus Ex feeling of having plenty of choices and consequences. Nevertheless, it is less refined than its predecessor regarding character and story development.
The “Breach” game mode is used as an implausible justification to introduce micro transactions to the main game, which is a disgrace to the Deus Ex franchise. The time and effort to flesh out that game mode, which could have been easily a game of its own, should have been invested into the storyline and the main quest journey of the singleplayer campaign.

Revolution Ace is a rather amateurish vertical shoot 'em up.
The game feels quite heavily influenced by the good old Raptor: Call of the Shadows. Unfortunately Revolution Ace is nowhere near as good as Raptor. It does have a number of decent ideas, but none of them are particularly well implemented.
The game goes for a kind of realistic art style (at least with the terrain) and this feels like a terrible choice. The backgrounds look extremely ugly and way too often the enemies and the bullets blend in the terrain. And good luck telling the air and ground targets apart when many of the ground units actually hover in the air too!
The audio isn't particularly impressive either. The sound effects feel quite weak and the soundtrack is rather repetitive as well. The weapons feel extremely weak too and even early enemies can take a massive amount of punishment before finally dying.
The ability to recharge your shields by not firing sounds like a good idea at first, but in practice it just leads to tedious gameplay where you take a break from the actual fighting and spend some time simply dodging bullets. The split between air and ground weapons is not particularly well done either and often ends up being more frustrating than anything else.
Overall I didn't find Revolution Ace particularly enjoyable and I gave up after playing for a bit over an hour. I wouldn't recommended it as there are far better shoot 'em ups available on Steam.
The good:
- Some nice ideas (even if they are not particularly well implemented)
The bad:
- Terrible graphics
- Poor audio
- Ground/air weapon split is poorly done
- Weapons feel extremely weak
- Enemy waves and bullet patterns are not very interesting
- Poorly designed perk system
- Terrible story and writing

This is proof that a good gameplay will keep you in the game even if the graphics aren't good.
I just got severely addicted to this game, even though it's frustrating at first, you don't know what to do and keep dying to 80 men armies, once you get the hang of it, it'll be a really fun experience, making you jump from the chair whenever you fight army vs army, or siege a castle, a city, or fight kings, and the accomplishment of beating a army with only your companions and yourself. There are the tense moments when a huge army faces off against you, you are cornered, the calm moments, and those where you are soo excited with the battle you actually do something wrong and lose everything, feeling in despair, only for you to go out and reconstruct your army.
I have some tips for new players if you want to have a good time on the game:
Fight in tournaments, bet on yourself. Beat everyone down as fast as you can. Seriously, you can make something close to 4k of denizens in just one tournament, which may help you buy that armour or weapon you wished for soo much, or the companion in that tavern. Ah, companions.
If a companion is specialist in something, FOCUS on that. Trust me, you won't regret it, specially after you have lots of companions.
Get a horse, a two handed weapon, a shield to cover your back, and a ranged weapon for emergencies. Don't bother picking the fastest horse, armour over everything. But still get a fast horse, because the faster you are, the more damage you do. And don't forget to move around so the enemies can't strike you, and take care of one by one. Recommended to have a bow though.
With these tips here, you can make your way to beating a 40 man army solo, or with the help of your companions(Even if they'll keep falling in battle.
The graphics in the game may not bid well for many people, but don't let that fool you, that graphics isn't the most important thing, but the incredible combat system it has, instantly putting you in excitement when facing 3 enemies at the same time, and being cornered, having to find a way to kill them all by finding which direction they won't block, just like For Honor, but better, no lock-on system necessary.
And if you're gonna try multiplayer, I hope you do your training well, because if you don't, most players will beat you down incredibly easy, or snipe a headshot outta nowhere.
I can just say, I love this game now. 33 hours well spent, and still counting after this review!

The in combat graphics dont matter that much; you have your army of troops and the simple graphics allow the large battles to run smoothly with no problems. There are however a few bugs, mostly with the ai and pathfinding, and some castles and towns having limited entries during sieges, resulting in clusters slowly tunneling in and getting mowed down. Its not that big of an issue though, since there are so many units in play its kind of to be expected.

GTA 5 was a masterful game when it came out in 2013. It still is, but now it is not as good as new games that came out more recently (or maybe because I have played this game too much, so that affects me).

however...is another story
What I have always wanted since I was younger (back when we used to play GTA: SA Multiplayer mod) was to have a truely open-world online game, that I can play with my friends, to do whatever we want that we can't in real life, and have fun in it.
GTA Online
that
Now that I have found 3 friends to play with, it kinna is fun. However...apart from the time that I play with my friends, GTA Online is pretty boring, grindy and frustrating.
, money and level is TOO important in this game. You need to gain levels to unlock weapons, and you need money to buy cars, houses, planes,...And the process to gain money is really slow. , one of the reason why everything takes so long is because of the LOADING TIME.

Store page says: "city building political strategy game with match-3 tower defense combat"
That is a lie. What is more, that is an unnecessary lie. Yeah this game has some building in it, but it is even more shallow than Facebook games like "Hayday". Yes, this game has some policy options which does not effect gameplay in any meaningful way. These two things are not main part of the game, they are just spices to make player sure that he actually is not playing some kind of "Candy Crush".
That is also a lie. This game heavily resembles Candy Crush. Actually, if I were to sum it up, "Candy Crush with tower defense elements." That is not as bad as it sounds, since we all know about addictiveness of candy crush. Gameplay mechanics are rather solid, most of the weapons and skills has their own uses. Policy options are just there for the sake of feeling like a king, not a 3-matcher. Soldiers have their own uses as well, but Scouts (the elite ones) maybe a bit unbalanced since they are the obvious choose for almost all missions.
I got this game from Humble Bundle, which also includes Paranautical Activity, Stacking and Windforge. The funny part is I got that bundle for Stacking. But this was the game I played most among those. Why? It is addicting. It gives sense of success. But if u despise mechanics of Candy Crush, you wont like this game. This is guaranteed, It has more complex mechanics when it comes to battles, but the main part is the same.
I have two more complaints. One: Resource system is a bit unbalanced. You earn money by waiting, you can earn some infinitesimal money in battle as well, which has no practical uses. Every thing needs wood. Almost nothing needs ore. And you wont need food after you upgraded your town center to level 5. Yes, it should not be more complex than this since this is basically a match 3 game but if these mechanics exist I would want it to be more gamey.
Second. After all this time, (and this is actually the second game first being Tower of Elements) there are still some gamebreaking bugs. If you use some spells which alters the gameboard too much (like Landslide, Tornado etc), and dont wait it to be completed, some cells includes two different colors which is practically impossible to complete the chapter after that. If you wait after using those spells no bug is there, I guess if there is a restriction on using heavy skills one after other, the way it is restricted should not be via a bug.
But still. If you find this game cheap. Real cheap. Under 4 dollars even, I would recommend it if you like such casual games. Since it got me hooked, and I actually finished it with most of achievements unlocked, I feel obliged to recommend it. By the way, this game will be fun for achievement hunters as well since it has well defined goals. Just dont be deceived by claims of the game about being a political simulator, true successor of Sim City 3000 etc, and if you cant find a good deal, go online and search for similar games for free.

I'll preface this by noting that ReignMaker is overall enjoyable, and has interesting and unique features compared to other match-3 games that I've played, but overall not worth the full asking price for the game.
The core of the game-play is a "targeted" match-3 tower defence concept. You will have enemies approaching from the side of your screen and must make matches in the same "row" as the enemy. (skeleton approaching at the next-to-top row of your screen? At least one of the element tiles in your match has to be somewhere in that next-to-top row to do any damage to the skeleton.) Matching tiles destroys the tiles, sends out an elemental bolt or fire/water/darkness/whatever ball streaking directly to the side that the enemies are approaching from. Any projectiles that hit an enemy do damage, and some enemies take more or less damage from different elements. This is an interesting change from the usual "make a match anywhere" of most match-3 games, but it can get quite frustrating on some of the boss fights where you need to deal a massive amount of damage to a relatively narrow area on the battlefield. Part of the game's charm, but also part of the frustration on harder bosses.
Most of the enemies are of the "advance across the screen and beat upon the wall" variety, but the bosses have some unique mechanics (such as throwing fireballs that you can destroy if you happen to make a match and toss out a fireball in the exact right place to impact the boss's projectile). These add some definate flavor to the fights, but the relative difficulty of preplanning where the tiles are going to fall make these boss abilities more of a "counter if you can" situation and can at times turn downright deadly (if a chain match suddenly bounces a bunch of your own shots off of a boss's reflective force field).
To help with this, you can use the resources you gather in town to research/craft/hire various spells/items/defenders. As you level up certain buildings in town, you gain access to more potent enhancements.
The spells are reusable abilities with no limt to number of uses but which require you to make a certain number of matches to "charge up" the spell. The charge level for each spell carries over from match to match, so you need to make decisions whether to use a spell to help finish a battle or save it to open with on the next battle. Spells can destroy tiles (dealing damage to enemies), heal your fortress, shuffle the board, etc.
Crafted items are consumeable (multiples can be stacked, but each time you use the item, your total available is reduced by 1 and you have to build/purchase more before you can use them again). Item effects range from stunning opponents to damaging them to preventing them from moving forward for a short time.
Defenders are guard units that walk up and down along the top of your wall, and heal you or shoot arrows/roll bolders at enemies or run and grab dropped treasure, etc. Like items, defenders are consumed on use, and more must be hired to keep a steady supply. You can have two types of defenders active at once (and only one of each can be active at a time).
All of these enhancements are bought/researched through the town building minigame, which feels very lackluster. Gold, food, wood, and metal are used as resources for upgrading buildings or purchasing items, etc. While gold is gathered on the battlefield, the other resources have to be gathered in town, by waiting for the appropriate resource-generating building to slowly (and automatically) fill up with a resource, choosing to harvest what's available, and then slowly letting the resource fill up again. While resource building structures automatically fill up with a resource, they do not automatically harvest it, so you have to remember to manually harvest your pumpkins or ironwood or the building will just sit there useless until you empty it out. This plays more like a freemium mobile game's time-limited resource production, and can get quite frustrating later on, when battles take significantly less time than needed for your crops to grow/wood to be milled. It gets quite annoying to have to log on every so often just to gather your resources so you can eventually afford the new spell/stonethrowing guard/shiney bomb that you're waiting for to tip the scales in your favor for the next boss fight.
Also with the city building, there is no customization for placing buildings where you want, or adding buildings to enhance particular resource production. You have one place to gather wood. One place to grow food. One place to research spells. Buildings grow as you level them up, but you can't move/rotate/remove/anything. There are a few different "town themes" but you can't do any significant customization.
The one feature of the town itself that isn't terribly boring is the townsfolk, which wander around and sometimes have thought bubbles that you can click on for an amusing quip. Also, the townsfolk react to some of your victories by asking for "policy decisions" where you can pick whether to protect forested areas, anger your local druids, be lenient with thieves, send a beaten boss monster back to a far-away forested area or kill her off, etc. Most of these are humorously written, none seem to have "wrong" answers, and none have any effect on game play as far as I can tell.
Even with the sometimes-frustrating fights, ReignMaker is a fun-for-a-bit casual match-3 game that's easy to pick up, put down for a few weeks, pick up again, etc., but it's not something that really grabs attention for hours on end. Between that and the lackluster town interface, resource gathering, and research/crafting system, I can't recommend paying full price for this game, especially compared to the asking price of some of the other match-3 games on Steam. If you can get it for 75% off or more (or part of a really-discounted bundle), it'll be an enjoyable game for occasional play. Just avoid buying it for full price unless you really MUST have every match-3 available.

After playing the Korea scenario in Civ V, it hit me that the only thing the game lacked was some real politics. Well, here it is in Urban Empire. The game is a mash-up of the Democracy series with the Civilization series, and plays with as much strategy as Plague Inc. There is also a heavy role-play element.

The story is a sweeping saga that spans 200 years in a small Austrian Empire backwater. The game presents four families. You start in era 1 with the ancestor of 1 family and build your city as an appointee of the emperor. Meanwhile the story of your family, your empire, and the world is revealed in the backdrop by flashing newspaper covers and random events triggered by the backstory. The events give you a choice of responses to make, with outcomes which will heavily affect both your stats and the direction of your game. It’s high in player agency and the roleplay is as satisfying as any rpg. The devs at Calypso Media have combined so many genres in one game, as to be ground-breaking.
As your character ages, and you learn his story, he will pass the city down to his progeny. Some of the descendants of each family are female as well as male. This pc aspect is pervasive, meaning that you will face racial, sexual, and political issues throughout the game, as you move from the Industrial Revolution, through the sexual revolution, two world wars, and a cold war. But, war is not a direct feature of your life in this backwater. It’s all there in the background of your provincial life, making for a nostalgic experience you won’t want to miss. You will be sure to find much replay value, as you explore the stories of each family.
Your story (and your job-security) will change mid-game as the empire fades, and you will then have to face a merciless 5-year election cycle. The council parties seem to forget quickly the years of dedication your family has given to the city then and you have to prove your worth, or maneuver and backstab your way through the rest of the game. My first game ended in that 3rd era, after the 3rd election. But, I moved on to another family for the 2nd game and achieved a very fun time victory by surviving to the end of the 5th era in 2020. There are also Science, Economic, Political, and ‘Remarkable City’ victories that can be obtained. But, these are much more involved than the typical 4x fare.
Though simple to learn, the game has much to be discovered through multiple play-throughs. The interface is clearly labeled, with tooltips that are informative and useful. The tutorial can be activated in a game to get you started. It merely describes the WASD controls and the basic moves that you will be using to play the game. Most everything else is easily discovered by checking out the User Interface.
You start by placing a district in a spot on the map. You are able to set the dimensions, the density, and other features, along with adjusting the shape of the roads. But, Urban Empire is NOT a city builder. You will not find the mindless micro-managing in this game. That’s all done for you by the game engine. You define the spread of residential, commercial, and industrial buildings. Then, as they are built by the engineers and your district expands, you may select buildings to view the population and business stats. You may choose to endorse a building, move it, or destroy it altogether, as with whole districts, if it is losing you money.
Colorful lighted symbols appear over different buildings frequently, notifying you visually of changing stats, related to the numbers all displayed directly above the map in the toolbar. Here, you may choose to micro-manage the industry, especially if you are the OCD type. But, even if you just let the district run itself, it performs well. And the stats screens will tell you if a district is still profitable or not.
Much of the game takes place in the Council screen, where you see the political parties, vote, pass edicts, make appeals to get your agendas passed, blackmail opposing parties, and other general political intrigues. This is perhaps the most fun aspect of the game, as you will find great glory in forcing your will on the city as it spans the ages.
The camera controls are great, allowing for two different ways of viewing the world. In standard play, you are locked-in to a low horizon almost top-down view of the map for building and control. This can be fully manipulated 360 degrees by Q & E and pressing the wheel. But, pressing F10 will launch the screenshot mode, which gives you a skyline view of your whole empire, without the overlays. While in F10, you have the same camera controls and are able to zoom in and out as well.
The tech cloud in the game is great. Components from each era are webbed within the next era, and you expand outward as the centuries unfold their sweeping changes for the world. You may choose to skip certain techs altogether, or skip ahead to future eras if you’ve made the right connections. The techs go beyond the typical, to include sociological elements of societal and political change as well. You may choose to adopt or ignore any civil rights. And, they are not required to win the game.
Besides the families in the regular campaigns, the game currently includes 3 scenarios, which I’ve not yet played and am anxious to get to myself.
Some gamers have reported dropping framerates, to which the devs always reply. By lowering graphics settings and tweaking the settings, I found a wide range of performance. But, some of the settings appeared to be nonexistent, as in the fog which is apparently not in the game. There are lengthy loading screens, like in the Civ series. But, the game looks great.

The art style is what Civ VI could have been if the franchise had NOT chosen to go with the cartoon art map in this installment. I myself love both the art style of Civ V and Civ VI, though many veterans of the genre were not as thrilled with the loss of realism. In Urban Empire, you find an environment that is reminiscent of Civ V’s realism and modern. But, it is much more detailed, giving a range of historical costumes and scenery to set the stage for a tale of epic proportions, though provincial. The water moves, sound effects accompany, and the ‘mayor player’ is immersed in the environment of a German-esque island coast.
The soundtrack itself is comprised of a sweeping range of orchestral music from Tapani Siirtola, who also created for Assassin’s Creed: Unity, among other notable titles. I found the complete audio files in my Steam music library free. My favorite track is a lovely melody called ‘Emerging Vision,’ which is both haunting and inspiring. The voice acting is in high quality audio by Alan Orpin, appearing mostly in the reading of quotations that appear after researching techs.

*Urban Empire is an artform/ not just a game.
*Political Intrigue that will have you controlling the Council
*Roleplay with a historical flavor
*City Ruling simulation
*Ground-breaking & genre-busting

*Framerates are still being tweaked according to the devs.
*I’ve spotted a couple or three typos and grammatical errors.
*The game is pricey. I don’t forsee a drop in that price though, as it’s worth the cost with replay value.

Sadly, I cannot reccommend this game. There's many reasons but I'll keep it brief.
The way this game sells itself as a political/city builder hybrid is true to an extent, except that each aspect is way too shallow.
First the city building, or lack thereof. You only really build service buildings - schools, police stations, clinics, etc. - and you are stuck building your city using a district mechanic, which involves just clicking and dragging over an area. The roads and zones are automatically done for you. There's much more to say but if you're looking for a city builder - don't look here.
Secondly, and most disappointingly (as I knew the city-builder aspect was second fiddle to this part) the political simulator is just not good, at all. The parties are hard-wired to rise and fall depending on the eras, so no matter what decisions you make - there will be the same parties.
The political decisions themselves wreak of a liberal, socialist bias. The game sort of forces you to adopt progressive policies because the benefits are simply all positive and there's no counterbalance to give you pause for not adopting it. There's literally no reason to play with a conservative minded playstyle, you will be far behind somebody who just adopts all the progressive policies as they become available.
I had high hopes for this game, but I have to say it's one of the most disappointing purchases I've ever made.

After spending the last week playing this game, 42 hours in total, I have found the game to have some serious issues. The game economy is completely unbalanced. The infrastructure, like electricity, for example, has no positive net value in the long run and costs way too much. You end up spending way more money on infrastructure upkeep than you get back from benefactors (like industry) in return so the game forces you to increase taxes which kills city growth. The game also has issues with zone density. Increasing the density of a zone should not cost any money or have any upkeep, but the game developers decided that rezoning a district from light density to medium density should completely wipe out whatever funds you have saved up, with an upkeep so high that by the time the area deveopls with medium density and money is flowing again, you're in the hole 3 or 4 thousand (which is a lot in this game), and you're not making a whole lot more than before the rezoning. So the incentive to increase city density (which should be really fun to do), isn't there. In fact, it's the opposite. You avoid rezoning to higher densities, and that to me defeats the purpose of a city building game. I do not recommend this game unless the developers fix these disastrous gameplay issues.

Back in the early 90's almost every game was a platformer, so I had quite enough of them. Nowadays, I tend to avoid platformers for that very reason.
Surprisingly, Trine 2 is an exception to the rule. If you remember The Lost Vikings, then you'll see a lot of similarities between that and the Trine series. In Trine, you also get 3 different characters good for their own abilities that help you solve puzzles and progress.
The knight is for fighting the goblins and breaking things. The thief is about shooting arrows and climbing places with her rope (sometimes pushing goblins into pits in the process). The wizard is about conjuring boxes and planks, building from them and levitating everything that he can get ahold of.
Unlike the retro platformers, this one is heavily based on physics. This applies to rocks, conjured items and monsters. It also makes the wizard a really fun character to play as.
Another distinct feature of the Trine series is the graphics. The living backgrounds are beautiful and the colors are vivid, which can make Trine look better than many AAA titles.
Compared to the original Trine game, the most obvious new feature of Trine 2 is its multiplayer mode that allows up to 3 players to play simultaneously. It makes it more fun and helps solving the in-game puzzles as well as finding all the experience and secrets on every map.
On top of the above, and going away from the gameplay itself, Trine 2 is packed with little bonuses here and there. It's one of the very few games that support all kinds of 3D glasses out of the box (anaglyph, passive, active). It's also properly configured to be played with a gamepad. There's full Linux and Mac OS support too. And of course it's tightly integrated with Steam, having almost 100 achievements, trading cards and storing your saved games to the cloud.

If you drop the somewhat iffy Terminator-like background story and the hangar where you can customize your air vehicle of destruction, this reminds me very much of an old Sega Shootemup called Thunder Blade from the 80's - the game I liked a lot back then, even with all its home computer port clunkiness compared to the sleek machine of destruction that the arcade hall version was. The 3rd person perspective is missing, but the vertical dashes and objects coming towards your very face from the battlefield are  there, not to mention the overall feel plus both air and ground targets to be destroyed either with projectiles or missiles.
Nostalgia aside, this mindless-but-fun intended little vehicle has more clunkiness than it should for the maximisation of said / promised mindless destructive fun. You choose your weapons (and buy more when you get cash and level up, increasing your weapon slots and thus firepower), you fly, you select whether to shoot air or ground targets with them, you fight the end level boss (sometimes mid-bosses too), you collect your exp and cash, next level, repeat, etc. etc. Despite of the vehicle customization options that grow rather nicely when advancing the levels and experience, the game still is tactically shallow and has frankly few winning weapon combos that are most probably used in expese of every other gun there is. What is the worst, it gets repetetive quite fast no matter ho hard it tries with the variation of enemies to shoot and weapons to shoot them at.
Granted, it looks, sounds and feels like a nostalgia time machine with some modern game design twists and therefore has some charm, and I can't complain of any bugs or bad controls. Still, I feel it falls short even in the retro destruction department. Blowing this much stuff up with heavily armed flying death machine really shouldn't feel this... dull. So far I have plodded through for around 15 or so missions of the campaign mode and I'm daft enough to soldier them all through, but only because I'm stubborn that way. For you, there are better and more versatile shooters out there.

Devil May Cry 4 is one of my favorite games in the franchise as far as gameplay is concerned.  When I first read of a special edition coming around that, I was excited and went and read up more info about it before deciding to pre-order it.  Given how much time I invested in the game and it was only $25, I easily got my money's worth.  Fair warning, I strongly recommend a gamepad for this game, I would never try a game like this without one.
You may already be aware of this by now, but just in case, I'm going to clarify on this.  This is essentially Devil May Cry 4 with three additional playable characters and alternate costumes for all of the characters in the game.  The game's story is exactly the same, the missions are exactly the same, and aside from some general changes to mechanics (for example, Speed activates near instantaneously now outside of combat, but takes significantly longer during combat, if at all) and how Red Orb and Proud Soul accumulation works (thankfully, you earn Proud Souls
faster now and it no longer takes an eternity to learn every skill in the game; if for whatever reason you don't like that, there's a code you can punch in at the title screen that reverts Red Orb and Proud Soul accumulation back to their vanilla values), that's more or less the same; if you're expecting anything more, you're going to be disappointed.
So what is actually new then?  As mentioned, the main attractions are the three new playable characters (Vergil, Lady, and Trish), all of which have unique play styles and mechanics associated with them, and every character in the game has alternate costumes to use; Dante, Nero, and Vergil have a unique costume already available (Dante and Vergil have Legendary Dark Knight skins, which also includes a Sparta Devil Trigger which is pretty cool, while Nero's is based on concept art before his final design was chosen, I actually really like this one and think it suits the game better), while Lady and Trish's unique costume must be purchased as DLC; every character can also unlock an EX costume, which is just a recolor of their default costume (thankfully, there are mods out there that can change these lame ones into something cooler).  The game's split between three campaigns: Nero/Dante which is basically vanilla DMC4, Vergil where Vergil goes through the entirity of the game himself, and Lady/Trish, where Lady does Nero's segiments while Trish handles Dante's; all of which are also avaiable from the start.  It should be noted that there's only one save file and progression, aside from story progression per difficulty level, is shared, so each campaign will share items, life and magic upgrades, Red Orbs and Proud Souls, and unlocking difficulties with one campaign unlocks them in the others.
As far as DLC goes, the only one I'd even bother buying is the aforementioned Lady and Trish costumes: they are the only ones of the listing that cannot be acquired in the game at all otherwise and I personally think it's a lot more satisfying to unlock Super Dante/Nero/Vergil yourself rather than forking money over (unfortunately, there are no Super Lady and Trish variants out there).  It's largely up to you if you think it's worthwhile, I pre-ordered the game so I got them for free: Lady's costume is her outfit from DMC3 which is pretty cool, but Trish's costume is
Apparently anyone who has Windows 10 may have issues with the game randomly crashing or something because the game only uses DirectX10, which Microsoft apparently broke during one of their updates that was implemented into Windows 10.  As a Windows 10 user, I haven't had this happen to me personally and have spent long periods of time playing this in one sitting more times than I can remember, but your mileage may vary.
Overall, even though I'm giving this a positive review, it's difficult to recommend this to everyone.  If you didn't care for DMC4 to begin with, chances are this won't change your mind.  If you liked DMC4 or felt it could've used just a little more extra content, then you'll probably love this.

Okay, so I'm having a hard time trying to recommend this game, so I made the decision to not do so.
It's a match three game, mixed with a rather basic city building type of game, and by very basic I mean, click this, see if you have the resources, build, then job done! Not complicated in any way, very simple and easy to get the hang of, but it's honestly nothing special. Now on to the actual gameplay!
Like I said, the game is a match three game, so the main gameplay is just swiping so you get a line of three or more, but where it is a little different is the mechanic of the battles. On one side is you, which is a building filled with your gems/runes that you need to match three in order to use as an attack. On the other side is where the enemies will slowly encroach upon your castle, and it's your job to match those gems, be it horizontal or vertical to fire a spell at the enemy. You'll slowly whittle the enemy down with your matching abilities and the battle will be over and you'll be sent back to your village.
The combat isn't overly-complicated, and you will be getting extra abilities that you can unlock to help you along the way, but it's all simply "okay." And that's how I'd describe this game in a nutshell. It's merely okay. I'm not the biggest fan of the graphics style, but I can live with that. The combat is fairly simple, but it's nothing spectacular, and the whole village gimmick kind of makes you feel like you're playing a FaceBook game as you have to wait for your buildings to give you the resources you want. If you want to sit and wait and just watch that timer slowly tick down so you can get that extra little bit of ore, then you can, but I can't admit being the biggest fan of having to wait on real time to get something a little extra in a game.
I don't hate the game, but at the same time I can't say I like it either. Which is why I'm not going to be recommending it, because an "okay" game does not make it necessarily a good one.

The year is 2007. It is the future. The world has been overrun by killer cyborgs, and only one cyber commando can stop them. This is Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon, an amazing FPS that takes its weaponry and style from the films of the 80s and its missions and attitude from the FPSs of the 90s. It packs more memorable moments into its $15 price point than most FPSs nowadays can fit in at $60. The weapons, from Arnie's shotgun from T2, to Robocop's handgun, have a distinct kick that makes the combat addictingly fun. You could spend hours planning out stealth runs to take out dudes with shuriken and a neon katana, or you can charge in with your minigun and a sniper rifle that shoots explosive rounds. I haven't even mentioned the dragons that shoot lasers out of their eyes.
When you were a kid, this is the type of video game you dreamed about playing, and it was worth the wait. There wasn't another game this entire year that ripped my attention away from Blood Dragon, and after three playthroughs it still feels amazing. You're doing yourself a disservice by not playing it right now, even if you've already completed it.

This game...This game is brilliantly crafted, the amount of hours you are able to play this and still find something new is astonishing.

If you are going to play it, purely F2P, you can, by grinding TP ( Turbine Points ).
You can basically get the whole game that way, at the cost of several months of straight-up farming/grinding.
I highly recommend that you play with other people, whether you know them or not. Playing solo is boring, as it is slow. Some classes can actually make soloing easy. However, playing solo is entirely viable. At the moment, any class can mow down tons of enemies on their own. At levels 1-90, you will hardly find anyone to play with, there isn't enough people to do stuff with, or they don't have the content, as they have to buy it.
There's also a bunch of classes with their own mechanics, the most basic of them being the Guardian.
If you like LOTR lore, this is for you, however, don't expect amazing end-game stuff, and don't expect a top-of-the-line story.
Some may enjoy the story of LOTRO, as it ties you with the main characters from LOTR, but some may also be bored with the main stuff, rather quickly.
The PVP is...meh. There isn't any structured PVP so it's all in a region called the Ettenmoors. The balance is for PVP has always been bad/awful, as there is always something OP.
The community is fairly helpful compared to many other games, but there is always an occasionally jerk/idiot/whatever.
If you come expecting amazing, you'll kinda feel let down. But it's good enough to say the least.                                                                 Try the game, see if you like it. It's free.

The first thing I'd like to note before really getting into this game is that no: You do not need a controller. I played it on a keyboard and while I'm sure it would have made controlling the characters less frustrating; you are not required to have one.
That said: I did enjoy the game. The music was beautiful; especially during the more somber moments and the art-style was lovely. There were things going on in the background of the different set pieces that made it feel more alive. I did have a few problems with the game - the controls at time were frustrating and there were two or so lever puzzels that just took forever to finish. (Though maybe that was on me; I just for the life of me couldn't figure out how to get them to turn the cranks faster).
The game sits somewhere between a walking similator and a platformer. You're traversing the areas, moving from one venue to another: You can interact with a few things in the enviroment, (And at the beginning; the younger brother, Neiee, is almost downright unlikeable. He's a bratish little punk that a bit cruel to people: But he likes animals, so he has that going for him (I was so nervous the first time I had him interact with an animal because he just smashed a flower pot the last time I had him interact with something, but no, he petted it nicely), but mostly you're just walking - making sure you don't let the brothers stray too far from each other (They will complain and call out to the other if one of them gets too far behind)
The story also has a very fairytale quality to it - as I said, you move from one set-piece to another with little things happening to the brothers along the way. The story; perhaps, was a little simplistic (and at one point down right predictable), but enjoyable all the same. I'd probably only suggest buying this game when it's on sale due to how short it is and it doesn't have much replayabity beyond getting the achievements (which are easy enough to get on the first play through), but yeah. I suggest it.

This is the only game that I can confidently say every single person should play. Buy it, sit down, play it through. You won't regret it. This game is the proof that video games can be art.

Gameplay:
The controls take little getting used to (because your controlling two characters at once), but are generally fine. Note that you will definitely require a control pad - this isn't a shoddy console port, its just that the gameplay itself is built around two analogue sticks). The game itself is made up of environment puzzles that require you to combine the skills of the two characters. Honestly, its pretty easy... I'm not sure I'd even call them puzzles so much as hold ups. Nonetheless, they are interesting and make good use the environment. They also integrate well with the overall narrative.
Art:
This is where the game shines. Honestly, the game looks incredible. Some of the later areas are particularly breathtaking/interesting. I took a lot of screen shots.
Music:
The music was also very good. Haunting melodies mostly. I'll probably try and get a copy of the soundtrack to relax too.
Narrative:
For a story told using a made up language, the narrative is shockingly effective. I nearly cried at the end. More than that though, is there is a general tone that is simultaneouls beautiful and bleak. The only way I can think to describe it is: "That got dark quickly".
Overall:
Well worth a purchase. I think I paid $1.50 in the last Steam sale, so its good value too. I recommend setting aside 3 hours and just playing it from start to finish. It's pretty much perfect that way.

This is not a NOT RECOMENDED review. Im mainly pointing out the flaws of the game; dont look at this review as a "dont try this game" but rather a "here are the flaws, look at the recomended for more details on the good points." Why? because, although i have the pros here listed, i only describe my point of view on the flaws.
Dont get me wrong, i love this game, i do, and i play it quite often.
Pros:
+Great, solid, super smash bros-like game with interesting mechanics and frenetic gameplay.
+No pay2win, there are coins that you can purchase with real money, but they only serve to buy skins, sidekicks and taunts. The rest-characters, colors-is completely free, and can be bought ONLY with in game gold.
+Good variety of characters and weapons, with about one new character every 2 weeks being released, along with bug fixes and server improvement.
+No buffs. No nerfs. Every character has diferent kits instead: some give armour, others speed, and others offense. But this can be quite the problem too.
Cons:
-Ranked. Ok, lets talk ranked. The 2v2 is a great way of going up ranks with your SO, friend, or family member. But the thing that keeps me playing only 1v1 ranked is, you can actually hit your teammate. Now, i know what youre thinking: "Thats an interesting way of adding strategy and teamwork to the games, how can it be a con?". Little jimmy, its a con because the opposite team, if they are skilled enough, can lure you to attack your teammate everytime. If not skilled, they can just turn you into a ping-pong ball and attack you until youre red, and then one  of them throws the finalblow by just simply pressing the RMB2. Oh, did i mention that just spamming the RMB2 can get you up the ranks?
-The shield. The shield is absolutely useless-for the purpose it was made for. Most of the times i find myself pressing the shield button and getting hit (after actually pressing the shield and seeing it activate on-screen). Now, i dont know if this is a bug, or i just press the button in the worst possible moments, in wich the game decides to deny me protection, but this is annoying as hell.
-Unbalance. Now, as i stated before, each character has their kit, and you gain more and more as you level up with that characters. In ranked, no, you can only play as the 1st kit the character has. Again, i know what you are probably thinking:"But thats to make the rankeds a balanced experience, so no characters have advantage over others...right?" WRONG. Now, little jimmy, even with only the basic kits, some characters have a crushing advantage over the rest; Thats because the basic kit isnt the same for all characters, some have offence, some have defence, some have speed, etc. This is a nice feature, dont get me wrong, it adds variety to the game. But most of the times, on 2v2 for example, a Koji-Hatori team will easily crush any opponent-unless they are really really bad players at those characters. And on 1v1, if you wanna go up the ranks fast, consider picking Hatori, Lucien, Azura (or whatever she is called) or Koji.
EDIT 8/3/2017
The weapon giving system has been updated, therefore i deleted my con about it. However, ive played recently and the game is still somewhat unbalanced and the shield is still useless.

When this game first released it was a buggy unplayable mess, but after months of patching alot of the offline issues were fixed. The only thing stopping me from recommending Mortal Kombat X was the abysmal netcode and insulting micro transactions. Whilst the micro transactions are still there, the netcode has been completely overhauled, and the new developers have even restored some features previously unavailable to PC players. Like native PS4 support, lag simulation for offline play (sounds like a negative but it helps you improve your timing when playing online) and unlocking extra skins via the MK app on mobile.
The gameplay feels like a nice middle ground between Street Fighter and Tekken. It's also the perfect place to start for players new to the fighting genre. Easy to get into, but hard to master. Things like pulling off 'Brutalities' are also a great way to encourage new players to learn how to chain special moves with combos and so on.
With all the work that QLOC have put into fixing the netcode, even going as far to give that away for free. I don't see why they shouldn't be rewarded. I definitely recommend picking up Kombat Pack 2 if you own MKX. or picking up the MKXL if you were previously interested in the game, but were turned off by the bugs and shoddy netcode.

Let's get straight to the point. Mount and Blade: Warband is not the prettiest game on the market. If games were women, Mount and Blade: Warband would be that girl with a hormone disorder that made her have kind of a beard. But like beard-girl, Warband has a really good personality and if you close your eyes when you kiss you can pretend that the facial hair is just a scarf or something. Know what I'm talking about?
Warband is the stand-alone expansion to the original Mount and Blade, released towards the end of 2008. Being a stand-alone, you don't need the original game to play. In Warband, like the original, you take the role of an individual on a fictional landmass known as Calradia, and are basically free to do whatever you want. The game definitely nudges you in certain directions, but following those suggestions or completely forging your own path is ultimately up to you. In this sense it is very similar to the Elder Scrolls games, except not even remotely technically groundbreaking.
At its best, Warband looks like the missing link between Morrowind and Oblivion. At its worst – which is basically any indoor location, most towns, and the overworld – it looks like it was released a decade ago. Character models and structures all have quite low polygon-counts, and most walls have pretty low-rez textures. Open areas look a great deal nicer, but even then, there's never a jaw-dropping or even a "ooh, that's pretty!" moment.
Open areas don't look too bad.
But for all the ugly, Warband has a lot going on under the hood. Gameplay has a few different layers, and each of these layers houses a great deal of complexity. Take, for example, the game's combat system. Each weapon deals a certain kind of damage, and most can be used in several different ways. On horseback, a voulge may only function as a thrusting-weapon, but when you dismount, you can swing away for much more damage. That's just the basics, though. The direction you swing from, whether or not you're moving – and which direction you're moving in – and the proximity of your enemy to you can all affect how much damage each swing of your weapon inflicts. Thrusting forward while you're on horseback will deal much more damage than trying to back-slash someone as you ride past them. Learning all the little tricks to maximize your damage, and even just the timing of your hits, means Warband has a rather steep learning curve that must be tackled before you start having fun.
The economy-side of the game is fascinating, and it can take a while to learn what's worth buying at what price, and where the best places to sell it are. Trying to balance your income and outgoing expenses adds yet another complication into the game's thick broth of gameplay elements. As you gain ground and become stronger, you will have to fend off attackers, manage your lands, keep your allies in line and keep your growing costs down, making the game's steep difficulty curve even steeper.

When I first read about this upcoming game many months ago, I thought this was going to be a dream of mine come true, a hybrid between Cities in Motion, Tropico, Cities Skylines, and Civilization, a city and development planner with a strong historical perspective. As someone who is obsessed with government simulation and strategy games, I saw this game and immediately pre-ordered it. I watched numerous videos of gameplay and it appeared to be just my cup of tea. Upon release, and several hours of playtime, I feel as though I've had my fill, not $34 worth, but a fill.
The initial era is perhaps the most enjoyable portion of the game, it feels busy, turbulent, just as you begin your city—in other words, it feels as though you are truly engaged in creating a city, executing its policy, improving infrastructure, et cetera—however after the inital issues are settled, it slows down significantly. Oftentimes you find yourself barely making enough money to pay for simple improvements like gravel to cobblestone roads, and virtually never are able to increase taxes unless the deficit is immense, and even then it can be a struggle. By about era IV, you end up focusing less on improving and expanding your city through public works projects and legislation, and far more on simply hoarding goodwill so that you can sway the parties each time a mayoral election comes around (perhaps it's user error, or perhaps simply a reflection of the reality of politics?).
Though at first I noticed a trend towards more left-wing parties and policies having a sort of inevitable quality to them (which, mind you, I do not mind being a very liberal/left-wing person myself), the reality of it is that no matter how much you support these parties (such as supporting their legislation or merely being cordial to them), they almost always end up stabbing you in the back by the time elections come around—I've found myself having no other choice than to threaten the parties in order to remain in office by the later eras.
On the more technical aspects, the game itself is good-looking (though draw distance is far shorter than it should) and the graphics, though perhaps not revolutionary, are fitting, and the visuals do not leave me disappointed in the slightest. The game runs very smoothly on my PC (despite it not being necessarily a ultra-powerful machine) on the highest settings. Overall, I have encountered no game-breaking bugs or issues that have ruined the gameplay simply because of developer error. On that same note, responding to pop-up events is in many ways taking a shot in the dark, as the impacts of the decisions aren't known until after it has been made (though truthfully after some playtime one can guess to a point the impacts they will have), and if I would request a specific addition to be made to the game, it would be to add the statistics to the decision screen so that more informed decisions can be made. Additionally, I would like to see difficulty settings and/or different gamemodes that cater to players' different playstyles or fortés, or merely adjustable/toggleable settings for campaigns that can add diversity to each playthrough, something that I believe would be a welcome addition, especially taking into account how repetitive and grinding the game can become as early as 1-2 hours into a campaign. Being as this focus more specifically on political aspects of governing a city, I might also recommend a system be put in place that would allow a player to create their own party, that way they could fight to pass their own policies and work to elect their own councilmembers rather than be limited to merely courting the leadership and membership of other parties which may or may not help fulfill the mayor's agenda. Though the political aspects of this game are a refreshing change for a "city builder/ruler," they could use more fleshing out, as it feels very disconnected and two-dimensional in its current state.
Long story short, Urban Empire is an interesting and rather ingenuitive approach to the age-old city builder genre, however it is executed in a way that feels shallow and repetitive to experienced and newcomers to the genre alike. I will likely play this game more, nevertheless, and look forward to future updates and DLC, though I hope that the developers will heed the input of the community and release a significant amount of free content to improve upon a regrettably barebones game. As previously stated, I am someone who plays strategy/simulation games all the time, I love the idea, and the game is far from bad as some other reviews have stated, but it needs more draw and replay value to keep even the most battle-hardened strategy gamers coming back for another playthrough, and quite honestly I am on the cusp of recommending to that demographic in particular, but widespread appeal to people not as weird as me is, unfortunately, lacking.
Final conclusion: amazing concept, needs more work.

So far, I have 21 hours in Urban Empire. I really want to like it, but it needs some fixing. Some of the points I'm bringing up have probably been brought up, and I have noticed that the developer is paying attention to the reviews, so they may already be working on fixing the issues. Anyway, I need to share the things I have reacted to.
1. The FPS
When my city was growing bigger and bigger, I noticed a drastic drop in FPS. My PC can handle many demanding games without any major issues, but for some reason it doesn't work here. I tried lowering the graphics setting as low as possible to try to fix it, but the problems remained. In my case, my city was around 70.000 inhabitants and sometimes the FPS went below 10 FPS. I'm wondering if it's at all possible to get higher than 60 FPS in-game, because it feels like an FPS lock. I wouldn't have a problem with that if it ran at 60 FPS the entire game, but it doesn't.
2. Lack of clear information
From the get go, I was really confused with all the information that was given to me. I still have trouble finding information about different things, however that may be my fault. One thing is really bugging me whenever you resolve an event and get bonuses to some of the different aspects (social life, happiness, security etc.): sometimes you get an indication to what is affected in what way when you hover over with your mouse indicator, other times it doesn't. Also, there are times when text is missing in dialogue windows. It feels very inconsistent and should be considered for a patch.
3. Repetitive events
Whether it's about the sucurity in a district, the circus coming to town, or getting criticism from a local journalist, many events show up one too many times during your ruling. So many times, in fact, that you could learn what option to choose to get the best result every time. If they would be reused after the end of time victory I wouldn't mind, but as of now it's a little too repetetive.
4. Consequences?
My first game I learned about the concequenses of having low goodwill towards many of the parties. But as soon as I just focused on districts and kept an eye on the taxes, I could cruise through the game without having to worry about anything political. Well, apart from the majoral election. I was so nervous the first couple of times, but as time went on I barely had to appeal to any parties to make it through to the next period. Maybe a higher difficulty setting option could be in its place.
Then there are features I would like to be included, such as:
- Being able to control where the RCI zones are placed in a district
- Going backwards in modifying a district without having to cancel the entire modification to fix something you want to change (it's really bugging me)
- Being able to zoom out even more than is possible at the moment, I want to see my entire city in all it's glory (granted if I can run it with the highest graphics setting)
To be clear, I really want to like it. I'm really close to liking it. I have played some city simulators before, and even though they are fun I really want this concept city ruling to be great. After patching I think this game has great potential. I really like that the developer are keeping an eye on the feedback and wish them the best of luck in making this game the best it can possibly be.
As of now, I can't fully recommend Urban Empire. I want to, but I can't. I sort of like it, I want to really like it. It's not a terrible game, but it's not a great game yet.
EDIT: Ignore what I said about going backwards in modifying a district. Turns out that I was blind and missed that feature.

ReignMaker is a casual game that combines tile swapping, tower defense, idle clicking (gathering resources for upgrading your village) and even some light-hearted decision making that might grant you some bonuses.
There's some good potential in tile swapping / tower defense combo and I admit that some of the levels are pretty fun because the tiles are locked or corrupted etc.
The reason I'm still giving this game thumbs down is that I didn't enjoy the town building stuff at all. At the point the levels finally offered some real challenge, upgrading the town and dealing with the seemingly pointless decision making started to get annoying. There isn't enough stuff going on in the village to justify the fact that it's a pretty big part of the game. The village mechanics are very basic and the graphics are unappealing. It takes time for the derpy villagers to gather resources and research spells, and the only way to pass that time is to replay old levels again and again until I finally get the upgrade I need.
Maybe I'm just impatient, I don't know. Life is short.
So yeah, the game's mildly amusing, but the village business slows things down. Just my two cents, though.  ReignMaker seems popular enough, so do give it a try if you can get it for a couple of dollars. (I personally don't think it's worth more than that.)
EDIT: The resource system is definitely unbalanced. You can hoard all the money you want, but there's not enough wood. No matter how many lumberjacks you have roaming about your village, there's simply not enough wood. I would get that if this was a micropayment game, but there's no option to buy resources to speed things up.

An interesting take on the Match-3 Puzzle 'Genre' that is sure to keep your senses occupied.
Take your standard Match-3 game with the usual difficulty of adding special tiles with certain requirements to clear.. now tie that mechanic to a 'tower/base defending game' to introduce even more difficulty as well as a bit of strategy. Add progression through town building and management, where you can build, craft, recruit soldiers and even decide on policies that will affect your kingdom as well as how your story will unfold. That's Reignmaker in a nutshell.
As someone who likes this particular sub-genre, I have to say this game may have just become my new top favourite amongst it's kind. The extra layer of difficulty and depth by adding and combining it with elements from other specific genres compliment it very well. That said however, this is not a game where you can just sit back and relax for a casual game of matching colors. It starts out easy, getting gold and perfects on the first few towers but the difficulty ramps up pretty quickly.
I could elaborate on that.. but basically what it comes down to is that your eyes, hand(s) and mind will be having a field trip with this game. If you're a fan of match-3 games or love a good 'action' puzzle challenge, I'd say it's definitely worth the price.

This one is a definite must-own and must-play.  It's fun and satisfying to treat the game like a big toybox playground of action figures from the 80s with you running around like a maniac at cyborg-enhanced speed blasting crowds of bad guys and finishing them off with shurikens and swords.
The humor, music, and visuals are also all great.  The neon-on-black aesthetic makes the whole game feel like you're running around inside a giant arcade from the 80s.
The only real downside is the major gameplay drag that was present in farycry 3 - the game, even on 'hard' mode, is still too easy.  The enemy AI is pretty dim and the enemies are far too easy to kill in general - even the blood dragons are chumps when you figure out their weakness.
There was also an opportunity with this game to make more threatening enemies - for example, stalker cyborgs that might be a combination of Terminator, bits of the predator, and the stalkers from the Running-Man movie.  Basically, things that could be a tough match for Rex Power Colt to deal with.
This game is also a budget spinoff made in-house, and it shows - they re-use assets for most of the game, and the game lacks a lot of features that would be great to have in a fully priced release - like epic boss battles and more variety.
As it is though, this is one of those 'must-play' games.  You will feel like your dreams from childhood of being a cybernetic soldier of the future who gets to cuss all he wants and be the coolest kid on the playground are being realized.
Oh and this game features one of the funniest sex scenes in anything.
I look forward to seeing this game get its own true release in sequel/remake/spinoff form - everything from boss battles to coop play to more area, enemy, and mission variety needs to happen.  Rex Power Colt shall rise again.
PS - When you play this game, unless you're rescuing a hostage or don't want to deal with a blood dragon at the moment, don't worry in the least about exercising caution.  Even on hard mode, you can pretty much run around like a maniac meleeing and stopping to blast a few enemies, so long as you run around behind cover a lot and use commo sense about not over-extending.  You're a superpowered cyborg after all, so you can do a lot more running and jumping than a human being  - might as well dash around like the Terminator stabbing people in the face.
